\section{Real closedness and completion without a defect argument}
\label{pma:ser:sec:realclosed}

To connect these fields to integer-part arithmetic, we specialize to a real
closed coefficient field. A useful proof avoids importing a full theory of
henselian defect. The sole substantial algebraic input is the classical
Newton--Puiseux theorem in characteristic zero: for an algebraically closed
field $K$ of characteristic zero, $\bigcup_n K((t^{1/n!}))$ is algebraically
closed. Poonen gives this as Corollary~7 \cite{Poonen}.

\begin{lemma}[Completion preserves algebraic closedness]
\label{pma:ser:lem:completionac}
The metric completion of a non-Archimedean valued algebraically closed field
is algebraically closed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Write $|\cdot|$ for the multiplicative real-valued absolute value; it is not
the truncated metric. Let $K$ be the field and $\widehat K$ its completion.
Take a monic polynomial
\[
 P(X)=X^d+\sum_{i<d}a_iX^i\in\widehat K[X],\qquad d\geq1.
\]
Choose monic polynomials $P_n\in K[X]$ of degree $d$ whose coefficients
converge to those of $P$, and positive real numbers $\varepsilon_n\to0$
such that every coefficient of $P_{n+1}-P_n$ has absolute value at most
$\varepsilon_n$. There is a common real bound $M\geq1$ for $1$ and for the
absolute values of all coefficients of all $P_n$.
Every root $z$ of any $P_n$ satisfies $|z|\leq M$: otherwise the monic term
would strictly dominate every lower-degree term.

Choose a root $z_0$ of $P_0$. Having chosen $z_n$, factor
$P_{n+1}(X)=\prod_{j=1}^d(X-w_j)$ over $K$. Since $P_n(z_n)=0$,
\[
 \prod_{j=1}^d|z_n-w_j|
 =|P_{n+1}(z_n)|
 \leq \varepsilon_n M^{d-1}.
\]
Some root $w_j$ therefore satisfies
$|z_n-w_j|\leq(\varepsilon_n M^{d-1})^{1/d}$.
Choose it as $z_{n+1}$. Consecutive distances tend to zero, and the
ultrametric inequality then makes $(z_n)$ Cauchy: the distance between any
two late terms is at most the largest intervening consecutive distance.
Let $z\in\widehat K$ be its limit. Continuity of polynomial evaluation and
coefficient convergence give $P(z)=0$. Thus every nonconstant polynomial
has a root, which is equivalent to algebraic closedness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Real closed Puiseux and Levi-Civita fields]
\label{pma:ser:thm:rc}
If $k$ is a real closed ordered field, then $\Pk$ and $\Lk$ are real closed.
In particular, this applies to the countable field $k=\ka$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $K=k(i)$, which is algebraically closed because $k$ is real closed.
Splitting coefficients into their real and imaginary parts gives
\[
 \mathcal P_K=\Pk(i),\qquad \mathcal L_K=\Lk(i).
\]
For the first identity, finitely many denominator bounds can be replaced by
one common bound; for the second, a finite union of left-finite supports is
left-finite. By Newton--Puiseux, $\mathcal P_K$ is algebraically closed.
By Proposition~\ref{pma:ser:prop:completion} and Lemma~\ref{pma:ser:lem:completionac}, so is
$\mathcal L_K$. The fields $\Pk$ and $\Lk$ are ordered and adjoining $i$
makes them algebraically closed; the standard characterization of real
closed fields therefore proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A ring-language separation]\label{pma:ser:cor:rclang}
For $k=\ka$, the field $\Pk$ has no Polish additive-group topology with
jointly Borel multiplication, even without a separately specified measurable
order. The field $\Lk$ does have such a topology, and it is unique.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Real closedness makes the order Borel by Corollary~\ref{pma:ser:cor:realorder}.
Apply Theorems~\ref{pma:ser:thm:puiseux} and~\ref{pma:ser:thm:lc}.
\end{proof}

Real closedness here is a classical algebraic property proved using a
classical input; it is not the proposed novelty. Its role is to remove the
order-measurability hypothesis from the final field-language contrast.

\section{Local Polish hulls, unbounded support ranks, and an exact cover number}
\label{pma:ser:sec:hulls}

The failure of Polishability for the full Hahn field is global, not an
obstruction to accommodating any prescribed countable collection of its
elements. This section proves that much stronger local positive statement.
In particular, the Levi-Civita field is a minimal completion, not a maximal
Polish subfield of the Hahn field.

\begin{lemma}[Metric completeness of the rational Hahn field]
\label{pma:ser:lem:hahncomplete}
For every field $k$, $k((t^\Q))$ is complete for the metric
$d(f,g)=\min\{1,2^{-v(f-g)}\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a Cauchy sequence, every prefix up to an integer $N\geq0$ eventually
stabilizes, just as in Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:lc}. This time a stabilized prefix
need not have finite support, but it has well-ordered support because it is
a prefix of a Hahn series. The compatible stabilized prefixes define a
coefficient function $f$.
Its support is well ordered: given any nonempty subset $S$ of that support,
choose $s\in S$ and an integer $N\geq\max\{0,s\}$. The nonempty set
$S\cap(-\infty,N]$ has a least element since it lies in the stabilized
well-ordered prefix. That element is also least in $S$, as all remaining
points exceed $N$. Thus $f$ is a Hahn series, and stabilization shows that
it is the limit of the original sequence.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Countable-parameter Polish hulls]\label{pma:ser:thm:hulls}
Let $k$ be countable and ordered, $H=k((t^\Q))$, and $A\subseteq H$ countable.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{pma:ser:eq:hull}
 F_A=\overline{k(t^\Q)(A)}^{\,v}\ \subseteq H
\end{equation}
is a complete separable ordered subfield containing $\Lk\cup A$.
Its valuation topology is its unique admissible Polish topology.
It is the smallest valuation-closed subfield of $H$ containing
$k(t^\Q)\cup A$.
Every valuation-complete separable intermediate field
$\Lk\subseteq F\subseteq H$ arises in this way.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The algebraic field $k(t^\Q)(A)$ is countable. Its closure is separable and
is complete by Lemma~\ref{pma:ser:lem:hahncomplete}. Closure preserves addition and
multiplication by continuity, and preserves inversion at every nonzero limit
by the inverse-difference identity. Thus $F_A$ is a subfield.
The closure of $k(t^\Q)$ in $H$ is exactly $\Lk$: it is dense in $\Lk$,
and $\Lk$ is complete and hence closed in the metric space $H$.
Therefore $\Lk\subseteq F_A$.
The valuation and order topologies agree, and
Corollary~\ref{pma:ser:cor:unique} gives uniqueness. Minimality follows directly
from taking closure. Finally, for a complete separable intermediate field
$F$, choose a countable valuation-dense subset $A\subseteq F$.
Completeness makes $F$ closed in $H$, and \eqref{pma:ser:eq:hull} then gives
$F_A=F$.
\end{proof}

Taking $A=\{y\}$ for the bounded infinite support in
\eqref{pma:ser:eq:boundedhahn} immediately gives
\[
 \Lk\subsetneq F_{\{y\}}\subsetneq H.
\]
The second strict inclusion follows from Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:hahn}.
Thus bounded infinite supports do not individually prevent Polish field
arithmetic. What is impossible is allowing all independently varying bounded
prefixes at once.

\begin{theorem}[A support bound for every separable family]
\label{pma:ser:thm:rankbound}
Let $X\subseteq H=k((t^\Q))$ be valuation-separable, and let $D\subseteq X$
be countable and dense. Then
\begin{equation}\label{pma:ser:eq:rankbound}
 \operatorname{ot}(\supp f)
 \leq\beta_D:=\sup_{d\in D}\operatorname{ot}(\supp d)<\omega_1
 \qquad(f\in X).
\end{equation}
Here the empty support has order type $0$. In particular, every admissibly
Polish intermediate field has a uniform countable support-order bound.
There is no uniform countable bound valid for all Polish hulls $F_A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $f\in X$ and every integer $N\geq0$, density supplies a $d_N\in D$
with $v(f-d_N)>N$. Their prefixes through $N$ agree. Hence
\[
 \operatorname{ot}(\supp f\cap(-\infty,N])
 \leq\operatorname{ot}(\supp d_N)\leq\beta_D.
\]
These prefixes are increasing initial segments whose union is the support
of $f$, so their order types have supremum
$\operatorname{ot}(\supp f)$. This proves \eqref{pma:ser:eq:rankbound}.
The supremum defining $\beta_D$ is countable because $D$ and all rational
supports are countable.

For an admissible topology, a countable dense set remains valuation-dense
by Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:refinement}, so the preceding argument applies.
For the last assertion, let $\alpha$ be any countable ordinal. Embed its
linear order into $\Q\cap(0,1)$ and let $h_\alpha$ have coefficient $1$
on that support and $0$ elsewhere. It belongs to the Polish hull
$F_{\{h_\alpha\}}$ and has support order type $\alpha$.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} Source~03's \cref{pma:bor:thm:bounded} proves a uniform
countable support bound for every Borel coefficient-observable family by
analytic boundedness; \cref{pma:ser:thm:rankbound} is the elementary
counterpart for separable families, as source~09 says below.

This bound uses separability and prefix stabilization, not analytic
boundedness or a Borel-domain hypothesis. It is a specialized elementary
counterpart of the support bounds in the preceding Borel-support manuscript.
It also makes the failure of maximality explicit.

\begin{corollary}[No maximal admissibly Polish intermediate field]
\label{pma:ser:cor:nomax}
Every admissibly Polish field $F$ with
$k(t^\Q)\subseteq F\subseteq H$ is properly contained in another such
field. The larger field can have an element whose support order type exceeds
all support order types in $F$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Choose a countable dense set $D$ in the admissible topology of $F$ and let
$\beta_D$ be as in Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:rankbound}. Choose a Hahn series $h$
with support order type $\beta_D+1$.
The hull $F_{D\cup\{h\}}$ contains the valuation closure of $D$, and hence
contains $F$. It also contains $h\notin F$. Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:hulls} proves
that it is admissibly Polish.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Real-closed, truncation-closed hulls}

With $k=\ka$, a hull can be required to preserve both real closedness and
all rational truncations. Full Hahn real closedness follows from the
classical algebraic-closedness theorem for Hahn fields with algebraically
closed coefficients and divisible exponent group
\cite[Corollary~4]{Poonen}, applied after adjoining $i$.

\begin{theorem}[A strengthened hull with a countable truncation core]
\label{pma:ser:thm:rchull}
Let $H=\ka((t^\Q))$ and let $A\subseteq H$ be countable. There exist a
countable real closed truncation-closed subfield $B\subseteq H$ and a field
$C=\overline B^{\,v}$ such that
\[
 k(t^\Q)\cup A\subseteq B\subseteq C,
\]
$C$ is real closed and admissibly Polish, and every rational prefix of every
$f\in C$ belongs to $B$:
\begin{equation}\label{pma:ser:eq:trunccore}
 T_{\leq q}(C)\subseteq B\qquad(q\in\Q).
\end{equation}
In particular, $C$ is truncation-closed and contains $\Lk\cup A$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Start with the countable field $B_0=k(t^\Q)(A)$.
Given $B_n$, adjoin $T_{\leq q}b$ for all $b\in B_n$ and all $q\in\Q$,
then take its real closure inside the real closed field $H$ to obtain
$B_{n+1}$. Each step is countable: there are countably many truncations and
countably many elements algebraic over a countable field.
The union $B=\bigcup_nB_n$ is a countable field, is truncation-closed, and
is real closed. For the last assertion, any finite list of polynomial
coefficients and any positive element occur at one stage, and the requisite
odd-degree roots and positive square roots occur at the next stage.

The field $C=\overline B^{\,v}$ is complete and separable, hence admissibly
Polish by the same argument as Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:hulls}.
For $f\in C$ and $q\in\Q$, choose $b\in B$ with $v(f-b)>q$.
Then $T_{\leq q}f=T_{\leq q}b\in B$, proving \eqref{pma:ser:eq:trunccore}.
To prove real closedness, regard $B(i)$ inside $H(i)$.
The coefficientwise valuation satisfies
\[
 v(a+ib)=\min\{v(a),v(b)\}\qquad(a,b\in H).
\]
Consequently its completion is $C(i)$. Since $B$ is real closed, $B(i)$ is
algebraically closed; Lemma~\ref{pma:ser:lem:completionac} makes $C(i)$ algebraically
closed. As $C$ is ordered, it is real closed.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact global invariant}

Let $\operatorname{pcov}_k(H)$ be the least cardinality of a family of
admissibly Polish intermediate subfields $k(t^\Q)\subseteq F\subseteq H$
whose union is $H$. The topology on a covering field need not initially be
the inherited valuation topology.

\begin{theorem}[The Polish field-cover number]\label{pma:ser:thm:covernumber}
For every countable ordered coefficient field $k$,
\[
 \operatorname{pcov}_k\bigl(k((t^\Q))\bigr)=2^{\aleph_0}.
\]
For $k=\ka$, the same minimum holds even if all covering fields are required
to be real closed, truncation-closed, and Polish in their valuation topology.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the upper bound, $|H|=2^{\aleph_0}$, and the fields $F_{\{h\}}$ from
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:hulls}, one for each $h\in H$, cover $H$.
For real algebraic coefficients use the stronger hulls from
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:rchull} instead.

For the lower bound, use the continuum-sized binary family
\[
 h_b=\sum_{n\geq0}b(n)t^{1-1/(n+2)},\qquad b\in2^\N.
\]
Distinct centers differ in absolute ordered value by more than $2t$.
In any one admissibly Polish intermediate field, the intervals of radius
$t$ about the centers it contains are nonempty, open, and pairwise disjoint.
It therefore contains only countably many members of this binary family.
A union of $\kappa<2^{\aleph_0}$ such fields contains at most
$\kappa\cdot\aleph_0<2^{\aleph_0}$ members of the family, and cannot cover
$H$. This cardinal calculation is in ZFC and uses no continuum hypothesis.
\end{proof}

The local and global statements now fit together exactly. Every countable
collection of Hahn data is contained in one well-behaved Polish field;
no such field is maximal; nevertheless continuum many are necessary to
cover all Hahn data. These conclusions are not consequences of the mere
cardinality $|H|=2^{\aleph_0}$: the lower bound uses the fixed-scale
separation forced by arithmetic and order.

\section{A countable omnific integer part and its exact floor regularity}
\label{pma:ser:sec:floor}

Throughout this section $k=\ka\subseteq\R$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{pma:ser:eq:integerpart}
 \Ik=\Z\oplus\bigoplus_{q\in\Q_{<0}}kt^q.
\end{equation}
Thus an element has finitely many negative-exponent terms and an ordinary
integer constant term. The direct sum is literal finite support; replacing it
by arbitrary Hahn support would change the ring.

\begin{theorem}[A common integer part]\label{pma:ser:thm:commonip}
The ring $\Ik$ is countable and discretely ordered. It is an integer part of
both $\Pk$ and $\Lk$. If
\[
 f=p+c+u,
\]
where $p$ is the negative principal part, $c=f_0\in k$, and $u$ has only
positive exponents, then
\begin{equation}\label{pma:ser:eq:floor}
 \floorI{f}
 =p+\lfloor c\rfloor-\begin{cases}
  1,&c\in\Z\text{ and }u<0,\\
  0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Finite rational supports with coefficients in a countable field form a
countable set. Addition and multiplication preserve finite negative support
and integer constant terms, so $\Ik$ is a countable unital subring.
If a nonzero element has a negative leading exponent, its absolute ordered
value exceeds every positive ordinary integer. Otherwise it is a nonzero
ordinary integer. Hence $1$ is its least positive element.

For $f\in\Lk$, left-finiteness makes $p$ finite, and every nonzero $u$ is
smaller in absolute ordered value than every positive constant of $k$.
If $c\notin\Z$, both $c-\lfloor c\rfloor$ and
$\lfloor c\rfloor+1-c$ are positive constants; the infinitesimal $u$
cannot change either inequality. If $c\in\Z$ and $u\geq0$, the floor is
$p+c$. If $c\in\Z$ and $u<0$, the floor is $p+c-1$.
In every case the stated element $a$ satisfies $a\leq f<a+1$.
Uniqueness follows because distinct elements of $\Ik$ differ by at least
$1$ in absolute ordered value. Since $\Pk\subseteq\Lk$ and contains
$\Ik$, the same result holds in $\Pk$.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} With $t^q\mapsto\omega^{-q}$, formula \eqref{pma:ser:eq:floor}
is the collection's floor rule \replabel{odg:thm:floor}, proved in Lean for
every surreal, and source~03's \cref{pma:bor:lem:floor}. For $k=\ka$, the
ring $\Ik$ is source~03's finite principal-part ring $\A$ with coefficients
restricted to $\ka$ (with $X=t^{-1}$), a countable subring of it; it is also
the Shepherdson ring used by batch~86's manuscript~10 in
\fn{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/docs/surreal/discrete-initial-subgroups-and-omnific-normalization}.

Formula~\eqref{pma:ser:eq:floor}, particularly its correction for a negative
infinitesimal at an integer constant, is a specialization of the omnific
normal-form floor rule already documented in ProveIt \cite{s09:ProveIt}.
It is not claimed as a new floor formula. The following topological
consequences are the point of its use here.

\begin{theorem}[Exact discontinuity set and Baire class]
\label{pma:ser:thm:floorregularity}
Give $\Lk$ its unique admissible Polish topology and $\Ik$ the discrete
topology. The floor map $\floorI{\cdot}:\Lk\to\Ik$ is Baire class one.
Its set of discontinuities is exactly $\Ik$, a countable closed nowhere-dense
subset of $\Lk$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Its fibers are the half-open intervals $[a,a+1)$ for $a\in\Ik$.
If $f\notin\Ik$ and $a=\floorI f$, then $a<f<a+1$, so a sufficiently
small order neighborhood of $f$ lies in the same fiber. The floor is
continuous there. At $a\in\Ik$, the sequence
$a-t^n$ converges to $a$, while
\[
 \floorI{a-t^n}=a-1\ne a=\floorI a.
\]
Thus the discontinuity set is exactly $\Ik$.

For $n\geq0$ let $T_n f=\sum_{q\leq n}f_qt^q$, a finite polynomial.
The map $T_n$ into its discrete, countable range is locally constant:
$v(f-g)>n$ implies $T_nf=T_ng$.
Consequently
\[
 F_n(f)=\floorI{T_nf}
\]
is a continuous map $\Lk\to\Ik$. These maps converge pointwise to the
floor, and indeed are eventually equal to it at each input. The negative
principal part and constant are already fixed for all $n\geq0$.
When the constant is an integer and the positive tail is nonzero, the sign
needed for the correction is determined by the first positive exponent,
which is included once $n$ is large enough. In all other cases no such
correction can change. This proves the Baire class one assertion.

Closed discreteness follows from Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:integerparts}. Its interior
is empty because every neighborhood of $a\in\Ik$ contains
$a+t^n\notin\Ik$ for large $n$. Hence it is nowhere dense.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Boundary tests]
The formulas include
\[
 \floorI{-t}=-1,\qquad
 \floorI{7-t^{1/3}}=6,\qquad
 \floorI{7+t^{1/3}}=7,
\]
and
\[
 \floorI{3t^{-2}-5t^{-1/2}+\tfrac32-t^{10}}
   =3t^{-2}-5t^{-1/2}+1.
\]
A finite-precision procedure that ignores a small negative tail at an integer
constant is wrong exactly at the kind of boundary detected by the theorem.
The continuous approximants above permit eventual correction; they do not
provide an input-uniform stage at which correction is finished.
\end{example}

\subsection{Floors in the larger Polish hulls}

The strengthened hulls of Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:rchull} support the same regularity
without restricting their negative principal parts to finite support.

\begin{theorem}[Canonical integer parts in real closed Polish hulls]
\label{pma:ser:thm:hullfloor}
Let $B\subseteq C\subseteq\ka((t^\Q))$ be as in
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:rchull}. Then
\[
 J_C=\{f\in C:\supp f\subseteq\Q_{\leq0},\ f_0\in\Z\}
\]
is a countable closed discrete integer part of $C$, and $J_C\subseteq B$.
Its floor is Baire class one as a map into discrete $J_C$, with discontinuity
set exactly $J_C$. Under the surreal normal-form embedding it is a subring
of the omnific integers.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $f\in C$, the principal part
$p=T_{\leq0}f-f_0$ belongs to $B$ by \eqref{pma:ser:eq:trunccore}. Thus the formula
\[
 \lfloor f\rfloor_{J_C}
 =p+\lfloor f_0\rfloor
  -\mathbf1_{\{f_0\in\Z,\ f-T_{\leq0}f<0\}}
\]
defines an element of $C$ with no positive exponents and integer constant.
The same leading-term comparisons as in Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:commonip} prove
the integer-part inequalities and discrete order. Ring closure follows from
convolution: negative exponents cannot contribute to the constant term.
Every $j\in J_C$ equals $T_{\leq0}j$, so lies in the countable set $B$.
Closed discreteness also follows from Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:integerparts}.

For each nonnegative integer $n$, the map $T_{\leq n}:C\to B$, with $B$
given the discrete topology, is locally constant. The maps
$f\mapsto\lfloor T_{\leq n}f\rfloor_{J_C}$ are therefore continuous and
are eventually equal to the floor at each input. Only the first nonzero
positive term is needed to decide the possible correction. The interval
fibers and the sequence $a-t^n\to a$ give the exact discontinuity set as
before. Finally, replacing $t^q$ by $\omega^{-q}$ turns the nonpositive
support and integer constant conditions into the omnific normal-form
conditions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The target topology matters]
The Baire class one assertion is about a \emph{discrete} integer-part target,
not just its inclusion in the field. It is stronger than merely producing
continuous real-valued approximants to the ordinary floor on $\R$.
Indeed, the ordinary floor $\R\to\Z_{\mathrm{discrete}}$ is not Baire class
one: every continuous map from connected $\R$ to discrete $\Z$ is constant,
and a pointwise convergent sequence of constant maps has a constant limit.
The locally constant prefix maps are a genuine non-Archimedean resource.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The common integer part satisfies open induction}

The classical relationship between integer parts of real closed fields and
open induction is often called the integer-part characterization of open
induction. For our specific ring the needed implication has a short proof.

\begin{proposition}[Open induction]\label{pma:ser:prop:iopen}
The nonnegative cone $\mathcal I_{k,\geq0}$ satisfies $Q+\mathrm{IOpen}$ in the
language of ordered arithmetic, with parameters allowed in the induction
scheme.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The elementary axioms of discretely ordered semiring arithmetic hold in the
nonnegative cone of any discretely ordered unital ring. Every positive
$a\in\Ik$ has predecessor $a-1\geq0$.

A quantifier-free formula in one variable with parameters from $\Ik$ is a
Boolean combination of polynomial equations and inequalities. In the real
closed field $\Lk$, the real roots of its finitely many nonzero polynomials
partition the line into finitely many intervals and points on which the
formula has constant truth value. Every nonempty trace of one of these pieces
on $\mathcal I_{k,\geq0}$ has a least element: the lower endpoint, when included and
already in $\Ik$, or the first integer-part element above that endpoint,
with $0$ serving as a lower bound when needed. The floor property supplies
this first element. Therefore every nonempty quantifier-free definable subset
of $\mathcal I_{k,\geq0}$ has a least element.

If a quantifier-free formula held at $0$ and were preserved by successor but
failed somewhere, its counterexamples would have a least element $a$.
Then $a>0$ and the formula holds at $a-1$, contradicting preservation by
successor. This is open induction.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} This is the route of \replabel{dsn:cor:openinduction} and
of source~03's \cref{pma:bor:thm:arithmetic}, which proves open induction for
$\A$; the Shepherdson model is classical \cite{Shepherdson}.

\begin{corollary}[Arbitrary countable support complexity in countable arithmetic]
For every countable ordinal $\alpha$, there is a real closed Polish
truncation-closed field $C\subseteq\ka((t^\Q))$ whose countable canonical
integer part $J_C$ contains an element with support order type $\alpha$.
The nonnegative cone of $J_C$ satisfies $Q+\mathrm{IOpen}$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Embed $\alpha$ into $\Q\cap(-2,-1)$ and take the Hahn series with coefficient
$1$ on that support. Put it in a strengthened hull using
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:rchull}. Its support is negative and its constant is $0$,
so it belongs to $J_C$. The proof of Proposition~\ref{pma:ser:prop:iopen} applies
verbatim with this integer part and its real closed ambient field.
\end{proof}

There is no conflict with Glazer's result: the arithmetic model
$\mathcal I_{k,\geq0}$ is countable. Its uncountable real closed ambient field
$\Lk$ is not a discretely ordered arithmetic model. Moreover, $\Pk$ and
$\Lk$ share this same integer part even though only the latter supports
admissible Polish field arithmetic.

\subsection{Why the finite integer part does not extend to the full Hahn field}

The element
\[
 z=t^{-2}y=\sum_{n\geq2}t^{-1-1/n}\in\Hk,
\]
where $y$ is from \eqref{pma:ser:eq:boundedhahn}, has infinitely many negative terms.
For every $a\in\Ik$, at least one negative coefficient of $z-a$ remains
nonzero; its leading exponent is negative, so $|z-a|>1$. Hence $\Ik$ is
not an integer part of $\Hk$.

Replacing finite negative support in \eqref{pma:ser:eq:integerpart} by arbitrary
well-ordered negative support gives an integer part of $\Hk$, with the
same coefficientwise floor rule. This larger ring is uncountable: binary
choices along the support of $z$ already produce continuum many elements.
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:integerparts} supplies another obstruction to admissible
Polish arithmetic on this full Hahn field. Here that argument agrees with,
but is less general than, Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:hahn}.

\section{Surreal realization and a formalization interface}
\label{pma:ser:sec:surreal}

\subsection{A set-sized embedding, not a topology on a proper class}

With $k=\ka\subseteq\R$, the normal-form assignment
\begin{equation}\label{pma:ser:eq:surreal}
 \iota\!\left(\sum_{q\in\Q}a_qt^q\right)
       =\sum_{q\in\Q}a_q\omega^{-q}
\end{equation}
realizes the three fields as set-sized subfields of the surreal numbers.
Well-ordered support in the $q$-variable becomes reverse-well-ordered support
in the Conway growth exponents $-q$. The normal-form rules preserve addition,
multiplication, and order; $t$ corresponds to $\omega^{-1}$.
The image of $\Ik$ has only positive growth exponents and an integer
constant term, so lies in $\Oz$.

This is a formal normal-form embedding. It does not assert that an arbitrary
infinite series can be evaluated at an infinite real or surreal argument by
ordinary analytic convergence. In particular, the direction of the exponent
change in \eqref{pma:ser:eq:surreal} is essential.
The full proper class $\No$ is never asserted to be a Polish space.
The series carriers have cardinality continuum and can be constructed as
subsets of the set $k^\Q$. Only afterwards are they identified with surreal
normal forms.

The project documentation is an interface to these structures, not a proof
that the new topological statements have already been formalized. The
reported kernel checks in ProveIt concern the repository's declared
constructions and theorems. No new kernel run was performed for this article.

\subsection{A modular Lean development plan}

A formalization need not begin with surreal arithmetic. Most of the proof is
independent of it. A suitable division into modules is as follows.

\paragraph{Category and ordered groups.}
Formalize the Baire-order local-bound lemma over a linearly ordered abelian
group, separately from the field specialization. Its interface should return
an order bound $a>0$ and a neighborhood inclusion, not an implicit assertion
that the ambient topology is the order topology. Import a proved Pettis
lemma and Borel-homomorphism automatic continuity at clearly stated instances.

\paragraph{Ordered rings and fields.}
Prove automatic discreteness using one scalar $a+1$, and prove the field
refinement theorem using $(a+1)/\varepsilon$. These are different lemmas:
quotient scalars are not available in a general ordered ring.
Then prove closed discreteness and countability of any integer-part subring
without assuming its carrier is measurable.

\paragraph{Series and topology.}
Construct left-finite coefficient functions as a subtype of $\Q\to k$.
Give finite-below-cutoff witnesses explicitly. Prove convolution finiteness,
the inverse construction, valuation identities, and metric completeness.
The countable dense subspace consists of finitely supported functions.
A separate theorem identifies the metric and order topologies.

\paragraph{Obstruction certificates.}
Formalize the binary family from Lemma~\ref{pma:ser:lem:separated}; the only infinite
support needed for the negative result has order type at most $\omega$.
For Puiseux, package the general countable proper-subfield-cover theorem,
then prove each lattice-support stage is closed. This separation prevents a
proof of incompleteness of one metric from being mistaken for a proof of
absolute non-Polishability.

\paragraph{Integer parts and measurable floors.}
First prove \eqref{pma:ser:eq:floor} in the left-finite series subtype. Then identify
this ring with the corresponding set-sized subring of the repository's
omnific integers. The exact discontinuity theorem and the pointwise eventually
constant sequence $(F_n)$ can be formalized independently of the full surreal
field.

\paragraph{Descriptive complexity.}
The explicit maps in \eqref{pma:ser:eq:rowcode} and the $\FIN$ reduction are the
finite combinatorial portion. The well-founded-tree reduction and
Lusin--Souslin step belong in a separate descriptive-set-theory layer.
They are not required for the core Hahn classification or the positive
Levi-Civita construction.

This architecture leaves no proper-class quantification in the main proof.
Universe parameters are needed only when identifying the set-sized series
carrier with a universe-relative surreal implementation. No additional large
cardinal assumption is used.

\section{Consequences for exact symbolic arithmetic}
\label{pma:ser:sec:computing}

An exact coefficient stream and a valuation-Cauchy name provide different
information. A coefficient stream reports one coefficient at a time. A
valuation-Cauchy name eventually fixes \emph{all} coefficients below a
specified cutoff. In a left-finite representation, certifying a completed
prefix therefore includes a support bound, not just a list of currently
observed nonzero terms.

Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:lc} supports continuous arithmetic in the second
representation. Proposition~\ref{pma:ser:prop:sameborel} says that the measurable
information is the same, but it does not turn these representations into the
same effective oracle. No computability claim follows merely from Borel
equivalence.

For an exact rational-coefficient prototype one can represent finite
truncations by dictionaries $q\mapsto a_q$ with $q,a_q\in\Q$.
When multiplying to cutoff $B$, lower bounds on the two supports determine
which input prefixes suffice: terms of the first factor above $B-v(g)$,
and terms of the second above $B-v(f)$, cannot affect the result. For
inversion of $a t^q(1+h)$, a positive lower bound
$\delta\leq v(h)$ bounds the number of geometric powers needed below any
fixed cutoff. These are mathematically certified finite reductions, not
numerical approximations to real coefficients.

Floor is different. Its Baire class one approximants may change once the
first nonzero infinitesimal term is revealed at an integer boundary. No
continuous exact floor algorithm on the whole field can exist, because the
mathematical function is discontinuous there. The theorem pinpoints the
necessary limitation instead of attributing it to a poor choice of code.

The accompanying Python program uses rational exponents and coefficients to
check finite algebraic identities, truncated geometric inverses, the floor
inequalities, and finite instances of the support witnesses. The deterministic run passed 20,116 finite assertions; its output
records the counts by test family. These tests catch implementation mistakes in
the supplied examples; they cannot establish Baire category, quantification
over all Polish topologies, infinite support completeness, or real closedness.
The conventional proofs are the basis of those assertions.

\section{Further research questions and concrete targets}
\label{pma:ser:sec:questions}

The following questions are proposed next steps. They are not asserted to be
previously published open problems, and no novelty claim is inferred from
failure to locate an answer in the inspected sources.

\begin{question}[Intermediate-field rigidity]\label{pma:ser:q:intermediate}
Let $k$ be countable and ordered, and let
$\Pk\subseteq F\subseteq k((t^\Q))$.
If $F$ has an admissible Polish topology, must its valuation topology be
complete, and must the admissible topology equal the valuation topology?
\end{question}
The prefix criterion gives countably many prefixes, but it does not prove
completeness of a coarser topology. A proof must close precisely that gap;
one cannot appeal to the open mapping theorem until both topologies are known
to be Polish.

\begin{question}[Classification of Polish hulls]
Within a fixed standard Borel family of coefficient-observable parameters,
what is the descriptive complexity of equality and inclusion between the
countable-parameter hulls $F_A$? Can one construct useful canonical dense
cores or invariants for their ordered-field isomorphism types?
\end{question}
The existence of proper Polish extensions of $\Lk$ and the absence of maximal
ones are settled by Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:hulls} and Corollary~\ref{pma:ser:cor:nomax}.
The remaining issue is classification, not existence. The ambient parameter
space must be specified: the full Hahn coefficient domain is not standard
Borel.

\begin{question}[Minimal scalar hypotheses]
How few Borel scalar maps suffice to force the order topology in the
rational-exponent setting? Can a specified countable set of monomial
multiplications replace all scalar maps under additional algebraic or
truncation-closure assumptions?
\end{question}
The current proof uses a scalar depending on the local order bound and the
target interval. An answer should identify which part of that freedom is
essential, rather than dropping scalar regularity altogether.

\begin{question}[Order-free non-real-closed fields]
For countable ordered $k$ that is not real closed, can the Hahn and Puiseux
nonexistence statements be derived from a Polish additive group and jointly
Borel multiplication alone, without requiring the displayed order to have the
Baire property?
\end{question}
Corollary~\ref{pma:ser:cor:realorder} settles the real closed case. In general a field
may have several orders, and the image-of-squares argument does not identify
one positive cone.

\begin{question}[Other support completions]
Extend the left-finite construction and its classification to countable
ordered exponent groups of higher rank. Which support restrictions give
separable complete field topologies, and which admit a countable cofinal
valuation scale but still fail by a proper-subfield cover?
\end{question}
The inverse proof in Proposition~\ref{pma:ser:prop:lcfield} explicitly uses
$n\delta\to+\infty$ in an Archimedean exponent group. It cannot be copied
unchanged into a lexicographic higher-rank group.

\begin{question}[Descriptive ranks beyond the trichotomy]
Which Borel ranks can occur for coefficient-code domains of admissibly Polish
subfields of $k((t^\Q))$? Is there a useful algebraic characterization of
when a Borel support family yields a Polishable additive group?
\end{question}
Table~\ref{pma:ser:tab:trichotomy} shows that a smaller rank is not sufficient.
A productive refinement should combine support closure, completeness of
prefixes, and the proper-subfield obstruction.

\begin{question}[The least support bound of a one-parameter hull]
For $y=\sum_{n\geq2}t^{1-1/n}$, determine the least countable ordinal bounding
all support order types in $F_{\{y\}}$. How does that least bound change when
real closure and closure under all rational truncations are imposed before
metric completion?
\end{question}
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:rankbound} proves existence of a bound but does not compute
it. A solution would require quantitative control of support order types
under convolution, inversion, algebraic extension, and stabilized-prefix
limits. It would turn the qualitative local-hull theorem into an ordinal
complexity calculation.

\begin{question}[Other integer parts and floor discontinuities]
Classify integer parts of $\Lk$ and the larger real closed Polish hulls up to
field automorphisms. Which floors admit canonical or effective locally
constant approximants for presentations not built from truncations?
\end{question}
Countability and closed discreteness hold for every integer part by
Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:integerparts}. The discontinuity set of its floor is also
its integer part in the order topology. The strengthened hulls retain explicit truncation approximants. The
remaining constructive issue is canonical or effective approximation for
other presentations, together with a classification of the integer parts.

\begin{question}[A uniform effective presentation]
For computably presented $k$, construct a certified Type-2 representation of
$\Lk$ with computable arithmetic, explicit precision transfer for products
and inverses, and a finite-mind-change floor procedure for $k=\ka$.
\end{question}
The representation must include effective support-completion information.
Bare enumerations of nonzero coefficients do not suffice to know that a
prefix is complete. Any claimed effective embedding into Baire space should
state which oracle representation is being used.

\begin{question}[Formal proof milestones]
Can the local order-bound theorem, automatic discreteness, and full Hahn
classification be formalized as a small reusable library independent of the
full surreal development? What is the minimal imported descriptive-set-theory
interface for the exact code-complexity theorems?
\end{question}
These are concrete implementation tasks. The first milestone is the
category-to-order bridge; the coanalytic lower bound should not block the
rest of the project.

\begin{question}[Positive cones versus groups of differences]\label{pma:ser:q:cones}
Characterize Borel discretely ordered semirings whose positive cones admit
Polish continuous addition but whose groups of differences are not Polishable
with measurable multiplication. Which hypotheses force a topology to extend
from the cone to its group completion?
\end{question}
This returns directly to the boundary emphasized by Glazer's arithmetic
questions and the earlier Presburger constructions. Theorem~\ref{pma:ser:thm:discrete}
provides an obstruction on the group side, not a classification of monoid
presentations.

\noindent\writetag{} This is source~08's \cref{pma:lc:q:completion}; source~06's
cone of $\Z+t\R[t]$ is a data point (\cref{pma:cp:sec:meet}).

\begin{question}[Weak choice and category]
Which portions of the classification survive in weaker choice settings?
Separate the dependent choices used to build the bounded increasing exponent
sequence, the Baire theorem, and the selections of representatives of
countably many prefix classes.
\end{question}
The present paper works in ZFC and makes no choice-free assertion. A
foundational analysis would be a distinct project rather than an automatic
consequence of the set-sized constructions.

\section{Conclusions of Part V}

The main dividing line is not whether exact infinite series can be assigned
Borel codes. It is whether their arithmetic, order, and completeness fit
within a separable Polish group.
A Baire-measurable order and Borel scalar arithmetic force local order bounds
and hence the order topology. Full Hahn support then admits too many
mutually separated prefixes, except in the countable-coefficient Laurent
case. Puiseux support avoids that obstruction but fails a different category
test because it is a countable union of proper measurable subfields.
Left-finite completion avoids both obstructions and supplies a unique Polish
topological field. Countable-parameter hulls go further: arbitrary countable
Hahn data fit into a Polish subfield, even with real closedness and truncation
closure over real algebraic coefficients. There is no maximal Polish
intermediate field, while the exact cover number of the full field is the
continuum.

The integer-part consequences connect this topological classification to
arithmetic and surreal normal forms, including arbitrary prescribed countable
support types inside suitable countable integer parts. A Polish ordered field cannot hide an
uncountable discrete integer part, even a nonmeasurable one. The real
algebraic-coefficient Levi-Civita field nevertheless supports a countable
omnific integer part with open induction, and its floor has exactly
controlled discontinuities. These results supply a precise next layer beyond
Borel support analysis while leaving topology rigidity on intermediate fields and the broader
positive-cone classification open.

\part{Baire order forces arithmetic rigidity}\label{pma:part:br}

prepared with ChatGPT for Vladimir Reshetnikov''), pinned to repository

(\texttt{pma:br:cor:signed-presburger}). Source~10's
$\operatorname{Fin}(A)$, the ordinary-integer-bounded part, is printed with
roman type and is not Part~II's set $\Fin$ of finite sets; its unit-image
spectrum $\mathcal S(G,e)$ is printed $\mathcal U(G)$, source~12's name for the
same set. \Cref{pma:sec:notation} lists these and the other conventions
of Parts~VI--IX; in particular source~12's $t$ and source~10's $X$ are the
same positive \emph{infinite} variable of $\Z+t\R[t]$, as in \cref{pma:part:cp}.

\section{The research intersection and the question answered}
\label{pma:br:sec:intersection}

The point of contact is the topology of arithmetic structures: how much
arithmetic can coexist with a well-behaved additive topology? Glazer's
\emph{A Topological Tennenbaum Theorem} rules out uncountable Polish
models of $Q+\IOpen$ with continuous addition and Borel multiplication
\cite[Corollary 1]{Glazer}. His Question 2 asks about continuous addition
for uncountable Polish Presburger models. ProveIt contains complementary
interfaces: integer Presburger elimination and ordered surreal and
omnific constructions \cite{s12:ProveItPresburger,s12:ProveItSurreal}.
This suggests examining what happens when an additive presentation is
required to support a full, order-compatible multiplication.

An earlier project report established a local-compactness obstruction
\cite{s12:PriorLC}. Its first research question in Section 14 asks whether an
uncountable discretely ordered ring can carry a Polish additive-group
topology with Borel order when multiplication has no regularity assumption.
The answer proved here is \emph{no}. More strongly, Borelness can be weakened
to the Baire property of a single cone, and Polishness can be weakened to
Baire plus the countable chain condition.

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=The principal result]
\textbf{Baire-category rigidity.}
If a discretely ordered ring $R$ has a Hausdorff Baire additive-group
topology and a positive cone with the Baire property, then
\[
 c(R)=d(R)=|R|.
\]
If this topology satisfies the countable chain condition, then $R$ is
countable and the topology is discrete.

\smallskip
There is no regularity hypothesis on multiplication.
\end{tcolorbox}

Here $c(R)$ is cellularity and $d(R)$ is density. The cardinal equality is
not merely an upper-bound obstruction: the proof explicitly constructs
$|R|$ disjoint open translates. It identifies a mechanism that persists far
beyond the finite-dimensional locally compact setting of the previous
report.

\subsection{What advances beyond the earlier work}

The local-compactness argument used structural information about locally
compact abelian groups. The proof below needs no decomposition into real
components, no finite-dimensional flag, and no regularity of scalar
multipliers. Its central interface is just an order-bounded neighborhood.
This makes the argument both more general and shorter to formalize.
The main consequences developed here are as follows.

\begin{enumerate}
\item A universal packing theorem gives exact density and cellularity,
with both Baire-category and Haar-measure routes to its hypothesis.
\item The images of a least positive element under \emph{all} ordered
additive self-embeddings are order-bounded in every uncountable Baire ccc
presentation; no regularity of the embeddings is required.
\item An uncountable such ordered group admits no compatible unital
ordered-ring multiplication, and its nonnegative cone admits no unital
semiring multiplication with the prescribed addition and unit.
\item Polynomial examples explain why Baire category, ccc, and regularity
of order cannot simply be deleted. A natural completion destroys discrete
order even before topology is considered.
\end{enumerate}

These statements are established within the manuscript. We do not claim
that each auxiliary lemma is historically new. Pettis's theorem and its
measure counterpart are classical; the contribution here is their use
with discrete arithmetic separation, the resulting sharp conclusions,
and the resolution of the specified project question.

\subsection{The scope is not Glazer's entire setting}
\label{pma:br:subsec:scope}

A positive arithmetic structure has an additive \emph{monoid}. Our central
hypothesis is a topology on its signed additive \emph{group}, with
continuous inversion as well as continuous addition. Algebraically taking
differences does not, by itself, construct a Polish group topology.
Therefore the theorem below is not a replacement for Glazer's theorem
under weaker hypotheses on the same objects. The carrier and topology
requirements are different.

Glazer's Question 1 concerns provability in $\mathrm{ATR}_0$
\cite[Question 1]{Glazer}; we do not settle that question. Nor do we
re-present the earlier affirmative Presburger construction
\cite{s12:PriorPresburger} as a new answer. The exact open question answered
here is the one in the preceding local-compactness report.

is source~08, \cref{pma:part:lc}; its ``first research question in

order is the fourth question of that section (\cref{pma:lc:q:weakenborel}).
The ``earlier affirmative Presburger construction'' \cite{s12:PriorPresburger}
is source~05, \cref{pma:part:pr}. Source~12's pin precedes the placement of
Parts~III--V, so it did not see source~09 (\cref{pma:part:ser}).

\subsection{The intersection and the result as source 10 states it \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:intro}

The topic is the boundary between topological presentations of arithmetic
and the algebra of non-Archimedean integer systems. It connects a specific
part of Elliot Glazer's published research with two concrete parts of
ProveIt, rather than relying on a speculative account of his interests.
In \emph{A Topological Tennenbaum Theorem}, Glazer proves, in particular,
that an uncountable Polish model of $\mathsf Q+\mathrm{IOpen}$ cannot have
continuous addition and Borel multiplication \cite[Corollary~1]{Glazer}.
ProveIt develops Cooper elimination for Presburger arithmetic and an
ordered surreal/omnific algebra \cite{s10:RepoPres,s10:RepoSurreal}. These are
natural interfaces at which to ask whether an additive presentation can
be expanded by multiplication.

Two earlier project manuscripts supply the immediate starting point.
\emph{Local Compactness Forces Arithmetic Rigidity} proves a
locally compact, second-countable version without regularity assumptions
on multiplication, and explicitly asks whether local compactness can be
removed \cite{s10:Local}. \emph{Polishability at the
Hahn--Puiseux--Levi-Civita Boundary} isolates the category argument that
makes a Baire order locally bounded \cite{s10:Hahn}. The present article
combines that local bound with a different quotient construction. The
quotient has a countable kernel even when the open subgroup is neither
divisible nor finite dimensional.

\begin{tcolorbox}
\textbf{Main conclusion.} Let $A$ be a nonzero discretely ordered ring.
If $(A,+)$ is a Polish topological group and $\{x\in A:x>0\}$ has the
Baire property, then $A$ is countable and its topology is discrete.
Multiplication is an arbitrary algebraic operation compatible with the
ordered-ring axioms; it is not required to be measurable.
\end{tcolorbox}

Thus the answer to the general Polish-group question posed in
\cite{s10:Local} is negative: there is no uncountable example. We actually
prove the stronger Baire--ccc statement. Here \emph{ccc} means that every
family of pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets is countable.

\subsubsection{What changes in the proof}

The earlier locally compact argument finds an open real vector component
and uses multiplication to move an uncountable divisible subgroup into
its quotient. That approach makes finite-dimensional structure appear
essential. Instead, for a positive element $a$, consider
\[
 H_a=\{x\in A: |x|\le n a\text{ for some ordinary }n\in\N\}.
\]
This is a convex additive subgroup. Its elements need not be bounded by a
\emph{single} multiple of $a$; the ordinary integer $n$ may depend on $x$.
Nevertheless,
\[
 ax\in H_a\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 |x|\le n1\text{ for some ordinary }n.
\]
For a discretely ordered ring, the right side says exactly that
$x\in\Z1$. Therefore multiplication by $a$, followed by the additive
quotient map, has the countable kernel $\Z1$ on \emph{all} of $A$.
When $H_a$ is open, ccc makes the target countable. No continuity of this
map is needed: an algebraic injection is enough.

The signed-group hypothesis matters. A Polish topology on a positive
arithmetic monoid does not automatically extend to a Polish topology on
its group of differences. We return to this distinction in
\cref{pma:br:sec:monoids}. We also do not claim to settle Glazer's reverse-
mathematical Question~1, which concerns an $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ proof of his
Theorem~2 \cite{Glazer}.

\section{Conventions and elementary ordered algebra}
\label{pma:br:sec:conventions}

All structures and topological spaces in the theorems are sets, and the
ambient foundation is ZFC. We use the usual standard natural numbers when
writing an external countable union or a sequence indexed by $\N$.

\begin{definition}
A \emph{discretely ordered ring} is a nonzero unital ring $R$ with a total
order such that addition preserves order, the product of two strictly
positive elements is strictly positive, and $1$ is the least strictly
positive element. Unless stated otherwise, rings are commutative.
\end{definition}

This is the standard discrete-order convention used in weak arithmetic
\cite{s12:Mohsenipour}. It is not a statement that a supplied topology is
discrete. In fact, distinguishing those two meanings of discreteness is
central to the problem.

The ring order makes the additive group ordered and torsion-free. For
$x\in R$ put $|x|=\max(x,-x)$. Directly from the order axioms,
\begin{equation}
 x\ne y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad |x-y|\geq1,
 \qquad |xy|=|x|\,|y|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:unit-separation}
\end{equation}
There are no zero divisors: the absolute value of a product of nonzero
elements is positive.

\begin{lemma}[Ordinary integers form a convex subring]
\label{pma:br:lem:convex-integers}
If $R$ is discretely ordered and $0\leq x\leq n$ for an ordinary natural
number $n$, then $x$ is one of $0,1,\ldots,n$. Consequently, either
$R=\Z$ as an ordered unital ring, or there is $c\in R$ with $c>n$ for every
ordinary $n\in\N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first assertion follows by external induction on $n$. If $x>0$, then
$x\geq1$, so $0\leq x-1\leq n-1$. For the second assertion choose an
element outside the ordinary integer subring and take its absolute value.
If it were bounded by any ordinary natural number, the first assertion
would put it in that subring. Thus its absolute value is larger than all
ordinary natural numbers.
\end{proof}

This uses no induction axiom \emph{inside} the ring. It is an ordinary
metatheoretic proof about a finite integer interval.

\begin{definition}
An \emph{additive-group topology} on $R$ is a topology making
$(R,+,0,-)$ a topological group. We always require it to be Hausdorff.
We make no compatibility assumption between this topology and the order
topology. Write $P=\{x\in R:x>0\}$.
\end{definition}

A set has the \emph{Baire property} if its symmetric difference with an
open set is meager. A space is \emph{Baire} if no nonempty open set is
meager in the space. These are distinct notions: a positive cone may
have the Baire property in a space that is itself meager.

A space satisfies the \emph{countable chain condition}, abbreviated ccc,
if every family of pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets is countable.
Its cellularity $c(X)$ is the supremum of the cardinalities of such
families. Its density $d(X)$ is the least cardinality of a dense subset.
For any space,
\begin{equation}
 c(X)\leq d(X)\leq |X|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:cardinal-basic}
\end{equation}
Indeed, each member of a disjoint open family meets a dense set, and the
chosen intersection points are different. Separability implies ccc.
A Polish space is separable and completely metrizable, and is Baire.

For Borelness, regularity of the binary order and regularity of its cone
are equivalent in an additive topological group: the cone is a section
of the order relation, and
\[
 x<y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in P.
\]
Our category theorem needs only the Baire property of $P$ itself. It does
not quantify over the Borel complexity of every definable relation.

\subsection{Conventions of source 10 \src{10}}\label{pma:br:s10:sec:conventions}


Throughout the main development, an \emph{ordered ring} is a nonzero
commutative unital ring $A$ with a translation-invariant total order such
that $x,y>0$ implies $xy>0$. This is the strict ordered-domain convention.
It implies cancellation of positive factors in inequalities. We do not
use the weaker convention allowing positive zero divisors. The
noncommutative extension is recorded in \cref{pma:br:rem:noncomm}.

Write $\std n=n1_A$ for an ordinary integer represented in $A$.
An ordered ring is \emph{discretely ordered} when $1_A$ is its least
positive element. This is an algebraic property, not a statement about
the topology. The standard examples and the connection to weak
arithmetic are discussed in \cite{s12:Mohsenipour}. All uses of induction
on an ordinary integer in this paper are external finite mathematical
arguments; no first-order induction axiom inside $A$ is assumed.

The topology $\tau$ is a topology on the additive group: addition and
negation are continuous. Unless stated separately, multiplication is
not a topological operation. The topology need not agree with the order
topology. We write
\[
 P=\{x\in A:x>0\},\qquad |x|=\max(x,-x).
\]
The set $P$ \emph{has the Baire property} if it differs from an open set
by a meager set. This condition on the positive cone is exactly the
regularity used. In particular, a Borel positive cone suffices. We do not
silently replace it by a stronger hereditary condition on every closed
subspace, nor do we need such a condition.

A space is \emph{Baire} when each countable intersection of open dense
sets is dense. In a Baire space, no nonempty open set is meager. Open
subspaces of a Baire space are Baire. A Polish space is separable and
completely metrizable, so it is Baire and ccc. For the latter fact,
a countable dense set meets each nonempty member of a disjoint open
family at a different point.

All structures in the theorems are sets, and all arguments take place
in ZFC. Quotients such as $A/H$ are quotients of \emph{additive groups},
unless explicitly specified otherwise. No ideal property is presumed.
When $\No$ or $\Oz$ appears, we apply the result only to specified
set-sized subrings or to a fixed universe-bounded formal model.
There is no Polish topology on a proper class in the sense used here.

\section{From category to an order-bounded neighborhood}
\label{pma:br:sec:category}

The following elementary form of the Pettis lemma is the only category
input beyond the definition of a Baire space. We include the proof to
make the later dependency boundary explicit \cite{s12:Pettis}.

\begin{lemma}[Pettis difference lemma]
\label{pma:br:lem:pettis}
Let $G$ be a Baire topological abelian group. If $A\subseteq G$ has the
Baire property and is nonmeager, then $A-A$ contains an open neighborhood
of $0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
There is a nonempty open set $U$ on which $A$ is comeager. For any
$h\in U-U$, the intersection $U\cap(h+U)$ is nonempty and open. Both
$A$ and $h+A$ are comeager in that intersection. Since a nonempty open
subspace of a Baire space is Baire, they meet there. Thus
$h=x-y$ for some $x,y\in A$. We have proved
\[
 U-U\subseteq A-A.
\]
The set $U-U$ is open and contains $0$.
\end{proof}

Pettis alone is not enough: differences of an arbitrary positive set need
not be order-bounded. A reflection supplies the missing bounded set.

\begin{lemma}[Bounded-neighborhood lemma]
\label{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}\label{pma:br:lem:localbound}
Let $G$ be a nontrivial linearly ordered abelian group with a Hausdorff
Baire group topology. If its strict positive cone $P$ has the Baire
property, then there are $a>0$ and an open neighborhood $W$ of $0$ such
that
\begin{equation}
 0\in W\subseteq(-a,a).
 \label{pma:br:eq:bounded-neighborhood}
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If the topology is discrete, take $W=\{0\}$ and any $a>0$.
Suppose it is nondiscrete. A Hausdorff topological group with an isolated
point is discrete, so $\{0\}$ is closed with empty interior and hence
nowhere dense. Because
\[
 G=P\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{0\}\mathbin{\dot\cup}(-P)
\]
and inversion is a homeomorphism, $P$ cannot be meager: otherwise $G$
would be meager in itself, contrary to the Baire assumption.

Choose a nonempty open $U$ in which $P$ is comeager, and choose
$u\in U\cap P$. Reflection $x\mapsto2u-x$ is a homeomorphism. Therefore
$2u-P$ is comeager in $2u-U$. The open set
\[
 V=U\cap(2u-U)
\]
contains $u$. On $V$, both $P$ and $2u-P$ are comeager. Hence
\[
 A=P\cap(2u-P)=(0,2u)
\]
is nonmeager and has the Baire property. By \cref{pma:br:lem:pettis}, there is an
open neighborhood $W$ of $0$ with $W\subseteq A-A$. If $x,y\in A$, then
$-2u<x-y<2u$. Thus $W\subseteq(-2u,2u)$, and $a=2u$ works.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood} is source~09's
\cref{pma:ser:lem:bound}, stated there for Polish groups and proved by the same
reflection-and-Pettis argument; \cref{pma:br:lem:pettis} is the Baire-group
form of \cref{pma:ser:lem:pettis}. Source~12 states both for Hausdorff Baire
groups and does not cite source~09, which it had not seen. Source~10 states the
lemma as its Lemma~4.2 (\texttt{pma:br:lem:localbound} is a second label of
\cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}), credits the Polish version to
source~09, and proves it without Pettis's lemma, as follows.
\label{pma:br:s10:sec:category}

The category mechanism is elementary and is related to the usual
Pettis sumset argument; \cite{Chen} discusses Pettis's theorem and its
connections with automatic continuity. We supply the full argument
because its hypotheses are central to the result. The Polish version
of the local-bound lemma was already isolated in \cite{s10:Hahn}.

\begin{lemma}[Comeager semigroups have interior \src{10}]\label{pma:br:lem:sumset}
Let $G$ be a Baire topological group, written additively and assumed
abelian here. Suppose a set $P$ is comeager in a nonempty open set $O$
and satisfies $P+P\subseteq P$. Then $O+O\subseteq P$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take $z\in O+O$. The set $W=O\cap(z-O)$ is nonempty and open.
The sets $P$ and $z-P$ are both comeager in $W$: the second assertion
uses that reflection followed by translation is a homeomorphism.
Because $W$ is Baire, these two comeager subsets intersect. Choose
$x$ in their intersection. Then $x\in P$ and $z-x\in P$, hence
$z=x+(z-x)\in P+P\subseteq P$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof of \cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood} \src{10}]
Source~10 writes $c$ and $U$ for the bound $a$ and the neighbourhood $W$.

For a discrete group use $U=\{0\}$ and any $c>0$.
Otherwise every singleton is closed with empty interior and hence
nowhere dense. Inversion takes the positive cone $P$ to $-P$.
If $P$ were meager, the partition
$G=P\cup(-P)\cup\{0\}$ would make $G$ meager in itself, a contradiction.
Thus $P$ is nonmeager. Since it has the Baire property, it is comeager
in some nonempty open set $O$.

Choose $p\in O\cap P$. By \cref{pma:br:lem:sumset}, $O+O\subseteq P$.
The element $2p$ lies in this open set, so there is a symmetric
neighborhood $U$ of $0$ with $2p+U\subseteq O+O$.
For $u\in U$, both $u$ and $-u$ belong to $U$. Therefore
$2p+u>0$ and $2p-u>0$. These inequalities say
$-2p<u<2p$. Set $c=2p$.

\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The lemma applies to ordered \emph{groups}, not just rings. The order may
have many Archimedean levels, the group may be infinite-dimensional or
non-locally-compact, and its positive cone need not be open, closed, or
Borel. Inversion and translation are used; multiplication is absent.
\end{remark}

The proof needs one locally comeager part of the positive cone, then a
symmetric overlap. This is why there is no need to classify Borel orders
or to restrict them to real subspaces or compact subgroups.

\section{Algebraic packing and maximal cellularity}
\label{pma:br:sec:packing}

\begin{lemma}[Arithmetic packing]
\label{pma:br:lem:packing}
Let $R$ be a discretely ordered ring with an additive-group topology.
Suppose that an open neighborhood $W$ of $0$ satisfies
$W\subseteq(-a,a)$ for some $a>0$. Set $b=2a+1$. Then
\begin{equation}
 \{br+W:r\in R\}
 \label{pma:br:eq:packing-family}
\end{equation}
is a family of $|R|$ pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every translate is open and nonempty. Suppose $r\ne s$. By discrete
order, $|r-s|\geq1$, and therefore
\begin{equation}
 |b(r-s)|=b|r-s|\geq b=2a+1>2a.
 \label{pma:br:eq:large-separation}
\end{equation}
On the other hand, $W-W\subseteq(-2a,2a)$. If $br+w_1=bs+w_2$ for
some $w_1,w_2\in W$, then $b(r-s)=w_2-w_1\in W-W$, contradicting
\eqref{pma:br:eq:large-separation}. Thus the translates are pairwise disjoint.
Since they are nonempty, distinct indices give distinct sets.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why no scalar continuity is hidden]
It is not asserted that $bW$ is open, that $r\mapsto br$ is continuous,
or that its graph is measurable. The open sets are \emph{translates of
one fixed open set} $W$. The scalars merely choose their centers.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Maximal cellularity and density]
\label{pma:br:thm:main}
Let $R$ be a discretely ordered ring with a Hausdorff Baire additive-group
topology. If $P=\{r:r>0\}$ has the Baire property, then there is a family
of $|R|$ pairwise disjoint nonempty open subsets of $R$. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{c(R)=d(R)=|R|.}
 \label{pma:br:eq:main}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Use \cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood} to obtain $W\subseteq(-a,a)$, and
apply \cref{pma:br:lem:packing}. This proves $|R|\leq c(R)$. Combine this with
\eqref{pma:br:eq:cardinal-basic}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Ccc rigidity]
\label{pma:br:cor:ccc}\label{pma:br:s10:thm:main}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{pma:br:thm:main}, if the topology satisfies ccc,
then $R$ is countable and the topology is discrete.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The explicit family in \cref{pma:br:lem:packing} and ccc imply countability.
A countable Hausdorff nondiscrete topological group has every singleton
nowhere dense, so it is meager in itself. This contradicts the Baire
assumption. Hence the group is discrete.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Polish rigidity; answer to the earlier question]
\label{pma:br:cor:polish}
Every discretely ordered ring with a Polish additive-group topology and
a positive cone having the Baire property is countable and discrete.
In particular, an uncountable discretely ordered ring cannot have a
Polish additive-group topology with Borel order, regardless of the
regularity of multiplication.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A Polish space is Baire and separable; separability implies ccc.
Borel sets have the Baire property. Apply \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc}.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} is source~10's main theorem, its
Theorem~5.1 (\texttt{pma:br:s10:thm:main}); source~10's proof, through the
principal-hull quotient embedding, is printed in \cref{pma:br:sec:main}.
With \cref{pma:br:cor:polish} it answers \cref{pma:lc:q:removelc} of
\cref{pma:part:lc} negatively. Source~10 states the Polish case as an exact
criterion:

\begin{corollary}[Exact Polish presentation criterion \src{10}]\label{pma:br:s10:cor:polish}
A discretely ordered ring admits a Polish additive-group topology with
a Baire-property positive cone if and only if its underlying set is
countable. Every such topology is discrete.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Polish spaces are Baire, Hausdorff, and ccc, so necessity and uniqueness
of the possible topology follow from \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc}. Conversely, a
countable ring with the discrete topology is a Polish topological ring,
and all subsets, in particular its positive cone, are Borel.
\end{proof}

Here ``uniqueness'' refers to the topology for a fixed underlying ring:
it must be the discrete topology. The theorem does not classify
countable discretely ordered rings up to isomorphism. There are many
nonstandard ones, including $\Z[X]$ ordered with $X$ positive infinite.


\begin{remark}[Countable does not mean standard]
A countable nonstandard discretely ordered ring can carry the discrete
Polish topology. The corollary does not assert that the ring is $\Z$;
it asserts that its cardinality is countable and its given Baire ccc
group topology is discrete.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[A separable category dichotomy]
\label{pma:br:cor:dichotomy}
Let a discretely ordered ring have a separable Hausdorff additive-group
topology and a positive cone with the Baire property. Then either it is
countable discrete, or it is meager in itself.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If the topology is Baire, use \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc}. Otherwise some nonempty
open $U$ is meager in the group. Let $D$ be countable and dense. For each
$x$, the nonempty open set $x-U$ meets $D$, so $x\in D+U$. Thus
$G=\bigcup_{d\in D}(d+U)$ is a countable union of meager sets.
\end{proof}

The same packing proof works for noncommutative discretely ordered
unital rings, provided the order axioms make products of positives
positive: left multiplication by $b>0$ is order-preserving and satisfies
$|bx|=b|x|$. Commutativity of multiplication is not essential to
\cref{pma:br:thm:main}.

\begin{remark}[Noncommutative extension \src{10}]\label{pma:br:rem:noncomm}
The main proof also applies to an associative unital ring with a total
translation-invariant order and strictly positive products, without
commutativity. Use left multiplication $x\mapsto ax$. For $a>0$,
$|ax|=a|x|$, positive left multiplication reflects inequalities, and
ordinary integer multiples of $1$ commute with $a$. These are all the
multiplicative facts used in the kernel computation. The quotient maps
remain homomorphisms of the abelian additive groups. We keep the
commutative convention elsewhere to match the arithmetic and omnific
applications.
\end{remark}

\section{Principal convex subgroups and a second obstruction}
\label{pma:br:sec:convex}

There is a useful purely algebraic form of the argument. It reveals why
an open convex subgroup cannot rescue an uncountable ring presentation.

For an ordered abelian group $G$ and $a>0$, define the principal convex
subgroup
\begin{equation}
 H_a=\{x\in G:\text{for some ordinary }n\geq1,\ |x|\leq na\}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:Ha}
\end{equation}
It is a subgroup by the triangle inequality, and it is convex by
construction. The indexing quantifier is external and ranges over the
ordinary natural numbers.

\begin{proposition}[An open principal convex subgroup]
\label{pma:br:prop:open-convex}\label{pma:br:prop:openhull}
Every nontrivial ordered Hausdorff Baire topological abelian group whose
positive cone has the Baire property has an open subgroup $H_a$ of the
form \eqref{pma:br:eq:Ha}. If the topology is ccc, $G/H_a$ is countable.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose $W\subseteq(-a,a)$ using \cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}. Then
$W\subseteq H_a$. A subgroup containing a neighborhood of the identity
is open, because it is the union of its translates of that neighborhood.
Its cosets are disjoint nonempty open sets, so ccc makes the coset space
countable.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} Source~10 states \cref{pma:br:prop:open-convex} for
ordered rings, with $a\geq1$ so that $\FinA(A)\subseteq H_a$ (its
Proposition~4.3, \texttt{pma:br:prop:openhull}), and adds that the open
subgroup $H_a$ is also closed, its complement being a union of open cosets.
Its proof is the one above. Source~10 continues \src{10}:

It is important that $H_a$, rather than the interval $[-a,a]$, is the
subgroup used in the proof. The interval need not be a subgroup.
Conversely, $H_a$ need not be bounded by one fixed element of $A$.
Only membership in some ordinary multiple of $[-a,a]$ is needed.


\begin{theorem}[Every principal convex quotient is as large as the ring]
\label{pma:br:thm:convex-index}
Let $R\ne\Z$ be a discretely ordered ring. For every $a>0$,
\begin{equation}
 [R:H_a]=|R|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:convex-index}
\end{equation}
More explicitly, choose $c>n$ for every ordinary natural number $n$, and
put $b=(a+1)c$. The map
\begin{equation}
 R\longrightarrow R/H_a,\qquad r\longmapsto br+H_a
 \label{pma:br:eq:quotient-injection}
\end{equation}
is injective.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Such a $c$ exists by \cref{pma:br:lem:convex-integers}. For every ordinary
$n\geq1$,
\[
 b=(a+1)c>(a+1)n>an.
\]
If $r\ne s$, then $|r-s|\geq1$, so $|b(r-s)|\geq b>na$ for every
ordinary $n$. Therefore $b(r-s)\notin H_a$, proving injectivity in
\eqref{pma:br:eq:quotient-injection}. The quotient has at most $|R|$ elements,
so its cardinality is exactly $|R|$.
\end{proof}

No ideal is being asserted here. $H_a$ is an additive convex subgroup;
$R/H_a$ is used only as an additive quotient. Confusing a convex subgroup
with a ring ideal would obscure the purpose of the construction.

Combining \cref{pma:br:prop:open-convex,pma:br:thm:convex-index} gives another proof
of the countability part of \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} for $R\ne\Z$. This route uses
an infinite element to make a quotient injection. By contrast, the
packing proof uses only the finite expression $2a+1$, works uniformly
for $R=\Z$, and directly attains the full cellularity bound. It is the
preferred proof of the main theorem.

\begin{example}[Polynomial interpretation]
In $\Z+t\Q[t]$, ordered by the leading coefficient with $t$ infinite,
$H_{t^d}$ consists exactly of polynomials of degree at most $d$.
Multiplication by $t^{d+1}$ sends every nonzero difference outside that
subgroup. Thus a principal convex quotient retains at least as much
cardinality as the entire ring, despite discarding a complete finite
range of growth degrees.
\end{example}

For real rather than rational coefficients, the same description holds:
each individual leading coefficient is bounded by an ordinary integer.
This observation will also be useful in the sharpness constructions.

\subsection{The principal-hull quotient embedding \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:algebra}

\subsubsection{The ordinary-integer-bounded part}

\begin{definition}[\src{10}]
For an ordered ring $A$, define
\begin{equation}
 F=\FinA(A)=\{x\in A:\exists n\in\N\ (|x|\le\std n)\}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:finitepart}
\end{equation}
For $a>0$, define its principal convex additive hull by
\begin{equation}
 H_a=\{x\in A:\exists n\in\N\ (|x|\le n a)\}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:principal}
\end{equation}
The quantifiers over $\N$ in these definitions are external ordinary
quantifiers, not quantifiers over a nonstandard arithmetic model.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[\src{10}]\label{pma:br:lem:hulls}
The set $F$ is a convex additive subgroup and a unital subring of $A$.
For every $a>0$, $H_a$ is a convex additive subgroup, the smallest such
subgroup containing $a$. If $a\ge1$, then $F\subseteq H_a$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The triangle inequality gives closure under addition, and absolute value
gives closure under negation. Bounds by ordinary integers multiply, so
$|x|\le\std n$ and $|y|\le\std m$ imply $|xy|\le\std{nm}$.
Thus $F$ is a subring containing $1$. If $|z|\le |x|$ and $x$ belongs to
either hull, the same bound puts $z$ in that hull; this proves convexity.
Any convex additive subgroup containing $a$ contains all $na$ and all
intervals $[-na,na]$, hence contains $H_a$. Finally,
$\std n\le na$ when $a\ge1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Finite elements in a discretely ordered ring \src{10}]
\label{pma:br:lem:std}
If $A$ is discretely ordered, then $\FinA(A)=\Z1_A$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For each ordinary $n\ge0$, we prove externally that
$[0,\std n]=\{\std0,\ldots,\std n\}$. At $n=0$ this is immediate.
If $0<x\le\std{n+1}$, discreteness gives $x\ge1$, and consequently
$0\le x-1\le\std n$. Apply the induction hypothesis. Negating deals
with negative finite elements. Conversely, every ordinary integer is
bounded by its ordinary absolute value.
\end{proof}

The loss of finiteness in $F$ is precisely what permits uncountable
ordered fields such as $\R$ to escape the arithmetic obstruction. The
next theorem separates this algebraic issue from topology entirely.

\subsubsection{A quotient embedding with exactly known kernel}

\begin{theorem}[Principal-hull amplification \src{10}]\label{pma:br:thm:principal}
Let $A$ be an ordered ring and $a>0$. The additive homomorphism
\begin{equation}
 T_a:A\longrightarrow A/H_a,\qquad T_a(x)=ax+H_a
 \label{pma:br:eq:T}
\end{equation}
has kernel exactly $\FinA(A)$. It induces an ordered additive embedding
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_a:A/\FinA(A)\hookrightarrow A/H_a,
 \qquad x+\FinA(A)\longmapsto ax+H_a.
 \label{pma:br:eq:Phi}
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
 |A/\FinA(A)|\le |A/H_a|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:quotientbound}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Distributivity makes $T_a$ additive. Since $a>0$, absolute values and
positive cancellation give the equivalences
\begin{align*}
 T_a(x)=0
 &\iff ax\in H_a\\
 &\iff \exists n\in\N\ \bigl(|ax|\le na\bigr)\\
 &\iff \exists n\in\N\ \bigl(a|x|\le a\std n\bigr)\\
 &\iff \exists n\in\N\ \bigl(|x|\le\std n\bigr)\\
 &\iff x\in\FinA(A).
\end{align*}
The induced additive map is therefore well defined and injective.

Both quotient orders are defined because their subgroups are convex.
A positive nonzero class $x+\FinA(A)$ has a representative satisfying
$x>\std n$ for every ordinary $n$. Hence $ax>na$ for every $n$.
Every member of $H_a$ is at most some $na$, so $ax+H_a$ is positive
and nonzero. Applying the same reasoning to $-x$ proves that signs,
and hence all comparisons of distinct classes, are preserved.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why this is not a continuity argument \src{10}]
The map $T_a$ is used only as a homomorphism of abstract additive groups.
It may be discontinuous or nonmeasurable. The quotient $A/H_a$ need not
be a ring, and multiplication by $a$ need not descend to any endomorphism
of $A/H_a$. What descends is exactly the map from $A/\FinA(A)$ specified
in \eqref{pma:br:eq:Phi}. No other descent is asserted.
\end{remark}

\begin{corollary}[\src{10}]\label{pma:br:cor:unitwhole}
If an ordered ring has an additive order unit $a>0$, so that $H_a=A$,
then $A=\FinA(A)$. A discretely ordered ring with an additive order unit
is therefore just its standard integer subring.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The target in \eqref{pma:br:eq:Phi} is zero, so the source is zero. Apply
\cref{pma:br:lem:std} in the discrete case.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The change from the earlier amplification theorem \src{10}]
The order-unit theorem in \cite{s10:Local} uses a subgroup avoiding nonzero
ordinary integers in order to obtain an injective map \emph{before}
quotienting its domain. Here there is no reason to avoid those integers.
They are precisely the kernel, and their countability is harmless.
Taking the principal convex hull makes an order unit available without
any local compactness, vector structure, or divisibility assumption.
\end{remark}

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:lem:std} is the first assertion of
\cref{pma:br:lem:convex-integers} and of source~08's \cref{pma:lc:lem:finite}.
\Cref{pma:br:thm:principal} generalizes part~(1) of source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:thm:amplification}: it needs neither an integer-free subgroup nor
an order unit, and it holds in every ordered ring.

\subsection{Arithmetic rigidity without local compactness \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:main}

Source~10's main theorem is \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc}; its proof is a second
proof of that corollary.
\begin{proof}[Second proof of \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} \src{10}]

By \cref{pma:br:prop:open-convex}, some principal convex subgroup $H_a$ is open.
Its cosets are pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets, so ccc implies that
$A/H_a$ is countable. By \cref{pma:br:thm:principal,pma:br:lem:std}, there is an injection
\[
 A/\Z1_A\hookrightarrow A/H_a.
\]
Thus $A/\Z1_A$ is countable. Each coset of $\Z1_A$ is countable,
so $A$ is countable.

A countable Hausdorff Baire group must be discrete. Otherwise it has
no isolated point, since any isolated point can be translated to $0$
and then to every other point. Every singleton would consequently be
nowhere dense, and their countable union would make $A$ meager in
itself. This contradicts the Baire hypothesis.

\end{proof}

\subsection{The cardinal theorem for general ordered rings \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:cardinal}

The argument has a useful form before discreteness of the order is
imposed. It measures the topological size needed to accommodate the
quotient by ordinary-integer-bounded elements.

For an infinite space $X$, let $\cell(X)$ be the supremum of the
cardinalities of disjoint nonempty open families, $\dens(X)$ the least
cardinality of a dense subset, and $\ext(X)$ the supremum of the
cardinalities of closed discrete subsets. We use the usual infinite-
cardinal convention for the Lindel\"of degree $L(X)$: every open cover
has a subcover of size at most $L(X)$.

\begin{theorem}[Relative cardinal obstruction \src{10}]\label{pma:br:thm:relative}
Let $A$ be an ordered ring with a Hausdorff additive-group topology.
Suppose some neighborhood of $0$ is order bounded. Then there is an
open convex additive subgroup $H$ such that
\begin{equation}
 A/\FinA(A)\hookrightarrow A/H
 \label{pma:br:eq:relativeembedding}
\end{equation}
is an ordered additive embedding. In particular,
\begin{equation}
 |A/\FinA(A)|\le |A/H|\le\cell(A)\le\dens(A).
 \label{pma:br:eq:relativecard}
\end{equation}
Moreover, $A$ has a closed discrete subset of cardinality $|A/H|$.
The order-bounded-neighborhood hypothesis follows from a Baire group
topology and a Baire-property positive cone.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Choose $a\ge1$ so that the neighborhood lies in $[-a,a]$, and put
$H=H_a$. The proof of \cref{pma:br:prop:open-convex} shows that $H$ is open
without needing Baire once the neighborhood bound is given.
Apply \cref{pma:br:thm:principal}. The cosets form a disjoint nonempty open
family, proving the middle bound. A dense set must meet every member
of any such family, proving the last bound.

Choose one representative from each coset and call the resulting set
$T$. Each point of $T$ is isolated in $T$ by its coset. To see that
$T$ is closed, take $x\notin T$. Its coset contains exactly one selected
