point $t$. Since the group is Hausdorff, the coset with $t$ removed is
an open neighborhood of $x$ disjoint from $T$. Thus $T$ is closed
and discrete, and $|T|=|A/H|$. The last sentence is
\cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cardinality of the finite part \src{10}]\label{pma:br:cor:finitecard}
For a Hausdorff Baire ccc additive presentation of an ordered ring with
a Baire-property positive cone,
\begin{equation}
 |A|=|\FinA(A)|=\max\bigl(\aleph_0,|[0,1]_A|\bigr).
 \label{pma:br:eq:finitecard}
\end{equation}
Consequently a countable unit interval forces a countable, discrete
additive group.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{pma:br:thm:relative}, $A/\FinA(A)$ is countable. The group $\FinA(A)$
contains $\Z1$ and is infinite. A countable union of its cosets has the
same cardinality as $\FinA(A)$, giving the first equality.

Every ordinarily bounded element lies in an ordinary integer translate
of $[0,1]$. Indeed, inside a fixed finite interval $[-\std n,\std n]$,
one can choose the largest ordinary integer $k$ not exceeding that
element, using only a finite search. Hence
\[
 \FinA(A)=\bigcup_{k\in\Z}\bigl(\std k+[0,1]_A\bigr).
\]
This proves the upper bound for the second equality; the reverse
bound follows from the inclusions of $[0,1]$ and $\Z1$ in $\FinA(A)$.
A countable Hausdorff Baire group is discrete as in \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc}.
\end{proof}

This relative formulation does not exclude the usual real field:
its finite part is all of $\R$, and its unit interval already has its
full cardinality. Nor does it exclude every non-Archimedean ordered
field. Its conclusion is an exact restriction on how much cardinality
can occur beyond the finite part in a ccc presentation.

\begin{theorem}[Maximal topological size \src{10}]\label{pma:br:thm:maximal}
Let $A$ be an uncountable discretely ordered ring equipped with a
Hausdorff Baire additive-group topology and a Baire-property positive
cone. Then some open convex additive subgroup $H$ has
\begin{equation}
 |A/H|=|A|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:maxindex}
\end{equation}
There is a closed discrete subset of $A$ of size $|A|$, and
\begin{equation}
 \cell(A)=\dens(A)=\ext(A)=L(A)=|A|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:maximal}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Every coset of $\Z1$ is countable. Since $A$ is uncountable,
cardinal arithmetic gives $|A/\Z1|=|A|$.
By \cref{pma:br:thm:relative}, an open $H$ satisfies
$|A|\le|A/H|\le|A|$, proving \eqref{pma:br:eq:maxindex} and the existence
of the closed discrete transversal.

The cosets witness $\cell(A)\ge|A|$, and no disjoint family can have
more members than there are points. A dense set must meet every coset,
so $\dens(A)=|A|$. The closed discrete transversal gives the equality
for extent. Finally, the coset cover has no proper subcover and has
$|A|$ members, while any open cover of a space of size $|A|$ has a
subcover of size at most $|A|$, by choosing one covering set per point.
This proves the equality for $L(A)$.
\end{proof}

Thus a nonseparable counterexample cannot be merely a little larger
than a Polish space in its supply of disjoint open sets. It must have
as many disjoint open cosets, and as many points in one closed discrete
set, as it has elements altogether. The explicit locally compact
example in \cref{pma:br:subsec:nonsep-example} attains this conclusion.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:thm:maximal} and source~12's
\cref{pma:br:thm:main} overlap: source~12 proves $c(R)=d(R)=|R|$ for every
discretely ordered ring with a Hausdorff Baire topology and a Baire-property
cone, with no uncountability assumption; source~10 adds, for uncountable rings,
an open convex subgroup of full index, a closed discrete set of full size, and
the equalities for extent and Lindel\"of degree. Source~10's $\cell$ and
$\dens$ are source~12's $c$ and $d$.

\subsection{A complementary bounded-subgroup amplification \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:bounded}

The principal-hull theorem is the shortest route to the main result.
A different amplification statement retains information about multiple
independent additive copies and is useful for algebraic certificates.
Here a subgroup is bounded by one element, which is stronger than
having an order unit.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded-subgroup amplification \src{10}]\label{pma:br:thm:bounded}
Let $A$ be a discretely ordered ring, and let $H\le(A,+)$ satisfy
$|h|\le c$ for every $h\in H$, where $c\ge0$.
If $b>c$, then $bH\cap H=\{0\}$ and the additive map
\[
 H\longrightarrow A/H,\qquad h\longmapsto bh+H
\]
is injective. With $a=c+2$, the finite-sum map
\begin{equation}
 \Psi:\bigoplus_{j\ge0}H\longrightarrow A,
 \qquad (h_j)\longmapsto\sum_{j\ge0}a^j h_j
 \label{pma:br:eq:boundedpoly}
\end{equation}
is an ordered additive embedding when the source is ordered by the
sign of its highest-index nonzero coordinate. Its restriction to the
positive-index summands remains injective after quotienting by $H$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $h\ne0$, then $|h|\ge1$, so $|bh|=b|h|\ge b>c$.
Thus $bh\notin H$. This proves the first assertion and the coset
injection.

For the second, take a nonzero finite tuple and let $k$ be the largest
index with $h_k\ne0$. If $k=0$, the conclusion is immediate. For $k>0$,
the magnitude of its lower terms is at most
\[
 B=c\sum_{j<k}a^j.
\]
The geometric-sum identity and $a-1=c+1$ give
\[
 (a-1)B=c(a^k-1)<(a-1)a^k.
\]
Indeed, subtracting the middle expression from the right gives
$a^k+c>0$. Cancelling $a-1>0$ yields $B<a^k$.
Since $|h_k|\ge1$, the leading term has magnitude
$a^k|h_k|\ge a^k>B$. The sum is therefore nonzero and has the sign
of $h_k$. Distributivity gives additivity; applying the sign conclusion
to differences gives the order embedding.

If a positive-index sum belongs to $H$, subtract that element as the
zeroth coefficient in \eqref{pma:br:eq:boundedpoly}. Injectivity of $\Psi$
forces every coefficient to vanish.
\end{proof}

No divisibility, convexity, ideal property, or integer-disjointness is
assumed of $H$. The source is an additive direct sum, not a polynomial
ring with coefficient ring $H$. Its ordered embedding gives more
structure than a cardinal inequality, although countable direct sums
do not increase an infinite cardinal.

\subsubsection{Two initial approaches become corollaries}

A non-Archimedean topological group has a basis at the identity of open
subgroups; this terminology is standard in Polish group theory
\cite{s10:KechrisNA}. If the additive group in \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} is
non-Archimedean, a bounded neighborhood contains an open bounded subgroup
$H$. Then \cref{pma:br:thm:bounded} injects $H$ into the countable coset
space $A/H$, yielding countability. This is a valid proof in that case,
but the principal-hull argument makes the non-Archimedean assumption
unnecessary.

Likewise, an open real topological vector subgroup can be treated by
order-unit amplification. If $U\subseteq[-u,u]$ is a neighborhood in
that subgroup, then $v/n\to0$ implies $|v|\le nu$ for some ordinary
$n$, making $u$ an order unit. Divisibility makes each nonzero member
larger in magnitude than every ordinary integer. Multiplication by $u$
then injects the subgroup into its additive quotient, as in
\cite{s10:Local}. This works in infinite as well as finite dimension.
Again, \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} is stronger and needs neither vector structure
nor an open subgroup of a prescribed kind.

These two arguments help explain the discovery path, but they should
not be mistaken for the endpoint. Arbitrary Polish additive groups,
including mixed or otherwise unclassified ones, are covered by the
principal-hull proof.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:thm:bounded} is a variant of parts~(2)
and~(3) of source~08's \cref{pma:lc:thm:amplification}, with a bound by one
element in place of an integer-free subgroup with an order unit.

\section{Arbitrary self-embeddings have bounded unit images}
\label{pma:br:sec:embeddings}

The topological obstruction has an interpretation that does not mention
multiplication. It restricts purely algebraic ordered self-embeddings.

Let $G$ be an ordered abelian group with a least positive element $e$.
Write $\Emb(G)$ for the set of injective additive maps $f:G\to G$ that
preserve strict order. The maps are not required to preserve $e$, nor to
be continuous or measurable. Define the unit-image spectrum
\[
 \mathcal U(G)=\{f(e):f\in\Emb(G)\}.
\]
This terminology refers only to a distinguished least positive element;
$G$ need not be a ring.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded unit-image spectrum]
\label{pma:br:thm:unit-spectrum}
Suppose $G$ is uncountable and has a Hausdorff Baire ccc group topology,
an invariant total order, and a positive cone with the Baire property.
If $e$ is its least positive element, then $\mathcal U(G)$ is bounded
above in $G$. In fact, if $W\subseteq(-a,a)$ is the neighborhood from
\cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}, then
\begin{equation}
 f(e)\leq2a\qquad\text{for every } f\in\Emb(G).
 \label{pma:br:eq:embedding-bound}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose $f(e)>2a$. For distinct $x,y\in G$, discreteness gives
$|x-y|\geq e$. Additivity and order preservation imply
\[
 |f(x)-f(y)|=f(|x-y|)\geq f(e)>2a.
\]
Consequently the sets $f(x)+W$, indexed by all $x\in G$, are pairwise
disjoint by the same difference argument as in \cref{pma:br:lem:packing}.
This contradicts ccc because $G$ is uncountable.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Cofinal unit movement is impossible]
\label{pma:br:cor:cofinal-unit}
An uncountable discretely ordered abelian group with a family of ordered
additive self-embeddings whose values at the least positive element are
cofinal cannot have a Hausdorff Baire ccc group topology with a
Baire-property positive cone.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A cofinal subset cannot be bounded above in a nontrivial ordered group,
since adding a positive element always produces a larger element.
Apply \cref{pma:br:thm:unit-spectrum}.
\end{proof}

For a discretely ordered ring, the maps $x\mapsto bx$ for $b>0$ are
ordered additive embeddings, and their values at $1$ range over the
entire positive cone. The main ccc obstruction is therefore a special
case of this cofinal-unit-movement obstruction. The formulation is useful
for other algebraic structures equipped with an expansive family of
endomorphisms, even before a ring structure is supplied.

\subsection{A spectrum can be infinite and still bounded}

Consider
\begin{equation}
 G_\R=\R\lex \Z,
 \qquad e=(0,1),
 \label{pma:br:eq:real-lex}
\end{equation}
with the product topology $\R_{\rm usual}\times\Z_{\rm discrete}$ and
lexicographic order in which the real coordinate is more significant.
This is an uncountable Polish ordered group with least positive element
$e$. Its cone is
\[
 (\R_{>0}\times\Z)\ \cup\ (\{0\}\times\Z_{>0}),
\]
a $\Dtwo$ set.

For each ordinary $k\geq1$, the map $(r,n)\mapsto(r,kn)$ is an ordered
additive embedding. Thus $\mathcal U(G_\R)$ is infinite, although all
these images are less than $(1,0)$.
In fact these are exactly the possible images of $e$.
To see this, an additive map from the divisible group $\R$ to $\Z$ is
zero. Therefore an ordered additive embedding restricts on
$\R\times\{0\}$ to $r\mapsto(\alpha(r),0)$, where $\alpha$ is an
increasing additive injection. It follows that $\alpha(r)=\lambda r$
for some $\lambda>0$: first prove the identity on rationals, then squeeze
an arbitrary real between rationals. Write $f(e)=(b,k)$. Positivity
excludes $b<0$. If $b>0$, choose $r>0$ with $\lambda r<b$; then
$(r,0)>e$ but $f(r,0)<f(e)$, a contradiction. Thus $b=0$ and $k\geq1$.
Hence
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U(G_\R)=\{(0,k):k\in\Z_{>0}\}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:exact-spectrum}
\end{equation}
This illustrates why \cref{pma:br:thm:unit-spectrum} gives an \emph{order bound},
not a finite bound on the number of embeddings or possible unit images.

\subsection{All four clauses of the bounded spectrum \src{10}}\label{pma:br:s10:sec:embeddings}

Source~10 proves \cref{pma:br:thm:unit-spectrum} as clause~(3) of the
following theorem; clauses~(1), (2) and~(4) are additional. Its own section
reads \src{10}:

The proof uses less than a ring multiplication. This gives an independent
result about ordered additive groups and explains which part of
multiplication is incompatible with the topology.

\begin{definition}[\src{10}]
For a discretely ordered abelian group $(G,+,<,e)$ with least positive
$e$, define the \emph{unit-image spectrum}
\[
 \mathcal U(G)=\{f(e): f:G\longrightarrow G
      \text{ is an additive order embedding}\}.
\]
No continuity or measurability is required of $f$.
For $a>0$, define $H_a=\{x:|x|\le na\text{ for some }n\in\N\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded unit-image spectrum \src{10}]\label{pma:br:thm:spectrum}
Let $G$ be an uncountable discretely ordered abelian group with a
Hausdorff Baire ccc group topology and a Baire-property positive cone.
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $f:G\to G$ is an additive order embedding and $a=f(e)$,
      there is an ordered additive embedding $G/\Z e\hookrightarrow G/H_a$.
\item For every $a\in\mathcal U(G)$, the subgroup $H_a$ is not open.
\item There is $b>0$ such that $0<a<b$ for every
      $a\in\mathcal U(G)$.
\item Each subgroup $H_a$ with $a\in\mathcal U(G)$ is meager.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For the first assertion use $x\mapsto f(x)+H_a$.
Additivity and order reflection imply
\[
 |f(x)|\le na
 \iff f(|x|)\le f(ne)
 \iff |x|\le ne.
\]
The ordinarily bounded elements of a discretely ordered abelian group
are exactly $\Z e$, by the finite-interval proof of \cref{pma:br:lem:std},
which uses no multiplication. The kernel is therefore $\Z e$.
The sign proof for the quotient is the same as in \cref{pma:br:thm:principal}.

If $H_a$ were open, ccc would make $G/H_a$ countable. The injection
would make $G/\Z e$, and then $G$, countable, contrary to hypothesis.
For the third assertion, the local-bound lemma provides $b>0$ with
$H_b$ open. If $a\ge b$, then $H_b\subseteq H_a$, so $H_a$ is open.
Thus no such $a$ can lie in the spectrum.

Finally, each interval $[-na,na]$ has the Baire property, since it is
formed from translates of the positive cone, their complements, and
singletons. Therefore $H_a$, their countable union, has the Baire
property. A subgroup with the Baire property that is nonmeager in a
Baire group is open: if it is comeager in an open set $O$, the usual
intersection argument shows that $O-O$ is contained in the subgroup.
This is an open neighborhood of zero. Since the second assertion
excludes openness, $H_a$ is meager.
\end{proof}

The final assertion concerns \emph{each} hull separately. It does not
say that the spectrum itself, or the union of all these hulls, is
meager. Such a union may have uncountably many terms.

Every positive scalar in an ordered ring gives an additive order
embedding by multiplication. Thus its unit-image spectrum contains all
positive elements. The bounded-spectrum theorem prohibits this in an
uncountable Baire ccc discrete ordered group, independently of any
compatibility among the individual embeddings. Associativity and the
existence of one binary multiplication are not needed for this reduct
obstruction.

This is also a useful self-embedding result for a set-sized integer-like
ordered group. A Polish presentation may allow many discontinuous
additive order embeddings, but they cannot send the least positive
element to arbitrarily large scales. It is not a theorem about field
self-embeddings of $\No$: those fix $1$, and $\No$ is not discretely
ordered in the first place.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:cor:cofinal-unit} contains source~15's
\cref{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction} of \cref{pma:part:lcc}: a
positive endomorphism $T$ with $T(e)>0$ is an ordered additive embedding, so
endomorphisms with $T_a(e)=a$ for every $a>0$ give cofinal unit images, and
Part~VI needs only a Baire-property cone and no regularity of the maps (note in
\cref{pma:lcc:sec:borel-multiplication-obstruction}). The exact
spectrum~\eqref{pma:br:eq:exact-spectrum} extends Part~I's
\cref{pma:pr:thm:realendos} (unital endomorphisms of $\MR$) to all ordered
self-embeddings of $G_\R=\R\lex\Z$, not necessarily unital.

\section{Ring expansions, positive semirings, and Presburger arithmetic}
\label{pma:br:sec:expansions}

\begin{corollary}[No ordered-ring expansion]
\label{pma:br:cor:ring-expansion}\label{pma:br:cor:noexp}
Let $G$ be an uncountable ordered abelian group with least positive
element $e$, a Hausdorff Baire ccc group topology, and a positive cone
having the Baire property. No multiplication on the set $G$ makes
$(G,+,\cdot,0,e,<)$ a discretely ordered unital ring.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Such a multiplication would satisfy the hypotheses of \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc},
contradicting uncountability. Equivalently, its positive left multipliers
would contradict \cref{pma:br:cor:cofinal-unit}.
\end{proof}


The multiplication is ruled out algebraically relative to the prescribed
addition, order, and unit. The statement is stronger than saying that a
particular candidate multiplication is not Borel.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 states this corollary for Polish topologies (its Corollary~5.3, \texttt{pma:br:cor:noexp}) and adds:

This excludes the existence of the multiplication itself, not merely
its continuity or Borel measurability. It is therefore stronger than a
regularity obstruction on the specified additive presentation. It does
not, however, remove the topological-group hypothesis or the Baire
condition on order.


\begin{theorem}[No positive-semiring expansion]
\label{pma:br:thm:semiring}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{pma:br:cor:ring-expansion}, let
$M=G_{\geq0}$. There is no associative unital semiring multiplication on
$M$ with its given addition, zero, and unit $e$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Suppose there were such a multiplication. Every $g\in G$ is a difference
of two elements of $M$, and addition on $M$ is cancellative. Extend the
multiplication to differences by
\begin{equation}
 (a-b)(c-d)=(ac+bd)-(ad+bc),\qquad a,b,c,d\in M.
 \label{pma:br:eq:groth-product}
\end{equation}
We verify that it is independent of representatives. If $a-b=a'-b'$,
then $a+b'=a'+b$ in $M$. Multiplying this identity on the right by
$c\in M$ and using distributivity gives
$ac+b'c=a'c+bc$, so $ac-bc=a'c-b'c$ in $G$. The same holds with $d$;
subtracting gives independence of the first difference. Left
distributivity proves independence of the second. Expanding finite
products proves associativity and both distributive laws on $G$; $e$
remains the unit. Thus this is a unital ring extension.

Products of nonnegative elements are nonnegative because they belong to
$M$. For strictly positive $x,y\in M$, the least-positive-element
property gives $x=e+u$ and $y=e+v$ with $u,v\in M$. Therefore
\[
 xy=e+u+v+uv\geq e>0.
\]
The extended ring has the original discrete order. This contradicts
\cref{pma:br:cor:ring-expansion}.
\end{proof}

This proof does not assume commutative semiring multiplication: the
formula and positivity argument still work, and the main packing theorem
also has the required noncommutative version. Additive cancellation is
available because $M$ is a cone in a group.

\subsection{Application to signed Presburger models}

A signed Presburger model is a model of the complete ordered additive
theory of the integers. In particular, it is an ordered abelian group
with a least positive element $1$ and the standard-integer
division-with-remainder laws. We use only the ordered-group and
least-positive-element properties in the obstruction; quantifier
elimination and induction are unnecessary.


\begin{corollary}\label{pma:br:cor:signed-presburger}
An uncountable signed Presburger model with a Polish additive-group
topology and a Borel positive cone has no compatible unital ordered-ring
expansion. Its nonnegative cone has no unital semiring expansion with
its prescribed addition and unit.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{pma:br:cor:ring-expansion,pma:br:thm:semiring}.
\end{proof}

The group $G_\R$ in \eqref{pma:br:eq:real-lex} is a concrete example of the
additive behavior that survives. For a fixed ordinary $m>0$, divide the
real coordinate by $m$ and use the ordinary residue of the integer
coordinate. This provides the familiar split signed Presburger example;
its positive counterpart was studied in the earlier report
\cite{s12:PriorPresburger}. The new general theorem explains the obstruction
to multiplication independently of its particular coordinate system.

\subsection{The group-completion boundary}
\label{pma:br:subsec:completion-boundary}

For an abstract cancellative commutative monoid, the algebraic
Grothendieck group always exists. Given a \emph{topology} on the monoid,
several additional questions arise: whether the difference quotient is
Hausdorff, whether addition and inversion are continuous, whether the
original cone embeds topologically, and whether the resulting group is
Baire and ccc. None is supplied by the purely algebraic construction
\eqref{pma:br:eq:groth-product}.

A useful conditional consequence is therefore precise. If a positive
arithmetic presentation admits an order-compatible embedding as the
nonnegative cone of a Hausdorff Baire ccc topological group with a
Baire-property positive cone, and its carrier is uncountable, then no
unital semiring multiplication can extend its addition. But without
that group-topology hypothesis, this manuscript makes no such general
claim. The classical literature on topological semigroup embeddings
\cite{s12:Rothman} is relevant to that remaining boundary; no unverified
embedding criterion from that literature is being used here.

\subsection{Presburger arithmetic: presentations but no expansions \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:presburger}

\subsubsection{Signed models and the universal obstruction}

A \emph{$\Z$-group} is a discretely ordered abelian group with named
least positive element $1$ in which every element has a unique standard
remainder modulo each positive ordinary integer $m$:
\begin{equation}
 \forall g\ \exists!(q,r)\in G\times\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}:
 \qquad g=mq+r1,
 \label{pma:br:eq:division}
\end{equation}
The usual interpretation is
as a model of signed Presburger arithmetic. Cooper elimination reduces
formulas to inequalities and congruences; the relevant finite-residue
mechanism is the one formalized in ProveIt \cite{s10:RepoPres}.
For clarity, the transfer argument needed for this abstract
characterization is included in \cref{pma:br:app:presburger}.

\begin{corollary}[All uncountable Polish signed Presburger groups \src{10}]
\label{pma:br:cor:presburger}
Let $G$ be an uncountable $\Z$-group with a Polish additive-group
topology and a Baire-property positive cone. It has no expansion to a
discretely ordered ring with the same addition, order, and named $1$.
The proposed multiplication may be arbitrary and need not be definable.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Apply \cref{pma:br:cor:ring-expansion}. The standard division axioms of a $\Z$-group
are not needed for this obstruction.
\end{proof}

The last observation is useful: the obstruction belongs to the weaker
ordered-group reduct. Presburger quantifier elimination explains why
many such reducts exist and are well behaved, but the contradiction
requires no quantifier elimination or induction.

\subsubsection{Divisible-plus-integer examples}

Let $D$ be a divisible linearly ordered abelian group. Put
\begin{equation}
 G_D=D\overrightarrow{\times}\Z,
 \qquad 1_G=(0,1),
 \label{pma:br:eq:GD}
\end{equation}
where the first coordinate is compared first. The element $(0,1)$ is
least positive. If $g=(d,n)$ and $m\ge1$ is ordinary, write
$n=mq+r$ with $0\le r<m$. Then
\begin{equation}
 (d,n)=m(d/m,q)+r(0,1).
 \label{pma:br:eq:GDdivision}
\end{equation}
Uniqueness follows from torsion-freeness and the ordinary remainder
uniqueness in $\Z$. Thus $G_D$ is a $\Z$-group.

Three useful choices are
\[
 D=\R,\qquad
 D=\Q^{\N},\qquad
 D=\ell^2(\N,\R).
\]
Use the usual order on $\R$, and on either sequence space compare at the
first nonzero coordinate. Use the ordinary real topology in the first
case, the product of discrete rational topologies in the second, and
the norm topology in the third. These are divisible ordered groups;
the order is defined additively and need not be a lattice order in a
functional-analytic sense.

Each $G_D$ is an uncountable Polish additive group with a Borel order.
For the sequence cases its strict positive cone is
\begin{equation}
 P_D=\bigcup_{j\ge0}
 \{d:d_0=\cdots=d_{j-1}=0,\ d_j>0\}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:firstnonzero}
\end{equation}
In $\Q^{\N}$ each displayed condition is clopen. In $\ell^2$, each
term is the intersection of a closed set with an open set and is
$F_\sigma$, since the space is metrizable. Thus $P_D$ is $F_\sigma$.
Its complement is $-P_D\cup\{0\}$, also $F_\sigma$, so $P_D$ is
$\Dtwo$. The corresponding cone in $G_D$ is
\[
 (P_D\times\Z)\ \cup\ (\{0\}\times\Z_{>0}),
\]
again $\Dtwo$. The same conclusion is immediate for $D=\R$.

These constructions, including the real-coordinate model, belong to the
existing Presburger project context and are not claimed as new here
\cite{s10:Local}. What \cref{pma:br:cor:presburger} adds is a theorem covering
\emph{all} uncountable Polish signed models with the stated order
regularity, not only these examples or the locally compact ones.

\subsubsection{Positive cones still give Polish arithmetic monoids}

Since the nonnegative cone $G_D^{\ge0}$ is $G_\delta$ in a Polish space,
it is Polish with its subspace topology. Addition restricts continuously,
and this cone is a model of nonnegative Presburger arithmetic.
For $D=\R$ it is explicitly
\begin{equation}
 M_{\R}=(\R_{>0}\times\Z)\ \cup\ (\{0\}\times\N).
 \label{pma:br:eq:positiveR}
\end{equation}
Thus additive Polish arithmetic is not ruled out. What fails is its
ordered-ring expansion on the corresponding signed group.

For these explicit cones, even an ordered semiring multiplication
compatible with the given addition and order is impossible when its
ring of differences uses the displayed signed ordered group. The
extension of such a multiplication to differences is algebraic; the
compatible Polish signed topology is already provided by $G_D$.
This is more specific than asserting the same conclusion for every
Polish monoid, a step not justified by the present proof.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:cor:presburger} assumes a Baire-property
cone where source~12's \cref{pma:br:cor:signed-presburger} assumes a Borel one;
the semiring clause of the latter is \cref{pma:br:thm:semiring}. The models
$G_D$ with $D=\R$ and $D=\Q^{\N}$ are Part~I's $\GD$ (\cref{pma:pr:sec:main});
their cones are $\MR$ and $\MB$. Source~10 credits these constructions to
source~08 \cite{s10:Local}; they are source~05's, \cref{pma:pr:thm:main}.
The case $D=\ell^2(\N,\R)$ is new here.

\subsection{Positive monoids, group completion, and the exact boundary \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:monoids}

The group structure is used twice in the category proof: inversion
exchanges $P$ and $-P$, and reflection $x\mapsto z-x$ is a
homeomorphism. Neither operation is available on an arbitrary positive
monoid. These are substantive uses, not notational conveniences.

For a cancellative commutative monoid $M$, its algebraic Grothendieck
group can be formed from pairs $(x,y)$, with
\[
 (x,y)\sim(x',y')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x+y'=x'+y,
\]
interpreted as formal differences. A semiring multiplication extends
algebraically to this group by
\[
 (x-y)(u-v)=(xu+yv)-(xv+yu).
\]
However, none of these formulas proves that the quotient has a
compatible Hausdorff Polish group topology, or that the original
positive cone embeds with its original topology. Quotient topologies
can fail the required separation or completeness properties.

\begin{proposition}[Conditional completion obstruction \src{10}]
\label{pma:br:prop:monoidcompletion}
Let $M$ be an uncountable cancellative ordered semiring whose signed
ring of differences $A$ is discretely ordered. Suppose $A$ admits a
Polish additive-group topology with a Baire-property positive cone.
Then such a semiring cannot exist. In particular this applies whenever
a specified topological group completion supplies those properties.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The natural map from $M$ to $A$ is injective by cancellation, so $A$
is uncountable. The ring then contradicts \cref{pma:br:s10:cor:polish}.
\end{proof}

For the explicit models $G_D^{\ge0}$ in \cref{pma:br:sec:presburger}, the signed
topology is already available. For an arbitrary positive model, it is
not. Therefore the present proof does not by itself remove the Borel
multiplication assumption from Glazer's positive-model theorem. The
relationship between those results is a comparison of different
hypothesis sets, not an unconditional strengthening in every setting.

Glazer's Question~2 asks for an uncountable Polish Presburger model with
continuous addition \cite{Glazer}. The additive examples recalled here
belong to the already developed affirmative constructions in the project;
they are not presented as a new resolution in this manuscript.
Our new conclusion is their universal signed ordered-ring
non-expandability under Baire comparison, and the general rigidity
mechanism behind it.

\section{Borel structures, Polishability, and meager embeddings}
\label{pma:br:sec:borel}

\begin{definition}
For this section, a \emph{Polish group presentation of a fixed Borel
structure} is a Polish additive-group topology whose Borel sets are
exactly the specified Borel sets. This is a requirement, not an automatic
consequence of having a standard Borel group.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[No compatible Polish group presentation]
\label{pma:br:thm:nonpolishable}
Let an uncountable discretely ordered ring have a specified standard
Borel structure in which its positive cone is Borel. There is no Polish
additive-group topology generating that Borel structure. No Borelness
of multiplication is assumed.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In such a topology the cone would remain Borel, so
\cref{pma:br:cor:polish} would force the carrier to be countable.
\end{proof}

The result distinguishes two failures. A displayed metric may merely
fail to be complete; \cref{pma:br:thm:nonpolishable} rules out \emph{every}
compatible Polish group topology preserving the prescribed Borel sets.
It does not rule out a Polish topology after the measurable structure
and the order's regularity have been changed.

\begin{theorem}[Borel ordered-ring subgroups are meager when uncountable]
\label{pma:br:thm:meager-subgroup}
Let $K$ be a Polish abelian group. Suppose $A\subseteq K$ is an
uncountable Borel subgroup, equipped algebraically with a discretely
ordered ring structure whose addition is the inherited group addition.
If its positive cone is Borel as a subset of $K$, then $A$ is meager in
$K$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
If $A$ were nonmeager, \cref{pma:br:lem:pettis} would show that
$A-A=A$ contains a neighborhood of $0$. Thus $A$ is open. An open
subgroup is also closed, since its complement is a union of open cosets.
Consequently $A$, with the inherited topology, is a Polish group. Its
positive cone is Borel, so \cref{pma:br:cor:polish} makes $A$ countable,
contradicting the hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Closed subrings and integer parts]
\label{pma:br:cor:integer-part}
In the setting of \cref{pma:br:thm:meager-subgroup}, a closed subgroup admitting
a discretely ordered ring structure with Borel cone must be countable
and discrete in its subspace topology. More generally, an uncountable
Borel integer part of an ordered field with a Polish additive topology
and Borel order must be meager in the ambient additive group.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
A closed subgroup of a Polish group is Polish, so the first statement
is \cref{pma:br:cor:polish}. An integer part is a discretely ordered subring;
its positive cone is the intersection of its carrier with the field's
positive cone. Thus the second statement follows from
\cref{pma:br:thm:meager-subgroup}.
\end{proof}

An integer part here means a discretely ordered subring $I$ such that
for every field element $x$ there is $i\in I$ with $i\leq x<i+1$.
The approximation clause is not needed for this corollary; only discrete
order and subring structure are used. This is another instance where
weaker algebraic hypotheses suffice than full arithmetic.

\section{A parallel Haar-measure theorem}
\label{pma:br:sec:measure}

The bounded-neighborhood mechanism can also be obtained from measure
rather than category. This gives a separate improvement of the order
regularity hypothesis in the locally compact setting. We use a regular
Haar measure and its completion; no assumption about restrictions to
null subgroups is imposed.

\begin{lemma}[Positive-measure differences]
\label{pma:br:lem:steinhaus}
Let $G$ be a Hausdorff locally compact abelian group with regular Haar
measure $\mu$. If a compact set $K$ has $\mu(K)>0$, then $K-K$ contains
a neighborhood of $0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose an open $U\supseteq K$ of finite measure with
$\mu(U)<2\mu(K)$. Compactness and continuity of addition give a
neighborhood $W$ of $0$ such that $K+W\subseteq U$. For $h\in W$, the
sets $K$ and $K+h$ both lie in $U$, so
\[
 \mu\bigl(K\cap(K+h)\bigr)
 \geq2\mu(K)-\mu(U)>0.
\]
Thus they meet, and $h\in K-K$.
\end{proof}

This is the compact-set form of the classical Steinhaus difference-set
principle \cite{s12:Steinhaus}; the displayed argument establishes the
locally compact version actually needed here.

\begin{lemma}[Haar-measurable order gives a bounded neighborhood]
\label{pma:br:lem:haar-bounded}
Let $G$ be a nontrivial ordered abelian group with a Hausdorff locally
compact group topology. If its positive cone is measurable for the
completion of a regular Haar measure, then $0$ has an order-bounded
open neighborhood.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The discrete case is immediate. Otherwise $\mu(\{0\})=0$: an atom at
$0$, together with translation invariance and a compact neighborhood
of finite measure, would force that neighborhood to be finite, and
the Hausdorff group would then be discrete.

Choose a compact set of positive finite measure. Its partition by
$P$, $-P$, and $\{0\}$ shows that one of the first two pieces has
positive measure. Invert the negative piece if necessary. Inner
regularity for completed Haar-measurable sets provides a compact
$B\subseteq P$ with $0<\mu(B)<\infty$.

All integrations that follow may be performed in a sigma-compact open
subgroup containing $B$. Such a subgroup exists: take a compact
identity neighborhood, adjoin $B$ and $-B$, and take the subgroup
generated by their union. It is a countable union of compact sets and
contains an open identity neighborhood. Haar measure restricted to it
is sigma-finite. Tonelli's theorem and translation invariance give
\begin{align}
 \int_G \mu\bigl(B\cap(a-B)\bigr)\,d\mu(a)
 &=\int_G\int_G \mathbf1_B(x)\mathbf1_B(a-x)\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(a)
 \notag\\
 &=\mu(B)^2>0,
 \label{pma:br:eq:haar-convolution}
\end{align}
where the integrands vanish outside that subgroup and its relevant
compact sumsets. Hence there is an $a$ such that
$K=B\cap(a-B)$ has positive measure. It is compact. For any $x\in K$,
both $x$ and $a-x$ are positive, so $0<x<a$ and in particular $a>0$.
Thus $K\subseteq(0,a)$ and $K-K\subseteq(-a,a)$. Apply
\cref{pma:br:lem:steinhaus}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Haar-measurable arithmetic rigidity]
\label{pma:br:thm:haar}
Let a discretely ordered ring have a Hausdorff locally compact
additive-group topology. If its positive cone is measurable for the
completion of a regular Haar measure, then
\[
 c(R)=d(R)=|R|.
\]
If the topology is ccc, it is countable and discrete. In particular,
this conclusion holds for second-countable locally compact
additive-group topologies with Haar-measurable order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Combine \cref{pma:br:lem:haar-bounded,pma:br:lem:packing} with
\eqref{pma:br:eq:cardinal-basic}. Under ccc the ring is countable. Locally
compact Hausdorff spaces are Baire, so the same singleton argument
as in \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} makes it discrete.
\end{proof}

The earlier report asked how to weaken Borel order without assuming
that ambient measurability automatically passes to every closed
subgroup \cite[Section 14]{s12:PriorLC}. This proof avoids that issue:
it works directly with a positive-measure compact subset of the
ambient cone. The sole restriction used for Tonelli is to an \emph{open}
sigma-compact subgroup containing that compact subset. No conclusion
about measurability on a null closed subgroup is required.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:thm:haar} answers source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:q:weakenborel} for ambient Haar measurability, and
\cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood} answers it for the Baire property: in
both routes the regularity of the cone for the given topology suffices, and no
condition on restrictions to compact subgroups or closed real subspaces is
needed. \Cref{pma:br:thm:haar} also strengthens \cref{pma:lc:thm:headline}
from Borel to Haar-measurable order, and removes second countability from its
cardinal part.

\section{Sharpness: three topologies on one polynomial ring}
\label{pma:br:sec:sharpness}

The same algebraic example isolates the role of the principal
hypotheses. Let
\begin{equation}
 A=\Ap
 =\left\{z+\sum_{j=1}^{N}r_jt^j:
       z\in\Z,\ r_j\in\R,\ N\in\N\right\}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:polynomial-ring}
\end{equation}
Order a nonzero polynomial by the sign of its leading coefficient, so
that $t$ is larger than every ordinary real constant wherever that
comparison is made in $\R[t]$. This is an ordered ring: leading
coefficients multiply, and comparison is invariant under translation.
If a positive element has degree zero, it is a positive integer; if it
has positive degree, it exceeds every ordinary integer. Hence $1$ is
its least positive element. The cardinality of $A$ is $\cc$.


\noindent\writetag{} Source~10 prints the same three topologies on this
ring (written $\Z+X\R[X]$) as its Examples~9.1, 9.3 and~9.4; their labels
are second labels of the three subsections below. The ring is source~08's
$A_*$ (\cref{pma:lc:ex:nonsep}) and source~06's $\Z+t\R[t]$
(\cref{pma:cp:thm:polynomial}).
\label{pma:br:sec:examples}

\subsection{A separable metrizable ring that is meager in itself}
\label{pma:br:subsec:meager-example}


\label{pma:br:ex:incomplete}\label{pma:br:subsec:incomplete}

Identify a polynomial with its coefficient sequence and give $A$ the
subspace topology from
\[
 \Z_{\rm discrete}\times\R^{\N_{>0}}.
\]
The higher-coordinate sequence has finite support. The ambient space
is metrizable and second countable, so $A$ is separable and metrizable.
Addition and inversion are continuous. Multiplication is jointly
continuous as well, since its $n$th coefficient is the finite polynomial
expression
\begin{equation}
 (fg)_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n}f_i g_{n-i}.
 \label{pma:br:eq:convolution}
\end{equation}
Continuity into the product follows coordinate by coordinate; the
product lies again in the finite-support subring.

For $N\geq0$, let $A_N$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most $N$.
It is closed: all higher coefficients vanish. It has empty interior,
because a basic open set constrains only finitely many coordinates,
and a nonzero term can be inserted at a still higher degree. Thus
\begin{equation}
 A=\bigcup_{N\geq0}A_N
 \label{pma:br:eq:meager-union}
\end{equation}
is meager in itself.

Nevertheless the cone has low Borel complexity. For $d\geq1$, the
condition
\[
 f_j=0\text{ for all }j>d,\qquad f_d>0
\]
is the intersection of a closed set and an open set. In a metrizable
space every open set is $F_\sigma$, so this condition is $F_\sigma$.
The positive degree-zero polynomials form a countable union of closed
singletons. Taking the countable union over $d$ proves that $P$ is
$F_\sigma$. Its complement is $(-P)\cup\{0\}$, also $F_\sigma$.
Therefore $P$ is $\Dtwo$.

This example has continuous multiplication, not merely arbitrary
multiplication. It shows that the Baire hypothesis cannot be replaced
by metrizability or separability. By \cref{pma:br:thm:nonpolishable}, there is
also no Polish additive-group topology generating the same Borel
structure: the defect is not repaired by choosing another compatible
complete group metric.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 adds:

This example shows why a separable metrizable topology with Borel order
is not enough, even when multiplication happens to be continuous.
The failure occurs in the Baire hypothesis, not in the algebra.
For an even smaller example, $\Z$ with its $p$-adic subspace topology is
a countable, nondiscrete, non-Archimedean topological ring; every subset
is Borel, but it is again meager in itself.


\subsection{A locally compact Baire ring presentation without ccc}
\label{pma:br:subsec:nonsep-example}

\label{pma:br:ex:nonccc}


Decompose the additive group as
\begin{equation}
 A=\R t\oplus D,
 \qquad D=\Z\oplus\bigoplus_{j\geq2}\R t^j,
 \label{pma:br:eq:nonsep-topology}
\end{equation}
and give it the product topology with $\R t$ usual and $D$ discrete.
This is a Hausdorff locally compact metrizable topological group and
is Baire. It is not separable: the distinct sets $\R t+d$, $d\in D$,
are $\cc$ disjoint open subsets.

Its cone is again $\Dtwo$. When the high-degree part of $d$ is nonzero,
its leading coefficient determines the sign of $rt+d$ independently
of $r$. Such a coset is either wholly positive or wholly negative.
When $d=z\in\Z$, positivity is determined by $r>0$, or by $r=0$ and
$z>0$. Thus the positive cone is the union of an open set and the
closed set of positive integer points at $r=0$. The negative cone
has the analogous form. Metrizability gives the claimed $\Dtwo$
complexity.

Choosing rational $r$ in each open coset gives a dense set of size
$\cc$. The disjoint cosets give the matching lower bound. Hence
\[
 c(A)=d(A)=|A|=\cc,
\]
exactly as \cref{pma:br:thm:main} predicts.
The ring multiplication is not continuous in this topology. Indeed,
$t/n\to0$ whereas multiplication by $t$ sends that sequence to
$t^2/n$, which does not converge to $0$ in the discrete $D$ coordinate.
This is permitted by the theorem, which assumes nothing about
multiplication.

\noindent\writetag{} This is source~08's \cref{pma:lc:ex:nonsep}.
\src{10} Source~10 adds the extent and the Lindel\"of degree: by
\cref{pma:br:thm:maximal}, or directly by choosing one point on each line,
$\cell(A)=\dens(A)=\ext(A)=L(A)=|A|=\cc$. It notes:

This is not asserted to be a topological ring. The continuity of
addition is all the main theorem assumes, and multiplication in this
example fails continuity for many fixed scalars; see
\cref{pma:br:sec:scalars}.


\subsection{A Polish additive topology with a non-Baire positive cone}
\label{pma:br:subsec:pathological-order}

\label{pma:br:ex:nonbp}


Let $V=t\R[t]$, regarded only as a rational vector space. Its dimension
is $\cc$: it contains a copy of the rational vector space $\R$, and
its cardinality is $\cc$. The vector space $\Q^{\N}$ also has dimension
$\cc$. To justify the latter assertion, its cardinality is $\cc$; over
a countable field, an infinite-dimensional vector space has cardinality
the maximum of its dimension and $\aleph_0$. A countable-dimensional
one would be countable. These facts force the dimension to be $\cc$.

Using bases, choose a rational-linear isomorphism
\[
 \psi:V\longrightarrow\Q^{\N}.
\]
Transport the Polish group topology of
$\Z_{\rm discrete}\times\Q_{\rm discrete}^{\N}$ to the additive group
$A=\Z\oplus V$ through $z+v\mapsto(z,\psi(v))$. The ring and its
original leading-coefficient order remain algebraically unchanged.
The new topology is Polish and makes addition and inversion continuous.
By \cref{pma:br:cor:polish}, its positive cone does \emph{not} have the Baire
property.

This is an existence construction using choice of vector-space bases,
not a computable coding. It shows that regularity of order cannot be
omitted from the theorem. No claim is made that multiplication is
Borel in the transported presentation.

\noindent\writetag{} This is a variant of source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:ex:wildorder}, which transports $\R^d\times\Z$ and calls the order
necessarily non-Borel; here the transported topology is that of
$\Q^{\N}\times\Z$ and the conclusion is that the cone lacks the Baire property.
\src{10} Source~10's version of the example ends:

The isomorphism is chosen using vector-space bases. It is not an
algorithm, and the construction gives no Borel multiplication or
regular comparison procedure. Its point is exact: additive Polishability
alone does not prohibit uncountable discretely ordered rings. Order
regularity is an indispensable part of the theorem.


\subsection{Other indispensable distinctions}

The ordinary real field is an uncountable Polish ordered ring with
continuous operations and open positive cone. It does not contradict
our theorem because it has no least positive element. Thus discrete
order is essential.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 adds:

The usual real field is an uncountable Polish topological ring with
open positive cone. It escapes \cref{pma:br:cor:ccc} because it has elements
strictly between $0$ and $1$. In the relative theorem, its finite part
is already all of the ring. This is the correct boundary, not a failure
of Baire category or of the chain condition.


The group $G_\R$ from \eqref{pma:br:eq:real-lex} is uncountable, Polish,
locally compact, discretely ordered as a group, and has a $\Dtwo$
positive cone. It lacks any compatible unital ordered-ring expansion
by \cref{pma:br:cor:ring-expansion}. Thus continuous addition and regular
discrete order alone are not contradictory. It is the combination with
an unrestricted positive multiplier family that creates the packing.

\section{Continuous scalar maps beyond the separable setting \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:scalars}

Once ccc is imposed, the main theorem already gives discreteness.
The following observation is instead meaningful for nondiscrete,
necessarily non-ccc Baire presentations such as \cref{pma:br:subsec:nonsep-example}.

\begin{proposition}[A bounded subring of continuous scalars \src{10}]
\label{pma:br:prop:scalars}
Let $A$ be a discretely ordered ring with a nondiscrete Hausdorff Baire
additive-group topology and a Baire-property positive cone. Define
\[
 \Cont(A)=\{a\in A: L_a:A\to A,\ L_a(x)=ax,
                    \text{ is continuous}\}.
\]
Then $\Cont(A)$ is a unital subring containing $\Z1$, and for some
$c>0$ it is contained in $[-c,c]$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The identities $L_{a+b}=L_a+L_b$, $L_{-a}=-L_a$, and
$L_{ab}=L_a\circ L_b$ prove the subring assertion. Integer scalar
maps are continuous because the additive operations are continuous.
Choose a neighborhood $U\subseteq[-c,c]$ by local boundedness.
If $|a|>c$, then for every nonzero $x$, discreteness gives
$|ax|=|a||x|\ge|a|>c$. Hence $L_a^{-1}(U)=\{0\}$.
Continuity of $L_a$ would make $\{0\}$ a neighborhood and the group
discrete. Therefore such $a$ cannot belong to $\Cont(A)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[\src{10}]\label{pma:br:cor:allscalars}
A discretely ordered ring with a Hausdorff Baire additive topology,
a Baire-property positive cone, and continuous multiplication by every
fixed scalar is discrete. No separability or ccc assumption is needed.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
If the topology were nondiscrete, \cref{pma:br:prop:scalars} would bound all
of $A$ by one $c$, contradicting the existence of $c+1$.
\end{proof}

In \cref{pma:br:subsec:nonsep-example}, the continuous-scalar subring is exactly $\Z$.
Every integer works. If $a$ has positive degree $k$ and leading
coefficient $\alpha\ne0$, the restriction of $L_a$ to the open line
$\R X$ has degree-$(k+1)$ coefficient $r\mapsto\alpha r$ in the
discrete factor $D$. This is not continuous, so $L_a$ is not continuous.
Thus the bounded-scalar conclusion is nonvacuous and can be exact.

We deliberately do not identify Borel scalar maps with continuous ones
in this nonseparable discussion. Standard automatic-continuity
statements for Borel homomorphisms between Polish groups do not
license that substitution for an arbitrary nonseparable target.
In the Polish case of the main theorem, every map is already continuous
because the topology has been proved discrete.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:br:cor:allscalars} generalizes source~09's
\cref{pma:ser:thm:discrete} in another direction: continuous scalar maps
replace Borel ones, and no separability is assumed. Compare source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:thm:scalars}, which counts the Borel scalars of an integral-domain
multiplication unrelated to the order.

\section{Completion, units, and omnific applications}
\label{pma:br:sec:completion}

\subsection{Completion may destroy discrete order algebraically}

The additive completion of the coefficient-topology example in
\cref{pma:br:subsec:meager-example} is
\begin{equation}
 \widehat A=\Z+t\R[[t]].
 \label{pma:br:eq:completion}
\end{equation}
The higher coefficients may now have infinite support. The topology
is the full product topology, and \eqref{pma:br:eq:convolution} defines a
jointly continuous multiplication. Every coefficient sequence is the
limit of its finite truncations, so $A$ is dense. Completeness of the
product additive group gives the asserted completion.

One might try to extend the leading-degree discrete order to this
Polish ring. The obstruction is stronger than failure of Borelness:
\emph{there is no discrete ring order on this completion at all}.

\begin{lemma}[Units in a discretely ordered ring]
\label{pma:br:lem:units}
Every unit of a discretely ordered ring is $1$ or $-1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $uv=1$ and $u>0$, then $v>0$, and discreteness gives $u,v\geq1$.
If $u>1$, then $u\geq2$, and hence $uv\geq2$, a contradiction.
Thus $u=1$. If $u<0$, apply the positive case to $-u$ and $-v$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[No discrete order on the coefficient completion]
\label{pma:br:prop:completion-no-order}\label{pma:br:prop:completion}
The ring $\widehat A=\Z+t\R[[t]]$ admits no unital discrete ring order.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The element $1-t$ is a unit with inverse
\[
 1+t+t^2+\cdots.
\]
This identity is a formal coefficient identity, not an analytic
convergence assertion. It also follows from the exact finite identity
\begin{equation}
 (1-t)\sum_{j=0}^{N}t^j=1-t^{N+1}
 \label{pma:br:eq:geometric}
\end{equation}
by passing to the coefficient limit. But $1-t$ is neither $1$ nor
$-1$, contrary to \cref{pma:br:lem:units}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Second proof \src{10}]

Truncations show that the polynomial ring is dense in the product
coefficient group of all such formal series. This product is completely
metrizable, and the coefficientwise ring operations extend by the
finite convolution formulas.

In any discretely ordered ring, the only units are $1$ and $-1$.
Indeed, if $uv=1$, then $|u|,|v|\ge1$ and
$1=|u||v|\ge|u|\ge1$, so $|u|=1$.
In $\widehat A$, however, the element $1-X$ is a unit with inverse
$\sum_{n\ge0}X^n$. It is neither $1$ nor $-1$ as a formal series.
This contradicts the necessary unit property.

\end{proof}


The example separates three issues: the finite-polynomial ring has
a discrete order and a useful incomplete topology; its completion has
excellent topological ring operations; and the completion loses the
algebraic possibility of discrete order. It would be incorrect to
attribute this last failure only to descriptive-set-theoretic
complexity.

\subsection{Set-sized omnific subrings}

ProveIt's surreal development describes the omnific ring as the
normal-form elements with nonnegative exponents and integer constant
term; it records in particular the least-positive-element property
\cite{s12:ProveItSurreal}. The present theorem uses only the resulting
ordered-ring laws. It does not use the deeper claims in the repository's
unrefereed reports.

\begin{corollary}[Omnific presentation obstruction]
\label{pma:br:cor:omnific}
Let $B$ be any uncountable set-sized unital subring of the omnific
integers, with its inherited order. It admits no Polish additive-group
topology in which the inherited positive cone has the Baire property.
More generally, any Hausdorff Baire additive-group topology with such
a cone satisfies $c(B)=d(B)=|B|$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
An ordered unital subring of a discretely ordered ring is discretely
ordered: its positive elements are positive in the larger ring and
therefore at least $1$. Apply \cref{pma:br:thm:main,pma:br:cor:polish}.
\end{proof}


\noindent\src{10} Source~10 proves the same corollary with the cardinal equalities of \cref{pma:br:thm:maximal}:

The inspected ProveIt surreal README describes the construction of the
omnific ring, its least positive element $1$, its constant-term
homomorphism to $\Z$, and the fact that an omnific integer bounded by
an ordinary real is an ordinary integer \cite{s10:RepoSurreal}.
The first two properties already make its set-sized unital ordered
subrings eligible for the present theorem. We do not need the full
normal-form theory, constant-term retraction, or real closedness of the
surreal field for the obstruction.

\begin{corollary}[Set-sized omnific presentations \src{10}]\label{pma:br:s10:cor:omnific}
Let $A$ be a set-sized unital ordered subring of $\Oz$. If its additive
group is given a Polish group topology and the inherited positive cone
has the Baire property, then $A$ is countable and the topology is
discrete. If instead the topology is Hausdorff and Baire and $A$ is
uncountable, a Baire-property positive cone forces a full-cardinality
closed discrete subset and the equalities of \cref{pma:br:thm:maximal}.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The inherited order is discrete, with least positive element $1$.
Apply \cref{pma:br:s10:cor:polish,pma:br:thm:maximal}.
\end{proof}

A frequent coding pattern is a closed additive subgroup of a countable
product of countable discrete groups. Such a group is Polish: use a
complete product metric and restrict it to the closed subgroup. Its
finite-coordinate agreement subgroups are open and form a basis.
Thus an uncountable exact-stream representation of a set-sized omnific
subring in this format cannot simultaneously give continuous additive
group operations and a Baire comparison predicate.

This does not rule out countable notation systems, incomplete spaces of
finite expressions, non-Baire comparisons, non-Polish presentation
spaces, or purely algebraic formalizations. A kernel proof of field or
ring laws does not produce a Polish presentation or a measurable order
algorithm. Likewise, being homeomorphic to Baire space as a bare space
does not by itself give a non-Archimedean \emph{group} topology.

Finite polynomial expressions
\[
 z+r_1\omega+r_2\omega^2+\cdots+r_N\omega^N
\]
provide the direct connection with \eqref{pma:br:eq:polynomial-ring}. Finite
normal-form arithmetic identifies their ring and order with
$\Z+t\R[t]$ through $t\mapsto\omega$. The sharpness examples are thus
also examples on an explicit set-sized omnific subring; one does not
need the full proper class of surreal numbers to see the obstruction.

An additive fragment such as $\R\omega+\Z$ behaves differently. It is
closed under addition but not under multiplication, since $\omega^2$
lies outside it. Giving that fragment the topology of $G_\R$ is
compatible with a regular discrete additive order. The theorem explains
why expanding it to a ring while retaining that additive presentation
is impossible.

\subsection{Foundations and universe boundaries}

No theorem above treats the proper class $\Oz$ as a Polish space.
A Polish space is set-sized. To discuss the entire surreal or omnific
class in a class theory, one must separately specify which collections
of classes and which class maps are allowed; none of that is needed
for \cref{pma:br:cor:omnific}.

In a type-theoretic implementation, fix a universe containing the
carrier of the ring or additive group and a universe large enough for
its topology and cardinal invariants. The packing map is a set-indexed
family within those universes. If a universe-relative construction of
surreals is used, first identify the desired set-sized unital subring
and its order. A birthday cutoff or a finite list of permitted scales
must not be assumed to be a subring without proving closure.

The finite-polynomial example can instead be defined from scratch,
without any surreal ontology: its coefficient sequences are finitely
supported functions on the ordinary naturals, with an integer constant
term. This is a particularly clean target for a foundationally modest
formalization of the examples.

\subsubsection{Universe discipline \src{10}}

A proper class such as the full $\No$ or $\Oz$ is not an underlying set
for the theorems here. In a set-theoretic treatment, first choose a
set-sized subring closed under the needed operations. In a dependent-
type-theoretic treatment, first specify a universe level and a type
carrying the actual ordered ring, rather than a type of arbitrary
syntax with an unproved interpretation map. The theorem then concerns
that type's underlying set in a metatheoretic model.

The quotient $A/\Z1$ is a set-sized additive quotient. No ``set of all
class functions'', class-valued probability space, or topology on all
proper-class subsets is formed. These restrictions are part of the
statement, not a later repair to its proof.

\section{Formalization architecture and proof audit}
\label{pma:br:sec:formalization}

The repository snapshot used for the interface review is
\begin{center}\small\snap.\end{center}
The inspected Presburger README describes an integer-specific Cooper
eliminator with syntax, normalization, elimination, and a decision
procedure. The inspected surreal README records the ordered omnific
construction and distinguishes proved-library interfaces from research
reports \cite{s12:ProveItPresburger,s12:ProveItSurreal}. We have not built the
repository or independently verified those advertised audit results.

The central theorem can be formalized independently of Cooper
elimination, nonstandard-model syntax, or the full surreal construction.
Its proof should be split into interfaces that expose exactly what is
used.

\subsection{The algebraic interface}

The first component is a discretely ordered ring and its absolute-value
inequalities. The core certificate is the statement
\begin{equation}
 r\ne s,\ a>0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 2a<\left|(2a+1)(r-s)\right|.
 \label{pma:br:eq:formal-gap}
\end{equation}
Next, a set-level lemma says that if $W\subseteq(-a,a)$, the translates
$(2a+1)r+W$ are disjoint for distinct indices. Neither lemma needs
Baire category, cardinal arithmetic, topological continuity of scalar
multiplication, or properties of a particular ring.

For Lean, a robust design would expose the least-positive-element
property explicitly as a hypothesis on the ordered ring, rather than
assuming that a convenient name for a discrete-order typeclass matches
the required semantics. The proof only needs the implication
$0<x\Rightarrow1\leq x$. A Rocq development can package precisely the
same fields in a record. This paragraph is a design specification,
not a claim that any particular library API has been tested.

\subsection{The topological and category interface}

The second component concerns an ordered additive group with a
Hausdorff group topology. It should prove, in order:
\begin{enumerate}
\item a nondiscrete Hausdorff topological group has nowhere-dense
singletons;
\item a nonmeager Baire-property set has differences containing a
neighborhood of zero;
\item reflection of a locally comeager part of the positive cone
produces a nonmeager interval $(0,2u)$;
\item a Baire-property positive cone yields an order-bounded
neighborhood.
\end{enumerate}
The last statement should be written for groups rather than rings,
so that the self-embedding theorem can reuse it without introducing
unneeded multiplication.

The ccc consequence need not formalize general cardinal invariants
first. It can directly turn the family of translates into an injection
from the carrier into a countable family. The exact cardinal equalities
can be added later. This keeps the first kernel-checking target small.

\subsection{Separate modules and theorems}

A reasonable dependency order is:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{.28\textwidth}p{.64\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Module & Mathematical boundary \\
\midrule
DiscreteOrderGap & \eqref{pma:br:eq:unit-separation} and \eqref{pma:br:eq:formal-gap} \\
DisjointTranslates & The packing lemma, with an arbitrary bounded set \\
BaireOrderedGroup & Pettis and the bounded-neighborhood lemma \\
ArithmeticRigidity & Baire ccc and Polish conclusions \\
UnitImageSpectrum & All ordered additive self-embeddings, no regularity \\
PositiveExpansion & Difference-ring construction and semiring obstruction \\
PolynomialExamples & Finite-support ring and the completion unit witness \\
OmnificApplication & An adapter using proved subring and discrete-order laws \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The measure theorem belongs in a later module, because it adds Haar
measure, compact inner regularity, and Tonelli. It is logically
independent of the category route to the principal theorem.

\subsection{Trust boundaries of this package}

The package contains mathematical proofs and an executable exact
arithmetic script. It does not contain a new Lean or Rocq proof, and no
such toolchain was run during preparation. The tests check finite
polynomial identities in $\Z+t\Q[t]$. They do not certify Baire category,
all Borel sets, uncountable cardinalities, arbitrary semiring
completions, or a theorem for every ordered ring.

The most important audit questions are therefore mathematical. Does
one mistakenly use continuity of $r\mapsto br$? No: only translates
of $W$ are used. Does the reflection require multiplication? No:
$2u-x$ is formed in the additive group. Is an open convex subgroup
assumed to be an ideal? No. Is a positive monoid silently given a
Polish group completion? No. Is the proper class of all omnific
integers treated as a set? No. The manuscript's statements are
formulated to keep each of these distinctions visible.

\subsection{A small algebraic core before topology \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:formal}

A sensible implementation order is the following.

\paragraph{Layer A: finite intervals and hulls.}
Prove finite-interval exhaustion from least positivity of $1$; define
$\FinA(A)$ and $H_a$ using ordinary natural numbers; prove their additive
subgroup and convexity properties. Keep the hull's external ordinary
index distinct from an element of a nonstandard model.

\paragraph{Layer B: the exact kernel.}
Build the additive map $x\mapsto ax+H_a$ and prove that its kernel is
$\FinA(A)$. Obtain the quotient injection by a general additive-group
quotient theorem. This layer should depend only on ordered algebra,
not topology, measurable spaces, or surreal normal forms.
The bounded-direct-sum theorem can be implemented independently using
finite supports and a largest nonzero index.

\paragraph{Layer C: the category interface.}
Prove \cref{pma:br:lem:sumset,pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}. The only topological input needed
by the algebraic layer is one bounded neighborhood. Explicitly expose
that interface before connecting it to the Baire-property positive
cone. This makes the theorem reusable with other sources of local
boundedness.

\paragraph{Layer D: quotient cardinality and discreteness.}
Prove that an open subgroup has at most countably many cosets in a ccc
group. Combine the injection with countability of $\Z1$. Finish with
the elementary countable-Hausdorff-Baire-group lemma. A separate
cardinal module can produce the closed discrete transversal and the
maximal-cardinality results using choice.

\paragraph{Layer E: syntax and applications.}
Connect the theorem to the actual omnific ordered ring and to abstract
$\Z$-groups. ProveIt's Presburger development exposes affine syntax,
coefficient normalization, a normalized Cooper step, and a full Lean
sentence decision procedure, while its Rocq development independently
checks the decisive one-variable step \cite{s10:RepoPres}. Transfer to
abstract $\Z$-group semantics is a separate theorem; an integer
implementation alone is not evidence that the transfer has been
formalized.

No new source file is labeled ``Lean verified'' in this package. The
repository was inspected at the snapshot recorded in the source audit;
its builds were not rerun. The mathematical arguments above do not
rely on the repository's unrelated research claims.

\section{Further research questions and concrete next targets}
\label{pma:br:sec:questions}

The following questions are proposed research directions arising from
the proved results. Except for the earlier project questions explicitly
identified in \cref{pma:br:sec:intersection,pma:br:sec:measure}, we do not claim that
a complete literature search has established their open status.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 introduces its twelve questions as follows. Each
one that asks the same as a question of source~12 is printed after it; the
other four follow in \cref{pma:br:sec:q10}.

The general Polish signed-group question is resolved by
\cref{pma:br:cor:ccc}; it should no longer appear on the open list. The
following questions identify extensions not settled by this paper.
Unless attributed explicitly, they are proposed research targets,
not assertions that a problem's literature-wide open status has been
certified.

\noindent\writetag{} The question that both sources answer is
\cref{pma:lc:q:removelc} of \cref{pma:part:lc}; their answers are
\cref{pma:br:cor:ccc,pma:br:cor:polish}. Source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:q:weakenborel} is answered as stated (note after
\cref{pma:br:thm:haar}); the questions below on weaker regularity ask for
more.
\label{pma:br:s10:sec:questions}

\begin{question}[Positive monoids beyond Polishable signed groups]
Can an uncountable Polish continuous-addition positive arithmetic model
admit an algebraically compatible unital semiring multiplication when
no compatible Baire ccc signed-group presentation with regular order
exists?
\end{question}
The new obstruction shows exactly where a positive example would have
to escape: failure of an appropriate group topology or failure of
order regularity after passage to differences. Requiring stronger
arithmetic, such as $Q+\IOpen$, also invokes Glazer's obstruction if
multiplication is Borel. The non-Borel multiplication case and the
weaker algebraic case should be kept separate.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 asks:

\begin{question}[Positive arithmetic without a signed topology \src{10}]
Can an uncountable Polish positive arithmetic monoid with continuous
addition and suitably regular order carry an ordered semiring
multiplication when no regularity of that multiplication is assumed?
\end{question}
The task is to recover a replacement for the group reflection argument,
or to construct a genuine example escaping it. A result must state
its arithmetic axioms and must not silently assume a Polish group
completion. Glazer's positive-model work is the closest published
starting point, but its Borel multiplication hypothesis changes the
available tools.

\begin{question}[A usable group-completion criterion]
Which conditions on a Polish cancellative ordered monoid ensure that
its algebraic difference group has a Hausdorff Baire ccc topology with
a Baire-property cone and the required compatibility with the original
presentation?
\end{question}
The first useful outcome would be a sufficient criterion stated in
terms of translations and the difference quotient map. A proof must
check the quotient topology rather than appealing only to algebraic
cancellation. A converse would identify the precise gap between the
signed theorem here and the positive-monoid setting.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 asks:

\begin{question}[A usable group-completion criterion \src{10}]
Which Polish cancellative Presburger monoids embed topologically as the
positive cone of a Hausdorff Polish topological group?
\end{question}
A promising formulation would use translation embeddings, local
neighborhood compatibility, and a complete uniform structure on formal
differences. Both the topology on the original monoid and the
regularity of the completed order must be tracked. Such a criterion
would turn \cref{pma:br:prop:monoidcompletion} into a practical obstruction.

asked also by source~09 as \cref{pma:ser:q:cones}, for Baire ccc completions
with a Baire-property cone.

\begin{question}[The topology of regular ordered additive groups]
For a fixed Polish abelian group, which discrete invariant orders have
a Baire-property positive cone, and which open principal convex
subgroups can they produce?
\end{question}
\Cref{pma:br:prop:open-convex} provides an open principal convex subgroup with
countable quotient. This is necessary, not a classification. One can
ask whether recursive data from open convex subgroups and their
ordered quotients give complete invariants in natural classes such
as non-Archimedean Polish groups.

\begin{question}[Exact unit-image spectra]
Which subsets of the positive cone occur as $\mathcal U(G)$ for
uncountable Baire ccc discretely ordered groups with regular cone?
\end{question}
The spectrum is bounded by \cref{pma:br:thm:unit-spectrum};
\eqref{pma:br:eq:exact-spectrum} gives one exact infinite example. Possible
next invariants include its cofinality within the convex subgroup it
generates, closure under ordinary multiplication of indices when
available, and the effects of restricting to continuous or elementary
self-embeddings. These restrictions need not produce the same spectrum.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 asks:

\begin{question}[The intrinsic unit-image spectrum \src{10}]
For an uncountable Baire ccc discretely ordered group with regular
order, how can $\mathcal U(G)$ be classified algebraically and
descriptively?
\end{question}
The spectrum is order bounded and each of its principal hulls is
meager. Determining when the spectrum itself is meager, Borel, analytic,
or definable requires additional information. One should first analyze
explicit divisible-plus-integer examples, then groups without a global
additive order unit.

\begin{question}[Cardinal and component spectra]
For a fixed uncountable discretely ordered ring, which Hausdorff Baire
regular-order group topologies realize the forced equality
$c(R)=d(R)=|R|$, and what weights and connected-component structures
can occur?
\end{question}
The equality itself is settled here. The remaining realization problem
is more refined: prescribed local compactness, completeness,
metrizability, or topology on selected coefficient subgroups.
\Cref{pma:br:subsec:nonsep-example} shows that local compactness can coexist
with exact maximal cellularity on a continuum-sized ring.

\noindent\src{10} Source~10 asks:

\begin{question}[Optimal nonseparable presentations \src{10}]
Which discretely ordered rings admit nondiscrete Hausdorff Baire
additive topologies with Borel order, and which full-cardinality open
quotient structures can occur?
\end{question}
The polynomial example realizes maximal cellularity with an open real
line. The cardinal lower bound is exact, but it does not classify
possible local groups or orders. A classification for rings
$\Z+I$ with a specified divisible additive ideal $I$ would make the
boundary concrete.

\cref{pma:lc:q:sizespectra}: the equality $c=d=|R|$ is now proved.

\begin{question}[Regularity weaker than Baire or Haar measurability]
What assumptions on an ordered positive cone are sufficient to force
an order-bounded neighborhood without requiring the full Baire

The proof isolates a concrete intermediate property: some order-bounded
set has a difference set containing a neighborhood of zero. A productive

groups, any proposed measure substitute needs a carefully specified
notion of null set and invariance; there is no general locally finite

or definability hypothesis that still forces a bounded neighborhood?

A positive result needs an explicit substitute for the nonmeager-cone

\begin{question}[Definability of integer parts in Polish fields]
What descriptive complexities can occur for uncountable integer parts
inside ordered fields with Polish additive topology and Borel order?

A Borel integer part is meager by \cref{pma:br:cor:integer-part}, and its

when uncountable. These obstructions leave room for finer questions
about Borel ranks, analytic presentations, and the complexity of

\begin{question}[Which completions preserve discrete order?]
For natural additive topologies on discretely ordered subrings, which
completions avoid new units and retain any discrete ring order?
\end{question}
The unit witness in \cref{pma:br:prop:completion-no-order} gives an algebraic
necessary condition independent of Borel complexity. It is not

producing an order need not make it regular. A useful theory would
separate these three successive obstructions.

without introducing new nontrivial units or other elementary

The coefficient completion in \cref{pma:br:prop:completion-no-order} fails before

Supplying an open set and a coded meager exceptional set may change the

The initial milestone should be the packing lemma with its full

A certificate could expose a positive scale, an open principal hull,

\subsection{Further questions of source 10 \src{10}}\label{pma:br:sec:q10}

\begin{question}[Beyond cardinality: quotient order types \src{10}]
What additional restrictions does the ordered embedding
$A/\FinA(A)\hookrightarrow A/H_a$ impose on cofinalities, convex-subgroup
chains, and ordered ranks?
\end{question}
The main theorem uses only cardinality. The embedding preserves order,
so it may yield sharper obstructions for proposed arithmetic reducts
whose quotients have small rank even when both cardinalities are large.
A useful first target is a uniform rank calculation for iterated
polynomial and lexicographic extensions.

\begin{question}[The bounded continuous-scalar subring \src{10}]
Which subrings can occur as $\Cont(A)$ in a nondiscrete Baire
presentation with regular order?
\end{question}
It must contain the ordinary integers and be bounded in the ambient
order. The example here realizes exactly $\Z$. Constructing examples
with prescribed larger scalar subrings, or finding new algebraic
restrictions on them, would sharpen the link with topological algebra.
Borel and continuous scalars must be kept separate outside the
separable setting.

\begin{question}[Countable unit intervals in general ordered rings \src{10}]
How restrictive is the relative criterion
$|A|=\max(\aleph_0,|[0,1]_A|)$ when combined with model-theoretic
conditions on $A$?
\end{question}
The theorem isolates the finite part as the possible location of
uncountability. Investigating ordered fields, integer-part extensions,
and definable subrings with controlled bounded intervals may yield
applications beyond discretely ordered arithmetic.

\begin{question}[Definability of the transported counterexample \src{10}]
What is the best possible descriptive complexity of an ordered-ring
comparison relation after transporting its addition to
$\Q^{\N}\times\Z$?
\end{question}
The cone cannot have the Baire property, so it cannot be Borel or
analytic in that Polish presentation. The basis-selected construction
does not provide any finite projective definition. The problem should
be treated with explicit set-theoretic assumptions rather than assuming
that a nonconstructive transport is an effective code.

\section{Conclusions of Part VI}


The decisive topological resource is an order-bounded neighborhood,
not local compactness. Category regularity of an invariant positive
cone provides such a neighborhood in every Hausdorff Baire group.
Discrete ring arithmetic then amplifies the unit gap into a maximal
family of disjoint open translates:
\[
 \text{regular cone}
 \ \Longrightarrow\ W\subseteq(-a,a)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \{(2a+1)r+W:r\in R\}\text{ disjoint}.
\]
This resolves the earlier local-compactness-removal question and gives
the sharp equality $c(R)=d(R)=|R|$. A separate measure argument obtains
the same conclusion from ambient Haar measurability in locally compact
groups.

The consequences are both restrictive and diagnostic. They prohibit
arbitrary ordered-ring and positive-semiring expansions of a broad
class of Polish additive presentations, constrain all ordered additive
self-embeddings, and explain why natural coefficient completions of
omnific polynomial fragments must fail somewhere. At the same time,
the examples show that uncountable continuous addition, nonseparable
Baire ring presentations, and pathological Polish ordered algebra can
all exist outside the precise hypothesis boundary.

\paragraph{Source 10\textquoteright s conclusion \src{10}.}


The decisive improvement is to retain the ordinary-integer kernel
instead of trying to eliminate it before forming a quotient. A Baire
order provides an open principal convex additive hull. Multiplication
by its defining positive scale sends the quotient by finite elements
injectively into its open coset space. In discretely ordered arithmetic,
finite elements are exactly the ordinary integers. A countable open
coset space therefore leaves no room for an uncountable ring.

This resolves the project's remove-local-compactness question for
signed additive groups, strengthens it from Polish to Baire--ccc
topologies and from Borel order to the Baire property, and gives an
exact cardinal obstruction outside the separable setting. It also
identifies a purely ordered-group limitation on additive self-embeddings.
The remaining boundary is not local compactness or infinite dimension;
it is the passage from positive monoids to signed topological groups,
along with the precise regularity of order.
