\section{The research intersection and the contribution}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:intersection}

The relevant intersection is topological and effective model theory of
weak arithmetic. Glazer's paper \cite{Glazer} asks whether an
uncountable Polish space can support a model of Presburger arithmetic
with continuous addition. It also proves strong obstructions once
multiplication and suitable induction are available. The distinction
between continuous basic operations and the regularity of definable
operations is therefore mathematically consequential.

\repo\ provides two direct connections. Its Presburger project
formalizes an executable Cooper elimination procedure over the ordinary
integers, with an independent Rocq proof of the finite-residue core
\cite{s13:proveit-presburger,s13:proveit-syntax,s13:proveit-decision}. Its surreal
project develops the ordered field of surreal numbers and the omnific
integers \cite{s13:proveit-surreal}. These connections are established by
mathematical sources and actual repository material; the inaccessible
LinkedIn profile supplied in the request is not used to infer a current
appointment or professional affiliation.

\subsection{What was already in the repository}

At the inspected revision, the incoming directory contained three
related research packages. Two independently develop Polish Presburger
models \cite{s13:prior-one,s13:prior-two}; the third concerns Borel presentations
and support barriers in Hahn and omnific arithmetic \cite{s13:prior-three}.
The repository's own triage records a README-level inventory rather
than a validation of those proofs \cite{s13:repo-triage}. For this article
the three LaTeX manuscripts were extracted and read directly.

The first two packages already contain the positive cones
\[
 M_D=(D_{>0}\times\Z)\cup(\{0\}\times\N),
 \qquad D=\R\text{ or }\Q^\omega,
\]
continuous addition and fixed division, low Borel complexity of all
definable relations, examples of discontinuous definable operations,
and embedding results. The first package even classifies all
self-embeddings of its rational-stream model. Repeating these claims
would not constitute a further result for the present request.

Instead, the present work addresses their questions about nonsplit
presentations, exact discontinuity profiles, optimal finite revisions
of truth values, and complete metrics with uniform addition. The
connection to omnific arithmetic uses the repository's existing
classification: splitting over the standard integers is exactly the
obstruction to a unital additive ordered realization in $\Oz$
\cite{s13:omnific-prior}. The new models provide concrete Polish
applications of that obstruction.

\subsection{Scope of the claims}

An ``open question'' from an earlier repository manuscript means a
question that that manuscript explicitly left unresolved. It does not
assert that the question had independently become a recognized open
problem throughout the literature. The present results settle the
specified cases with proofs. They do not resolve Glazer's separate
question about the reverse-mathematical strength of his multiplication
theorem, and they do not classify arbitrary Polish topological monoids.

Several ingredients are classical: the theory of $\Z$-groups,
Presburger quantifier elimination, elementary facts about Polish
spaces, and the ordered-group universality of the surreal numbers.
These are cited where used. Their applications and the additional
arguments are supplied in full. In particular, a computational
diagnostic is never substituted for an infinitary proof.

\section{Arithmetic models and their two topologies}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:preliminaries}

We work in ordinary classical mathematics. A Polish space is separable
and admits a compatible complete metric. Unless stated otherwise, all
groups and parameter tuples are sets. The appearances of $\No$ and
$\Oz$ will be confined to embeddings with set-sized domain and image.

\subsection{Presburger groups and positive cones}

Write
\[
 \PrA_{\N}=\Th(\N;0,1,+),\qquad
 \PrA_{\Z}=\Th(\Z;0,1,+,-,<).
\]
Order is definable in the monoid language by
$x\leq y\iff\exists z\,(x+z=y)$. A \emph{$\Z$-group} is a linearly
ordered abelian group $G$ with least positive element $1_G$ such that
$G/\Z1_G$ is divisible. The classical characterization says that these
are exactly the models of $\PrA_{\Z}$; their nonnegative cones are
exactly the associated models of $\PrA_{\N}$
\cite[Section 2]{jerabek}. This includes the full first-order induction
scheme with parameters, not only the elementary equations for addition.

For every standard integer $m\geq1$ and every $g\in G$, there are
unique $q\in G$ and $r\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ such that
\begin{equation}
 g=mq+r1_G.
 \label{pma:nsp:eq:division}
\end{equation}
To see existence, divisibility of the quotient gives $g=mq_0+k1_G$;
ordinary integer division of $k$ gives the asserted remainder. For
uniqueness, if $m(q-q')=(r'-r)1_G$, convexity of the standard integers
forces $q-q'$ to be standard and the usual remainder argument applies.
If $g\geq0$, then $q\geq0$: a negative quotient would be at most $-1_G$
and would make $mq+r1_G<0$.

After congruence predicates are named, quantifier elimination reduces
each formula, uniformly over $\Z$-groups, to a finite Boolean combination
of affine inequalities, equalities, and congruences
\cite{s13:cooper,jerabek}. Transferring this theorem to a positive cone
means relativizing each quantified variable to $x\geq0$ before
elimination. No multiplication of two variables is introduced.

The word ``uniformly'' matters. A subset of a nonstandard group that is
invariant under adding a standard integer $m$ need not be invariant
under adding every member of $mG$. Presburger congruence predicates
have the latter, full-coset invariance. The earlier packages correctly
isolate that condition when adapting Cooper's finite-boundary proof
\cite{s13:prior-one,s13:prior-two}. The formal source inspected here evaluates
its syntax specifically in $\Z$; a model-uniform formalization remains
a separate task.

\subsection{The real and stream coefficient groups}

Let $D$ be either $\R$ with its usual topology and order, or
\[
 D_\omega=\Q^{\N}
\]
with each rational factor discrete. The latter carries the
first-difference lexicographic order: a nonzero sequence is positive
exactly when its first nonzero coefficient is positive. Both groups
are divisible Polish topological groups. Their strict positive and
negative cones are open; for $D_\omega$ they are countable unions of
finite-prefix cylinders.

Let $G_D=D\lex \Z$, with the $D$ coordinate dominant and
the integer coordinate discrete. Its positive cone is $M_D$ as above,
and $1=(0,1)$. The integer quotient in \eqref{pma:nsp:eq:division} is explicit:
\begin{equation}
 q_m(u,n)=\left(u/m,\left\lfloor n/m\right\rfloor\right),
 \qquad r_m(u,n)=n\bmod m.
 \label{pma:nsp:eq:splitdivision}
\end{equation}
These maps, as well as addition, are continuous in the specified
topology. We denote the real model by $\MR$ and the stream model by
$M_{\omega}$.

For clarity, the arithmetic order is not the topology being imposed.
Every arithmetic element has a successor, while zero is topologically
nonisolated. For example,
\[
 (1/j,0)\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in }\MR,
 \qquad(e_j,0)\longrightarrow0\quad\hbox{in }M_{\omega}.
\]
Here $e_j$ is the stream with a single coefficient $1$ at position $j$.
Each displayed nonzero element is greater in arithmetic order than
every standard integer. Convergence of these elements is one reason
that arithmetic order and continuous subtraction cannot be silently
assumed.

\subsection{Polishness, Baire space, and definable relations}

The cone $M_D$ is open in the closed Polish subspace
$D_{\geq0}\times\Z$: its complement there is
$\{0\}\times\Z_{<0}$, a closed set. Open subspaces of Polish spaces
are Polish. In the real model the integer slices are copies of
$[0,\infty)$ or $(0,\infty)$, so the space is perfect and locally compact.

The stream model is zero-dimensional and nowhere locally compact.
Every neighbourhood contains a closed cylinder with one positive
coordinate fixed and infinitely many free rational coordinates. Such a
cylinder is homeomorphic to $\Q^{\N}$ and cannot be compact, since a
free rational coordinate has an infinite discrete image. The standard
characterization of Baire space therefore gives
$M_{\omega}\cong\N^{\N}$ \cite{Kechris}. The earlier packages provide
explicit coding homeomorphisms as well \cite{s13:prior-one,s13:prior-two}.

Every parameter-definable relation on $M_D$ is $\Dtwo$ in this topology.
Indeed, a strict affine inequality is the union of an open leading-sign
condition and a closed leading-zero condition with a discrete integer
test. Its complement has the same form. Equalities are closed and
congruences are clopen, since $mG_D=D\times m\Z$. Quantifier elimination
then gives the claim. This background bound concerns sets and graphs;
it does not by itself prove a target-valued Baire-class bound for
functions. That distinction will become explicit below.

\noindent\writetag{} This section recalls Part~I, as source~13 says:
$M_D$ and its Polishness are \cref{pma:pr:thm:main,pma:pr:thm:criterion},
the homeomorphism $M_\omega\cong\Baire$ is \cref{pma:pr:thm:baire}, and the
$\Dtwo$ bound is \cref{pma:pr:thm:delta2,pma:pr:thm:definableborel}. Source~13's
$D_\omega=\Q^{\N}$ and $M_\omega$ are Part~I's $D_{\mathrm B}$ and $\MB$ (the
same group, order and topology); its $\mathbb Q^\omega$ is $\Q^{\N}$.



\section{A nonsplit countable arithmetic core}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:nonsplit-core}

The split constructions in the incoming reports do not exhaust the Polish
possibilities.  Nonsplit countable $\mathbb Z$-groups are classical, and the
repository already contains an explicit profinite-parameter family
\cite[section ``An explicit factorial family of nonsplit models'']{s13:omnific-prior}.  The following localization presentation is a
particularly elementary member of that family.  Its elements and its
fixed-division algorithms use ordinary rational arithmetic only.  The new
topological step below is to transfer arbitrary countable arithmetic cores
to perfect Polish universes while preserving their nonsplitting obstruction.

Put
\[
 A=\mathbb Z_{(2)}
   =\{a/b:a\in\mathbb Z,\ b\in\mathbb N_{>0}\text{ odd}\},
 \qquad
 B=\mathbb Z[1/2]
   =\{c/2^\ell:c\in\mathbb Z,\ \ell\in\mathbb N\},
\]
and let $K=A\times B$ with coordinatewise addition.  Its distinguished unit is
$e=(1,1)$.  Define
\[
 \pi:K\longrightarrow\mathbb Q,\qquad \pi(u,v)=v-u.
\]
Order $K$ by declaring
\begin{equation}
 (u,v)>_K0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 v-u>0\ \text{ or }\ (u=v\text{ and }u>0).
 \label{pma:nsp:eq:core-order}
\end{equation}
The second case involves an ordinary integer, since $A\cap B=\mathbb Z$.

\begin{proposition}[Explicit nonsplit $\mathbb Z$-group; a member of the family of \replabel{isg:cf:prop:family}]
\label{pma:nsp:prop:nonsplit-core}
The ordered group $(K,+,<_K,e)$ is a model of the ordered-group version of
Presburger arithmetic.  The sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathbb Z
 \xrightarrow{\ n\mapsto ne\ } K
 \xrightarrow{\ \pi\ }\mathbb Q
 \longrightarrow0
\]
is exact and does not split.  In fact,
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}(K,\mathbb Z)=0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Div}(K)=0,
\]
where $\operatorname{Div}(K)$ is the largest divisible subgroup.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The equality $A\cap B=\mathbb Z$ follows by writing a rational in lowest
terms: its denominator must be both odd and a power of two.  Every rational
belongs to $A+B$.  Indeed, write its denominator as $2^\ell b$ with $b$ odd,
and choose integers $s,t$ with $s2^\ell+tb=1$; then
\[
 \frac a{2^\ell b}=\frac{as}{b}+\frac{at}{2^\ell}.
\]
Replacing the first summand by its negative shows that $\pi$ is onto.
Its kernel is exactly $\mathbb Ze$.

Formula~\eqref{pma:nsp:eq:core-order} is the lexicographic extension of the usual
orders on $\mathbb Ze$ and $K/\mathbb Ze=\mathbb Q$.  It therefore defines a
translation-invariant linear order.  The subgroup $\mathbb Ze$ is convex;
$e$ is the least positive element; and the quotient is divisible.  The
standard characterization of $\mathbb Z$-groups now applies: a discretely
ordered abelian group is a Presburger group precisely when its quotient by
the subgroup generated by its least positive element is divisible
\cite[\S2]{jerabek}.

For completeness, the two assertions about homomorphisms and divisibility
are elementary.  The group $A$ is divisible by $3^j$ for every $j$.
Consequently, the image of any $a\in A$ under a homomorphism $A\to\mathbb Z$
would be divisible by every $3^j$, hence would be zero.  The same argument
with powers of two applies to $B$.  Thus every homomorphism
$K=A\times B\to\mathbb Z$ is zero.  A splitting over $\mathbb Ze$ would give
a retraction taking $e$ to $1$, which is impossible.

There is no nonzero infinitely $2$-divisible element of $A$, and no nonzero
infinitely $3$-divisible element of $B$.  For example, if $a/b\ne0$ is in
lowest terms with $b$ odd, $(a/b)/2^j$ fails to belong to $A$ for all
sufficiently large $j$.  Hence a divisible subgroup of either factor is zero.
Projection of a divisible subgroup of $K$ to either factor is divisible, so
the divisible subgroup itself is zero.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Exact relation to the repository's profinite family}

Let $\varepsilon_2\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}=\prod_p\mathbb Z_p$ have
$2$-adic coordinate $1$ and every odd-prime coordinate $0$.  The canonical
residue homomorphism of $K$ is
\[
 r_K(u,v)_2=u,\qquad r_K(u,v)_p=v\quad(p\text{ odd}),
\]
where each rational is interpreted in the indicated $p$-adic integer ring.
In particular, $r_K(-1,0)=-\varepsilon_2$.

This identifies $K$ explicitly with the repository family member
$G_{\varepsilon_2}$.  To verify the identification without any extension
classification, let $S_n$ be the ordinary residue of $\varepsilon_2$ modulo
$n!$, and put
\[
 H=\bigcup_{n\ge1}
 \left(\mathbb Z(1/n!,S_n/n!)+\mathbb Z(0,1)\right)
 \subseteq\mathbb Q\lex \mathbb Q.
\]
The map $T(u,v)=(v-u,v)$ is a unital ordered group embedding.  Writing
$n!=2^hm$ with $m$ odd, the congruences
$S_n\equiv1\pmod{2^h}$ and $S_n\equiv0\pmod m$ show that every
displayed generator of $H$ belongs to $T[K]$.  Conversely, write
$T(u,v)=(k/n!,l/n!)$ for sufficiently large $n$.  The condition
$u\in A$ gives $2^h\mid l-k$, and $v\in B$ gives $m\mid l$.
Hence $n!\mid l-kS_n$, proving
\[
 T(u,v)=k(1/n!,S_n/n!)+\frac{l-kS_n}{n!}(0,1)\in H.
\]
Thus $T[K]=H=G_{\varepsilon_2}$.  The localization presentation is a
transparent specialization of the existing family, rather than an
independent claim of algebraic priority.

\noindent\writetag{} As source~13 says, $K$ is a member of the factorial
family of the \fn{discrete-initial-subgroups-and-omnific-normalization} report:
$K\cong G_{\varepsilon_2}$ in the notation of \replabel{isg:cf:prop:family}, and
its nonsplitting is the case $\zeta=\varepsilon_2\notin\Z$ of
\replabel{isg:cf:thm:familytest}. The localization coordinates and the
fixed-division algorithm below are source~13's.

\subsection{An exact fixed-division algorithm}

Let $n\ge1$, and write $n=2^km$ with $m$ odd.  For an input
$x=(u,v)\in K$, choose presentations
\[
 u=\frac ab\quad(b\text{ odd}),\qquad
 v=\frac c{2^\ell}.
\]
There is a unique integer $r\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 r&\equiv a b^{-1}\pmod{2^k},\\
 r&\equiv c(2^\ell)^{-1}\pmod m.
 \end{split}
 \label{pma:nsp:eq:core-crt}
\end{equation}
Congruences modulo $1$ impose no condition.  Both indicated inverses exist,
and the Chinese remainder theorem gives $r$.  Define
\begin{equation}
 q_n^K(u,v)=\left(\frac{u-r}{n},\frac{v-r}{n}\right),
 \qquad r_n^K(u,v)=r.
 \label{pma:nsp:eq:core-division}
\end{equation}
Then $q_n^K(u,v)\in K$ and
\[
 (u,v)=nq_n^K(u,v)+r e.
\]
The first congruence in~\eqref{pma:nsp:eq:core-crt} removes exactly the forbidden
power-of-two factor from the denominator of $(u-r)/n$; the second removes
exactly the forbidden odd factor from the denominator of $(v-r)/n$.
Conversely, membership of both quotient coordinates in $A$ and $B$ forces
these two congruences.  This also proves uniqueness of $q$ and $r$ directly.

If $x\ge_K0$, then $q_n^K(x)\ge_K0$.  If $\pi(x)>0$, use
$\pi(q_n^K(x))=\pi(x)/n>0$.  If $\pi(x)=0$, then $x=te$ with an integer
$t\ge0$, and the formula reduces to ordinary Euclidean division of $t$.
Thus this is also the fixed-division algorithm for the nonnegative cone.

\section{Transferring every countable core to a perfect Polish universe}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:countable-core-transfer}

The preceding core can be replaced by any countable Presburger group.  Let
$(K,+,<,e)$ be such a group, equipped with its discrete topology, and let
$D$ be either
\[
 D=\mathbb R\quad\text{with its usual topology},
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 D=\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N}\quad\text{with its product of discrete topologies}.
\]
In the second case, order $D$ lexicographically at the first differing
coordinate.  Let
\[
 G=D\lex K,
 \qquad 1_G=(0,e),
 \qquad P=G_{\ge0},
\]
and give $G$ the product topology.  Its nonnegative cone is
\begin{equation}
 P=(D_{>0}\times K)\ \cup\ (\{0\}\times K_{\ge0}).
 \label{pma:nsp:eq:transferred-cone}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Countable-core transfer]
\label{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}
The ordered group $G$ is a $\mathbb Z$-group, and $P$ is an uncountable
Presburger model with continuous addition.  The space $P$ is perfect and
Polish.  It is locally compact when $D=\mathbb R$, and is homeomorphic to
Baire space when $D=\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N}$.

All fixed standard quotient and remainder functions on $P$ are continuous.
Every Presburger-definable relation on any finite power of $P$ is Borel;
indeed, it belongs to $\boldsymbol\Delta^0_2$ in these two presentations.
The map $k\mapsto(0,k)$ embeds $K$ as a closed discrete elementary
substructure of $G$.

There is a unit-preserving homomorphism $G\to\mathbb Z$ if and only if there
is one $K\to\mathbb Z$.  In particular, taking the core of
Proposition~\ref{pma:nsp:prop:nonsplit-core} gives nonsplit models in both topological
types, and their largest divisible subgroup is exactly $D\times\{0\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The element $(0,e)$ is least positive.  The quotient by its integer multiples
is $D\oplus(K/\mathbb Ze)$, which is divisible.  This proves the arithmetic
claim by the characterization of $\mathbb Z$-groups.

Both choices of $D$ are Polish topological groups.  For both, $D_{>0}$ is
open and $D_{\ge0}$ is closed.  For rational streams, a nonzero sequence's
sign is fixed by its first nonzero coordinate, which proves the open-cone
assertion.  The slice of $P$ at a fixed $k\in K$ is $D_{\ge0}$ when $k\ge0$,
and $D_{>0}$ when $k<0$.  It is therefore Polish, and $P$ is a countable
topological disjoint union of Polish spaces, hence Polish.  Equivalently,
$P$ is a $G_\delta$ subset of $D\times K$.  It need not be closed there:
if $k<0$, positive $d_j\to0$ give $(d_j,k)\in P$ converging in $G$ to
$(0,k)\notin P$.  No completeness claim is made for the restriction of the
ambient product metric.

Addition is the restriction of the continuous group addition on $G$.
Every point of either cone $D_{\ge0}$ or $D_{>0}$ is nonisolated.  This is
immediate for $\mathbb R$; for rational streams, one can change a sufficiently
late coordinate while preserving every prescribed initial coordinate and,
when necessary, keep the first nonzero coordinate positive.  Hence $P$ is
perfect and uncountable.

For $D=\mathbb R$, the slices are $[0,\infty)$ and $(0,\infty)$, so $P$ is
locally compact.  For rational streams, the slices, and hence $P$, are
zero-dimensional.  No nonempty open subset of $P$ is compact: inside every
nonempty basic neighborhood one can find a closed cylinder in which a
later rational coordinate is unrestricted; its projection onto the
infinite discrete space $\mathbb Q$ is onto, contradicting compactness.
For clarity at the all-zero stream, first choose a sufficiently late
coordinate to be $1$, then leave a still later coordinate unrestricted.
Thus $P$ is nowhere locally compact.  The classical characterization of
Baire space as the nonempty zero-dimensional Polish space with no nonempty
compact open subsets yields $P\cong\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}$.

Write $k=nq_n^K(k)+r_n^K(k)e$, with $0\le r_n^K(k)<n$.  On $G$ set
\[
 q_n^G(d,k)=(d/n,q_n^K(k)),\qquad r_n^G(d,k)=r_n^K(k).
\]
These are continuous, since division by $n$ is continuous on $D$ and every
map from the discrete factor $K$ is continuous.  For a nonnegative input,
the quotient remains nonnegative, by the sign of $d/n$ when $d>0$ and by
the ordinary Presburger division axiom in $K$ when $d=0$.  Restriction gives
the desired maps on $P$.

The strict order on $G$ is
\[
 (d,k)<(d',k')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 d<d'\ \text{ or }\ (d=d'\text{ and }k<k').
\]
The first condition is open; the equality condition is closed; and the
condition on the discrete coordinates is clopen.  Hence the order is
$\boldsymbol\Delta^0_2$.  Linear equality is closed, congruence modulo each
standard $n$ is clopen, and integer-affine maps are continuous.  Presburger
quantifier elimination expresses every definable relation as a finite
Boolean combination of these atomic relations
\cite[\S2]{jerabek}.  Finite Boolean combinations of
$\boldsymbol\Delta^0_2$ sets remain $\boldsymbol\Delta^0_2$.  Restricting to
the cone and its finite powers preserves the conclusion.  This argument
concerns definable sets, and by itself does not assert a target-valued Baire
class for every definable function.

The copy $\{0\}\times K$ is closed and discrete.  It is elementary because
it is itself a unit-containing $\mathbb Z$-subgroup, or directly by the same
quantifier elimination.  Finally, every homomorphism $D\to\mathbb Z$ is zero
because $D$ is divisible.  Thus any unit-preserving homomorphism
$G\to\mathbb Z$ restricts to one on $K$, and any such map on $K$ extends by
zero on $D$.  For the explicit reduced core, projecting a divisible subgroup
of $G$ to $K$ gives zero, while $D\times\{0\}$ is divisible.  This proves the
last assertion.
\end{proof}

The transfer is algebraically nonsplit over the distinguished standard
$\mathbb Z$, although it is deliberately a product with a discrete
\emph{countable core}.  These two statements are compatible.  Confusing
them would erase exactly the distinction resolved by the construction.


\noindent\writetag{} \textbf{One construction in three sources.} With
$D=\R$ and a countable nonsplit core, \cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}
is the construction of source~14's \cref{pma:atr:prop:polish-D}
(\cref{pma:part:atr}), whose core $K_*$ is the member $G_{\zeta_*}$ of the
same factorial family, and of source~15's \cref{pma:lcc:thm:boundary-realization}
(\cref{pma:part:lcc}), whose core is the difference group of an arbitrary
countable Presburger model. The construction is printed here, once, in its
general form; Parts~VIII and~IX print those two statements with their own
proofs, flagged as instances, because they add the omnific obstruction and the
boundary identification respectively. With
\cref{pma:nsp:thm:polish-group-unit-splitting} below, the theorem answers the
existence half of Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:beyondsplit} and, for countable
cores, Part~III's \cref{pma:cp:q:nonsplit}: every ordered extension
$0\to\Z\to G\to D\oplus(K/\Z)\to0$ obtained from a countable nonsplit
$\Z$-group $K$ has a Polish positive cone with continuous addition. Neither
question asks only for existence, and neither classification is attempted.
\subsection{Continuum many topological examples}

\begin{corollary}[Many nonsplit Polish arithmetic structures]
\label{pma:nsp:cor:continuum-polish-cores}
There are $2^{\aleph_0}$ pairwise nonisomorphic Presburger structures on
locally compact perfect Polish spaces having continuous addition and every
standard fixed-division operation, with no retraction onto the standard
integers.  There are likewise $2^{\aleph_0}$ such structures whose
underlying spaces are homeomorphic to Baire space.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Use the countable cores $G_\zeta$ from the repository's factorial family,
with $\zeta\in\widehat{\mathbb Z}\setminus\mathbb Z$, and apply
Theorem~\ref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}.  The family has
$2^{\aleph_0}$ extension classes modulo endpoint-preserving isomorphism:
the parameters $\zeta,\eta$ define the same such class exactly when
$\zeta-\eta\in\mathbb Z$.  Every nonsplit core is reduced, meaning that
its largest divisible subgroup is zero
\cite[section ``An explicit factorial family of nonsplit models'']{s13:omnific-prior}.

For either fixed choice of $D$, the maximal divisible subgroup of
$D\lex G_\zeta$ is $D\times\{0\}$.  Thus a unital
group isomorphism between two transferred groups would induce a unital
\emph{abstract group} isomorphism between their reduced quotients
$G_\zeta$ and $G_\eta$.  Such an isomorphism induces multiplication by
some nonzero rational on the quotient $\mathbb Q$ of the cores.  There
are only countably many possibilities.  For each such quotient map,
at most one endpoint-marked extension class is possible: comparing two
isomorphisms with the same quotient map gives an endpoint-preserving
isomorphism between their targets.  Consequently, each abstract unital
group isomorphism type accounts for at most countably many marked
extension classes, leaving $2^{\aleph_0}$ different transferred types.
An isomorphism of positive cones would extend to their Grothendieck
groups, so the same conclusion holds for the Presburger monoids.

Only an abstract quotient by the maximal divisible subgroup is used in
this argument.  That subgroup need not be convex, and no ordered quotient
by it is asserted.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} By source~15's \cref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones}
(\cref{pma:part:lcc}), the locally compact models of this corollary all live on
the one space $X_{\mathrm{lc}}$; source~15's
\cref{pma:lcc:thm:continuum-lc-models} gives $2^{\aleph_0}$ split models on
that space with standard boundary. The two continuum families are disjoint:
one is nonsplit, the other split.



\section{Canonical residues and automatic topological splitting}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:splitting}
The algebraic criterion recalled below is already present in \repo\ \cite{s13:omnific-prior}; the residue kernel is standard \cite{jerabek}. The topological consequences are developed separately.


In this section $G$ is a $\mathbb Z$-group: a discretely ordered
abelian group with named least positive element $1_G$ such that
$G/\mathbb Z1_G$ is divisible.  Standard division with remainder
gives, for every integer $m\geq1$, a homomorphism
\[
 r_m:G\longrightarrow\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z,
 \qquad r_m(1_G)=1,
\]
whose kernel is $mG$.  The maps are compatible, giving the canonical
residue homomorphism
\[
 r:G\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathbb Z}
       =\varprojlim_m\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z.
\]
Let
\[
 D=\ker r=\bigcap_{m\geq1}mG.
\]

\begin{lemma}[The divisible kernel]
\label{pma:nsp:lem:divisible-kernel}
The group $D$ is the largest divisible subgroup of $G$, and
$D\cap\mathbb Z1_G=\{0\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The group $G$ is torsion-free.  If $x\in D$ and $m\geq1$, there
is a unique $y\in G$ with $my=x$.  For every $n\geq1$, choose
$z\in G$ with $mnz=x$.  Cancellation gives $y=nz$, so
$y\in\bigcap_n nG=D$.  Hence $D$ is divisible.  Conversely, every
divisible subgroup lies in each $mG$, and therefore in $D$.
If $k1_G\in D$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$, then $m$ divides $k$ for
every standard positive $m$, which forces $k=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Algebraic splitting criterion; part of \replabel{isg:cf:main:presburger}]
\label{pma:nsp:thm:algebraic-unit-splitting}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is a group homomorphism
      $\rho:G\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$ with $\rho(1_G)=1$.
\item $G=D\oplus\mathbb Z1_G$ as abelian groups.
\item $r(G)$ is precisely the standard diagonal copy of
      $\mathbb Z$ in $\widehat{\mathbb Z}$.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, $\rho$ is unique, its kernel is $D$,
and the group decomposition is lexicographic for the induced order
on $D$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume (1) and put $K=\ker\rho$.  The map
$k\mapsto k+\mathbb Z1_G$ is an isomorphism
$K\cong G/\mathbb Z1_G$: subtracting $\rho(g)1_G$ from $g$
proves surjectivity, and the intersection is trivial because
$\rho(1_G)=1$.  The quotient is divisible, so $K$ is divisible
and $K\subseteq D$.  Conversely, every homomorphism from a
divisible group to $\mathbb Z$ is zero, so $D\subseteq K$.
Thus $K=D$, proving (2).

Assume (2).  Every $d\in D$ has zero residue modulo every $m$,
so $r(d+k1_G)=r(k1_G)$.  Since all standard integer elements
occur, this proves (3).

Assume (3).  For each $g\in G$, there is a unique standard
$k\in\mathbb Z$ with $r(g)=r(k1_G)$.  Define $\rho(g)=k$.
Injectivity of the diagonal map $\mathbb Z\to\widehat{\mathbb Z}$
and the homomorphism property of $r$ show that $\rho$ is a
homomorphism with $\rho(1_G)=1$.  This proves (1).

Every such retraction vanishes on $D$ and fixes the integer
summand, so it is unique.  Finally, $\mathbb Z1_G$ is convex in
$G$.  Any nonzero element of $D$ lies outside this convex
subgroup, and its sign is unchanged by adding a standard integer.
Thus the decomposition has the order of
$D\lex \mathbb Z$.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:nsp:thm:algebraic-unit-splitting} is part of
\replabel{isg:cf:main:presburger}, as the opening sentence of this section
says; \cref{pma:nsp:lem:continuous-residues-polish-group} and
\cref{pma:nsp:thm:polish-group-unit-splitting} are new.

\subsection{Automatic continuity in Polish topological groups}

The next theorem assumes a \emph{group} topology: addition and
inversion on the entire signed group $G$ are continuous.  It is
not a theorem about an arbitrary topology on the positive monoid.
No Borelness or compatibility assumption for the arithmetic order
is needed in this theorem.

\begin{lemma}[Finite residues are automatically continuous]
\label{pma:nsp:lem:continuous-residues-polish-group}
If a $\mathbb Z$-group $G$ carries a Polish group topology, every
$mG$ is open and closed, every $r_m$ is continuous, $r$ is
continuous, and $D$ is a closed Polish subgroup.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The map $g\mapsto mg$ is continuous, so its image $mG$ is
analytic and has the Baire property.  There are exactly $m$
cosets, represented by $0,1_G,\ldots,(m-1)1_G$.  The Baire
category theorem implies that $mG$ is nonmeagre.

For completeness, a subgroup $A$ of a Polish group which has the
Baire property and is nonmeagre is open.  There is a nonempty
open set $V$ on which $A$ is comeagre.  For all sufficiently
small $u$, the open overlap $V\cap(u+V)$ is nonempty.
On that overlap, $A$ and $u+A$ are both comeagre, hence
intersect.  Thus $u\in A-A=A$, proving that $A$ contains a
neighbourhood of $0$.  Apply this fact to $A=mG$.

An open subgroup is also closed, since its other cosets are open.
The fibres of $r_m$ are these open cosets, proving continuity.
The inverse-limit map $r$ is continuous because all its
coordinates are continuous.  Its kernel $D$ is closed; a closed
subgroup of a Polish group is Polish.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Topological splitting criterion]
\label{pma:nsp:thm:polish-group-unit-splitting}
Let $G$ be a $\mathbb Z$-group carrying a Polish group topology.
The conditions of Theorem~\ref{pma:nsp:thm:algebraic-unit-splitting}
are equivalent to the existence of a continuous unit-preserving
retraction $\rho:G\to\mathbb Z$, where $\mathbb Z$ is discrete.
When they hold, the canonical map
\[
 D\times\mathbb Z\longrightarrow G,
 \qquad(d,k)\longmapsto d+k1_G
\]
is a topological group isomorphism and an isomorphism of the
corresponding lexicographically ordered groups.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Only automatic continuity and the topological assertion require
proof.  Under algebraic splitting, $D$ is closed by
Lemma~\ref{pma:nsp:lem:continuous-residues-polish-group}, and its cosets
$D+k1_G$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, cover $G$.  If $D$ had empty
interior, every such closed coset would be nowhere dense,
contradicting the Baire category theorem.  Thus $D$ is open.
Its cosets are the fibres of $\rho$, so $\rho$ is continuous
into discrete $\mathbb Z$.  The displayed map is continuous,
and its inverse is
\[
 g\longmapsto(g-\rho(g)1_G,\rho(g)),
\]
which is continuous.  The order statement is already proved in
Theorem~\ref{pma:nsp:thm:algebraic-unit-splitting}.
\end{proof}

In particular, every positive cone with the topology inherited
from a Polish topological $\mathbb Z$-group has continuous fixed
residues.  Since each residue class occurs, such a cone is
disconnected (already reduction modulo $2$ gives a nontrivial
clopen partition).  This does not settle the connected-universe
question for arbitrary Polish monoids with continuous addition:
one would first need an appropriate Polish group completion.

\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) This settles Part~I's
\cref{pma:pr:q:connected} and Part~III's \cref{pma:cp:q:connected} negatively
for cones whose topology is inherited from a Polish topological $\Z$-group:
such a cone is disconnected. Source~15's
\cref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones} gives the locally compact case
again, with the exact carrier. For a topology on the cone alone both
questions stay open, as source~13 says.

\subsection{Compatibility with the nonsplit example}

The nonsplit construction with
$L=\mathbb Z_{(2)}\times\mathbb Z[1/2]$ and diagonal unit
$e=(1,1)$ is consistent with all of these conclusions.  In
$G=\mathbb Q^\omega\lex L$, with $L$ discrete,
the maximal divisible subgroup is
$D=\mathbb Q^\omega\times\{0\}$.  It is clopen.  Its quotient
is the countable discrete group $L$, rather than $\mathbb Z$.
The finite residue maps are continuous, but their coherent
values cannot be represented by a single standard integer for
every element.  The failure of an integer-coordinate retraction
is algebraic, not a failure of continuity of individual residues.



\section{The existing omnific criterion and its new Polish applications}
The equivalence in this section is recalled from \cite[Presburger initiality criterion and unit-preserving omnific embeddings]{s13:omnific-prior}, which proves a stronger result about initial images. It is not claimed as a new theorem here. The normal-form proof below is included to make the application independent of that stronger initiality machinery.

\label{pma:nsp:sec:omnific-criterion}

The following equivalence is included as background and an independently
checkable explanation of the obstruction, not as a new classification.
The repository manuscript \cite{s13:omnific-prior}, theorem labelled
\texttt{isg:cf:main:presburger}, already proves a stronger criterion with
\emph{initial} realizations in $\mathbf{No}$ and $\mathbf{Oz}$.  Here we need
only ordered additive embeddability, and the sufficiency proof uses a common
monomial shift instead of initial-realization theory.

An omnific integer has a Conway normal form whose exponents are
nonnegative and whose coefficient at exponent zero is an ordinary integer
\cite[Section 6]{EhrlichKaplan}.  Denote its constant coefficient by
\[
 c_0:\mathbf{Oz}\longrightarrow\mathbb Z.
\]
Normal-form addition is coefficientwise, so $c_0$ is additive and
$c_0(1)=1$.  In fact it is a unital ring homomorphism: a sum of two
nonnegative exponents is zero only when both are zero.  Only its additive
property is needed below.  No continuity or measurability of $c_0$ is
assumed.

\begin{lemma}[Moving a set-sized group into purely infinite surreals]
\label{pma:nsp:lem:purely-infinite-copy}
Every set-sized divisible ordered abelian group $D$ admits an ordered
additive embedding into the group of purely infinite omnific integers.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Use the standard embedding theorem that every divisible ordered abelian
group has an isomorphic copy as an ordered additive subgroup of
$\mathbf{No}$; the stronger initial-subgroup result is recalled in
\cite[Introduction]{EhrlichKaplan}.  Let $i:D\to\mathbf{No}$ be such an
embedding.  Since $D$ is a set and every surreal has a set-sized Conway
support, the union
\[
 S=\bigcup_{d\in D}\operatorname{supp}(i(d))
\]
is a set of surreal exponents.  Choose a surreal $\beta$ satisfying
\[
 \beta>0,\qquad \beta>-s\quad(s\in S).
\]
For example, the surreal cut $\{\{0\}\cup\{-s:s\in S\}\mid\varnothing\}$
has this property.  Multiplication by the positive monomial $\omega^\beta$
shifts every exponent $s$ to $\beta+s>0$.  Thus
\[
 j(d)=\omega^\beta i(d)
\]
has only strictly positive exponents, is an omnific integer, and has zero
constant coefficient.  Multiplication by a fixed positive surreal preserves
addition and strict order, so $j$ is the desired embedding.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Omnific criterion, recalled; \replabel{isg:cf:main:presburger}, \replabel{isg:cf:cor:unit}]
\label{pma:nsp:thm:omnific-criterion}
Let $G$ be a set-sized $\mathbb Z$-group with least positive element $1$.
The following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is a unital additive homomorphism $G\to\mathbf{Oz}$, with no
      assumption of injectivity or order preservation.
\item There is a unital ordered additive embedding $G\hookrightarrow
      \mathbf{Oz}$.
\item There is an additive retraction $\rho:G\to\mathbb Z$ with
      $\rho(1)=1$.
\item $G$ is isomorphic, as an ordered group with distinguished unit, to
      $D\lex \mathbb Z$ for some divisible ordered abelian
      group $D$.
\item The canonical residue homomorphism
      $r:G\to\widehat{\mathbb Z}$ has image exactly the standard diagonal
      copy of $\mathbb Z$.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, the retraction is unique and $\ker\rho$ is the
largest divisible subgroup of $G$.  The same conditions characterize the
existence of a unital additive homomorphism from $G_{\ge0}$ to
$\mathbf{Oz}$, or of a unital ordered additive embedding from $G_{\ge0}$
to $\mathbf{Oz}_{\ge0}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Condition (ii) implies (i).  If $f$ witnesses (i), then $\rho=c_0\circ f$
witnesses (iii).

Suppose (iii).  Algebraically,
\[
 G=\ker\rho\oplus\mathbb Z1,
 \qquad g=(g-\rho(g)1)+\rho(g)1.
\]
The kernel $D=\ker\rho$ is divisible.  One can see this from
$D\cong G/\mathbb Z1$, or directly as follows.  If
$d=nq+s1$ with $0\le s<n$, then $0=n\rho(q)+s$, so $s=0$ and $\rho(q)=0$.
Thus $d/n\in D$.

Every nonzero $d\in D$ is larger in absolute value than every standard
integer.  Otherwise, discreteness and a finite induction would place $d$
in $\mathbb Z1$, contradicting $D\cap\mathbb Z1=0$.  Consequently the sign
of $d+n1$ for $d\ne0$ is the sign of $d$.  This proves that the displayed
algebraic decomposition has the lexicographic order required in (iv).

Suppose (iv).  Choose $j:D\to\mathbf{Oz}$ as in
Lemma~\ref{pma:nsp:lem:purely-infinite-copy}.  Then
\[
 f(d,n)=j(d)+n
\]
is additive and preserves the unit.  Its nonzero purely infinite part
dominates every integer, so it is an ordered embedding.  This proves (ii).

For the residue formulation, recall that for each standard $n>0$ there is
a unique homomorphism $r_n:G\to\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ taking $1$ to $1$;
the compatible system forms $r:G\to\widehat{\mathbb Z}$
\cite[\S2]{jerabek}.  If (iii) holds, uniqueness gives
$r_n(g)=\rho(g)\bmod n$, so $r(G)$ is exactly diagonal $\mathbb Z$.
Conversely, under (v), define $\rho(g)$ to be the unique integer whose
diagonal residue is $r(g)$.  This is the required additive retraction.

Two retractions differ by a homomorphism vanishing on $\mathbb Z1$.
Their difference therefore factors through the divisible group
$G/\mathbb Z1$, and every homomorphism from a divisible group to
$\mathbb Z$ is zero.  This proves uniqueness.  A divisible subgroup of
$G$ is killed by $\rho$; since the kernel itself is divisible, it is
the largest one.

Finally, $G$ is the Grothendieck group of its nonnegative cone.  An additive
map from the cone to the additive group of $\mathbf{Oz}$ extends uniquely
by $\widetilde f(a-b)=f(a)-f(b)$; this is well defined because
$a-b=a'-b'$ implies $a+b'=a'+b$.  Thus a unital cone homomorphism implies
(i).  Conversely, the ordered embedding constructed above restricts to an
ordered embedding of the cones.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} The equivalence of (i), (ii) and~(iii) is
\replabel{isg:cf:cor:unit}, and (iii)$\Leftrightarrow$(iv)$\Leftrightarrow$(v)
is contained in \replabel{isg:cf:main:presburger}; source~13 recalls them and
supplies a direct normal-form proof.

\subsection{A two-element certificate excluding even a homomorphism}

For the explicit core, the failure is visible without any abstract
decomposition.  In its nonnegative cone put
\[
 x=(-1,0),\qquad y=(0,1)=x+e.
\]
Both are positive because $\pi(x)=\pi(y)=1$.  The element $x$ is divisible
in the positive cone by $3^j$ for every $j$, with quotient
$(-3^{-j},0)$; the element $y$ is divisible there by $2^j$ for every $j$,
with quotient $(0,2^{-j})$.

Suppose a unital additive map $f:K_{\ge0}\to\mathbf{Oz}$ existed.  The
integer $c_0(f(x))$ would be divisible by every $3^j$, so it would be zero.
Similarly, $c_0(f(y))=0$.  But $y=x+e$ would give
\[
 0=c_0(f(y))=c_0(f(x))+c_0(f(e))=0+1,
\]
a contradiction.  These same two points, placed in the fiber $D=0$, prove
the obstruction for both perfect Polish models of
Theorem~\ref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}.  In particular, neither a
different topology nor a loss of injectivity can repair the unital
additive embedding problem.

\subsection{The precise set/class boundary}

The theorem does not quantify over a set of all surreal numbers.  It can be
read in a conservative class framework such as NBG with the usual surreal
construction, while $G$, $D$, $i[D]$, and $S$ in the proof are sets.  In a
set-theoretic coding, surreal numbers are set-sized sign sequences and the
embedding has a set-sized graph.  Replacement bounds the birthdays of its
image and the supports occurring in the proof by a suitable ordinal.
The cut defining $\beta$ has set-sized left and right sides, so it is a
legitimate surreal cut.  After construction, all elements of the final
embedded group also belong to a sufficiently large set-sized birthday
stage.  No assertion that the whole proper class carries a Polish topology
is involved.

The set-size hypothesis is used decisively when taking the union of all
supports and choosing a common monomial shift.  This proof does not provide
the same conclusion for arbitrary proper-class groups.  It also proves an
additive and order-theoretic criterion only.  The embedding produced by
multiplying a group copy by one monomial is not asserted to preserve a
multiplication operation or to have an initial image in the simplicity
tree.

\subsection{Relation to the incoming research questions}

The countable-core transfer answers the existence part of the incoming
``beyond split topological models'' question.  It supplies explicit
uncountable Polish examples with continuous fixed divisions for which no
integer-coordinate retraction exists at all.  The omnific criterion
identifies exactly why the incoming additive realizations inside
$\mathbf{Oz}$ cannot cover these examples: preserving the standard unit
forces the entire coherent residue system to come from one ordinary
integer.  Thus the obstruction is algebraic and persists before imposing
any regularity on a proposed embedding.

The countable nonsplit algebra and the general omnific criterion have
explicit prior counterparts in the repository.  The contribution proposed
here is their transfer to perfect Polish models, together with elementary
CRT coordinates and a short divisibility certificate.  The searches
recorded for this project do not establish historical priority in the entire
literature.

\noindent\writetag{} The ``incoming `beyond split topological models'
question'' is Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:beyondsplit}; the existence half is
answered here, the characterization asked for there is not.




\section{Finite continuous branches for every definable function}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:branches}
Finite affine descriptions of Presburger functions are classical; see \cite{Cluckers}. We prove the precise candidate form needed for the topological arguments, directly from quantifier elimination.


Let $D$ be a divisible ordered abelian group, and put
$G(D)=D\lex \mathbb Z$, with positive cone $M(D)$.
Write $q_m$ for Euclidean quotient by a positive standard integer $m$:
\[
 q_m(d,n)=\left(\frac d m,\left\lfloor\frac n m\right\rfloor\right).
\]
For the two topological models $D=\mathbb R$ and
$D=\mathbb Q^\omega$, every $q_m:G(D)\to G(D)$ is continuous.
Parameters are held fixed unless they are explicitly made variables.

\begin{theorem}[Finite continuous branches]\label{pma:nsp:thm:finite-branches}

Every Presburger-definable total function
$f:M(D)^k\to M(D)^r$, with a finite parameter tuple $a$, admits a finite
definable partition $C_1,\ldots,C_s$ of its domain and candidate maps
$F_j:G(D)^k\to G(D)^r$ such that $f=F_j$ on $C_j$. Each coordinate of
each candidate has the form
\[
 q_m\left(c+\sum_i b_i x_i+\sum_t c_t a_t\right),
 \qquad m\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\quad b_i,c_t\in\mathbb Z,
 \quad c\in\mathbb Z\mathbf1.
\tag{B1}
\]
The candidates and partition are obtainable by a finite syntactic
procedure from a formula for the graph. The same assertion holds with
arbitrary ambient inputs $G(D)^k$ provided the output is still in $M(D)^r$.
In the two topological models every candidate is continuous into the
ambient group. A candidate need not be $M(D)$-valued outside its own cell.

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}

First take a single output variable $y$. Relativize the original formula
to the ordered group and eliminate quantifiers. Conjoin $y\geq0$ and
put the resulting formula into disjunctive normal form. Replace an
equality by two inequalities, a disequality by a disjunction of strict
inequalities, and strict inequalities by weak inequalities with a unit
shift. Each disjunct is a conjunction of linear inequalities, congruence
conditions, and negated congruence conditions.

For a particular disjunct, take $L$ to be a common positive multiple of
the absolute values of all its nonzero coefficients of $y$, with
$L=1$ if needed. Substitute $u=Ly$ and add $L\mid u$. Multiplying an
inequality by a positive standard integer makes its coefficient of $u$
equal to $1$ or $-1$. A congruence with nonzero coefficient $b$ is
transformed using
\[
 d\mid (by+t)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 d\frac{L}{|b|}\mid
 \left(\operatorname{sgn}(b)u+\frac{L}{|b|}t\right).
\tag{B2}
\]
This equivalence follows by torsion-freeness from
$d\mid w\Longleftrightarrow cd\mid cw$ for positive standard $c$.
Terms independent of $u$ are left unchanged.

Let $m$ be a common multiple of $L$ and all transformed moduli. Split
into the finitely many standard residues $u\equiv r\pmod m$.
Within one such residue, all congruence literals reduce to conditions
on the inputs and parameters. The remaining constraints on $u$ have
the form
\[
 u\geq b_1,\ldots,u\geq b_p,\qquad
 u\leq c_1,\ldots,u\leq c_q,\qquad u\equiv r\pmod m,
\tag{B3}
\]
where all $b_i,c_i$ are affine group terms. The lower-bound list is
nonempty because $y\geq0$ supplied $u\geq0$.

Fix an input for which this disjunct has a solution. Let
$B=\max_i b_i$, and let $s\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ be the unique standard
integer such that $B+s\equiv r\pmod m$. Then $u_0=B+s$ is the least
element of this residue class above $B$. To check this in an arbitrary
nonstandard group, if $u\geq B$ has the same residue, write
$u=B+s+mv$. If $v<0$, discrete order gives $v\leq-1$, hence
$u\leq B+s-m<B$, a contradiction. Thus $u\geq u_0$.
Because some solution satisfies the upper bounds, so does $u_0$.
It therefore satisfies the entire disjunct. Since that disjunct lies
inside the graph of a function, its solution is unique, and the value
of $y$ is exactly $q_L(B+s)$. The expression $B$ is one of the finitely
many terms $b_i$, and $s$ belongs to a finite standard set. Enumerating
all such possibilities over all disjuncts gives the candidates (B1).

For vector outputs, apply this argument to each coordinate graph,
obtained by existentially quantifying the other coordinates, and take
finite products of candidate lists. To make a partition, assign an
input to the first candidate which satisfies the original graph. This
is a finite definable partition: quotient functions are themselves
Presburger definable, so their use here can be eliminated from formulas.
Continuity of the candidates follows from continuity of affine group
maps and of $q_m$. \end{proof}

\paragraph{Audit of the nonstandard step.}
The proof used the least element of a fixed congruence class above a
given bound, explicitly justified from division and discrete order.
It did not use an iteration of successor a nonstandard number of times,
or infer invariance modulo $mG$ from invariance under one standard
translation. This is the distinction highlighted in the archived
manuscripts' finite-residue proofs.




\section{An exact compiler for continuity loci}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:continuity}

Let $D$ denote either $\mathbb R$ with its usual topology and order, or
$\mathbb Q^\omega$ with its product-of-discrete topology and lexicographic
order. Put
\[
 G=D\lex \mathbb Z,
 \qquad M=G_{\geq0}
   =(D_{>0}\times\mathbb Z)\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb N).
\]
Coordinates of an input tuple are written
$x=(u,n)\in M^k$, where $u\in D^k$ and $n\in\mathbb Z^k$.
All definability below means Presburger definability, with a fixed finite
tuple of parameters, unless an expanded coordinate language is explicitly
specified. Coordinate projections themselves are not presumed to be
Presburger definable.

We use the finite-branch normal form: a definable total map
$f:M^k\longrightarrow M^r$ admits a finite definable partition
$C_1,\dots,C_s$ and maps $F_1,\dots,F_s:G^k\longrightarrow G^r$ such that
$f|_{C_j}=F_j|_{C_j}$ and each $F_j$ is continuous. Its $D$-coordinates
are rational-affine expressions in $u$; its integer coordinates are
integer parts of rational-affine expressions in $n$, with any needed
fixed residue partition absorbed into $C_j$. The extensions $F_j$ need
not have values in $M$ away from $C_j$. This causes no problem for the
continuity criterion, which compares limits in the ambient Hausdorff
group $G^r$.

Apply quantifier elimination to the cells. List their affine group forms
as
\[
 L_i(u,n)=\bigl(\ell_i(u),z_i(n)\bigr),\qquad
 \ell_i(u)=a_i\cdot u+b_i,\quad i=1,\dots,t.
\]
Here $a_i\in\mathbb Q^k$, $b_i\in D$ is a rational-linear combination of
parameter coordinates, and after clearing denominators $z_i$ is an
integer-affine expression. Atomic formulas compare $L_i$ with zero or
test an integer congruence. When $\ell_i(u)\neq0$, the sign of $L_i$ is
the sign of $\ell_i(u)$. When $\ell_i(u)=0$, it is the sign of $z_i(n)$.
An equality $L_i=0$ requires both coordinates to vanish. A congruence
depends only on integer coordinates.

\subsection{Rational directions describe all local sign possibilities}

Fix $x=(u,n)\in M^k$. The integer tuple $n$ is constant on a neighbourhood
of $x$. Let
\[
 I(x)=\{i:\ell_i(u)=0\},\qquad
 B(x)=\{q:u_q=0\}.
\]
For $i\notin I(x)$, the sign of $\ell_i$ is locally constant. For
$i\in I(x)$, a perturbation $\delta\in D^k$ changes its value to
$a_i\cdot\delta$. The only local domain restrictions are
$\delta_q\geq0$ for $q\in B(x)$: an input with zero $D$-coordinate has
nonnegative integer coordinate, and may move to zero or positive
$D$-coordinate, but not to negative $D$-coordinate.

\begin{lemma}[Rational directions suffice]\label{pma:nsp:lem:rational-directions}

A finite pattern of signs of the forms $a_i\cdot\delta$, together with
the restrictions $\delta_q\geq0$ for $q\in B(x)$, is realizable in
$D^k$ if and only if it is realizable by a rational vector
$v\in\mathbb Q^k$.

\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
 For $D=\mathbb R$, the conditions are a finite homogeneous
system of rational linear equalities, strict inequalities, and weak
inequalities. A nonempty rational polyhedral relatively open region
contains a rational point. More explicitly, solve the equality subsystem
over $\mathbb Q$, restrict to its rational basis, and approximate a real
solution closely enough to preserve the finitely many strict signs and
the face determined by any vanishing weak inequalities.

For $D=\mathbb Q^\omega$, suppose $\delta$ realizes the pattern. For each
nonzero form, include the coordinate at which its first nonzero entry
occurs, and do likewise for each nonzero $\delta_q$ appearing in a domain
restriction. Choose $N$ beyond all these finitely many coordinates and
put
\[
 v_q(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j=0}^{N}\delta_q(j)\varepsilon^j.
\]
Every required nonzero linear form in these polynomials has the sign of
its first nonzero coefficient when $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small.
Every required zero form is identically zero, since all its sequence
coordinates were zero. A sufficiently small positive rational
$\varepsilon$ therefore gives the required rational vector. Conversely,
a rational vector is realized in $\mathbb Q^\omega$ by putting it in a
single coordinate. \end{proof}

For the topological use, rational directions are not just witnesses to
abstract consistency. In the real model, $\delta=\varepsilon v$ tends to
zero as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. In the stream model, put
$\delta_q^{(N)}=v_q e_N$, where $e_N$ has a single $1$ in coordinate $N$.
Then $\delta^{(N)}\to0$. These perturbations preserve all inactive
nonzero signs eventually and realize the chosen active signs exactly.
If all required signs are zero, the constant zero perturbation is allowed;
this correctly accounts for a cell which contains $x$ itself.

\begin{theorem}[Exact local accessibility]\label{pma:nsp:thm:accessibility}

The following are equivalent for a cell $C_j$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x\in\overline{C_j}$, with closure relative to $M^k$.
\item There is $v\in\mathbb Q^k$ satisfying $v_q\geq0$ for
      $q\in B(x)$ such that the Boolean formula for $C_j$ is true after:
      freezing all integer coordinates at $n$; retaining the signs of
      the inactive $\ell_i(u)$; and replacing each active sign by
      $\operatorname{sgn}(a_i\cdot v)$.
\end{enumerate}

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
 A rational witness gives arbitrarily close points in the
cell by the perturbations just constructed. Conversely choose a point of
$C_j$ sufficiently close that the finitely many inactive signs and all
integer coordinates agree with those of $x$. Its displacement realizes
the required homogeneous sign pattern. Apply the rational-direction
lemma. \end{proof}

This theorem is an algorithm: enumerate the finitely many assignments of
signs $-1,0,1$ to the active forms, evaluate the Boolean cell formula,
and decide feasibility of the associated rational linear system. Strict
inequalities introduce no difficulty; a homogeneous feasible system with
finitely many strict positive requirements can be rescaled so that all
those positive quantities are at least $1$, and ordinary rational linear
feasibility then applies. If there are no strict requirements, solve the
weak system directly. Rational Fourier--Motzkin elimination is one
possible implementation.

\subsection{The continuity criterion and its finite output}

\begin{theorem}[The branch-limit criterion]\label{pma:nsp:thm:continuity}

For $x\in M^k$,
\[
 f\text{ is continuous at }x
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \forall j\,
 \bigl(x\in\overline{C_j}\ \Longrightarrow\ F_j(x)=f(x)\bigr).
\tag{C}
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
 Suppose $f$ is continuous and $x\in\overline{C_j}$.
Since the domain is metrizable there is a sequence $x_m\in C_j$ tending
to $x$. In $G^r$,
$f(x_m)=F_j(x_m)\to F_j(x)$ by continuity of $F_j$, and
$f(x_m)\to f(x)$ by continuity of $f$. Uniqueness of limits yields the
equality. The value $F_j(x)$ is allowed initially to lie outside $M^r$;
the conclusion rules that possibility out for accessible branches.

Conversely, assume every accessible branch agrees at $x$. For each
inaccessible branch choose a neighbourhood of $x$ avoiding its cell.
There are only finitely many such branches. On every remaining branch,
continuity of its ambient extension at $x$ gives the usual neighbourhood
estimate around $f(x)$. Intersect the finitely many neighbourhoods. This
proves continuity into $G^r$, hence into its subspace $M^r$.
\end{proof}

In particular, the discontinuity set is exactly
\[
 \bigcup_{i,j=1}^{s}
 \{x\in C_i:x\in\overline{C_j},\ F_i(x)\neq F_j(x)\}.
\tag{D}
\]
Using rational accessibility to compile the closure conditions produces
a finite formula for this set. Its atoms are signs and equalities of
rational-affine $D$-coordinate expressions, and Presburger conditions
on integer coordinates. It is crucial to describe this as an
\emph{external coordinate formula}. It need not be a formula in the
original Presburger structure.

\begin{corollary}[Exact form of discontinuity sets]\label{pma:nsp:cor:disc-regularity}

The discontinuity set of every definable $f:M^k\to M^r$ is a
$\Delta^0_2$ set. More strongly, it is a finite union of locally closed
sets and is contained in a finite union of closed nowhere dense affine
$D$-coordinate hyperplanes. Thus it is nowhere dense; its closure is
nowhere dense as well. It need not itself be closed.

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
 In both coefficient models, each strict sign set of a
continuous $D$-affine form is open and each zero set is closed. Integer
conditions are clopen because the integer-coordinate space is discrete.
Finite Boolean combinations therefore form finite unions of intersections
of an open and a closed set. Such locally closed sets and their finite
unions are $F_\sigma\cap G_\delta$ in a metrizable space.

If $x$ lies on none of the nonconstant hyperplanes
$\ell_i(u)=0$ associated with the cell partition, all cell truth values
are locally constant. Forms constant in the variable $u$ also have
locally constant truth values: they either have fixed nonzero sign, or
are decided by the locally constant integer tuple. Hence $f$ locally
agrees with one continuous candidate and is continuous. Each nonconstant
hyperplane is closed and nowhere dense relative to $M^k$: vary an input
coordinate with nonzero coefficient by an arbitrarily small positive
perturbation, retaining membership in $M$. In the stream model such a
perturbation may be placed arbitrarily far out in the sequence. A finite
union remains closed nowhere dense. \end{proof}

\subsection{Two exact examples and necessary qualifications}

Define
\[
 f(x,y)=\begin{cases}x,&y=0,\\0,&y\neq0.\end{cases}
\]
This map is Presburger definable, and in both models its exact
discontinuity set is
\[
 \operatorname{Disc}(f)=\{(x,0):x\neq0\}.
\]
At a point of this set, let the second input approach zero through
$(\varepsilon,0)$ in the real model or through $(e_N,0)$ in the stream
model. The outputs become zero, whereas $f(x,0)=x\neq0$. If $y\neq0$,
the function is locally zero since the complement of the closed singleton
$\{0\}$ is open. At $(0,0)$ every output is either zero or the first
input, so continuity holds. This discontinuity set is not closed.

For truncated subtraction
\[
 x\mathbin{\dot-}y=\max(x-y,0),
\]
write $x=(u,n)$ and $y=(v,m)$. The compiler gives
\[
 \operatorname{Disc}(\dot-)
   =\{((u,n),(v,m)):u=v,\ n\neq m\}.
\tag{M}
\]
If $u-v\neq0$, its sign is stable and one of the two continuous branches
is selected nearby. If $u=v$ and $n=m$, both ambient branches agree at
zero. If $u=v$ and $n\neq m$, arbitrarily small admissible perturbations
of the $D$-coordinates realize both signs of their difference; the branch
limits are the distinct points $(0,n-m)$ and zero in $G$. This proves
the formula, including boundary inputs with $u=v=0$.

The set in (M) is not Presburger definable, even with parameters. If it
were, its section at $y=0$, with the point $x=0$ added, would define
exactly the standard copy of $\mathbb N$ in $M$. That set contains zero
and is closed under successor, so the induction scheme with those
parameters would force it to be all of $M$, a contradiction. Thus an
exact continuity compiler must be allowed to output the expanded
coordinate description, rather than claiming definability in the input
language.

\paragraph{Strict signs cannot be removed from the output language.}
The archived research question proposed descriptions involving equalities
of divisible-coordinate affine expressions and residue conditions. That
fragment is too small in both models. Choose a parameter
$a=(\alpha,c)$ with $\alpha>0$, and define
\[
 g_a(x,y)=\begin{cases}1,&x>a\text{ and }y=0,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Writing $x=(u,n)$, the exact discontinuity set is
\[
 \operatorname{Disc}(g_a)=\{(x,0):u\geq\alpha\}.
\]
For $u>\alpha$ the output at $y=0$ is one and nearby nonzero $y$ gives
zero. For $u<\alpha$ a neighbourhood forces $x<a$, so the map is zero.
At $u=\alpha$, approaching from larger divisible coordinate gives one
with $y=0$, while approaching through nonzero $y$ gives zero, regardless
of the integer comparison at the point. At $y\neq0$, the map is locally
zero. These observations prove the formula in both models.

In either model restrict to $x=(t\alpha,0)$ with rational $t\geq0$, and
to $y=0$. Each affine equality in this remaining scalar variable holds
at at most one $t$ or at every $t$, because $D$ is torsion-free and
$\alpha\neq0$. A finite Boolean combination therefore defines a finite
or cofinite subset of $\mathbb Q_{\geq0}$. All residue conditions are
constant on this slice. But the resulting threshold $t\geq1$ is neither
finite nor cofinite. Thus the equality-and-residue-only proposal has a
negative answer; the additional sign predicates in the compiler are
necessary.

\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) This answers Part~I's
\cref{pma:pr:q:discprofiles}: the discontinuity set of every definable total
function is computed from the graph (\cref{pma:nsp:thm:continuity},
\cref{pma:nsp:thm:global-continuity}), and the fragment proposed there,
equalities of divisible-coordinate affine expressions and residue conditions,
is too small, by the example $g_a$. The formula (M) is Part~I's
\eqref{pma:pr:eq:disclocus} (\cref{pma:pr:thm:truncated}).
\Cref{pma:nsp:cor:disc-regularity} generalizes that theorem to every definable
function. The output is a formula in an expanded two-sorted coordinate
language, not a Presburger definition, as source~13 stresses (and the
Hilbert's-tenth programme's review of the arrival notes,
\cref{pma:app:provenance}).

\subsection{Deciding global continuity after coordinate elimination}

The output formula (D) lives in a two-sorted language. The first sort is
the divisible ordered abelian group $D$, with rational scalar maps; the
second is Presburger integer arithmetic. Each atomic relation belongs
entirely to one of the two sorts. The domain condition is the finite
Boolean combination
\[
 \bigwedge_{q=1}^{k}
 \bigl(u_q>0\ \vee\ (u_q=0\wedge n_q\geq0)\bigr).
\]
The apparent interaction between the sorts occurs only through Boolean
combinations. Consequently, after distributing a finite disjunction,
existential quantification of all input coordinates separates into
ordinary divisible-ordered-group feasibility and ordinary Presburger
integer feasibility.

\begin{theorem}[Effective global continuity criterion]\label{pma:nsp:thm:global-continuity}

Given a Presburger definition of a total function, with a finite
parameter tuple, one can effectively construct a finite Boolean
combination $\Psi$ of:
\begin{itemize}
\item signs and equalities of rational-linear expressions in the
      $D$-coordinates of the parameters; and
\item Presburger conditions on the integer coordinates of the parameters,
\end{itemize}
such that the function is globally continuous exactly when $\Psi$ holds.
The same procedure compiles continuity at a named point by treating that
point's coordinates as additional parameters.

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
 Apply (D), add the domain condition, and existentially
quantify the inputs. Perform quantifier elimination for divisible ordered
abelian groups and for Presburger arithmetic, then negate the result.
All preceding transformations are finite syntactic procedures. The
rational accessibility feasibility tests depend only on the rational
coefficients of the active forms and the selected zero-coordinate face;
they therefore may be performed at compilation time for every possible
finite sign pattern. \end{proof}

This yields a genuine ordinary decision algorithm when the needed
parameter sign/equality tests are decidable, in particular for rational
real parameters and for exactly represented finitely supported rational
sequences. With arbitrary infinite input or parameter streams, it yields
an oracle reduction, not an ordinary decision procedure. A zero-sequence
test is already discontinuous, so that distinction cannot be removed.
For the stream model, each finitely many affine sequence forms can be
scanned until its first nonzero coordinate is found, treating the form as
zero in the meantime; the Boolean answer has a computable eventually
stable approximation. A separate sharper rank argument may improve the
mind-change bound; it is not needed for the compiler theorem.


\section{Exact target-valued Baire classification}\label{pma:nsp:sec:baire}

Here ``Baire class one'' means a pointwise limit of continuous maps into
the stated target space, with that target's actual topology. It is not
being used as a synonym for having $F_\sigma$ inverse images of open sets.
That distinction is decisive for the real-coordinate model.

\subsection{The stream model: explicit locally constant approximations}

Let $D_\omega=\mathbb Q^\omega$ with discrete rational coordinates and
lexicographic order. Let $T_N:G(D_\omega)\to G(D_\omega)$ retain the first
$N$ rational coordinates, set all later rational coordinates to zero,
and retain the integer coordinate. Its image is the subgroup
$G_N\cong\mathbb Q^N\lex \mathbb Z$.
This is an additive projection and commutes with every $q_m$.
It need not preserve the positive cone: a positive element whose first
nonzero rational coordinate occurs after $N$, and whose integer
coordinate is negative, is sent to a negative element. The following
construction explicitly accounts for that issue.

\begin{theorem}[Locally constant approximation with eventual exact prefixes]\label{pma:nsp:thm:baire-stream}

Every parameter-definable total function
$f:M(D_\omega)^k\to M(D_\omega)^r$ is a pointwise limit of locally
constant functions $f_N$ with the same domain and target. Given a graph
formula and streams for its parameters, these functions can be computed
uniformly: $f_N$ requires only the first $N$ rational coordinates and
the integer coordinates of the inputs and parameters. For each fixed
input $x$, there is $N_x$ such that
\[
 f_N(x)=T_N f(x)\qquad(N\geq N_x).
\tag{B4}
\]

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}

Let $R(x,a,y)$ be an ambient group formula for the graph, explicitly
including $y\in M^r$. Replace it by the following totalized graph:
if there is a unique $y\in M^r$ satisfying $R(x,a,y)$, return that $y$;
otherwise return the zero tuple. This defines a function
$F:G^{k+p}\to M^r$ for every input and parameter tuple in every
$\mathbb Z$-group. It agrees with $f$ at the original parameter tuple
and at inputs in the original domain. The definition is a first-order
formula using existence and uniqueness; no choice operation is needed.

Evaluate this same totalized formula in the finite-coordinate model
$G_N$ on $(T_Nx,T_Na)$, and include its output in $M(D_\omega)^r$.
Call the resulting output $f_N(x)$. It always lies in the target,
even when a truncated input or parameter lies outside the positive cone.
Every $f_N$ depends on finite coordinate data and is therefore locally
constant. It is effective because arithmetic and order in
$\mathbb Q^N\lex \mathbb Z$ are decidable and the
finite-branch theorem provides a finite list of possible outputs.

Apply the finite-branch theorem and quantifier elimination to the
totalized graph, with the parameters treated as variables. In every
atomic cell condition, a nonzero affine rational-coordinate stream has
a first nonzero coordinate. After that coordinate is retained, its sign
is fixed forever. A zero stream remains zero in every truncation.
Integer equalities and congruences are unchanged. Consequently every
atomic truth value, and hence every cell truth value, eventually agrees
with its value at $(x,a)$. There are only finitely many atoms.
For all sufficiently large $N$, the selected candidate is therefore
the same candidate $F_j$ as at $(x,a)$. Since affine group terms and
fixed quotients commute with $T_N$,
\[
 f_N(x)=F_j(T_Nx,T_Na)=T_NF_j(x,a)=T_Nf(x).
\]
This proves (B4). Coordinate truncations converge in the product
topology, proving the asserted pointwise convergence. \end{proof}

The theorem gives an actual target-valued Baire-one approximation,
rather than only a classification of the graph or its coordinate
functions. The integer output coordinate stabilizes, and each desired
finite output prefix is eventually exact. There is no claimed effective
bound on the stabilization stage. A stream which vanishes for a long
initial segment may reveal its first nonzero coordinate arbitrarily late.

\paragraph{A dimension bound on branch revisions.}
Suppose there are $k$ input streams and $p$ parameter streams. Compile
the totalized function into a common finite list of quantifier-free cell
conditions, and let $\rho$ be the rational rank of the coefficient vectors
of all affine $D$-coordinate forms occurring in their comparisons.
Then the selected candidate index in the approximation above changes
at most $\rho\leq k+p$ times. The entire output integer tuple likewise
changes at most $\rho$ times.

Indeed, the finite-rank truth theorem, Theorem~\ref{pma:nsp:addthm:rank-truth},
applies simultaneously to all the cell atoms. A new stage at which an
as-yet-zero leading form becomes nonzero contributes an independent row
functional on the $\rho$-dimensional span of comparison forms, so there
are at most $\rho$ such stages. Between them every atom and hence the
selected branch is unchanged. For a fixed candidate, its output integer
tuple depends only on the input and parameter integer tuples, which
truncation leaves unchanged. This proves both bounds. It does not bound
the number of distinct full stream outputs: even a single fixed branch
can acquire further nonzero output coordinates at infinitely many stages.

\subsection{The real model: a complete criterion and a sharp obstruction}

Write $M_{\mathbb R}=M(\mathbb R)$. For
$n=(n_1,\ldots,n_k)\in\mathbb Z^k$, the input slice of fixed integer
coordinates is
\[
 X_n=\prod_{i=1}^{k} I_{n_i}\times\{n\},\qquad
 I_t=\begin{cases}[0,\infty),&t\geq0,\\(0,\infty),&t<0.\end{cases}
\tag{B5}
\]
Each $X_n$ is nonempty, connected, and clopen in $M_{\mathbb R}^k$.
For a vector-valued map, let $\pi_{\mathbb Z}f$ denote the entire tuple
of output integer coordinates.

\begin{theorem}[Exact real-model Baire classification]\label{pma:nsp:thm:baire-real}

For a Presburger-definable total function
$f:M_{\mathbb R}^k\to M_{\mathbb R}^r$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $f$ is Baire class one with target $M_{\mathbb R}^r$.
\item $f$ belongs to some countable Baire class with that target.
\item For every $n\in\mathbb Z^k$, the map
      $\pi_{\mathbb Z}f$ is constant on $X_n$.
\end{enumerate}
Thus every definable map admitted anywhere in the countable target-valued
Baire hierarchy already belongs to class one. Other definable maps are
outside that hierarchy altogether.

\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
\emph{Necessity.}
For every continuous $g:X_n\to M_{\mathbb R}^r$, its integer-coordinate
map is continuous into the discrete space $\mathbb Z^r$, so connectedness
forces it to be constant. This property is preserved by pointwise limits.
Indeed, suppose $g_m$ have constant integer tuples $c_m$ on $X_n$ and
$g_m\to g$ pointwise. At one fixed point of $X_n$, convergence in the
discrete coordinate forces $c_m$ eventually to equal one tuple $c$.
The same sequence $c_m$ occurs at every point, so
$\pi_{\mathbb Z}g$ is identically $c$ throughout $X_n$.
Transfinite induction over the usual countable Baire hierarchy proves
the claim for every countable Baire class, establishing $(2)\Rightarrow(3)$.

\emph{Sufficiency.}
In both coefficient models every definable cell is $\Delta^0_2$.
For completeness, a group equality is closed; a strict or weak order
condition is a finite union of an open strict sign condition on the
$D$-coordinate and a closed zero condition with a clopen integer test.
Both it and its complement are $F_\sigma$. Congruence predicates are
clopen. Quantifier elimination and finite Boolean closure prove the
assertion.

On a metric space the real-valued characteristic function of a
$\Delta^0_2$ set $C$ is Baire one. To see this directly, choose increasing
closed exhaustions $A_m\uparrow C$ and $B_m\uparrow(X\setminus C)$.
When both are nonempty, the continuous functions
\[
 u_m(x)=\frac{d(x,B_m)}{d(x,A_m)+d(x,B_m)}
\]
converge to $\mathbf1_C$. The denominator is positive because the two
closed sets are disjoint. If $A_m$ is empty use $u_m=0$; if only $B_m$
is empty use $u_m=1$. These conventions preserve eventual convergence.

Apply this construction to the finite partition in the finite-branch
theorem. If $H_j$ is the real-coordinate part of the continuous candidate
$F_j$, then the real-coordinate part $h$ of $f$ is
\[
 h=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\mathbf1_{C_j}H_j.
\]
Replacing each characteristic function by its continuous approximation
gives continuous maps $h_m$ into $\mathbb R^r$ converging pointwise to $h$.

Under condition (3), write the output integer tuple as $w(n)$; it is
a continuous function of the input because the slices $X_n$ are clopen.
For $m\geq1$ and output coordinate $j$, replace $h_{m,j}$ by
\[
 \widetilde h_{m,j}(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 \max\{h_{m,j}(x),0\},&w_j(n)\geq0,\\
 \max\{h_{m,j}(x),1/m\},&w_j(n)<0.
 \end{cases}
\]
These are continuous, land in the required real-coordinate half-lines,
and converge to $h_j$. Thus
$x\mapsto(\widetilde h_m(x),w(n))$ are continuous maps into the actual
target $M_{\mathbb R}^r$ converging pointwise to $f$.
This proves $(3)\Rightarrow(1)$; $(1)\Rightarrow(2)$ is immediate.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{A parameter-free example.}
The definable function
\[
 \operatorname{sgn}_M(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x=0,\\1,&x>0\end{cases}
\]
has a $\Delta^0_2$ graph and $\Delta^0_2$ inverse images of open sets.
On $M_{\mathbb R}$ it belongs to no countable target-valued Baire class:
its integer output is zero at the endpoint of $X_0$ and one elsewhere
on that connected half-line. On $M(D_\omega)$ it is Baire class one by
the explicit approximation theorem. This isolates the precise reason
that graph complexity alone cannot settle the target-valued question.

\paragraph{An effective addition to the classification.}
The criterion (3) can itself be compiled into the external two-sorted
coordinate language used by the continuity theorem: assert that there
are no two inputs with the same integer tuple but different integer
output tuples. Substitute the finite branch candidates, split the
finite cell cases, and eliminate the real-coordinate quantifiers by
divisible-ordered-group elimination and the integer quantifiers by
Presburger elimination. The result is a finite Boolean combination of
rational-linear sign tests on the real parts of the parameters and
Presburger conditions on their integer parts. Consequently membership
in the target-valued Baire hierarchy is decidable for parameter-free
definitions, and for parameter presentations with decidable required
real sign/equality tests. Arbitrary real streams do not supply those
tests as uniformly decidable operations.

\subsection{Topological extension to a countable discrete core}

\begin{corollary}[Regularity over every countable discrete core]\label{pma:nsp:cor:discrete-core-regularity}

Let $K$ be any countable $\mathbb Z$-group with the discrete topology,
let $D=\mathbb R$ or $D=\mathbb Q^\omega$ with the respective topologies
used above, and put
\[
 G=D\lex K,\qquad P=G_{\geq0}.
\]
For every parameter-definable total map $f:P^k\to P^r$, the following
topological conclusions continue to hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item There are finitely many continuous ambient quotient-affine
      candidates. The rational-direction accessibility criterion and
      branch-limit continuity criterion remain valid with the core
      coordinates frozen. Consequently $\operatorname{Disc}(f)$ is a
      finite union of locally closed sets contained in finitely many
      closed nowhere dense affine $D$-coordinate hyperplanes.
\item For $D=\mathbb Q^\omega$, there are locally constant maps
      $f_N:P^k\to P^r$ such that, for each $x$, eventually
      $f_N(x)=T_N f(x)$; here $T_N$ truncates only the rational stream
      and leaves the $K$-coordinate unchanged. In particular $f$ is
      target-valued Baire class one.
\item For $D=\mathbb R$, membership in any countable target-valued
      Baire class is equivalent to class one, and holds exactly when
      the output $K$-tuple is constant on every slice with fixed input
      $K$-tuple.
\end{enumerate}

\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}

The group $G$ is a $\mathbb Z$-group, and its standard quotient maps are
\[
 q_m(d,b)=(d/m,q_m^K(b)).
\]
They are continuous because $K$ is discrete. The finite-branch proof
uses only Presburger elimination, discrete order, and standard division,
so it applies unchanged. On a neighbourhood of an input, all core
coordinates are fixed. Every core affine equality, order test, and
congruence therefore has a fixed truth value. The only varying signs
are the same rational-affine $D$-coordinate forms as before. At a zero
$D$-coordinate the domain again allows exactly nonnegative directions.
The accessibility proof, branch-limit proof, and nowhere-dense
hyperplane argument are consequently unchanged. Core conditions are
clopen, so the finite locally closed description follows as well.

In the stream case, totalize the graph on the ambient group and evaluate
it on truncated inputs and parameters in
$\mathbb Q^N\lex K$. This is again a $\mathbb Z$-group,
so the totalized output exists uniquely and lies in its positive cone.
The resulting map is locally constant, because it depends only on a
finite rational prefix and discrete core data. All core tests remain
fixed while the leading-coordinate tests eventually stabilize.
Quotient-affine candidates commute with truncation, giving
$f_N(x)=T_Nf(x)$ eventually, exactly as before.

In the real case the fixed-core slices are products of $[0,\infty)$
and $(0,\infty)$, according to the signs of their core coordinates.
They are connected and clopen. Projection to the discrete target $K^r$
therefore gives the same transfinite constancy obstruction. For
sufficiency, approximate the leading real coordinates and clamp them
to $[0,\infty)$ or to positive values according to the constant output
core coordinate. The earlier construction then produces continuous
maps into $P^r$ converging pointwise to $f$. \end{proof}

This extension is purely topological. No computable presentation of
$K$ is assumed. Countability and discreteness alone do not supply an
algorithm for evaluating core arithmetic or make the displayed
locally constant approximants uniformly computable. Effective versions
must separately specify a presentation of $K$ and the available
operations and decision procedures.



\section{The exact number of changes of mind}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:truth}

The earlier \repo\ report \cite{s13:prior-two} proved a finite-change truth theorem and bounded
the number of changes by the number of equality and order atoms after
