quantifier elimination.  Its question entitled ``Optimal finite-mind-change
complexity'' asked for the smallest possible bound for an individual
formula.  We first give a bound by linear dimension, which is sharp as a
function of the number of input streams.  We then give a finite, effective
calculation of the optimum for each parameter-free formula.

\subsection{Presentation and counting convention}

Let
\[
 D=\mathbb Q^{\mathbb N},\qquad
 G=D\lex \mathbb Z,\qquad
 M=G_{\geq0},
\]
where a nonzero rational stream is positive when its first nonzero
coefficient is positive, and the $D$ coordinate precedes the integer
coordinate in the order on $G$.  Give $G$ the product topology in which
each rational coordinate and the integer coordinate are discrete.  An
element of $M$ has the form $x=(h,n)$, with
\[
 h\geq_{\mathrm{lex}}0,
 \qquad h=0\Longrightarrow n\geq0.
\]
Thus $n<0$ guarantees that $h$ has a positive first nonzero coefficient.
The earlier report provides a computable homeomorphism between this
presentation and a total coding by Baire space.  A valid coordinate code
can also be converted to that Baire code effectively: when $n<0$, search
for its guaranteed positive leading coefficient before producing the
corresponding negative-slice tag.

A \emph{truth approximation} for a relation $f:M^d\to\{0,1\}$ is a
sequence of continuous maps $A_s:M^d\to\{0,1\}$ satisfying
\[
 \lim_{s\to\infty}A_s(\bar x)=f(\bar x)
 \quad\text{for every }\bar x\in M^d.
\]
Its number of changes on $\bar x$ is
\[
 \#\{s\in\mathbb N:A_{s+1}(\bar x)\ne A_s(\bar x)\}.
\]
The initial output is not counted as a change.  A computable approximation
means that the stage maps are uniformly Type-2 computable.  Each output
must use only finite input information, but its computation may inspect
an input-dependent finite number of coordinates.  In particular, the
definition does not require an output before the integer coordinates
have been read.

Write $\mu(f)$ for the least uniform change bound among continuous
approximations, and $\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(f)$ for the corresponding minimum
among computable approximations.  The constructions below show that these
minima exist for the definable relations under consideration.

\subsection{The dimension bound}

Translate a Presburger formula on $M$ to the ordered group $G$ by
relativizing its quantified variables to the positive cone.  Effective
quantifier elimination for $\mathbb Z$-groups then produces a Boolean
combination of atoms
\[
 t_j(\bar x)>0,\qquad t_j(\bar x)=0,
 \qquad m_\ell\mid u_\ell(\bar x),
\]
where each affine term has integer coefficients.  For an order or
equality atom write
\[
 t_j(\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^d c_{ji}x_i+b_j\mathbf1,
 \qquad c_j=(c_{j1},\ldots,c_{jd})\in\mathbb Z^d.
\]
Repeated occurrences do not need to be duplicated in the following rank.
Define
\[
 U=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{c_j:
                  \text{$j$ is an order or equality atom}\},
 \qquad r=\dim_{\mathbb Q}U.
\]
Only these atoms enter $r$; congruence coefficients do not.

\begin{theorem}[Linear dimension bounds truth changes; sharpens \cref{pma:pr:thm:mindchange}]
\label{pma:nsp:addthm:rank-truth}
For every Presburger formula with $d$ external stream variables, effective
quantifier elimination and rational Gaussian elimination compute a
uniform truth approximation with at most
\[
 r\leq d
\]
changes on every input.  Here an external stream variable can be a free
variable or a parameter supplied as an oracle.  In particular, a
parameter-free formula in $k$ free variables requires at most $k$
changes, independently of its length and its quantifier alternation.
A formula in $k$ variables with $p$ supplied stream parameters admits
the uniform bound $k+p$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $x_i=(h_i,n_i)$.  First read all integer coordinates.  The integer
coordinate of $t_j$ is the exactly known integer
\[
 N_j=\sum_i c_{ji}n_i+b_j,
\]
and its stream coordinate is $\sum_i c_{ji}h_i$.  Congruence atoms are
decided immediately from the corresponding integer coordinate, since
\[
 mG=D\times m\mathbb Z.
\]

Let
\[
 v_a=(h_1(a),\ldots,h_d(a))\in\mathbb Q^d
 \qquad(a\in\mathbb N).
\]
At stage $s$, use the sign of the first nonzero value among
$c_j\cdot v_0,\ldots,c_j\cdot v_{s-1}$ if there is one.  Otherwise use
the sign of $N_j$.  This gives an approximation to every order atom.
For equality use the answer $N_j=0$ until a nonzero stream coefficient
is seen, at which point the answer is permanently false.  Evaluate the
fixed Boolean combination at each stage to obtain $A_s$.

There are finitely many atoms.  Every nonzero stream has a first nonzero
coefficient, so every atom eventually becomes permanently correct.
Consequently $A_s$ converges to the desired truth value.

To count changes, restrict the row functional $c\mapsto c\cdot v_a$ to
$U$, and denote the resulting element of $U^*$ by $\ell_a$.  Put
\[
 W_s=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}
                         \{\ell_0,\ldots,\ell_{s-1}\}\subseteq U^*.
\]
An order or equality atom has no witnessed nonzero stream coefficient
exactly when its coefficient vector is annihilated by all members of
$W_s$.  If $\ell_s\in W_s$, every such coefficient vector is also
annihilated by $\ell_s$.  Hence no unresolved atom can become resolved
at that stage.  Resolved atoms never change again, and congruence atoms
are already fixed.  Thus
\[
 A_{s+1}\ne A_s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
                       \dim W_{s+1}>\dim W_s.
\]
The dimension starts at zero and never exceeds $r$, which proves the
bound.  The construction is uniform and reads only finite prefixes at
each stage.  All its preprocessing is effective.
\end{proof}

The proof also gives the input-dependent bound
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{\ell_a:a\in\mathbb N\}$, which can be strictly
smaller than $r$.  It does not provide a computable time at which the
last change has occurred.  A new independent row can first appear
arbitrarily far along the input streams.

\paragraph{Many atoms, only two possible changes.}
For example, the formula
\[
 \bigl((x+y=0)\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}(x=y)\bigr)
 \ \wedge\
 \bigwedge_{m=1}^{32}\bigl(mx<(m+1)y\ \vee\ x=y\bigr)
\]
has many order atoms, but all their coefficient vectors lie in
$\mathbb Q^2$.  On inputs with integer coordinates zero, take row
$v_2=(1,1)$, row $v_7=(1,0)$, and all other rows zero.  The displayed
approximation has successive relevant answers $0,1,0$: the first row
resolves $x+y$, while the later row resolves $x-y$.  The many inequalities
remain true after the first row.  Both rank increases can therefore
matter to the final Boolean answer.

\subsection{Sharpness of the bound by arity}

\begin{theorem}[Exactly $d$ changes can be necessary]\label{pma:nsp:thm:arity}
For every $d\geq1$, the parameter-free Presburger relation
\[
 P_d(x_1,\ldots,x_d)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       \text{an odd number of the statements $x_i\ne0$ hold}
\]
satisfies
\[
 \mu(P_d)=\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(P_d)=d.
\]
Thus the dimension bound is sharp even when no order atoms or quantifiers
are used.  For any proposed computable approximation with fewer than $d$
changes, a violating input can be chosen computable and with every stream
of finite support.  For arbitrary continuous stage maps the same
lower-bound argument gives an existential violating input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound follows from the preceding theorem.  The parity relation
is a finite Boolean combination of the equality atoms $x_i=0$; it is
therefore a Presburger formula, with no parity operation added to the
language.

For the lower bound restrict to the closed slice on which all integer
coordinates are zero.  Initially let every stream be zero.  Its truth
value is zero, so convergence gives a stage $t_0$ at which the proposed
approximation outputs zero there.  By continuity, the value at that
stage is fixed on some finite-prefix neighborhood of this tuple.

Insert a single positive rational coefficient, sufficiently far out in
the first stream to remain in this neighborhood.  The tuple still belongs
to $M^d$, its first coordinate is now nonzero, and its truth value has
toggled to one.  Convergence gives a later stage $t_1>t_0$ outputting one.
Choose a finite-prefix neighborhood that fixes the outputs at both
chosen stages.  Insert a sufficiently delayed positive coefficient in
the second, previously zero, stream.  Its truth value toggles again.

Continue in this way through the $d$ streams.  At each step preserve all
previously selected output values, and choose the next correct output
at a strictly later stage.  The final tuple has finite support in each
stream and satisfies
\[
 A_{t_j}(\bar x)=j\bmod2\qquad(0\leq j\leq d).
\]
There must therefore be at least one change between every pair of
successive selected stages, giving at least $d$ changes altogether.

If the stage maps are computable, the construction is effective relative
to their index.  At each step the current finite-support input is
computable, so search for a stage with its known correct truth value.
The computation terminates by convergence.  Record the finitely many
input coordinates queried by all the selected computations and place
the next positive coefficient beyond them.  This preserves their
outputs and gives a computable final input.  Mere continuity supplies
the requisite neighborhoods without an effective procedure for finding
them, which is enough for the noneffective lower bound.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An exact finite calculation for every parameter-free formula}

The rank bound is often not the individual optimum.  For example,
$x_1=0\wedge\cdots\wedge x_d=0$ has coefficient rank $d$, but a single
change suffices: begin with the answer determined by the integer
coordinates and change permanently to false when a nonzero stream
coefficient appears.  The following finite construction computes the
exact optimum instead of just a rank bound.

Fix a parameter-free formula $\varphi(\bar x)$ and an effectively
obtained quantifier-free group formula $\Psi$ as above.  Include standard
numerals in the affine constants $b_j$.  Put
\[
 C=\{c_j\ne0:\text{$c_j$ occurs in an order or equality atom}\}
                  \cup\{e_1,\ldots,e_d\},
\]
where $e_i$ is the $i$th coordinate vector.  Retain just one copy of each
vector.  Including the coordinate vectors is essential: they record the
positivity requirements defining $M^d$.

\paragraph{Integer regimes.}
The truth of $\Psi$ at fixed stream signs depends on the integer tuple
$\bar n\in\mathbb Z^d$ only through finitely many data:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item the bits $\eta_i=[n_i<0]$;
 \item the signs
       $\alpha_j=\operatorname{sgn}(c_j\cdot\bar n+b_j)$
       for its order and equality atoms;
 \item the truth values $\beta_\ell$ of its congruence atoms evaluated
       on $\bar n$.
\end{enumerate}
A choice of all these data is an \emph{integer regime} $R$.
There are finitely many choices.  Whether a regime is nonempty is an
ordinary Presburger decision problem over $\mathbb Z$: ask whether
there exists an integer tuple having the stipulated signs and
congruences.  Discard every infeasible regime.

\paragraph{The finite sign-pattern poset.}
For a feasible regime $R$, let $\mathcal P_R$ be the set of vectors
\[
 \sigma(v)=\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(c\cdot v)\bigr)_{c\in C}
                   \in\{-1,0,1\}^{C}
\]
realized by rational vectors $v\in\mathbb Q^d$ satisfying
\[
 v_i\geq0\quad\text{for all }i,
 \qquad v_i>0\quad\text{whenever }\eta_i=1.
\]
Order these patterns by
\[
 \sigma\preceq\tau
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
       \forall c\in C\,
       (\sigma_c\ne0\Longrightarrow\tau_c=\sigma_c).
\]
In other words, passing upward can replace zeros by signs but cannot
change an already nonzero sign.  This is a finite partially ordered set.
It is computable: enumerate the finitely many proposed sign vectors and
decide the corresponding finite systems of rational linear equalities
and strict inequalities.  Rational linear elimination suffices.  Since
the systems are homogeneous, one can alternatively replace their strict
positive inequalities by inequalities at least one whenever there is a
strict inequality; a common positive rescaling proves equivalence.

Label each $\sigma\in\mathcal P_R$ by a bit $\lambda_R(\sigma)$, obtained
by evaluating $\Psi$ as follows.  For an order atom, use the nonzero
stream sign $\sigma_{c_j}$ when available and otherwise its integer sign
$\alpha_j$.  An equality atom holds exactly when both those signs are
zero.  A congruence atom has the fixed value $\beta_\ell$.
For a zero coefficient vector set $\sigma_0=0$ by convention.

Let
\[
 a(R)=\max_{\sigma_0\prec\cdots\prec\sigma_q\text{ in }\mathcal P_R}
          \#\{j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:
                    \lambda_R(\sigma_j)\ne\lambda_R(\sigma_{j-1})\},
 \qquad
 N_\varphi=\max_{R\text{ feasible}}a(R).
\]
Singleton chains are allowed and contribute zero.  The finite maximum
is effectively computable, for example by dynamic programming on the
finite partially ordered sets.

\begin{lemma}[Finite sign compression]\label{pma:nsp:lem:compression}
For any finite $C\subseteq\mathbb Q^d$, every sign pattern
\[
 \bigl(\operatorname{sgn}_{\mathrm{lex}}
                 (\textstyle\sum_i c_i h_i)\bigr)_{c\in C}
\]
of a tuple of rational streams is realized by a single rational vector.
If $C$ contains the coordinate vectors, the rational vector has exactly
the same zero and positive coordinate pattern as the streams.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose a finite prefix long enough to witness the first nonzero
coefficient of every nonzero linear combination indexed by $C$.
Let its rows be $v_0,\ldots,v_{L-1}$.  For a sufficiently small positive
rational $\varepsilon$, set
\[
 v=v_0+\varepsilon v_1+\cdots+\varepsilon^{L-1}v_{L-1}.
\]
For each $c\in C$ whose stream is nonzero, the first nonzero coefficient
of the polynomial $c\cdot v$ determines its sign for all sufficiently
small positive $\varepsilon$.  Finitely many such requirements can be
satisfied simultaneously.  A combination that is identically zero
annihilates every row and remains zero.  Applying this also to the
coordinate vectors proves the final assertion.  If all combinations
are zero, the zero vector suffices.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact computable change complexity]
\label{pma:nsp:thm:exact-changes}
For every parameter-free Presburger formula $\varphi$ on this presentation,
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \mu(\mathbf1_\varphi)
   =\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf1_\varphi)
   =N_\varphi\leq r\leq d.
 \quad}
\]
Thus the minimum possible number of changes of mind is computable from
the formula.  It is the maximum number of truth-value alternations
along a chain of feasible sign patterns, maximized over its finitely
many feasible integer regimes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, the sign-compression lemma shows that $\mathcal P_R$ describes
exactly the finite stream-sign patterns occurring on the integer slice
of any tuple $\bar n$ in regime $R$.  Coordinate signs enforce precisely
the necessary conditions: every stream is lexicographically nonnegative,
and a stream is nonzero when its integer coordinate is negative.
Conversely, a feasible rational vector gives a valid tuple by placing
that vector in the first row and making all later rows zero.

For the upper bound, read the integer coordinates and hence their
regime.  If $n_i<0$, scan until the positive leading coefficient of $h_i$
has been witnessed.  Validity of the input guarantees termination.
Choose $L$ beyond all these witnessed indices; if there are no negative
integer coordinates, use $L=0$.  This finite preliminary scan is part of
the computation of the first output, so it does not itself count as a
change.

At stage $s$ truncate all streams after their first $L+s$ coefficients,
and let $\sigma_s$ be their pattern on $C$.  Each truncated tuple is
still in the same integer slice of $M^d$, so by sign compression
$\sigma_s\in\mathcal P_R$.  Revealing a new row cannot change a
previously witnessed nonzero leading sign.  Therefore
\[
 \sigma_0\preceq\sigma_1\preceq\sigma_2\preceq\cdots.
\]
Output $A_s=\lambda_R(\sigma_s)$.  Every relevant linear combination
eventually has its correct sign, and only finitely many combinations
are involved, so these outputs converge to truth.  After repeated
patterns are removed, their path is a chain in $\mathcal P_R$.
Consequently it has at most $a(R)\leq N_\varphi$ changes.  All the
computations are effective and inspect finite input information.

For the lower bound, choose a feasible regime $R$ and a chain attaining
$N_\varphi$.  Remove consecutive portions with constant label to obtain
\[
 \sigma_0\prec\sigma_1\prec\cdots\prec\sigma_{N_\varphi},
 \qquad
 \lambda_R(\sigma_{j+1})\ne\lambda_R(\sigma_j).
\]
Fix an integer tuple $\bar n$ in that regime and a one-row rational
tuple realizing $\sigma_0$.  For any continuous truth approximation,
choose a stage $t_0$ outputting its correct label.

Suppose a finite-support tuple with pattern $\sigma_j$ has been chosen
and the outputs at the earlier selected stages have been fixed.
Take a finite-prefix neighborhood preserving all those outputs.  At a
coordinate beyond both that prefix and the current finite support,
append a rational row $v$ realizing $\sigma_{j+1}$.  Every previously
nonzero linear combination retains its old leading coefficient and
hence its sign.  Every combination previously zero acquires the sign
of $c\cdot v$.  By the defining extension order, the resulting tuple
has exactly pattern $\sigma_{j+1}$.  The coordinate vectors in $C$
ensure that the tuple remains in $M^d$ with the same integer regime.

Its truth value is the opposite label, so convergence yields a strictly
later stage $t_{j+1}>t_j$ with that value.  Continue until the end of
the chain.  The final tuple preserves alternating outputs at
$t_0<\cdots<t_{N_\varphi}$ and therefore forces at least $N_\varphi$
changes.  This lower bound holds even for arbitrary continuous stage
maps.  With computable stage maps, integer and rational witnesses can
be found effectively, and the finite-prefix neighborhoods can be
recovered from finite oracle-query traces.  The same argument then
constructs a computable finite-support witness.

Finally, along any chain of realizable sign patterns, let $Z_j$ be the
span of the order/equality coefficient vectors still assigned zero.
These subspaces form a descending chain.  Whenever one of these forms
becomes nonzero, the descent is strict: a rational vector realizing the
new pattern annihilates all still-zero forms but does not annihilate
the newly nonzero one.  A truth-value change requires at least one
order/equality form to become nonzero, because the integer regime and
all congruence values are fixed.  Thus every truth change strictly
decreases $\dim Z_j$, which starts at most $r$.  This proves
$N_\varphi\leq r\leq d$ and completes the argument.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A sharp obstruction when parameters are fixed}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform parameter optimization is impossible]\label{pma:nsp:thm:parameters}
For a fixed parameter $p\in M$, let $f_p(x)=\mathbf1_{x<p}$.  Then
\[
 \mu(f_p)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&p=0,\\
  1,&p>0.
 \end{cases}
\]
The same values hold for the minimum among approximations computable
relative to a supplied name of $p$.  There is no Type-2 computable
procedure that obtains this minimum uniformly from the name of $p$.
Even when $p$ is promised computable, there is no algorithm that obtains
the minimum from an index computing its stream.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The relation is empty when $p=0$, so its characteristic function is
constant.  For every $p$, the single inequality $x-p<0$ has coefficient
rank one in the two supplied streams and therefore has a uniform
one-change approximation relative to $p$.

Suppose $p>0$.  The element $x=p-\mathbf1$ belongs to $M$: if the stream
of $p$ is positive, subtracting one does not change that fact, and if
its stream is zero, its integer coordinate is at least one.  Let $e_N$
be the stream whose only nonzero coefficient is a one at coordinate $N$,
and put $\delta_N=(e_N,0)$.  In the product topology,
$\delta_N\to0$, whereas in the arithmetic order $\delta_N>\mathbf1$
for every $N$.  Thus
\[
 x+\delta_N\longrightarrow x,
 \qquad f_p(x)=1,
 \qquad f_p(x+\delta_N)=0.
\]
Consequently $f_p$ is not continuous.  A zero-change approximation is
constant in its stage index and equals its first continuous stage map,
so none can approximate this function.  Its optimum is exactly one.

The map from $p$ to this optimum is discontinuous at zero, as witnessed
by $\delta_N\to0$.  It therefore cannot be Type-2 computable.
For the stronger index statement, given a machine index $e$, define a
computable stream $h_e$ that has coefficient one at its halting time if
the machine halts and has all other coefficients zero.  Computing its
$j$th coefficient requires only a bounded simulation through step $j$.
The element $p_e=(h_e,0)$ is always a valid computable parameter, and
\[
 \mu(f_{p_e})=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
                            \text{machine $e$ halts}.
\]
A uniform algorithm for the minimum would decide the halting problem.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Scope of the resolution.}
This theorem completely answers the earlier report's individual-formula
optimization question for parameter-free formulas in the specified
rational-stream presentation.  A formula with parameters that are
allowed to vary as additional input streams is covered after those
parameters are made additional free variables.  For one fixed arbitrary
parameter tuple, the dimension bound remains valid uniformly relative
to its supplied names, but the exact finite-poset calculation just
proved is not asserted: fixing an infinite parameter stream can prevent
the free delayed tail modifications used in the lower bound.  The last
theorem shows that a uniform algorithm for arbitrary fixed computable
parameters is impossible, even for a single unary order formula.

The finite procedure is a decidability result about optimal change
counts, not an efficient quantifier-elimination or truth algorithm in
the ordinary running-time sense.  It can require a large quantifier-free
formula, many integer regimes, and many feasible sign patterns.  Nor
does a bound on changes identify a finite stopping stage for every
input.  These distinctions are essential to the statement.

\paragraph{Further questions suggested by the theorem.}
Classify fixed parameter tuples or restricted formulas for which a
finite effective replacement for the sign-pattern calculation exists,
despite the general obstruction just proved.  Study
the complexity of computing $N_\varphi$ from a formula already in
quantifier-free form, and compare the finite poset with effective
finite difference hierarchies.  Seek syntactic fragments for which the
integer regimes and sign-pattern chains can be analyzed without full
elimination.  Finally, formalize the finite-sign compression lemma,
rank argument, and delayed-tail lower bound as independently checkable
steps in ProveIt.


\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) This answers Part~I's

\section{A completeness obstruction beyond invariant metrics}\label{pma:nsp:sec:metric}

Let $M$ be a commutative cancellative monoid with identity $0$.  Assume
that its algebraic order
\[
 x\leq y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (\exists z\in M)\;x+z=y
\]
is a linear order.  In particular it is antisymmetric.  Define truncated
subtraction by
\[
 x\mathbin{\monus}y=
 \begin{cases}
 z,&y+z=x,\quad y\leq x,\\
 0,&x<y.
 \end{cases}
\]
Cancellation makes $z$ unique.  Let $M$ carry a metrizable topology in
which addition is continuous.

\begin{definition}
For a compatible metric $d$ on $M$, say that translations are
\emph{uniformly equicontinuous at the identity} if, for every
$\varepsilon>0$, there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $0$ such that
\[
 d(b+u,b)<\varepsilon\qquad(b\in M,\;u\in U).
 \tag{UE0}
\]
The same neighbourhood $U$ must work for all $b$.  Joint uniform
continuity of addition for the product metric
$\max\{d(x,x'),d(y,y')\}$ implies \textup{(UE0)} by comparing
$(b,u)$ with $(b,0)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Closed translates forced by complete uniformity]
\label{pma:nsp:thm:closed-translates-uniformity}
Suppose $x\mathbin{\monus}y$ is continuous at $(a,a)$ for every
$a\in M$.  If a compatible complete metric $d$ satisfies
\textup{(UE0)}, every translate $c+M$ is closed in $M$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $c\in M$ and a convergent sequence
$x_n=c+b_n\longrightarrow x$.  We prove that $(b_n)$ is $d$-Cauchy.
Given $\varepsilon>0$, select $U$ as in \textup{(UE0)}.  Continuity
of truncated subtraction at $(x,x)$, where its value is $0$, gives
a neighbourhood $V$ of $x$ such that
\[
 s,t\in V\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 s\mathbin{\monus}t\in U.
\]
For all sufficiently large $n,m$, both $x_n,x_m$ belong to $V$.
If $b_m\leq b_n$, write $b_n=b_m+z$.  Cancellation implies
$z=x_n\mathbin{\monus}x_m$, so $z\in U$, and
\[
 d(b_n,b_m)=d(b_m+z,b_m)<\varepsilon.
\]
If $b_n\leq b_m$, interchange the indices and use symmetry of $d$.
The order is total, so these cases cover every pair.  Thus $(b_n)$
is Cauchy.  Completeness gives $b_n\longrightarrow b\in M$.
Continuity of addition gives $x_n=c+b_n\longrightarrow c+b$.
Uniqueness of limits yields $x=c+b\in c+M$.  Metric spaces are
sequential, so $c+M$ is closed.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No complete metric with uniformly continuous addition; strengthens \cref{pma:pr:prop:invariantmetric}]
\label{pma:nsp:cor:no-complete-uniform-addition}
Under the hypotheses of the preceding theorem, suppose some translate
$c+M$ is not closed.  No compatible complete metric satisfies
\textup{(UE0)}; in particular no compatible complete metric makes
addition jointly uniformly continuous.
\end{corollary}

The theorem uses ordinary continuity at each individual diagonal
point.  It does not assume a uniform modulus for truncated subtraction.
Nor does it require translations to be isometries or their inverses
to be uniformly continuous.

\subsection{Application to the real and rational-stream cones}

Put $G=H\lex \mathbb Z$, with least positive
element $1_G=(0,1)$, and let $M=G_{\geq0}$ carry the subspace
topology of $H\times\mathbb Z$.  Here either
$H=\mathbb R$ with its usual topology, or
$H=\mathbb Q^\omega$ with discrete rational factors and
first-difference lexicographic order.

\begin{lemma}\label{pma:nsp:lem:diagonal}
Truncated subtraction on $M$ is continuous at every diagonal point.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $a=(h,k)$.  Near $(a,a)$ both integer coordinates equal $k$,
because the integer factor is discrete.  For
$x=(u,k)$ and $y=(v,k)$, therefore,
\[
 x\mathbin{\monus}y=((u-v)^+,0),
 \qquad w^+=\max\{w,0\}.
\]
For $H=\mathbb R$ the positive-part map is continuous.  For
$H=\mathbb Q^\omega$, it is continuous at $0$: if the first
$N$ coordinates of $w$ vanish, the first $N$ coordinates of
$w^+$ also vanish.  Since $u-v\longrightarrow0$ as
$(x,y)\longrightarrow(a,a)$, the displayed formula proves the
claim in both cases.
\end{proof}

Every nonzero element of $M$ has a predecessor, so
$1_G+M=M\setminus\{0\}$.  This translate is not closed.
Indeed, $((1/n),0)\longrightarrow0$ in the real example, and
$(e_n,0)\longrightarrow0$ in the rational-stream example, where
$e_n$ is the rational stream with a single $1$ in coordinate $n$.
All these points are nonzero.  Consequently
Corollary~\ref{pma:nsp:cor:no-complete-uniform-addition} applies.

Both spaces are nevertheless Polish and addition is continuous.
The obstruction concerns the simultaneous demands of a compatible
complete metric and uniform continuity.  The incomplete restriction
of an invariant metric from the ambient group has uniformly
continuous addition, so completeness is essential.

\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) \Cref{pma:nsp:cor:no-complete-uniform-addition}
answers Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:metrics} negatively for joint uniform
continuity of addition, and for uniform equicontinuity of translations at the
identity, in $\MR$, $\MB$ and the countable-core models; it strengthens
\cref{pma:pr:prop:invariantmetric}. The question's other parts (uniform
continuity of all translations in one direction, the distortion of their
inverses) stay open.



\section{Consequences, examples, and the formalization boundary}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:consequences}

The results separate three different forms of regularity. An arithmetic
operation can be continuous, uniformly continuous for an incomplete
metric, or uniformly continuous for a complete compatible metric. The
first two hold for addition in the explicit cones; the third is
impossible. A definable map can have a simple graph while failing to be a
pointwise limit of continuous maps into its actual target. Finally, a
truth value can be eventually correct after finitely many revisions
without there being an effective stage at which correctness can be
announced permanently.

\subsection{A compact comparison of the models}

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{.30\textwidth}YYY@{}}
\toprule
Property & $M_{\R}$ & $M_{\omega}$ & Nonsplit countable-core models\\
\midrule
Perfect Polish carrier & Yes, locally compact & Yes, Baire space &
Either type, by choice of coefficient group\\
Addition and fixed division & Continuous & Continuous & Continuous\\
All definable relations & $\Dtwo$ & $\Dtwo$ & $\Dtwo$\\
Retraction onto standard integers & Unique, continuous & Unique, continuous &
Absent for the explicit core\\
Unital additive map to $\Oz$ & Exists & Exists & Impossible for the explicit core\\
Every definable map target-valued Baire one & No; exact slice criterion &
Yes, explicit finite-prefix approximants & Stream: yes; real: exact core-slice criterion\\
Complete metric with uniform addition & Impossible & Impossible &
Impossible for both explicit coefficient choices\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The metric conclusion extends to the countable-core cones without any
new arithmetic assumption. Near a diagonal point the two discrete core
coordinates agree, so truncated subtraction is
$((u-v)^+,0_K)$. The diagonal continuity proof is unchanged. The
successor image again omits exactly zero, which is nonisolated.

The no-homomorphism result concerns $\Oz$, not all of $\No$. For example,
the countable core itself has the unital ordered additive embedding
\[
 (u,v)\longmapsto(v-u)\omega+v
\]
into $\No$. Its finite constant coefficient need not be an integer.
This example pinpoints why the omnific restriction matters.

\subsection{What the continuity procedure returns}

For a graph formula defining $f$, the procedure has a concrete finite
output: a Boolean expression describing $\Disc(f)$ in a language with
one divisible ordered group sort and one discrete integer sort.
It can also decide global continuity in the absence of arbitrary
undecidable parameter comparisons. A full implementation would perform
the following transformations.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Relativize the graph to the signed group and eliminate its
quantifiers; extract a finite list of affine quotient candidates.
\item Partition by the first successful candidate, and eliminate the
remaining quantifiers in its cell conditions.
\item For each possible pattern of zero and nonzero leading forms,
solve the finite rational directional-feasibility problems for the
accessible cells.
\item Compare every accessible candidate with the actual candidate at
the point, using the exact continuity criterion.
\item If global continuity is desired, eliminate the input coordinates
in the two separate sorts.
\end{enumerate}

This output language is necessary, even for a simple operation. In the
monus example the condition that two leading coordinates are equal
detects standard finite difference, which is unavailable as a
Presburger definition of the standard cut. Thus the compiler is an
analysis tool for the presentation, not an additional definability
theorem inside the original arithmetic.

\subsection{What can be formalized directly in \repo}

The inspected Lean syntax interprets affine expressions in lists of
ordinary integers, and its central theorem quantifies over
\code{List Int} \cite{s13:proveit-syntax,s13:proveit-decision}. It therefore
cannot be cited as an existing proof that every nonstandard
$\Z$-group validates the same elimination algorithm. That semantic
generalization has to be implemented and proved.

A useful implementation order is as follows. First define an abstract
discretely ordered abelian group with a named least positive unit and
standard division with remainder. Prove the full-coset finite-boundary
lemma and the model-uniform elimination theorem. These algebraic steps
support the finite-candidate theorem and the arithmetic correctness of
all the explicit models.

Next formalize rational sign feasibility, finite sign compression, and
the rank argument. These are finite algebraic statements plus an
elementary eventual-stabilization argument. The exact minimum theorem
then separates into a finite poset calculation and the delayed-tail
lower-bound construction. The existing integer eliminator can decide
the feasibility of each integer regime once its relation to the
abstract semantics has been established.

The topological component can be developed independently: the
positive-cone construction, the finite-branch continuity lemma, the
rational-direction realization, and the closed-translate metric
theorem. The last of these is particularly small and has no dependence
on surreal numbers, descriptive set-theoretic classification, or
Presburger quantifier elimination.

Finally, the omnific application needs the additive constant map and an
ordered embedding of a set-sized divisible group into $\No$.
The explicit two-element contradiction only needs the former. It is
therefore a shorter initial formalization target than the general
surreal embedding criterion.

\section{Further research questions and concrete next steps}
\label{pma:nsp:sec:future}

The questions below arise after the proved results. They are not
presented as already solved, and their scopes are narrower than a
blanket request for a new theory of all Polish arithmetic.

\begin{question}[Fixed-parameter revision complexity]
For a fixed parameter tuple, classify the exact degree of difficulty of
computing the optimal revision number. The uniform decision problem is
already obstructed by the threshold example above. Which representations
with certified zero tests, rational dependence data, or finite support
restore an effective finite classification?
\end{question}

The next attainable case is a tuple with explicitly supplied finite
supports. Its known initial coordinates can be incorporated into the
sign-pattern calculation, after which later perturbations see zero
parameter tails. The proof must account for the transition between
these fixed initial coordinates and the freely variable tail.

\begin{question}[Complexity of the exact finite algorithms]
How hard is it to compute the optimal revision number or the exact
continuity condition from a quantifier-free graph? Can the sign-pattern
search be compressed using the intersection lattice of the rational
hyperplanes, rather than enumerating all ternary patterns?
\end{question}

The theorems prove decidability, not a good running-time bound. It is
useful to separate the cost of Presburger elimination from the
combinatorial cost of feasible sign patterns and alternating chains.
A small verified implementation of the latter would already be a
substantive addition to the repository.

\begin{question}[Effective computation for countable cores]
For $D\lex K$, where $K$ is a countable $\Z$-group equipped with
the discrete topology, classify the oracle information needed for an
effective continuity compiler and for finite-prefix evaluation of
definable maps. How does the answer depend on the chosen presentation
of $K$ and the names of its parameters?
\end{question}

The purely topological continuity and Baire conclusions extend by the
same finite-branch proofs, as established above. Computation must
distinguish knowing a core element as a discrete topological point from
having algorithms for its arithmetic. A countable carrier does not by
itself provide decidable operations or order. A useful first case is a
computable presentation with a decidable atomic diagram and named
standard quotient functions.

\begin{question}[Connected Polish monoid presentations]\label{pma:nsp:q:connected}
Can a connected uncountable Polish space support Presburger addition
when no signed Polish group presentation is supplied?
\end{question}

The automatic continuity of standard residues settles the negative
answer for cones inheriting a Polish group topology. It does not settle
the question for arbitrary monoid topologies. The essential missing
step is a suitable group-completion theorem, or an example showing why
such a completion cannot be demanded.

\noindent\writetag{} This is Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:connected} and Part~III's
\cref{pma:cp:q:connected}, restricted to monoid topologies with no signed
Polish group presentation; see the note after
\cref{pma:nsp:thm:polish-group-unit-splitting}.

\begin{question}[Rigidity with continuous addition]\label{pma:nsp:q:rigidity}
Which rigid Presburger models admit a Polish topology with continuous
addition and Borel order? How does the answer change when one demands a
Polish topology on the entire signed group?
\end{question}

The split models have nontrivial positive dilations of their divisible
part. The nonsplit construction here retains such a divisible
coefficient part and is not a rigid example. Je\v r\'abek's structural
theory \cite{jerabek} gives algebraic constraints, but these do not
automatically produce or exclude a prescribed Polish topology.

\noindent\writetag{} Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:rigidity} asks the first sentence.

\begin{question}[Open divisible subgroups and continuous core decompositions]
In which Polish Presburger groups with Borel order is the maximal
divisible subgroup $\ker r$ open? When does the algebraic decomposition
admit a continuous splitting with a countable discrete reduced core?
\end{question}

The transfer examples have an open divisible factor and a countable
reduced core. The automatic-continuity theorem proves a different,
narrower statement: if a retraction onto the standard integers exists
algebraically, it is continuous. It does not classify arbitrary
countable cores or make every algebraic decomposition topological.

\begin{question}[Sufficiency in the metric problem]
For a cancellative linearly ordered Polish monoid with diagonal
continuity of monus, is closedness of all translates part of a useful
sufficient criterion for a compatible complete metric with uniformly
continuous addition? What additional hypotheses are necessary?
\end{question}

The closed-translate theorem supplies a necessary condition only.
One should first study concrete subclasses, such as cones with
continuous ambient subtraction or locally compact monoids, and keep
the uniform structure as part of the data.

\begin{question}[Embeddings between different countable cores]
Describe continuous elementary embeddings between $D\lex K$ and
$D'\lex K'$, especially when the cores are reduced and nonsplit.
Which information in the coherent residue image is preserved by a
topological or ordered embedding?
\end{question}

The automatic continuity theorem shows that all finite residue maps
are topologically visible on a Polish signed group. The distinction
between their separate continuity and a single integer retraction is
therefore a natural invariant to retain in such a classification.

\begin{question}[Minimal foundational and formalization requirements]\label{pma:nsp:q:foundations}
What is the weakest convenient subsystem in which the explicit
stream model, the rank bound, and the finite-pattern optimization can
be proved for coded inputs? Can the mathematical and computational
parts be isolated into small reusable proof-assistant modules?
\end{question}

This is a question about the positive construction and its
classification algorithms. It is separate from Glazer's published
reverse-mathematical question about the strength of the topological
Tennenbaum theorem. A proof of one would not be a proof of the other.

\noindent\writetag{} Compare Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:metatheory}. Source~14
(\cref{pma:part:atr}) claims an answer to Glazer's published question; it is a
different theorem from the positive construction, as source~13 says.

\section{The question, the intersection, and the contributions}
\label{pma:atr:sec:intro}

Elliot Glazer's research in set theory and formal systems, together with
his work on foundations of proof assistants, makes the interface between
arithmetic models, definability, and formalization a direct match for
\repo; an institutional author biography confirms these interests
\cite{s14:Epoch}. The particularly useful source is his
\emph{A Topological Tennenbaum Theorem} \cite{Glazer}.
The relevant part of \repo\ is its work on Diophantine exponentiation,
arithmetic coding, and Polish models of omnific arithmetic
\cite{s14:RepoPower,s14:RepoPresburger}.

In ordinary mathematics, Glazer proves that a model of
\(\mathsf Q+\ID+\Exp\) on an uncountable Polish space, with both
arithmetic operations Borel, cannot have either operation continuous.
His Question~1 asks whether this conclusion is provable in \(\ATR\).
The unresolved issue identified there concerns the descriptive
complexity of exponentiation and the choices used in the multiplicative
argument. We give a proof using internal MRDP, Borel regularization,
and category.

Here and below, \emph{uncountable} is external to the arithmetic
object structure; its precise coded meaning is specified in
Section~\ref{pma:atr:subsec:coding}. Arithmetic comparisons refer to the
model's order.
A Polish space is a separable space admitting a complete compatible
metric. Neither that topology nor its metric is assumed to agree with
the arithmetic order topology.

\begin{theorem}[Main theorem: cofinal unary discontinuity]
\label{pma:atr:thm:main}
Work in \(\ATR\), with the coded-presentation convention of
Section~\ref{pma:atr:sec:framework}. Let \(\mathcal M\) have an uncountable
Polish carrier \(M\) and Borel addition and multiplication.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If \(\mathcal M\models\mathsf Q+\IOpen\), then for every
\(b\in M\) there is an \(a\ge b\) such that
\[
 \tau_a:M\longrightarrow M,\qquad \tau_a(x)=a+x
\]
is discontinuous.
\item If \(\mathcal M\models\mathsf Q+\ID+\Exp\), then for every
\(b\in M\) there is an \(a\ge b\) such that
\[
 \lambda_a:M\longrightarrow M,\qquad \lambda_a(x)=2^a x
\]
is discontinuous.
\end{enumerate}
In particular neither addition nor multiplication is separately
continuous, and neither is jointly continuous, under the hypotheses
of \textup{(ii)}.
\end{theorem}

The two witnesses \(a\) need not be the same. \emph{Cofinal} here means
unbounded in the arithmetic order; it makes no assertion about
topological density, cardinality, or category of the set of parameters.

Part~(i) uses a weak theory already covered by Glazer's additive
obstruction. The substantive new connection for Question~1 is the
passage from a \emph{provably correct internal} Diophantine definition
to a Borel exponentiation map. Cofinality and the unary formulation
are additional consequences of the proof supplied here.

A second contribution records a concrete distinction that is useful
for the repository's surreal program.

\begin{theorem}[A nonsplit Presburger boundary; an instance of \cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}]
\label{pma:atr:thm:nonsplit-intro}
There is an explicitly described uncountable, locally compact, perfect
Polish model of Presburger arithmetic with jointly continuous addition
whose standard-integer subgroup is not a direct summand of its
Grothendieck group. The model has an ordered additive embedding into
the surreal numbers using expressions
\[
 x\omega^2+q\omega+p\qquad(x\in\R,\ p,q\in\Q),
\]
but has no additive map to the canonical omnific integers that sends
its unit to \(1\).
\end{theorem}

The abstract existence of nonsplit \(\Z\)-groups is classical
\cite{jerabek}; we supply an elementary explicit example, its Polish
realization, and the omnific obstruction. We do not claim the first
discovery of nonsplit Presburger groups.
