\section{Framework and the established inputs}
\label{pma:atr:sec:framework}

\subsection{Object arithmetic and external mathematics}

The object language contains \(0,1,+,\cdot,<\), with the usual
discretely ordered semiring conventions. The order may equivalently
be recovered from addition:
\[
 x<y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists z\;(x+z+1=y).
\]
We use \(\IOpen\) for induction for quantifier-free formulas and
\(\ID\) for induction for bounded formulas. Write
\[
 T_{\exp}=\mathsf Q+\ID+\Exp.
\]
The exponentiation axiom is the ordinary first-order assertion of
total exponentiation through finite-sequence coding, not an assumption
that an external exponential operation has already been supplied
as a Borel map. The standard equivalent formulations of elementary
arithmetic may be used.

The external theory \(\ATR\) is second-order arithmetic with
arithmetical transfinite recursion. Its natural role is that Borel
codes may require transfinite recursion to evaluate. The object
theory and the external theory do different jobs: \(T_{\exp}\)
controls the algebra in \(M\), while \(\ATR\) controls codes for
the Polish space and its Borel data.

\subsection{Coded-model convention}
\label{pma:atr:subsec:coding}

A coded Polish space is specified by a countable dense metric
presentation and its completion; a point is represented by a suitable
fast Cauchy name. Equality of names means equality of the represented
points. Borel maps are specified by standard Borel codes, including
uniform codes for inverse images of a countable basis.
All functions and relations must respect equality of point names.

For the reverse-mathematical statement, a coded space or coded Borel
subset \(A\) is \emph{uncountable} when no coded sequence of point
names covers it. In symbols, this is
\[
 \neg\exists(x_n)_{n\in\N}\;
 \forall x\bigl(x\in A\ \longrightarrow\ \exists n\;x=x_n\bigr),
\]
where membership is interpreted using the supplied Borel code.
The word external does not introduce an ambient cardinality predicate
unavailable in second-order arithmetic.

The notation \(\mathcal M\models T_{\exp}\) is ordinary semantic
notation in the mathematical exposition. For the reverse-mathematical
claim it is interpreted \emph{instance by instance}: every particular
first-order formula needed by the proof is translated directly into
second-order arithmetic, with its variables ranging over point names.
We do not postulate a truth predicate for all first-order formulas
on an uncountable carrier.

\begin{lemma}[Fixed-proof interpretation]
\label{pma:atr:lem:finite-proof}
Let \(\pi\) be a fixed finite first-order derivation of a sentence
\(\psi\) from a theory \(T\), and let \(\Gamma_\pi\) be the finite
collection of nonlogical axiom instances actually used.
For a coded real-domain structure, the direct translations of those
instances imply the direct translation of \(\psi\).
No uniform satisfaction predicate is required.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Translate each of the finitely many formulas in \(\pi\).
Object quantifiers become quantifiers over valid point names, and
atomic formulas use the specified equality and operation relations.
Logical axioms remain valid under this interpretation; modus ponens
and generalization remain valid as well. Thus the translated finite
derivation proves
\[
 \bigwedge_{\theta\in\Gamma_\pi}\theta^{\mathcal M}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \psi^{\mathcal M}.
\]
This is a fixed syntactic translation. It neither constructs a set
of truths nor proves uniform soundness for arbitrary proof codes.
The elementary logic involved is available already in the base
second-order framework, once the presentation laws are assumed.
\end{proof}

Consequently the main argument can be stated with a sufficient fixed
finite arithmetic package, giving an actual second-order sentence.
Using the familiar model-theoretic notation is harmless provided this
convention is kept explicit.

\subsection{The exact internal MRDP input}

The theorem of Gaifman and Dimitracopoulos needed here is the
following proof-theoretic form of MRDP \cite{s14:GD}. Its exact statement
is explicitly recorded in the recent research paper of
Chen, M\"uller, and Yokoyama: see its Section~1.4 and
Definition~5.2 \cite{s14:CMY}.

\begin{theorem}[Gaifman--Dimitracopoulos; established input]
\label{pma:atr:thm:GD}
For each fixed bounded arithmetic formula \(\theta(\bar x)\),
there are fixed polynomial terms \(P(\bar x,\bar u)\) and
\(Q(\bar x,\bar u)\), with natural-number coefficients, such that
\[
 T_{\exp}\vdash
 \theta(\bar x)\ \longleftrightarrow\
 \exists\bar u\;P(\bar x,\bar u)=Q(\bar x,\bar u).
\]
The same conclusion holds for each fixed \(\Sigma_1\) formula by
including its initial existential variables in \(\bar u\).
\end{theorem}

Only one standard instance, for the graph of \(2^x\), is essential to
the multiplicative theorem. No uniform formalization of the whole
MRDP theorem inside the external theory is needed. The theorem's
\emph{internal correctness} is essential: a polynomial that merely
agrees with exponentiation on standard integers would be insufficient.

The original 1982 contribution is a chapter in monograph no.~30 of
\emph{L'Enseignement Math\'ematique}, not an article in journal
volume~30. Its bibliography is confirmed by the author's publication
list \cite{s14:DimitracopoulosList}. An accessible scan of the original
chapter was not obtained in this audit; the precise input above is
corroborated by \cite{s14:CMY}, rather than inferred from a casual summary.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:atr:thm:GD} is a declared input. Source~14's
author did not see the original chapter \cite{s14:GD} and took the statement
from \cite{s14:CMY}; the intake did not check either source.

\subsection{Coded descriptive-set-theoretic inputs}\label{pma:atr:subsec:inputs}

We use the following standard results in their coded forms, available
in \(\ATR\); the relevant implementation of the perfect-set and order
steps is also described in Glazer's Optimization section
\cite{Glazer,s14:Simpson,s14:Blass}.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Disjoint analytic sets admit a Borel separator. In particular,
an analytic set with analytic complement has a Borel code.
\item Borel sets have the property of Baire, with an open approximant
and a coded countable cover of the error by closed nowhere-dense sets.
\item An uncountable Borel subset of a Polish space admits a
continuous injective Cantor map. For a Borel linear order, this may
be refined to an increasing continuous Cantor map.
\item The preceding perfect-set/order construction can be carried
out for a coded sequence of uncountable Borel sets without adding
a countable-choice principle for arbitrary relations.
\end{enumerate}

For the order refinement, pull the arithmetic order back along a
Cantor injection, color pairs by agreement with lexicographic order,
and use perfect-set homogeneity for a Borel two-coloring of pairs.
Reverse the Cantor order if necessary.
The uniform version asserts the existence of one real coding the
sequence of embeddings; it does not assert an effective or Borel
selection operator on all input codes. Apply the pseudohierarchy
construction relative to the join of the input codes, then one tagged
Baire approximation to the pullback pair-colorings, a common perfect
tree avoiding all errors, and the coded open-color homogeneous-tree
construction in each section. This is the common coding and
perfect-tree construction used in Glazer's optimization.

These are declared inputs, not hidden consequences of elementary
metric completeness. The new uses of them, particularly the tagged
continuity construction, are proved below.

\noindent\writetag{} These four coded inputs, together with
\cref{pma:atr:lem:perfect-order} and the evaluation of countable Borel
iterations along a pseudohierarchy in \cref{pma:atr:sec:atr-audit}, are where
the $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ bookkeeping of source~14 rests on statements it declares
rather than proves. Whether each holds in $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ in the uniform form
used is part of what an independent review would have to check.

\section{Internal Diophantine definitions become Borel maps}
\label{pma:atr:sec:borel}

\subsection{The functional projection principle}

\begin{lemma}[Total analytic functions]
\label{pma:atr:lem:analytic-function}
Let \(X,Y\) be Polish spaces. Suppose \(R\subseteq X\times Y\)
is analytic and for every \(x\in X\) there is exactly one \(y\)
with \(R(x,y)\). Then the function \(f(x)=y\) has a Borel graph
and is a Borel map. From the analytic data and the asserted
totality and uniqueness, the needed codes can be obtained in \(\ATR\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The complement of the graph is analytic because
\[
 \neg R(x,y)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists z\;(R(x,z)\wedge z\ne y).
\]
Here totality supplies an output, and uniqueness identifies all
other pairs as nongraph pairs. Analytic separation therefore gives
a Borel graph.

To obtain a map code explicitly, let \((U_j)_{j\in\N}\) be a
countable basis of \(Y\). Form the tagged sets
\[
\begin{split}
 A&=\{(j,x):\exists y\;(R(x,y)\wedge y\in U_j)\},\\
 B&=\{(j,x):\exists y\;(R(x,y)\wedge y\notin U_j)\}.
\end{split}
\]
They are analytic, disjoint, and exhaust \(\N\times X\).
One separator is therefore exactly \(A\). Its sections give all
the codes for \(f^{-1}(U_j)\) at once. This avoids a countable
sequence of independently chosen separators.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Automatic Borel definability]
\label{pma:atr:thm:automatic}
Suppose \(\mathcal M\models T_{\exp}\) has a Polish carrier and
Borel arithmetic operations. If a fixed \(\Sigma_1\) formula
\(\varphi(\bar x,y)\) provably defines a total single-valued
function in \(T_{\exp}\), then its interpretation in \(\mathcal M\)
is a Borel map.
Also, any relation whose positive and negative definitions are
provably \(\Sigma_1\) over \(T_{\exp}\) is Borel.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:GD} to write
\[
 \varphi(\bar x,y)
 \ \longleftrightarrow\
 \exists\bar u\;P(\bar x,y,\bar u)=Q(\bar x,y,\bar u)
\]
inside \(T_{\exp}\). Polynomial evaluation in \(\mathcal M\) is
Borel: the polynomial is a fixed finite expression built from Borel
operations. Equality of two values is a closed relation on the
carrier, so the equality locus is Borel. Projection over the finite
tuple \(\bar u\) makes the displayed relation analytic.
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:analytic-function} applies.

For a relation with positive and negative \(\Sigma_1\) definitions,
apply internal MRDP to both definitions and then analytic separation.
The transfer of each fixed arithmetic derivation is justified by
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:finite-proof}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
\label{pma:atr:cor:bounded}
Every fixed bounded arithmetic relation is Borel in a Borel
presentation of a model of \(T_{\exp}\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
A bounded formula and its negation are both bounded. Apply the
relational part of Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:automatic}.
\end{proof}

This corollary is not obtained by pretending that an internally
bounded quantifier ranges over an externally finite set. In an
uncountable nonstandard model, an interval \([0,a]\) can be
uncountable. The Diophantine translation is doing substantive work.

\subsection{Exponentiation is an instance of the principle}
\label{pma:atr:subsec:exp}

For clarity, one may use the standard remainder-based sequence
coding. Let
\[
 \beta(u,v,i)=u\bmod(1+(i+1)v).
\]
The assertion \(\beta(u,v,i)=r\) can be expanded using a bounded
quotient witness and a polynomial equality, so it is bounded
arithmetic syntax. The graph formula
\[
\begin{split}
 E(x,y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists u\,\exists v\,\bigl(&\beta(u,v,0)=1
 \ \wedge\ \beta(u,v,x)=y\\
 &{}\wedge\ \forall i<x\,
       \beta(u,v,i+1)=2\beta(u,v,i)\bigr)
\end{split}
\tag{3.1}
\]
is \(\Sigma_1\) after expanding the remainder notation. All intermediate
remainders and quotient witnesses can be bounded by terms in the
code parameters.

The usual arithmetic properties, proved internally in \(T_{\exp}\),
are
\[
 e(0)=1,\qquad e(1)=2,\qquad
 e(a+b)=e(a)e(b),\qquad
 a<b\ \Longrightarrow\ e(a)<e(b),
 \tag{3.2}
\]
where \(e(x)\) is the unique \(y\) satisfying \(E(x,y)\).
Only fixed proofs of these facts and of totality and uniqueness
are used.

\begin{corollary}[Borel internal exponentiation]
\label{pma:atr:cor:exp-borel}
In every Borel Polish presentation of a model of \(T_{\exp}\),
the internally defined function \(e(x)=2^x\) is Borel.
This conclusion, including a Borel-map code, follows in \(\ATR\).
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:automatic} to the fixed formula \(E\).
\end{proof}

The auxiliary Diophantine witnesses need not be unique. Only the
output \(y\) must be unique. Nor do we require that those witnesses
depend continuously or Borel-measurably on \(x\).
The argument concerns projection and the resulting function, not
a selection of polynomial solutions.

\section{A common Cantor set of continuity}
\label{pma:atr:sec:regularization}

The next lemma explains precisely how the Borel code for \(e\)
replaces higher-complexity choices.

\begin{lemma}[Simultaneous Cantor regularization]
\label{pma:atr:lem:regularization}
Let \(Y\) be a Polish space and let \((H_n)_{n\in\N}\) be a
uniformly coded sequence of Borel maps \(\Cantor\to Y\).
There is a continuous increasing injection
\(F:\Cantor\to\Cantor\), for the lexicographic order, such that every
\(H_n\circ F\) is continuous. The construction is available in
\(\ATR\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \((U_j)\) be a countable basis of \(Y\).
Apply the Baire-property construction to the single Borel set
\[
 A=\{(n,j,r):H_n(r)\in U_j\}
 \subseteq \N\times\N\times\Cantor.
\]
It gives open approximants \(V_{n,j}\) and, uniformly, a
countable family of closed nowhere-dense sets covering every
symmetric difference
\[
 H_n^{-1}(U_j)\mathbin{\triangle}V_{n,j}.
\]
Let \(G\) be the complementary dense \(G_\delta\) subset of
\(\Cantor\). On \(G\), every basis preimage for every \(H_n\) is
relatively open. Thus every \(H_n|G\) is continuous.

Write \(G=\bigcap_\ell W_\ell\), with each \(W_\ell\) dense
open. Construct nonempty clopen cylinders \(V_s\), \(s\in2^{<\omega}\),
so that the two successors lie inside \(V_s\cap W_{|s|}\),
are disjoint, occur in left-to-right lexicographic order, and
have lengths tending to infinity with \(|s|\). Each branch
has a unique intersection point. The branch map \(F\) is
continuous, injective, increasing, and has range in \(G\).
Therefore all \(H_n\circ F\) are continuous.
\end{proof}

The use of a single tagged set matters in weak metatheory.
It produces one coded family of approximations and errors;
it does not appeal to unrestricted countable choice.
The conclusion also does not say that the original \(H_n\)
are continuous on all of Cantor space.

\section{Arithmetic scales above any prescribed parameter}
\label{pma:atr:sec:scales}

We next replace informal fractional powers by exact floor
operations. This also makes the cofinal strengthening transparent.

\subsection{Borel arithmetic order, division, and square roots}

\begin{lemma}
\label{pma:atr:lem:basic-borel}
In a Borel presentation of a model of
\(\mathsf Q+\IOpen\), the arithmetic order is Borel.
Floor division by a positive element, its remainder, and the
function \(x\mapsto\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) are Borel.
Truncated subtraction is also Borel.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both \(x<y\) and its complement have existential definitions:
\[
 x<y\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists z\;(x+z+1=y),\qquad
 x\ge y\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists z\;(y+z=x).
\]
They are analytic, so separation gives a Borel order.

Open induction supplies Euclidean quotient and remainder and
the largest \(q\) with \(q^2\le x\). For example, the
quantifier-free inequality \(q^2>x\) holds at \(q=x+1\);
the least-transition argument supplied by open induction
gives a least such \(q\). The division argument uses
\(dq>x\), with \(d>0\), in the same way.

The characterizing graphs
\[
 x=dq+r,\quad r<d,
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 q^2\le x<(q+1)^2
\]
are Borel and define unique total outputs on their stated domains.
For coding purposes, extend quotient and remainder by zero at
divisor zero, so their domains are the Polish space \(M^2\).
The tagged inverse-open argument of
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:analytic-function} supplies map codes.
Truncated subtraction has the Borel graph
\[
 (y\le x\ \wedge\ y+z=x)\ \vee\ (x<y\ \wedge\ z=0),
\]
which again gives a unique total output. No continuity of subtraction
is asserted.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Uniform increasing Cantor maps; established input]
\label{pma:atr:lem:perfect-order}
For a Borel linear order on an uncountable Polish space, every
uncountable Borel subset contains an increasing continuous
Cantor image. Given a coded sequence of such subsets, the images
can be supplied by a single real coding a sequence of embeddings
in \(\ATR\).
\end{lemma}

This is the perfect-set/order-homogenization input described in
Section~\ref{pma:atr:sec:framework}. Its uniform form is the one used in
Glazer's weak-metatheory optimization \cite{Glazer}.
No uncountable choice of points is involved.

\subsection{The exact scale construction}

Fix any threshold \(b\in M\).
An increasing Cantor image in \(M\) supplies a \(c_0\) for which
\([0,c_0]\) is uncountable: take its upper endpoint.
Enlarge it to
\[
 c=\max\{c_0,(b+2)^4\}.
\]
Define, for external \(n\in\N\),
\[
 t_0=c,\qquad
 t_{n+1}=\lfloor\sqrt{t_n}\rfloor,\qquad
 q_n=\lfloor c/t_n\rfloor.
 \tag{5.1}
\]

Every interval \([0,t_n]\) is uncountable. To verify this without
induction on an assertion of uncountability, fix an arbitrary external
\(n\). At each level \(i<n\), quotient and remainder upon division
by \(t_{i+1}+1\) inject \([0,t_i]\) into \([0,t_{i+1}]^2\), since
\[
 t_i<(t_{i+1}+1)^2.
\]
Iteration along the finite binary tree gives an injection
\([0,c]\hookrightarrow[0,t_n]^{2^n}\). A coded enumeration of
\([0,t_n]\) would enumerate its finite Cartesian power. Reconstruct
the tree upward with \(x=(t_{i+1}+1)q+r\), retaining results in
\([0,c]\) and using zero otherwise. Every element of \([0,c]\)
would occur, contradicting its uncountability. Correctness of these
finite calculations uses arithmetic induction relative to their
evaluation traces, not induction on a projective uncountability
predicate. In particular every \(t_n\) exceeds every standard integer,
all the divisions in (5.1) are legitimate, and \(q_n\ge1\).

Set
\[
 X_n=\{q_n i:i<t_{n+2}\}.
 \tag{5.2}
\]
Each \(X_n\) is uncountable because multiplication by \(q_n>0\)
is injective. It is Borel by the direct description
\[
 X_n=\{x<q_nt_{n+2}:\remd(x,q_n)=0\}.
\]
Also \(X_n\subset[0,c)\), because \(q_nt_n\le c\)
and \(t_{n+2}<t_n\).

The scale separation has a short exact proof:
\[
 q_{n+1}\ge q_n t_{n+1}
          \ge q_n t_{n+2}^2
          >8q_n t_{n+2}.
 \tag{5.3}
\]
The first inequality follows from
\(c\ge q_nt_n\ge q_nt_{n+1}^2\), and the last uses
\(t_{n+2}>8\).

We use the shifted sets \(X_{n+1}\).
By Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:perfect-order}, choose uniformly increasing
continuous injections
\[
 f_n:\Cantor\longrightarrow X_{n+1}.
\]
Write \(\epsilon_k=\chi_{\{k\}}\), so \(\epsilon_k\to0^\omega\).
For a suitable increasing Cantor restriction \(F\), or simply
\(F=\mathrm{id}\), put
\[
 x_n=f_n(F(0^\omega)),\qquad
 h_{k,n}=f_n(F(\epsilon_k))-x_n.
 \tag{5.4}
\]
The subtraction denotes the unique nonnegative arithmetic
difference, not an assumed continuous operation.

\begin{lemma}[Separated perturbations]
\label{pma:atr:lem:perturbations}
The parameters in \textup{(5.4)} satisfy
\[
 b<h_{k,n},\qquad
 q_{n+1}\le h_{k,n}<q_{n+1}t_{n+3},\qquad
 x_n<c.
 \tag{5.5}
\]
Every choice \(h_n=h_{k_n,n}\) satisfies
\[
 h_{n+1}>8h_n.
 \tag{5.6}
\]
If \(F=\mathrm{id}\), then \(x_n+h_{k,n}\to x_n\).
If \(e\) is Borel and \(F\) is obtained by
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:regularization} for \(H_n=e\circ f_n\),
then
\[
 e(x_n+h_{k,n})\longrightarrow e(x_n).
 \tag{5.7}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The differences are positive multiples of \(q_{n+1}\), because
both endpoints lie in \(X_{n+1}\). They are smaller than
\(q_{n+1}t_{n+3}\).
Moreover
\[
 q_1\ge t_1\ge(b+2)^2>b,
\]
and (5.3) makes the subsequent \(q_n\) increase.
The scale inequality gives (5.6), independently of the choices of \(k_n\).
The convergence assertions follow from the specified continuity
and from \(\epsilon_k\to0^\omega\).
\end{proof}

Although \(t_n\) decreases and remains internally infinite for every
standard \(n\), no paradox is involved. The recursion is externally
countable, and internal nonstandard intervals need not behave like
standard finite intervals.

\section{A quantitative fusion lemma}
\label{pma:atr:sec:fusion}

The following metric estimate will serve both operations.
Suppose finite vertices \(V_s\in M\), \(s\in2^{<\omega}\), are
constructed level by level, with
\[
 V_{s0}=V_s.
\]
Assume vertices at each level are pairwise distinct. Put
\[
 \Delta_0=1,\qquad
 \Delta_n=\min\bigl(\{1\}\cup
 \{d(V_s,V_t):s,t\in2^n,\ s\ne t\}\bigr)\quad(n>0).
\]
Zero extensions imply \(\Delta_{n+1}\le\Delta_n\).

\begin{lemma}[Fusion estimate]
\label{pma:atr:lem:fusion}
If
\[
 d(V_s,V_{s1})<2^{-n-4}\Delta_n
 \qquad(s\in2^n),
 \tag{6.1}
\]
then
\[
 z_r=\lim_N V_{r|N}
\]
exists for every \(r\in\Cantor\), uniformly in \(r\), and the map
\(r\mapsto z_r\) is a continuous injection. More precisely,
\[
 d(V_{r|N},z_r)\le2^{-N-3}\Delta_N,
 \tag{6.2}
\]
and if \(r|N\ne s|N\), then
\[
 d(z_r,z_s)\ge(1-2^{-N-2})\Delta_N>0.
 \tag{6.3}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(i\ge N\), \(\Delta_i\le\Delta_N\).
The sum of the tail edge bounds is at most
\[
 \Delta_N\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}2^{-i-4}
   =2^{-N-3}\Delta_N.
\]
Completeness gives the limit and (6.2).
Since \(\Delta_N\le1\), the bound also gives a common Cauchy rate.
The finite-level maps \(r\mapsto V_{r|N}\) are locally constant,
so uniform convergence makes the limit map continuous.

If the prefixes at level \(N\) differ, their vertices are at least
\(\Delta_N\) apart. Subtracting the two tail bounds gives (6.3).
Thus distinct branches have distinct limits.
\end{proof}

At an implementation level, the search for (6.1) need not compare
arbitrary real numbers exactly. Choose rational lower bounds for
the finitely many positive separation distances and dovetail a
search for certified strict inequalities. The convergence used
below guarantees termination at each stage. This is a recursive
construction with supplied codes, not an arbitrary sequence of
choices.

\section{Cofinal discontinuity of additive translations}
\label{pma:atr:sec:addition}

We first give a full additive proof, including the category lemma
that will be reused.

\begin{lemma}[Category zero--one law for finite changes]
\label{pma:atr:lem:tail}
If \(D\subseteq\Cantor\) has the property of Baire and membership in
\(D\) is invariant under changing finitely many coordinates,
then \(D\) is meager or comeager.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(D\) is nonmeager, it is comeager in some nonempty basic
cylinder. Finite bit flips take this cylinder to every cylinder
of the same length. Invariance makes \(D\) comeager in every one
of them. There are finitely many such cylinders and they cover
Cantor space, so \(D\) is comeager.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
\label{pma:atr:thm:additive}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:main}\textup{(i)},
discontinuous translations occur cofinally in the arithmetic order.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(b\in M\), and suppose for contradiction that every
translation \(\tau_a\) with \(a\ge b\) is continuous.
Use Section~\ref{pma:atr:sec:scales} with \(F=\mathrm{id}\).
For every \(m\ge2c\), the translating constant \(m-x_n\)
is larger than \(c\), hence larger than \(b\). Therefore
\[
 m+h_{k,n}
 =(m-x_n)+(x_n+h_{k,n})\longrightarrow m.
 \tag{7.1}
\]
Only a fixed translation is used in this passage to the limit.

Choose \(h_n=h_{k_n,n}\) recursively and set
\[
 V_s=2c+\sum_{i<|s|,\ s(i)=1}h_i.
\]
At stage \(n\), (7.1) allows \(k_n\) to make every one of the
finitely many new edges satisfy (6.1).
The growth \(h_{n+1}>8h_n\) makes all subset sums at a fixed
level distinct. For example, induction gives the integer inequality
\[
 7\sum_{i<n}h_i<h_n;
\]
the largest differing summand dominates all earlier ones.
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:fusion} gives a continuous injection
\(r\mapsto z_r\).

Identify subsets of \(\N\) with their characteristic functions.
For \(j\notin A\), the exact finite-sum identities and continuity
of the fixed translation by \(h_j>b\) give
\[
 z_{A\cup\{j\}}=z_A+h_j.
 \tag{7.2}
\]
This identity, not continuity of order or subtraction, controls
the limits.

Let \(r^*\) denote coordinatewise complementation and define
\[
 E_n=\{r:z_{r^*}<z_r\le z_{r^*}+h_n\},\qquad
 D=\{r:\forall n\ (z_{r^*}+h_n<z_r)\}.
 \tag{7.3}
\]
These are Borel sets.

Let \(r(j)=0\) and let \(s\) be obtained by flipping the \(j\)th
bit. Equation (7.2) says
\[
 z_s=z_r+h_j,\qquad z_{r^*}=z_{s^*}+h_j.
 \tag{7.4}
\]
If \(r,s\in E_n\) and \(j>n\), then
\[
 z_{s^*}+h_j<z_r,\qquad
 z_r+h_j\le z_{s^*}+h_n.
\]
Adding and cancelling yields \(2h_j<h_n\), which is impossible.
Thus \(E_n\) is disjoint from its image under any sufficiently
far bit flip. If \(E_n\) were nonmeager, it would be comeager
in some cylinder. A flip beyond that cylinder's length would
give two disjoint comeager subsets of the same cylinder.
Hence each \(E_n\) is meager.

The set \(D\) is invariant under a single bit flip.
In the notation (7.4), \(r\in D\) immediately implies \(s\in D\).
Conversely, suppose \(s\in D\) and fix \(n\).
Choose \(k=\max(n,j)+1\); growth gives
\[
 h_k>h_n+2h_j.
\]
Then
\[
 z_{s^*}+h_k<z_s=z_r+h_j
\]
implies, after comparison and cancellation,
\[
 z_{r^*}+h_n=z_{s^*}+h_j+h_n<z_r.
\]
Thus \(r\in D\). Iterating proves finite-change invariance.

The sets \(D\) and \(D^*=\{r^*:r\in D\}\) are disjoint.
Their union is comeager, because \(z_r\ne z_{r^*}\) by injectivity,
and
\[
 \Cantor\setminus(D\cup D^*)
 \subseteq\bigcup_n(E_n\cup E_n^*).
 \tag{7.5}
\]
Complementation is a homeomorphism. Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:tail} says
\(D\) is meager or comeager. In the first case both \(D\) and
\(D^*\) are meager, contradicting their comeager union.
In the second case they are disjoint comeager sets, another
contradiction. This proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

The proof never takes an arithmetic inequality through a metric
limit. In particular it does not assert \(z_r\ge2c\) because
every approximating vertex has that property.

\section{Cofinal discontinuity of power-of-two multipliers}
\label{pma:atr:sec:multiplication}

We now prove the part that resolves the weak-metatheory question.

\begin{theorem}[A Borel exponential obstruction]
\label{pma:atr:thm:external-exp}
Suppose \(\mathcal M\models\mathsf Q+\IOpen\) has an
uncountable Polish carrier and Borel arithmetic operations.
Suppose in addition there is a Borel function \(e:M\to M\)
satisfying (3.2). Then, for every \(b\in M\), some fixed
multiplication map \(x\mapsto e(a)x\), with \(a\ge b\),
is discontinuous.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(b\), and assume that multiplication by \(e(a)\) is
continuous for every \(a\ge b\).
Construct \(c,t_n,q_n,X_n,f_n\) as in
Section~\ref{pma:atr:sec:scales}. Apply
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:regularization} to all maps \(e\circ f_n\),
and define \(x_n,h_{k,n}\) using the resulting common \(F\).
We have (5.7).

For each \(m\ge2c\), the parameter \(m-x_n>c>b\).
Using only continuity of multiplication by the fixed element
\(e(m-x_n)\), we obtain
\[
\begin{split}
 e(m+h_{k,n})
 &=e(m-x_n)e(x_n+h_{k,n})\\
 &\longrightarrow e(m-x_n)e(x_n)=e(m).
\end{split}
 \tag{8.1}
\]

Choose \(h_n=h_{k_n,n}\) recursively, write \(y_n=e(h_n)\),
and put
\[
 V_s=e(2c)\prod_{i<|s|,\ s(i)=1}y_i.
 \tag{8.2}
\]
Each current vertex is \(e(m_s)\), with
\(m_s=2c+\sum_{i<|s|,s(i)=1}h_i\ge2c\).
Thus (8.1) allows all new edges at stage \(n\) to satisfy
(6.1).

The arithmetic identities for \(e\) give
\[
 y_0\ge2,\qquad y_{n+1}>y_n^5.
 \tag{8.3}
\]
Let \(Q_n=\prod_{i<n}y_i\). Induction gives
\(Q_n^4<y_n\): it holds at \(n=0\), and
\[
 Q_{n+1}^4=Q_n^4y_n^4<y_n^5<y_{n+1}.
\]
Consequently the largest differing index in two finite products
dominates all preceding factors. The vertices at every level
are distinct. Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:fusion} again produces a continuous
injection \(r\mapsto z_r\).

For \(j\notin A\), continuity of multiplication by
\(y_j=e(h_j)\), whose exponent is \(h_j>b\), gives
\[
 z_{A\cup\{j\}}=y_jz_A.
 \tag{8.4}
\]
Every \(z_A\) is strictly positive. If \(z_A=0\), flip any bit.
Equation (8.4), and cancellation of the nonzero factor \(y_j\)
when the bit is removed, give a second input whose limit is zero.
This contradicts injectivity. The carrier is the nonnegative
arithmetic domain, so nonzero means positive.
No order-closedness assumption is used.

Define direct comparison events
\[
 E_n=\{r:z_{r^*}<z_r\le y_nz_{r^*}\},\qquad
 D=\{r:\forall n\ (y_nz_{r^*}<z_r)\}.
 \tag{8.5}
\]
They are Borel. With \(r(j)=0\) and \(s\) its one-bit flip,
(8.4) gives
\[
 z_s=y_jz_r,\qquad z_{r^*}=y_jz_{s^*}.
 \tag{8.6}
\]
If \(r,s\in E_n\) and \(j>n\), then
\[
 y_jz_{s^*}<z_r,\qquad
 y_jz_r\le y_nz_{s^*}.
\]
Multiplying the first inequality by \(y_j\), combining, and
cancelling \(z_{s^*}>0\), yields \(y_j^2<y_n\).
This contradicts (8.3). The same cylinder argument used in
Section~\ref{pma:atr:sec:addition} therefore makes each \(E_n\) meager.

The set \(D\) is invariant under one-bit flips.
If \(r\in D\), (8.6) immediately implies \(s\in D\).
For the converse, suppose \(s\in D\), fix \(n\), and put
\(k=\max(n,j)+1\). Then
\[
 y_k>y_ny_j^2.
\]
We have
\[
 y_jz_r=z_s>y_kz_{s^*}>y_ny_j^2z_{s^*}.
\]
Cancelling \(y_j>0\) proves
\(z_r>y_nz_{r^*}\), as required.

The category contradiction now finishes the proof:
\(D,D^*\) are disjoint, have a comeager union by
\[
 \Cantor\setminus(D\cup D^*)
 \subseteq\bigcup_n(E_n\cup E_n^*),
\]
and are interchanged by a homeomorphism.
Finite-change invariance gives the meager-or-comeager dichotomy,
which is incompatible with these two facts.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The answer to Glazer's Question 1, as claimed by source 14]
\label{pma:atr:cor:answer}
With the coding convention of Section~\ref{pma:atr:sec:framework},
Glazer's topological Tennenbaum theorem for
\(\mathsf Q+\ID+\Exp\) is provable in \(\ATR\).
In fact Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:main} holds.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{pma:atr:cor:exp-borel} supplies the Borel function \(e\)
and its internally proved algebraic properties.
Apply Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:external-exp} and
Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:additive}. Joint continuity implies continuity
of every unary section, so the original continuity conclusion
follows as well.
\end{proof}

\begin{tcolorbox}[title=Status of this answer \writetag]
\Cref{pma:atr:cor:answer} is a \textbf{claimed} affirmative answer to Glazer's
Question~1, which this report printed as open (\cref{pma:cp:q:glazerone};
\cref{pma:sec:glazer}). It is an unrefereed, AI-assisted manuscript's claim,
an upper bound under the coded-model convention of
\cref{pma:atr:subsec:coding}, and it has \textbf{not been independently
reviewed}: not by the intake, and not by the Hilbert's-tenth programme's
scoped review of the same archive, which read the internal-MRDP input and the
automatic-Borel argument and states that it does not certify the claimed
resolution (\cref{pma:app:provenance}). Its $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ bookkeeping rests
partly on declared inputs (note in \cref{pma:atr:subsec:inputs}), and its
author did not see the Gaifman--Dimitracopoulos chapter it relies on. No
reversal is claimed: $\mathsf{ACA}_0$ is not shown insufficient.
\end{tcolorbox}

\noindent\writetag{} Glazer names two places where his proof of Theorem~2
uses more than $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ \cite[p.~8]{Glazer}: the comprehension used to
define a partial map $g$ from preimages under $\exp\circ f_n$ in his Claim~2,
and $\boldsymbol\Sigma^1_2$-$\mathsf{AC}_0$ to choose the points $s_{k,n}$.
Source~14 replaces the first by the Borel exponentiation of
\cref{pma:atr:cor:exp-borel} and the common continuity restriction of
\cref{pma:atr:lem:regularization}, and the second by the finite searches of the
fusion estimate (\cref{pma:atr:lem:fusion}). Its additive part,
\cref{pma:atr:thm:additive}, strengthens Glazer's Corollary~1, which Glazer
already proves in $\mathsf{ATR}_0$ \cite[p.~7]{Glazer}, from measure to
category and to cofinal unary maps.

\section{Why the proof stays in \texorpdfstring{\(\ATR\)}{ATR0}}
\label{pma:atr:sec:atr-audit}

The new bridge is short, but its metatheoretic interpretation needs
care. The following table states the roles of the ingredients.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.29\textwidth}YP{0.23\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Operation & Data or justification & Choice or truth issue\\
\midrule
Internal exponentiation formula &
One fixed MRDP proof instance &
Finite proof translation only\\
Polynomial evaluation &
Finite composition of Borel operations &
No solution selector\\
Exponentiation map code &
One tagged analytic separator &
No separate separators chosen\\
Arithmetic scales &
Borel floor-root and quotient maps &
Coded recursive evaluation\\
Increasing Cantor maps &
Uniform perfect/order construction &
Use the coded uniform form\\
Common continuity restriction &
One tagged Baire approximation &
One exceptional cover\\
Metric fusion &
Finite searches with a common tail bound &
No arbitrary real choices\\
Tail contradiction &
Baire property and finite flips &
No measure theory\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\subsection{Countable iteration of Borel functions}

The sequence \(t_{n+1}=\lfloor\sqrt{t_n}\rfloor\) should not be
justified by an unexamined appeal to dependent choice.
Evaluation of the finitely many Borel maps involved can be organized
along a common countable well-order \(\alpha\). Successive evaluations
can then be performed along \(\alpha\cdot\omega\), with each block
using the point name produced by the preceding one.
This is arithmetical transfinite recursion, precisely the available
principle. The rational search used in fusion is handled within the
same coded evaluation framework.

\subsection{Uniform meager covers}

The passage from the individual meagerness of \(E_n\) to the
meagerness of their union also has a uniform implementation.
Apply the Baire-property construction to
\[
 \{(n,r):r\in E_n\}\subseteq\N\times\Cantor.
\]
Because each section is meager, each open approximant section must
be empty: a nonempty open subset of Cantor space cannot be meager.
The uniformly supplied error cover therefore covers every section.
Its sections, together with their complement-images, supply the
one countable cover needed in (7.5) and its multiplicative analogue.

\subsection{An upper bound, not a reversal}

An affirmative answer to the question about provability in \(\ATR\)
is an upper bound on the metatheory required.
Nothing here proves that the theorem is equivalent to \(\ATR\)
over \(\RCA\), or that \(\ACA\) cannot prove a suitably restricted
version. Those are separate questions, sensitive to how uncountability,
the Borel data, and the arithmetic hypotheses are coded.

Similarly, the proof does not construct a global satisfaction
predicate for \(T_{\exp}\), a set of all Borel functions, or a
collection of all models on an uncountable carrier.
The cofinality assertions themselves can be written as
second-order formulas about point names and the supplied Borel codes.

\subsection{Three tempting shortcuts that are insufficient}

First, a Diophantine representation proved only on standard \(\N\)
does not automatically identify the internally defined function in
an arbitrary nonstandard model. Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:GD} is the remedy.

Second, a Borel graph is not the chosen endpoint of the argument.
The tagged basis-preimage construction explicitly gives the
Borel-map information needed for regularization.

Third, transferring the topology along \(e:M\to e[M]\) does not
immediately reduce multiplication to addition. The Borel subspace
\(e[M]\) need not be Polish in the inherited topology, and a Polish
refinement can destroy the continuity one hoped to preserve.
The direct metric fusion works in the original complete carrier.

\section{A nonsplit Polish Presburger model}
\label{pma:atr:sec:nonsplit}

This supplementary section is ordinary set-theoretic mathematics.
The \(\ATR\) upper-bound claim concerns the coded topological-arithmetic
theorem above; no formalization of the surreal statements in
\(\ATR\) is asserted.

The preceding obstruction needs more arithmetic than addition alone.
To make that boundary concrete, we now construct a Presburger model
with continuous addition whose algebra differs from the split
examples already investigated in \repo.

\subsection{A countable nonsplit ordered group}

For \(n\ge1\), define
\[
 s_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}k!,\qquad
 e_0=(1,0),\qquad
 a_n=\left(\frac{s_n}{n!},\frac1{n!}\right)\in\Q^2.
 \tag{10.1}
\]
Let \(K_*\) be the subgroup generated by \(e_0,a_1,a_2,\ldots\).
Order \(\Q^2\) by the second coordinate first and then by
the first coordinate:
\[
 (p,q)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 q>0\ \text{or}\ (q=0\ \text{and}\ p>0).
\]

\begin{lemma}[$K_*=G_{\zeta_*}$ of \replabel{isg:cf:prop:family}]
\label{pma:atr:lem:D}
The group \(K_*\) is countable, \(e_0\) is its least positive
element, and projection onto the second coordinate induces
\[
 K_*/\Z e_0\cong\Q.
\]
The exact sequence \(0\to\Z e_0\to K_*\to\Q\to0\) does not split.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Countability is immediate.
If \(i\le N\), then
\[
 a_i=\frac{N!}{i!}a_N-\frac{s_N-s_i}{i!}e_0,
 \tag{10.2}
\]
and both coefficients are integers. Hence every finite linear
combination of generators has the form \(m e_0+k a_N\)
for suitable integers \(m,k\) and \(N\).
Its second coordinate is zero exactly when \(k=0\).
Thus the kernel of the projection is \(\Z e_0\).
The image contains \(1/n!\) for every \(n\), so it is all of
\(\Q\). An element with positive second coordinate is larger
than \(e_0\); an element with zero second coordinate is an
integer multiple of \(e_0\). This proves the least-positive claim.

The generators obey
\[
 (n+1)a_{n+1}=a_n+e_0.
 \tag{10.3}
\]
If a homomorphism \(\rho:K_*\to\Z\) satisfied \(\rho(e_0)=1\),
write \(b_n=\rho(a_n)\). Iterating (10.3) gives
\[
 n!b_n=b_1+s_n.
 \tag{10.4}
\]
Both \(s_n\) and \(n!-s_n\) tend to infinity.
For the second assertion, \(s_n\le2(n-1)!\) for \(n\ge3\),
so \(n!-s_n\ge(n-2)(n-1)!\).
For sufficiently large \(n\), (10.4) would therefore put the
integer multiple \(n!b_n\) strictly between \(0\) and \(n!\).
This is impossible. A splitting of the displayed exact sequence
would give such a retraction, proving nonsplitting.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} $K_*$ is the group $G_{\zeta_*}$, $\zeta_*=\sum_k k!$, of
the \fn{discrete-initial-subgroups-and-omnific-normalization} report
(\replabel{isg:cf:eq:explicitparameter}), with the two coordinates exchanged:
source~14's $a_n=(s_n/n!,1/n!)$ and $e_0=(1,0)$ are that report's
$x_n=(1/n!,S_n/n!)$ and $e=(0,1)$, with $S_n=s_n$, and
relation (10.3) of \cref{pma:atr:lem:D} is its transition relation with every
digit equal to~$1$. This lemma is therefore
\replabel{isg:cf:prop:family} with \replabel{isg:cf:thm:familytest} for
$\zeta_*$, proved with the same estimate $s_n\le2(n-1)!$
(\replabel{isg:cf:lem:noninteger}). Source~14 does not cite that report; its
statement that it does not claim the first discovery of nonsplit Presburger
groups stands.

This supplies all algebra needed here without invoking the
classification of extensions of \(\Q\) by \(\Z\).

\subsection{The Polish carrier}

Let
\[
 G=\R\lex K_*
\]
as an ordered group, with the real coordinate having priority.
Give it the product \emph{group topology}
\(\R\times K_{*,\mathrm{discrete}}\).
Its distinguished unit is \((0,e_0)\).
Let \(M=G_{\ge0}\), with the inherited topology and addition.

\begin{proposition}[an instance of \cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}]
\label{pma:atr:prop:polish-D}
The structure \(M\) is an uncountable, locally compact, perfect
Polish model of Presburger arithmetic with jointly continuous
addition. Its group completion is \(G\), and the standard-integer
subgroup of \(G\) is not a direct summand.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The group \(K_*\) is countable discrete, hence Polish.
The slices of \(M\) are
\[
 M\cap(\R\times\{d\})=
 \begin{cases}
 [0,\infty)\times\{d\},&d\ge0,\\
 (0,\infty)\times\{d\},&d<0.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{10.5}
\]
These slices are clopen in \(M\).
They are locally compact Polish spaces without isolated points.
A countable topological disjoint union of Polish spaces is Polish:
choose bounded complete metrics on the slices and a fixed positive
distance between distinct slices. This also proves local
compactness and perfectness directly.
The carrier is uncountable because any one slice is uncountable.
Addition is the restriction of continuous group addition on
\(\R\times K_{*,\mathrm{discrete}}\).

The least positive element of \(G\) is \((0,e_0)\), and
\[
 G/\Z(0,e_0)\cong\R\oplus\Q
\]
is divisible. The standard characterization of Presburger groups
as discretely ordered abelian groups with divisible quotient by
the subgroup generated by \(1\) therefore applies
\cite[Section~2]{jerabek}. Its nonnegative cone is a model of
Presburger arithmetic.

Every element of a linearly ordered group is a difference of
nonnegative elements, so \(G\) is the Grothendieck group of \(M\).
A retraction \(G\to\Z\) fixing its unit would restrict on
\(\{0\}\times K_*\) to the forbidden retraction in
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:D}. Thus the extension remains nonsplit.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:atr:prop:polish-D} is the case $D=\R$,
$K=K_*$ of source~13's \cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}, printed
there in general; source~14's proof is its own. Source~15 uses the same
construction in \cref{pma:lcc:thm:boundary-realization}.

In fact every first-order definable relation, with parameters, is
\(\Delta^0_2\) in this presentation. On each clopen discrete fiber
of a finite power of \(M\), a linear inequality is a real open or
closed half-space, with its equality boundary decided by the order
of \(K_*\). Both the inequality and its complement are \(F_\sigma\)
after taking the countable union of fibers. Congruence classes are
clopen unions of fibers: \(nG=\R\times nK_*\), so divisibility of
the real coordinate leaves the real part unrestricted.
Presburger quantifier elimination \cite{jerabek}, and closure of
\(\Delta^0_2\) under finite Boolean operations, prove the assertion.
Thus this is a Borel arithmetic presentation at the additive level.

\subsection{A surreal realization and an omnific obstruction}

For \((x,(p,q))\in G\), set
\[
 \Phi(x,(p,q))=x\omega^2+q\omega+p.
 \tag{10.6}
\]
These are ordinary finite Conway normal forms.

\begin{proposition}[second clause: \replabel{isg:cf:cor:unit}]
\label{pma:atr:prop:surreal}
The map \(\Phi:G\to\No\) is additive, injective, preserves
order, and sends the distinguished unit to \(1\).
There is nevertheless no additive map \(M\to\Oz\) that sends
the distinguished unit to \(1\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Addition of these finite normal forms is coefficientwise.
The sign of their difference is determined by its first
nonzero coefficient in the order
\(\omega^2,\omega,1\). This is exactly the order on \(G\),
so \(\Phi\) is an ordered additive embedding and has the
stated unit value.

For the second assertion, recall the defining normal-form
property of the canonical omnific integers: their constant
coefficient is an integer, and their normal forms have no negative
exponents \cite{s14:LM}. Taking that coefficient gives
an additive map
\[
 \ct:\Oz\longrightarrow\Z,\qquad \ct(1)=1.
\]
Suppose \(f:M\to\Oz\) were additive with \(f(1)=1\).
All \((0,a_n)\) lie in \(M\), since their second coordinate
inside \(K_*\) is positive. Thus
\(b_n=\ct(f(0,a_n))\in\Z\) would satisfy
\[
 (n+1)b_{n+1}=b_n+1
\]
by (10.3), and hence the impossible relation (10.4).
No extension of \(f\) to the group completion is needed for
this contradiction.
\end{proof}

Preservation of the unit is essential to the obstruction. The map
\[
 \Phi_\omega(x,(p,q))=\omega\Phi(x,(p,q))
             =x\omega^3+q\omega^2+p\omega
\]
is an ordered additive embedding into \(\Oz\), but sends the
distinguished unit to \(\omega\). Its constant term is zero.

\noindent\writetag{} The second assertion of \cref{pma:atr:prop:surreal} is
the case $G=K_*$ of \replabel{isg:cf:cor:unit} (a $\Z$-group admits an
additive map to $\Oz$ sending its least positive element to $1$ only if it
splits), and the embedding $\Phi_\omega$ is the one that report records after
that corollary, $(a,b)\mapsto a\omega^2+b\omega$ on $G_\zeta$. Source~13 gives
a two-element certificate of the same obstruction for its core
(\cref{pma:part:nsp}).

The distinction is algebraic. The topology under discussion is the
explicitly given Polish topology on \(G\) and \(M\). The image of
\(\Phi\) is discrete in the surreal order topology, since its
ordered-group gaps are at least \(1\). Consequently \(\Phi\) is
not a homeomorphic realization of the perfect Polish carrier in that
order topology.

The use of surreals creates no collection of all surreal
numbers as a set. Formula (10.6) describes a set-indexed
family of finite normal forms; it can be handled within
a sufficiently large set-sized stage, or as a class-valued
map in a conservative class framework. The nonexistence
argument is stronger and more general: it applies to any
target additive group that has a unit-preserving additive
map to \(\Z\).

\section{Consequences and a concrete formalization route}
\label{pma:atr:sec:repo}

\subsection{What the result says about representations}

In a Borel arithmetic presentation, internal exponentiation
can be discontinuous, but it cannot have arbitrary projective
complexity: its provable Diophantine definition supplies Borel
regularity. This amount of regularity is enough to find a
common perfect set on which the required countably many
exponential maps are continuous. Completeness then turns
small metric perturbations into a Cantor family of limits.
Arithmetic growth and finite-bit symmetries make that family
impossible if the relevant translations remain continuous.

The result distinguishes three notions that a representation
theorem must keep separate:
\begin{enumerate}
\item correctness on standard natural numbers;
\item correctness in every model of a specified weak arithmetic;
\item regularity of the interpreted operations in an external
topological presentation.
\end{enumerate}
The passage from the second to the third is the main bridge
of this article. The first alone does not imply either.

The cofinal strengthening says more than a failure somewhere
in a two-variable function. No final arithmetic segment of
translation parameters can consist entirely of continuous
maps; the same holds for exponents of continuous powers-of-two
multipliers. In particular the failure cannot be confined
to a bounded set of arithmetic constants.

\subsection{Existing interfaces and missing obligations}

The relevant Lean file is
\begin{quote}\small
\texttt{Logic/PeanoArithmetic/ListCoding/Lean/PAListCoding/}\\
\texttt{ExponentiationDiophantine.lean}.
\end{quote}
It imports Mathlib's Diophantine development and proves the
standard-natural graph statement using
\texttt{Dioph.pow\_dioph} \cite{s14:RepoPower}.
The corresponding Coq file provides explicit formula and
single-equation interfaces \cite{s14:RepoPowerCoq}.

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}P{0.26\textwidth}YY@{}}
\toprule
Layer & Existing or established material & Additional obligation\\
\midrule
Standard graph &
\(\N\)-valued exponentiation is Diophantine &
Keep the standard-domain scope explicit\\
Internal graph &
Gaifman--Dimitracopoulos theorem &
Extract one weak-arithmetic proof for \(E(x,y)\)\\
Presentation semantics &
Borel arithmetic operations on a Polish space &
Interpret the finite object proof on point names\\
Borel decoding &
Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:automatic} &
Formalize tagged analytic separation\\
Perfect restriction &
Lemma~\ref{pma:atr:lem:regularization} &
Formalize uniform Baire approximations and fusion\\
Continuity obstruction &
Sections~\ref{pma:atr:sec:addition}--\ref{pma:atr:sec:multiplication} &
Formalize limits, one-bit identities, and category\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

A practical development should proceed in this order.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Fix the arithmetic sentence.}
Choose one exact coded-sequence definition \(E\) and one
pair of polynomial terms. Record the finite weak-arithmetic
proof obligations connecting them. Do not silently substitute
a theorem about \(\N\).
\item \textbf{Separate interpretation from topology.}
Prove the fixed-proof interpretation lemma for the chosen
syntax and point-equality relation. This module should have
no claims about continuity.
\item \textbf{Prove the abstract Borel decoding lemma.}
Its inputs are analytic relation codes, totality, and uniqueness.
The result should include uniform inverse-basis codes.
\item \textbf{Formalize the metric and category core.}
The fusion estimate and one-bit contradiction can be verified
in ordinary mathematical foundations before reverse-mathematical
code bookkeeping is added.
\item \textbf{Assemble the exact upper bound.}
Audit every use of countable sequences. Tagged constructions
should replace implicit choices, and the final statement should
name the coding convention.
\end{enumerate}

No Lean or Coq file in this package is presented as a completed
formalization of these obligations. The included program checks
finite arithmetic estimates and the explicit nonsplit presentation;
it does not check the infinite-dimensional semantic theorem.

\section{Further research questions and topics}
\label{pma:atr:sec:questions}

\subsection{Reverse-mathematical strength}

\begin{question}
For a fixed, precise coding of Borel arithmetic presentations,
is the topological Tennenbaum statement equivalent to \(\ATR\)
over \(\RCA\), or does a weaker subsystem suffice?
\end{question}

The present proof provides an upper bound. A useful first step
is to separate the contribution of analytic separation from that
of the perfect-set/order lemma. Restrictions on the Borel ranks
of the supplied operations may allow a sharper statement.
A proposed reversal must specify the meaning of uncountability
and the available presentation codes; otherwise different
formulations can conceal different principles.

\subsection{Weaker object arithmetic}

\begin{question}
Can the power-of-two multiplier obstruction be established
under a strictly weaker arithmetic hypothesis than
\(\ID+\Exp\), without assuming a total Borel exponential
homomorphism as extra data?
\end{question}

Theorem~\ref{pma:atr:thm:external-exp} isolates exactly the usable
external substitute. The remaining task is to obtain enough
internally correct exponential behavior in weaker arithmetic.
This should not be confused with a claimed proof of MRDP
in \(\ID\); that is a separate longstanding problem
\cite{s14:CMY}. Partial exponentiation cuts are a natural
intermediate setting.

\subsection{How complicated are the discontinuous parameters?}

There is an immediate general upper bound. If
\(F:P\times X\to Y\) is Borel between Polish spaces, discontinuity
of the section \(F_p\) is equivalent to
\[
 \exists x\ \exists\varepsilon\in\Q_{>0}\ \exists(x_k)_{k\in\N}\
 \forall k\left[
 d_X(x_k,x)<2^{-k}\ \wedge\
 d_Y(F(p,x_k),F(p,x))\ge\varepsilon\right].
\]
The displayed witness relation is Borel, so the discontinuous-parameter
set is analytic and the continuous-parameter set is coanalytic.
The countable sequence of witnesses can be selected in \(\ATR\),
which already proves \(\Sigma^1_1\text{-}\mathsf{AC}_0\)
\cite[Theorem V.8.3]{s14:Simpson}. Apply this to the jointly Borel
families \(F(a,x)=a+x\) and \(F(a,x)=e(a)x\).

\begin{question}
For the arithmetic families above, is the coanalytic upper bound
sharp, or must the parameter sets
\[
 \{a:\tau_a\text{ is continuous}\},
 \qquad
 \{a:\lambda_a\text{ is continuous}\}
\]
be Borel under some natural additional hypotheses?
Can their complements be forced to be nonmeager, or must
one settle for arithmetic cofinality?
\end{question}

The theorem proves cofinal discontinuity, which does not settle
a topological size question. The outstanding problem is sharper
classification for arithmetic families, beyond the general
analytic/coanalytic bound just proved.

\subsection{Borel-rank bounds for internally computable functions}

\begin{question}
Given a fixed internal proof that a \(\Sigma_1\) graph is
total and single-valued, what bounds can one give on the
Borel complexity of its interpretation in terms of the
Borel codes for the primitive arithmetic operations?
\end{question}

The analytic-separation argument gives existence of codes,
not a small fixed finite rank. A quantitative version could
turn a qualitative impossibility theorem into an analysis
of the representation cost of arithmetic decoding.
One should distinguish graph ranks from ranks of
inverse images of open sets.

\subsection{The computational content of Borel decoding}

\begin{question}
What is the uniform computational strength of the operation
that takes coded Borel arithmetic and an internal
Diophantine correctness proof to a Borel exponentiation code?
\end{question}

A precise formulation can compare this operation with
analytic separation or transfinite Borel evaluation.
The fixed-proof theorem shows that uniform arithmetic truth
is not required. Determining whether separation is genuinely
necessary for the full code-construction problem would
clarify the source of noncomputability.

\subsection{Nonsplit Presburger topology}

\begin{question}
How can continuous unit-preserving homomorphisms and elementary
embeddings between the countable-slice Presburger models
\((\R\lex K)_{\ge0}\) be classified? Which additional specified
topological or definability conditions constrain the extension
class or force splitting?
\end{question}

The slice argument already applies to every countable
\(\Z\)-group \(K\) with its discrete topology. In particular, an
extension \(0\to\Z\to K\to V\to0\) with \(V\) countable,
divisible, and ordered carries the lexicographic order with convex
kernel \(\Z\), and yields the same locally compact Polish positive
cone and definability bounds. General existence is therefore settled
by this construction. Classification of maps, extension classes under
extra constraints, and other Polish carriers remains a separate task.

\noindent\writetag{} The general existence statement is source~13's
\cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}. With it, this answers the
existence part of Part~III's \cref{pma:cp:q:nonsplit} for countable cores.

\subsection{Which arithmetic fragments fit inside the omnific integers?}

\begin{question}
For set-sized Presburger groups admitting a retraction to \(\Z\),
which additional conditions allow unit-preserving omnific embeddings
with specified definability, topology, or initiality in the surreal
simplicity order?
\end{question}

Proposition~\ref{pma:atr:prop:surreal} supplies a necessary obstruction:
the constant-term map forces such a retraction.
The question concerns these extra requirements, rather than bare
ordered additive existence. The explicit formula (10.6) also makes
clear that an algebraic surreal realization need not carry the
desired topology. Any prescribed topology and notion of initiality
must be stated before an embedding classification is attempted.

\subsection{A proof-assistant milestone with a finite target}

\begin{question}
Can one extract and verify one explicit
\(\ID+\Exp\)-proof of the Diophantine correctness of \(E(x,y)\),
together with its finite semantic interpretation?
\end{question}

This is more focused than immediately formalizing every part
of MRDP or all reverse mathematics of Borel sets.
It would close the exact gap between the repository's
standard-natural exponentiation theorem and the principal
new application in this article. The tagged Borel lemma and
the metric/category core can then be developed independently.

\section{Verification, scope, and research status}
\label{pma:atr:sec:verification}

The mathematical review concentrated on the points where the
argument could otherwise fail:
\begin{enumerate}
\item internal, rather than merely standard, Diophantine correctness;
\item Borel-map codes in addition to graph codes;
\item uniformity of the perfect restriction and meager covers;
\item positivity of multiplicative limits without order continuity;
\item exact one-bit identities and inclusive comparison endpoints;
\item control of all continuity parameters above an arbitrary threshold;
\item the distinction between a fixed finite proof translation and
a global satisfaction construction.
\end{enumerate}
Separate in-session proof audits checked the arithmetic/descriptive
bridge and the metric/category argument. This is a mathematical
review record, not a substitute for independent external scrutiny.

The accompanying Python program uses exact integers and rational
numbers to check finite instances of the root-scale inequalities,
subset-sum separation, product-growth estimates in logarithmic
coordinates, factorial identities, and the finite obstruction
to a proposed retraction. These computations test concrete
algebraic details; they neither simulate a nonstandard model
nor prove the infinite topological theorem.

The claim about the question's status is deliberately precise.
The argument answers Question~1 \emph{as stated in the inspected
2023 paper}. The current repository manuscripts inspected for
this task leave that question open. Searches did not locate
a later arXiv version or a separate indexed solution.
This is not an exhaustive bibliographic priority determination.

The final package includes the complete LaTeX source, its compiled
PDF, build instructions, the finite-check program and its results,
and concise source and proof-audit records.

\section{The research intersection and the contribution}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:intersection}

The intersection chosen here is the topological model theory of weak
arithmetic, together with ordered additive groups and set-sized fragments
of Conway's omnific integers. It is supported by Glazer's own mathematical
paper, rather than inferred from a professional profile. In
\emph{A Topological Tennenbaum Theorem}, Glazer proves strong
nonexistence results for uncountable Polish models of arithmetic and asks
whether an uncountable Polish space can support Presburger arithmetic with
continuous addition \cite{Glazer}. The ProveIt repository contains both
an integer Cooper elimination development and a research manuscript on
Polish Presburger models inside the omnific integers
\cite{s15:proveitPresburger,s15:proveitPolish,s15:proveitOmnific}.

The repository manuscript already supplies an affirmative construction
for Glazer's Question~2 as it is stated in the cited 2023 paper. In
particular, the nonnegative cone of $\R\lex\Z$ works when the real
coordinate has its usual topology and the integer coordinate is discrete.
That construction, its Baire-space analogue, and the basic affirmative
answer are background for this article. Repeating them would not constitute
further progress. The present questions are what their locally compact
generalisations look like, whether their additive structures can support
multiplication, and how much arithmetic variation survives a fixed
underlying topology.

\subsection{Five principal results}

The following statements give a guide to the proofs. A Borel order below
means that the order relation is Borel for the specified topology. It
does not mean that the topology is the order topology.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Local compactness classification.}
For a Borel ordered abelian Polish group $G$, local compactness of
$G_{\geq0}$ at zero forces $G$ to be countable discrete or topologically
$\R\times A$ with $A$ countable discrete and torsion-free. These
conditions are also sufficient. If $G$ has a least positive element and
is uncountable, its cone is homeomorphic to
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:Xlc-intro}
 \Xlc=
 \left(\bigsqcup_{j\in\N}\R\right)
 \sqcup\left(\bigsqcup_{j\in\N}[0,\infty)\right).
\end{equation}

\item \textbf{An absolute multiplication obstruction in this case.}
If $H$ is an uncountable Archimedean additive subgroup of a discretely
ordered unital ring $R$, multiplication by any fixed $h>0$ in $H$
induces an injection $H\hookrightarrow R/H$. The locally compact
groups above have an Archimedean real subgroup of countable index.
Consequently their positive cones admit no unital semiring multiplication
with the same addition and prescribed unit, whether measurable or not.

\item \textbf{A Borel multiplication obstruction without local
compactness.}
In a Polish abelian group with Borel discrete order and least positive
element $e$, positive Borel endomorphisms cannot send $e$ to every
positive element unless the group is discrete. In particular, a
nondiscrete such cone admits no semiring multiplication for which each
fixed right-multiplier map is Borel. This is a group-theoretic extension
of Glazer's probabilistic mechanism, with a stronger topological
hypothesis and substantially weaker arithmetic assumptions.

\item \textbf{Optimal arithmetic diversity on one locally compact
space.}
There are exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ isomorphism classes of full Presburger
models with continuous addition on the space $\Xlc$. An explicit family
encodes subsets of $\N$ in its orders of Archimedean classes and admits
finite-normal-form realizations in the omnific integers.

\item \textbf{Arithmetic on the topological boundary.}
For an uncountable locally compact inherited Presburger cone, the
endpoints of its closed-ray components form a countable discrete
elementary initial submodel. Every countable Presburger model can occur
as this boundary. Even when the boundary is fixed to the standard
natural numbers, the continuum lower bound in the preceding item
persists.
\end{enumerate}

These results settle structural follow-up questions inside a precisely
specified class of presentations. They do not settle the existence of
all possible connected or zero-dimensional locally compact Polish
Presburger presentations. A topology on a positive monoid need not
extend to a Polish group topology on its difference group. That
distinction is essential and will be demonstrated by a counterexample.

\subsection{Existing results and the status of the extensions}

The probabilistic construction of rapidly convergent, rapidly growing
subseries, the use of complementation, and the final zero-one-law
contradiction come from Glazer \cite[Theorem~1]{Glazer}. Automatic
continuity of Borel homomorphisms is classical
\cite{s12:Pettis}. Measurable orders on locally compact abelian groups
have an extensive earlier theory, including the work discussed by
Asmar and Montgomery-Smith \cite{AsmarMS}; Borel ordered-group
classification also appears in Christensen, Kanovei, and Reeken
\cite{s15:ckr2001}. Neither the no-compact-subgroup lemma nor the real-line
order lemma is offered as a new discovery.

The contribution developed here is the exact condition that the
\emph{cone itself} be locally compact, its application to arithmetic
carriers, the cardinal-index obstruction, the boundary interpretation
and its realization converse, the optimal family on the classified
carrier, and a unified statement of the multiplier barrier
at the level of positive endomorphisms. The proofs are supplied in
full. A targeted source search did not establish publication priority
for these exact combined statements. They should be treated as proved
claims in an unrefereed research manuscript, with the standard
dependencies explicitly identified, rather than as a certified
historical first or an announced breakthrough.

\section{Arithmetic and topology: the precise framework}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:framework}

\subsection{Discrete order is independent of the chosen topology}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{discretely ordered abelian group with distinguished unit} is
an ordered abelian group $(G,+,0,<)$ with a least positive element
$1$. Its nonnegative cone is the cancellative commutative monoid
$M=G_{\geq0}$.
\end{definition}

For every standard $n$, the interval $[0,n1]$ consists exactly of
$0,1,\ldots,n1$. The assertion follows by external induction, using
the absence of an element strictly between successive translates of
$0$ and $1$. It does not bound nonstandard elements by standard
integers. The order topology of such a group or cone is discrete,
since each point has immediate neighbours, with the usual endpoint
modification at zero. Thus an uncountable Polish presentation must
use a different topology.

A \emph{Polish group} is a topological group whose topology is
separable and completely metrizable. An arbitrary compatible complete
metric need not be translation invariant. A Borel order can be
discontinuous: $\R\lex\Z$ with product topology is the basic example.
For a topological group, the positive cone is Borel if and only if
the entire order relation is Borel, since
$x\leq y$ exactly when $y-x$ is in that cone.

We use the phrase \emph{inherited group presentation} to mean exactly
that $M=G_{\geq0}$ has the subspace topology of a specified Polish
abelian group $G$ with Borel order. The phrase carries a genuine
hypothesis. It is not a theorem that every continuous-addition
Polish monoid has such a presentation.

\subsection{The coefficient construction and full induction}

Let $D$ be a divisible ordered abelian group. Its unique rational
division makes it a $\Q$-vector space. Set
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:coefficient-model}
 G_D=D\lex\Z,\qquad
 M_D=(D_{>0}\times\Z)\cup(\{0\}\times\N),
 \qquad1=(0,1).
\end{equation}
The $D$ coordinate is compared first. In particular, a negative
integer coordinate is compatible with being positive whenever the
$D$ coordinate is positive.

\begin{proposition}[The standard algebraic certificate; = \cref{pma:pr:cor:fullpresburger}]
\label{pma:lcc:prop:zgroup-certificate}
For every divisible ordered abelian group $D$, $M_D$ is a model of
the entire first-order theory of $(\N,0,1,+,<)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The group $G_D$ has least positive element $(0,1)$. For every
standard $m\geq2$, each $(d,k)$ has the unique decomposition
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:division-certificate}
 (d,k)=m\left(d/m,\lfloor k/m\rfloor\right)+(0,r),
 \qquad0\leq r<m,
\end{equation}
where $r$ is the ordinary remainder of $k$ modulo $m$. For positive
input, the quotient is nonnegative: it has positive $D$ coordinate
if $d>0$, and an ordinary nonnegative integer coordinate if $d=0$.

These are the axioms of a $\Z$-group: a discretely ordered abelian
group with exactly the standard residue classes modulo every
standard positive integer. The classical quantifier-elimination
theorem says that the theory of $\Z$-groups in the language expanded
by these congruence predicates is complete and is the theory of
the ordered integers; see \cite[Chapter~8]{s15:henson} and the
elimination method of \cite{s13:cooper}. Relativizing quantifiers to
the nonnegative cone gives the asserted elementary equivalence.
In particular every first-order Presburger induction instance
holds in $M_D$.
\end{proof}

This use of quantifier elimination is a classical dependency, not a
claim that verifying a few division equations alone proves arbitrary
induction. It also exposes the formalization boundary. ProveIt's
current executable semantics quantify over \texttt{Int}; the
nonstandard semantic theorem must be supplied before substituting
an arbitrary group $G_D$ for that type. In particular, invariance
under $x\mapsto x+m$ for standard iterations is weaker than
invariance under every shift in the full subgroup $mG_D$.

\subsection{Exactly when the inherited coefficient cone is Polish}

Equip $D$ with a Polish group topology and $\Z$ with the discrete
topology. Write $P=D_{\geq0}$. Each fixed-integer slice of $M_D$ is
homeomorphic to $P$ or $P\setminus\{0\}$.

\begin{proposition}[Positive-cone criterion; = \cref{pma:pr:thm:criterion}]
\label{pma:lcc:prop:positive-cone-criterion}
The space $M_D$ is Polish in the inherited product topology if and
only if $P$ is $G_\delta$ in $D$. In that case addition on $M_D$ is
continuous. If the condition holds, the strict positive cone and
the order relation on $G_D$ are also Borel.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If $M_D$ is Polish, its clopen slice at integer coordinate zero is
a Polish subspace of $D$ equal to $P$. A subspace of a Polish space
is Polish exactly when it is $G_\delta$. Conversely, if $P$ is
$G_\delta$, then $P\setminus\{0\}$ is $G_\delta$ as well. The
countable topological sum of the resulting Polish slices is
Polish. For example, choose bounded complete metrics on the slices
and set the distance between distinct slices equal to a fixed
larger constant. Addition is the restriction of the continuous
ambient group operation; the cone is closed under addition.
\end{proof}

For $D=\R$, the slice at $k\geq0$ is $[0,\infty)$ and the slice
at $k<0$ is $(0,\infty)$. Consequently $M_\R$ has the space
$\Xlc$ of \eqref{pma:lcc:eq:Xlc-intro}. It is locally compact and has no
isolated points. The map $r\mapsto\log r$ identifies an open ray
with $\R$ and supplies a compatible complete metric there. This
explains how a subspace defined using open rays can still be
completely metrizable.

For contrast, on $D=\R^2$ with its Euclidean topology and
lexicographic order,
\[
 P=\{(x,y):x>0\}\cup\{(0,y):y\geq0\}
\]
is $G_\delta$ and $F_\sigma$, but is not locally compact at zero.
Every relative neighbourhood of zero contains a sequence
$(1/j,-\varepsilon)$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$ whose ambient
limit $(0,-\varepsilon)$ is missing. A compact relative
neighbourhood would contain that limit, a contradiction. Thus
local compactness of the coefficient group is weaker than local
compactness of its cone.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:lcc:prop:zgroup-certificate,pma:lcc:prop:positive-cone-criterion}
are Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:thm:main,pma:pr:cor:fullpresburger} and
\cref{pma:pr:thm:criterion}, proved again; source~15 calls them background. The
lexicographic $\R^2$ example is the step $d\ge2$ of part~(3) of source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:thm:cones}.


\section{An induction-free obstruction to Borel multiplication}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:borel-multiplication-obstruction}

The construction of Polish positive cones with continuous addition raises a
natural strengthening question: can their addition be supplemented by a
measurable multiplication?  When the topology comes from a Polish additive
group, the answer has a particularly strong form.  No arithmetic induction
axiom is needed, and even separate Borel measurability in one argument is
already too much.

The probabilistic mechanism below is adapted from the proof of
Glazer's first topological Tennenbaum theorem
\cite[Theorem~1]{Glazer}.  We give every step of the group version.
The changes relevant here are that Borel multiplier maps become continuous
by automatic continuity, limits are taken in the ambient additive group,
and a finite-block probability estimate removes the need to construct an
injective map from Cantor space.  We present this as a consequence and
extension of that mechanism; we do not assert independent historical
priority for its ingredients.

\noindent\writetag{} \textbf{A special case of Part~VI.} The obstruction of
this section is subsumed by \cref{pma:part:br}, which source~15 did not see.
A positive additive endomorphism $T$ with $T(e)>0$ is an ordered additive
embedding: $x>0$ gives $x\ge e$ and $T(x)\ge T(e)>0$. So the endomorphisms
$T_a$ of \cref{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction} have cofinal unit
images, and source~12's \cref{pma:br:cor:cofinal-unit} already excludes an
uncountable group with a Baire-property cone, a Hausdorff Baire ccc group
topology and such a family, with no regularity of the $T_a$; a countable Polish
group is discrete. Likewise \cref{pma:lcc:cor:no-borel-semiring-expansion} is a
case of \cref{pma:br:thm:semiring}, \cref{pma:lcc:cor:polish-discrete-ordered-ring}
of \cref{pma:br:cor:polish} (and source~09's \cref{pma:ser:thm:discrete} with
right instead of left scalars), and \cref{pma:lcc:cor:ordered-ring-nonpolishable}
of \cref{pma:br:thm:nonpolishable}; none of the Part~VI versions needs Borel
multiplier maps. \Cref{pma:lcc:thm:archimedean-subgroup-cardinality} is a case
of source~10's \cref{pma:br:thm:principal} and of part~(1) of source~08's
\cref{pma:lc:thm:amplification}. The section is printed because its proof of
\cref{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction} is different: it adapts
Glazer's zero-one-law argument rather than packing open sets, and its proof of
\cref{pma:lcc:lem:borel-hom-continuous} is source~08's \cref{pma:lc:lem:auto}
and source~09's \cref{pma:ser:lem:automatic} again. Its mechanism is that of
source~06's \cref{pma:cp:thm:zero} in Part~III.

\subsection{Automatic continuity of individual multiplier maps}

Recall that an ordered abelian group is an abelian group equipped with a
translation-invariant linear order.  An endomorphism \(T:G\to G\) is
\emph{positive} if \(x\geq0\) implies \(T(x)\geq0\).  If \(e>0\) is the
least positive element, then
\[
  0\leq x\leq ne
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  x\in\{0,e,\ldots,ne\}
  \qquad(n\in\mathbb N).
\]
This elementary assertion is proved by ordinary, external induction on
the standard integer \(n\).  It is not an induction scheme imposed on the
ordered group as an arithmetic structure.

\begin{lemma}[Borel homomorphisms are continuous; = \cref{pma:lc:lem:auto}]
\label{pma:lcc:lem:borel-hom-continuous}
Let \(G\) be a Polish group and \(H\) a second-countable topological group.
Every Borel homomorphism \(f:G\to H\) is continuous.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We recall the category argument associated with the
Piccard--Pettis theorem \cite{s12:Pettis}.  First, if \(A\subseteq G\)
has the Baire property and is nonmeagre, there is a nonempty open set
\(O\) in which \(A\) is comeagre.  For every \(g\) sufficiently close to
the identity, \(O\cap gO\) is nonempty and open.  The sets \(A\) and
\(gA\) are comeagre in this intersection, so they meet.  Consequently
\(AA^{-1}\) contains a neighborhood of the identity.

Now let \(V\) be an identity neighborhood in \(H\), and choose an open
identity neighborhood \(W\) such that \(WW^{-1}\subseteq V\).
Second countability implies that the subspace \(f(G)\) is Lindel\"of.
The cover
\(\{f(g)W\cap f(G):g\in G\}\) therefore has a countable subcover,
with centers \(f(g_j)\).  If \(A=f^{-1}(W)\), then
\[
  G=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb N}g_jA.
\]
The set \(A\) is Borel and cannot be meagre, by the Baire category
theorem.  Thus \(AA^{-1}\) contains an identity neighborhood, and
\[
  AA^{-1}\subseteq f^{-1}(WW^{-1})\subseteq f^{-1}(V).
\]
This proves continuity at the identity, hence everywhere.
\end{proof}

For a ring whose addition makes it a Polish group, the map
\(x\mapsto xy\), for any fixed \(y\), is an additive homomorphism.
Accordingly, a Borel hypothesis on this one-variable map already gives
all the multiplication continuity used below.  Joint continuity of
multiplication is neither assumed nor needed.

\subsection{The positive-endomorphism obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[Borel multiplier obstruction; a case of \cref{pma:br:cor:cofinal-unit}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction}
Let \(G\) be a Polish abelian topological group with a Borel,
translation-invariant linear order and a least positive element \(e\).
Suppose that for every \(a>0\) there exists a positive Borel additive
endomorphism \(T_a:G\to G\) such that
\[
  T_a(e)=a.
\]
There is no required measurability or algebraic coherence in the
parameter \(a\).  Then \(G\) is discrete and consequently countable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that \(G\) is not discrete.  Fix a complete metric \(d\) inducing
its topology.  We do not assume that \(d\) is translation invariant.

\paragraph{A positive null sequence.}
There is a sequence of nonzero points \(v_j\to0\).  Put
\(u_j=|v_j|\), where this absolute value means
\(\max(v_j,-v_j)\) in the given group order.  Since both \(v_j\) and
\(-v_j\) tend to zero, so does \(u_j\), even though the absolute-value
map need not be continuous.  The finite set
\(\{e,2e,\ldots,5e\}\) does not contain zero.  After discarding
finitely many terms, discreteness of the order therefore gives
\[
  u_j>5e,\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad u_j\geq6e
  \quad\text{for every }j.
\]

\paragraph{Rapid topological convergence and rapid order growth.}
We recursively construct positive elements \(y_0,y_1,\ldots\), beginning
with \(y_0=e\), such that
\begin{equation}
  y_n>5y_{n-1}\qquad(n\geq1)
  \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-order-growth}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 d(s,s+y_n)<2^{-n}
 \quad\text{for every }\quad
 s\in
 \left\{\sum_{i<n}\varepsilon_i y_i:
                 \varepsilon_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.
 \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-metric-smallness}
\end{equation}
Suppose the elements before \(y_n\) have been chosen.
Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:borel-hom-continuous} implies that
\(T_{y_{n-1}}\) is continuous, so
\(T_{y_{n-1}}(u_j)\to0\).
For each of the finitely many \(s\) in
\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-metric-smallness}, continuity of addition gives
\[
  d\bigl(s,s+T_{y_{n-1}}(u_j)\bigr)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Choose \(j\) large enough for all these inequalities and set
\(y_n=T_{y_{n-1}}(u_j)\).  Positivity and additivity imply
\[
  y_n\geq T_{y_{n-1}}(6e)=6y_{n-1}>5y_{n-1}.
\]
This completes the recursion.

\paragraph{All binary subseries converge.}
For \(r\in2^{\mathbb N}\), define
\[
  s_N(r)=\sum_{i<N}r(i)y_i.
\]
If \(N\geq1\), consecutive partial sums either agree or differ by the
addition of \(y_N\).  Thus, uniformly in \(r\),
\[
 d(s_N(r),s_L(r))
 \leq\sum_{i=N}^{L-1}2^{-i}
 \qquad(L>N\geq1).
\]
Completeness gives a limit
\[
  z(r)=\lim_{N\to\infty}s_N(r)\in G,
\]
and the convergence is uniform in \(r\).  Since each \(s_N\) is
continuous on Cantor space, so is \(z\).  Write
\(\bar r(i)=1-r(i)\), and put
\[
  D(r)=z(r)-z(\bar r).
\]
The map \(D:2^{\mathbb N}\to G\) is continuous, and
\begin{equation}
  D(\bar r)=-D(r).
  \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-complement-symmetry}
\end{equation}
If \(r\) and \(s\) differ on only finitely many coordinates,
continuity of the group operations gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
  D(r)-D(s)=2\sum_i(r(i)-s(i))y_i.
  \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-finite-change}
\end{equation}
To see this, the corresponding identity for finite partial sums is
constant once the partial sums include every changed coordinate; then
take limits.

\paragraph{Order separation on a finite block.}
Let \(S_m=\sum_{i<m}y_i\).  From
\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-order-growth}, induction gives
\begin{equation}
  4S_m<y_m\qquad(m\geq1).
  \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-geometric-sum}
\end{equation}
Indeed \(4y_0<y_1\), and
\(4S_{m+1}=4S_m+4y_m<5y_m<y_{m+1}\).
If \(r\) and \(s\) differ finitely and \(m\) is their greatest
coordinate of disagreement, then
\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-finite-change} implies
\begin{equation}
  |D(r)-D(s)|
     \geq2(y_m-S_m)>y_m
     \qquad(m\geq1).
  \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-separation}
\end{equation}

Give \(2^{\mathbb N}\) the fair independent Bernoulli product
probability measure.  Fix \(n\geq0\) and \(k\geq1\), and consider the
block \(B=\{n+1,\ldots,n+k\}\).  Once all coordinates outside \(B\)
are fixed, at most one of the \(2^k\) assignments on \(B\) can satisfy
\[
  |D(r)|\leq y_n.
\]
Otherwise, two such assignments would have greatest disagreement
\(m\in B\), and \eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-separation} would give
\[
