  |D(r)-D(s)|>y_m\geq y_{n+1}>5y_n,
\]
whereas the triangle inequality in the ordered group would give
\(|D(r)-D(s)|\leq2y_n\).
The events are Borel because \(D\) is continuous and the order is
Borel.  Integrating the finite conditional counting bound yields
\[
  \mathbb P\bigl(|D(r)|\leq y_n\bigr)\leq2^{-k}.
\]
As \(k\) is arbitrary, this probability is zero.  Countable
additivity now gives
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb P\bigl(\forall n\;\;|D(r)|>y_n\bigr)=1.
  \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-large-almost-surely}
\end{equation}
In particular, \(\mathbb P(D(r)=0)=0\).  No injectivity assertion
about \(z\) was necessary.

\paragraph{A tail event with probability one half.}
Define
\[
  A=\{r:\forall n\;\;D(r)>y_n\}.
\]
By \eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-large-almost-surely}, almost every \(r\)
belongs either to \(A\) or to its reflected event
\(\{r:\forall n\;\;-D(r)>y_n\}\).
Complementation preserves product measure and interchanges these two
disjoint events by \eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-complement-symmetry}.
Consequently
\[
  \mathbb P(A)=\tfrac12.
\]

We verify directly that \(A\) is a tail event.  Suppose \(r\in A\)
and \(s\) differs from \(r\) only at coordinates at most \(m\).
Equations~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-finite-change} and
\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-geometric-sum} give
\[
  |D(s)-D(r)|\leq2S_{m+1}<y_{m+1}.
\]
For any given \(n\), choose \(j>\max(n,m+1)\).  The growth condition
implies
\(y_j>y_n+y_{m+1}\), and therefore
\[
  D(s)\geq D(r)-|D(s)-D(r)|
       >y_j-y_{m+1}>y_n.
\]
Thus \(s\in A\).  Reversing \(r\) and \(s\) proves invariance under
every finite coordinate change.

For each \(N\), membership in this Borel set is consequently
determined by the coordinates with index at least \(N\): replace the
first \(N\) coordinates by zero to obtain a Borel test on the
remaining tail.  Hence \(A\) belongs to the tail sigma-algebra.
Kolmogorov's zero-one law says that its probability is zero or one.
Indeed, a tail event is independent of every event determined by
finitely many coordinates.  The monotone-class theorem extends this
independence to all events in the product Borel sigma-algebra,
including \(A\) itself.  Thus
\(\mathbb P(A)=\mathbb P(A)^2\), contradicting
\(\mathbb P(A)=1/2\).
This proves that \(G\) is discrete.  Every discrete second-countable
space is countable, completing the proof.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Semiring expansions and the difference group}

\begin{corollary}[No Borel semiring expansion of a nondiscrete Polish cone; a case of \cref{pma:br:thm:semiring}]
\label{pma:lcc:cor:no-borel-semiring-expansion}
Let \(G\) be a nondiscrete Polish abelian group with a Borel,
translation-invariant linear order and least positive element \(1\).
Put \(M=G_{\geq0}\), with its inherited Borel structure.  There is no
semiring multiplication
\[
  \mu:M\times M\longrightarrow M
\]
having the original addition and zero, having \(1\) as multiplicative
identity, and satisfying the following weak regularity condition:
for every fixed \(a\in M\), the map \(x\mapsto\mu(x,a)\) is Borel.
In particular, there is no jointly Borel such multiplication.
The positive cone \(M\) need not itself be Polish.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The maps
\[
  x^+=\max(x,0),\qquad x^-=\max(-x,0)
\]
are Borel, take values in \(M\), and satisfy \(x=x^+-x^-\).
For \(a>0\), define
\[
  T_a(x)=\mu(x^+,a)-\mu(x^-,a).
\]
This is a Borel map \(G\to G\).  It is precisely the additive extension
of \(x\mapsto\mu(x,a)\) from \(M\) to its difference group \(G=M-M\).
For completeness, if \(b-c=b'-c'\) with \(b,c,b',c'\in M\), then
\(b+c'=b'+c\).  Distributivity gives
\[
  \mu(b,a)+\mu(c',a)=\mu(b',a)+\mu(c,a),
\]
so the difference of the two products is independent of the chosen
representation.  This also proves additivity of the extension.
For \(x\geq0\), \(T_a(x)=\mu(x,a)\geq0\), and
\(T_a(1)=a\).  Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction}
now contradicts nondiscreteness.
\end{proof}

If \(\mu\) is jointly Borel, its usual extension to the whole group
can be written explicitly as
\begin{align}
 \mu_G(x,y)
   ={}&\mu(x^+,y^+)+\mu(x^-,y^-)
       \notag\\[-2pt]
     &-\mu(x^+,y^-)-\mu(x^-,y^+).
 \label{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-group-completion}
\end{align}
Thus no measurable selection theorem is required for the passage to
differences.  The formula is Borel and biadditive.  The usual
well-definedness argument above, applied in both variables, proves
that it is the unique ring multiplication extending \(\mu\).
Associativity and the unit law extend from \(M\) by distributivity.
For the obstruction itself, only the individual \(T_a\) are needed.

\begin{corollary}[Polish discretely ordered rings; a case of \cref{pma:br:cor:polish}]
\label{pma:lcc:cor:polish-discrete-ordered-ring}
Let \(R\) be a unital ordered ring whose additive group is Polish and
whose order is Borel.  Suppose \(1\) is its least positive element
and, for every fixed \(a\in R\), right multiplication
\(x\mapsto xa\) is Borel.  Then the additive topology of \(R\) is
discrete and \(R\) is countable.
\end{corollary}

No form of \(\mathrm{IOpen}\), bounded induction, division with
remainder, roots, or exponentiation occurs in these statements.
Indeed, Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction} does not assume
a multiplication operation at all: it assumes only the listed
positive additive endomorphisms.  The order's least positive element,
Polish completeness, measurability of the order, and the multiplier
regularity supply the obstruction.

\begin{corollary}[Non-Polishability of the additive Borel group; a case of \cref{pma:br:thm:nonpolishable}]
\label{pma:lcc:cor:ordered-ring-nonpolishable}
Let \(R\) be an uncountable discretely ordered unital ring on a
standard Borel space, with Borel addition, negation, order, and
individual right-multiplier maps.  Its additive Borel group is not
Polishable: there is no Polish group topology on \((R,+)\) whose
Borel sets are the given ones.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
In any such topology the order and multiplier maps would remain
Borel.  Corollary~\ref{pma:lcc:cor:polish-discrete-ordered-ring} would force
\(R\) to be countable.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An algebraic cardinality obstruction}

For an important subclass, measurability can be removed completely.
A subgroup \(H\) of an ordered abelian group is called
\emph{Archimedean} if for all \(h,k>0\) in \(H\), some standard
positive integer \(n\) satisfies \(k<nh\).

\begin{theorem}[Archimedean subgroup versus quotient cardinality; a case of \cref{pma:br:thm:principal}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:archimedean-subgroup-cardinality}
Let \(R\) be a discretely ordered unital ring, and let
\(H\subseteq(R,+)\) be an uncountable Archimedean subgroup, with its
induced order.  Then there is an injective additive homomorphism
\[
  H\longrightarrow (R,+)/H.
\]
In particular,
\[
  |H|\leq |R/H|.
\]
Thus an ordered abelian group having an uncountable Archimedean
subgroup of countable index cannot be the additive ordered group of
a discretely ordered unital ring with the prescribed least positive
element as unit.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every \(a>0\) in \(H\) is larger than every standard integer multiple
of \(1\).  Otherwise, \(0<a\leq n1\) for some standard \(n\), and
discreteness of the ring order gives \(a=k1\) for a positive integer
\(k\).  Archimedeanness would then imply that each \(b>0\) in \(H\)
is bounded by \(ma=mk1\) for some standard integer \(m\).
Discreteness again gives \(b\in\mathbb Z1\), and hence
\(H\subseteq\mathbb Z1\), contradicting uncountability.

Fix \(h>0\) in \(H\).  For any \(a>0\) in \(H\), positivity of
multiplication yields
\[
  ah>nh\qquad\text{for every standard }n.
\]
Because \(H\) is Archimedean, the multiples \(nh\) are cofinal in
its positive part.  Consequently \(ah\) is larger than every
element of \(H\), and in particular \(ah\notin H\).  If \(a<0\),
applying this argument to \(-a\) likewise gives \(ah\notin H\).
The additive homomorphism
\[
  a\longmapsto ah+H
\]
therefore has trivial kernel.
\end{proof}

For example, suppose a coefficient group is algebraically
\(D=\mathbb R\oplus A\), where \(A\) is countable, and its order
restricts to an Archimedean order on the displayed copy of
\(\mathbb R\).  In \(G=D\lex \mathbb Z\), with the
integer summand least significant and its positive generator as
the proposed unit, take
\[
 H=\mathbb R\oplus\{0\}\oplus\{0\}.
\]
Then \(H\) is uncountable and \(G/H\cong A\oplus\mathbb Z\) is
countable.  There is no compatible semiring multiplication on the
positive cone, even with no regularity requirement whatever.
This applies to coefficient decompositions of this form supplied
by a classification of \emph{locally compact positive cones}.
Local compactness of \(D\) alone is a different hypothesis and
does not by itself supply this decomposition with a countable
quotient.

\subsection{Scope and sharpness of the hypotheses}

\paragraph{The countable discrete case is possible.}
The usual ordered ring \(\mathbb Z\), with its discrete topology,
satisfies all the hypotheses and all its operations are continuous.
Thus the conclusion cannot be strengthened to nonexistence of every
such ring.

\paragraph{Complete metrizability matters.}
Give the usual ordered ring \(\mathbb Z\) its \(2\)-adic topology,
whose basic neighborhoods are the congruence classes modulo \(2^k\).
Addition, negation, and multiplication are continuous.  The usual
order is Borel: every subset of the countable \(T_1\) space
\(\mathbb Z^2\) is a countable union of closed singletons.  The
element \(1\) remains the least positive element algebraically,
while the topology is nondiscrete.

This example is not Polish.  It is a countable metrizable space
without isolated points, so every singleton is nowhere dense; the
Baire category theorem rules out any compatible complete metric.
The familiar \(2\)-adic metric is explicitly incomplete: the integer
partial sums
\[
  q_N=\sum_{j=0}^{N}4^j
      =\frac{4^{N+1}-1}{3}
\]
are Cauchy and converge in the \(2\)-adic completion to \(-1/3\),
which is not an integer.  This is the same final-digits phenomenon
used in the topological arithmetic constructions of
Enayat, Hamkins, and Wcis\l{}o \cite[Section~2]{EHW}.

\paragraph{A least positive element matters.}
The ordinary ordered field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual topology,
is an uncountable Polish additive group with continuous
multiplication and a Borel order.  It has no least positive element.
Its null sequences have small order magnitude, so the recursion
forcing simultaneous order growth and topological convergence
cannot begin.

\paragraph{The ambient group topology is a real hypothesis.}
The corollaries concern a topology making \emph{both} addition and
negation continuous on the full difference group.  A Polish topology
on a positive cone alone does not automatically have this property.
One should therefore not infer a blanket nonexistence theorem for
all uncountable Polish models of the purely algebraic theory of
nonnegative parts of discretely ordered rings.  For any application,
the original addition, the distinguished element \(1\), the Borel
order, and the specific compatible Polish group topology must all
be identified.

Here is an explicit example demonstrating the distinction. The
polynomial construction is included as a boundary example; no
novelty is claimed for it.
Let
\[
  R_0=\mathbb Z+t\mathbb R[t],
\]
and order a nonzero polynomial by the sign of its highest-degree
coefficient.  This makes \(R_0\) a discretely ordered ring in which
\(t\) is larger than every integer and \(1\) is the least positive
element.  Let \(M_0=(R_0)_{\geq0}\).  Give \(M_0\) the topological
disjoint-union decomposition
\[
  M_0=
  \mathbb N\ \sqcup\
  \bigsqcup_{d\geq1}
   \bigl((0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^{d-1}\times\mathbb Z\bigr).
\]
The factor \((0,\infty)\) records the leading coefficient of a
degree-\(d\) polynomial, the middle factors its other nonconstant
coefficients, and \(\mathbb Z\) its constant coefficient.
The constants have the discrete topology.  This is an uncountable
Polish space, being a countable topological sum of Polish spaces,
and zero is isolated.  It is also locally compact.  Each stratum
is open and locally compact: near a nonconstant polynomial, fix
its integer constant coefficient and choose a bounded coefficient
box with closure keeping the leading coefficient strictly positive.
That closure is compact inside the same stratum.  An isolated
constant has its singleton as a compact neighborhood.

Addition and multiplication are jointly continuous.  On a fixed
pair of nonconstant degree strata, addition has degree equal to
the larger input degree and multiplication has degree equal to
their sum: positive leading coefficients prevent cancellation.
Within these fixed strata the coefficient formulas are continuous
polynomial functions.  Addition of a constant and multiplication
by a positive constant have the same property.  The remaining
cases involve the isolated zero or two isolated constants.

In fact its additive reduct is a model of \emph{full} Presburger
arithmetic.  The convex subgroup generated by \(1\) in \(R_0\) is
the constant copy of \(\mathbb Z\), and
\[
  R_0/\mathbb Z\cong t\mathbb R[t]
\]
is a divisible ordered abelian group.  The standard
\(\mathbb Z\)-group characterization therefore applies
\cite[Section~2]{jerabek}.
More explicitly, for each standard integer \(m>0\), write the
constant coefficient \(c\) of
\(p=c+\sum_{i=1}^d a_it^i\) as \(c=mq+r\), with \(0\leq r<m\).
Then
\[
  p=m\left(q+\sum_{i=1}^d\frac{a_i}{m}t^i\right)+r
\]
is its unique division by \(m\) with standard remainder.
When \(p\geq0\), its quotient is also nonnegative.  These division
schemes, together with the discrete ordered-group axioms, give the
complete Presburger theory on the nonnegative cone.

Thus \(M_0\) is an uncountable locally compact Polish model of full
Presburger arithmetic admitting a continuous semiring
multiplication.  It is a model of the algebraic theory
of nonnegative parts of discretely ordered rings, but it fails
open induction in the language \emph{with multiplication}
explicitly.  The quantifier-free formula with parameter
\(t\),
\[
  \varphi(x)\ \equiv\ x^2<t,
\]
holds in \(M_0\) exactly for the ordinary nonnegative integer
constants.  Hence \(\varphi(0)\) and
\(\forall x\,(\varphi(x)\Rightarrow\varphi(x+1))\) hold, while
\(\varphi(t)\) does not.

The additive Borel group of \(R_0\), using the corresponding
coefficient Borel structure, cannot carry a compatible Polish
group topology.  Besides
Corollary~\ref{pma:lcc:cor:ordered-ring-nonpolishable}, this has a direct
category proof.  Put
\[
  G_d=\{p\in R_0:\deg p\leq d\},\qquad d\geq0,
\]
including zero in every \(G_d\).  These are Borel additive
subgroups and \(R_0=\bigcup_dG_d\).  In a hypothetical Polish group
topology with these Borel sets, one \(G_d\) would be nonmeagre.
The Piccard--Pettis argument makes that subgroup open.
A second-countable group has at most countably many cosets of
an open subgroup.  But
\[
  G_{d+1}/G_d\cong(\mathbb R,+)
\]
already supplies uncountably many such cosets, a contradiction.
The obstruction therefore concerns the passage from a Polish
positive monoid to a Polish difference group, not the existence
of the displayed positive semiring itself.

\noindent\writetag{} The degree-stratum cone $M_0$ is batch-86 source~06's
cone of $\Z+t\R[t]$ in Part~III, with the same topology:
\cref{pma:cp:thm:polynomial,pma:cp:thm:openfailure}, and its group of
differences is not compatibly Polishable for the reason given in
\cref{pma:cp:sec:meet}; source~15 claims no novelty for it, and had not seen
Part~III. The $2$-adic example is new to this report; source~10 makes the same
remark for the $p$-adic topology (\cref{pma:br:subsec:meager-example}).


\section{Classification of locally compact coefficient presentations}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:lc-coefficients}

The positive-cone construction has a surprisingly rigid locally compact
case.  The result below classifies the topological spaces obtained by this
construction, including presentations whose coefficient group was not
initially assumed locally compact.  Its scope is precisely the inherited
product topology; arbitrary Polish presentations of Presburger arithmetic
are not covered.

Let $D$ be a divisible abelian Polish group with a translation-invariant
linear order $\prec$ whose positive cone is Borel.  Write
\[
 P=D_{\succeq0},\qquad P^*=D_{\succ0},\qquad
 M_D=(P^*\times\mathbb Z)\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb N),
\]
and give $M_D$ the topology inherited from $D\times\mathbb Z$, with
$\mathbb Z$ discrete.  Arithmetic is inherited from the lexicographic
ordered group $D\lex \mathbb Z$, and the distinguished
arithmetic zero is $(0,0)$.  In this section no preliminary assumption that
$P$ is $G_\delta$ is needed: in the cases classified as locally compact,
Polishness follows from the classification itself.

\subsection{A measurable-order obstruction to compact subgroups}

\begin{lemma}[compare \cref{pma:lc:lem:compact}]\label{pma:lcc:lem:no-compact-ordered-subgroup}
Let $G$ be a second-countable Hausdorff topological group with a translation-invariant linear
order whose positive cone is Borel.  If the order is invariant under left
translations, then $G$ has no nontrivial compact subgroup.  In particular,
this applies to the ordered abelian groups used here.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
An ordered group is torsion-free, so a nontrivial compact subgroup $K$
would be infinite.  Its normalized Haar measure $\mu$ is atomless: by
translation invariance, one positive point mass would give the same
positive mass to every point of the infinite group.

First consider the abelian case, which is all that is needed below.
The two sets $K_{\succ0}$ and $K_{\prec0}$ have the same Haar measure,
because inversion preserves Haar measure on a compact group.  They
partition $K\setminus\{0\}$, so each has measure $1/2$.  Let $X,Y,Z$ be
independent Haar-distributed points of $K$.  Ties have probability zero,
and exchangeability gives
\[
 \Pr(X\prec Z\ \text{and}\ Y\prec Z)=\frac13.
\]
Conditioning on $Z=z$, translation invariance makes $X-z$ and $Y-z$
independent Haar-distributed points.  The same probability must therefore
be $(1/2)^2=1/4$, a contradiction.

For a group with a merely left-invariant order, replace $X-z$ and $Y-z$
by $z^{-1}X$ and $z^{-1}Y$; inversion still interchanges the positive and
negative cones and preserves normalized Haar measure on a compact group.
The identical argument applies.
\end{proof}

The argument isolates the obstruction: a translation-invariant measurable
linear order is incompatible with a uniform distribution on a nontrivial
compact subgroup.  No continuity of the order relation is assumed.

\subsection{Local compactness at zero determines the coefficient group}

\begin{lemma}\label{pma:lcc:lem:cone-lc-implies-group-lc}
Let $D$ be a Hausdorff ordered abelian topological group.  If its
nonnegative cone $P$ is locally compact at zero in the subspace topology,
then $D$ is locally compact.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
There is a compact set $K\subseteq P$ which contains a neighborhood of
zero relative to $P$.  Choose an ambient open neighborhood $W$ of zero
such that $P\cap W\subseteq K$, and put $U=W\cap(-W)$.  Every $x\in U$
belongs to $K\cup(-K)$: if $x\succeq0$, then $x\in P\cap W$, and
otherwise $-x\in P\cap W$.  Thus $K\cup(-K)$ is a compact neighborhood
of zero in $D$.  Translation gives local compactness everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{pma:lcc:lem:locally-closed-total-cone}
Let $C$ be the nonnegative cone of a translation-invariant linear order on
the additive group $\mathbb R^n$.  If $C$ is locally compact at zero in
the Euclidean subspace topology, then $n\leq1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose a compact $K\subseteq C$ and a Euclidean open neighborhood $W$ of
zero such that $C\cap W\subseteq K$.  Since $K$ is closed in
$\mathbb R^n$ and $K\subseteq C$, the set $C\cap W=K\cap W$ is closed
relative to $W$.

The cone $C$ is invariant under multiplication by every positive rational
number.  Indeed, positive integral multiples preserve sign in an ordered
abelian group, and division in $\mathbb R^n$ is unique.  If $x_j\in C$
converges to $x$, choose a positive rational $q$ small enough that $qx\in
W$.  For all sufficiently large $j$, $qx_j\in C\cap W$.  Relative
closedness yields $qx\in C$, hence $x\in C$.  Thus $C$ is globally
closed.

If $n\geq2$, the sets
\[
 C\cap S^{n-1}\quad\text{and}\quad(-C)\cap S^{n-1}
\]
are nonempty disjoint closed sets covering the connected sphere
$S^{n-1}$.  This is impossible.  Nonemptiness follows by taking a nonzero
vector and its negative; closedness also implies that rescaling a positive
vector to the sphere preserves its sign, by rational approximation.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[= \cref{pma:lc:lem:flag} for $d=1$, with the Baire property]\label{pma:lcc:lem:borel-order-real-line}
A translation-invariant linear order on the additive group $\mathbb R$
whose positive cone has the Baire property is either the usual order or
its reverse.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $B$ be its strict positive cone.  The sets $B,-B$, and $\{0\}$
partition $\mathbb R$, so $B$ is nonmeager.  Since $B$ has the Baire
property, it is comeager in some nonempty bounded open interval $I$.
For every $t\in I+I$, the interval $I\cap(t-I)$ is nonempty.  The sets
$B$ and $t-B$ are both comeager there, so their intersection is nonempty.
Consequently
\[
 I+I\subseteq B+B\subseteq B.
\]
The interval $I+I$ does not contain zero, and thus lies entirely in one
of the two usual half-lines.  Positive rational dilations of a nonempty
open interval in $(0,\infty)$ cover $(0,\infty)$; the analogous statement
holds on the negative half-line.  The cone $B$ is invariant under these
dilations.  It therefore contains one usual strict half-line, and the
partition $B\sqcup(-B)=\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ prevents it from
containing anything else.
\end{proof}

The only structural theorem about locally compact groups needed next is
the classical principal structure theorem: a locally compact abelian
group has an open subgroup topologically isomorphic to
$\mathbb R^n\times K$, with $n<\omega$ and $K$ compact.  We use the
standard statement in Morris~\cite[Chapter~6, Theorem~25]{s15:Morris1977}; it
is also explicitly recalled by Gabriyelyan and
Morris~\cite[p.~68]{s15:GabriyelyanMorris2016}.

\begin{theorem}[Locally compact coefficient classification; extends \cref{pma:lc:thm:cones}(3)]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:lc-coefficient-classification}
For $D$ and $M_D$ as above, the following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $M_D$ is locally compact at its arithmetic zero $(0,0)$.
\item $M_D$ is locally compact.
\item As a topological group, $D$ is either a countable discrete
      $\mathbb Q$-vector space or $\mathbb R\times A$, where $A$ is a
      countable discrete $\mathbb Q$-vector space.
\end{enumerate}
In the first case $M_D$ is a countably infinite discrete space.  In the
second case $M_D$ is an uncountable locally compact Polish space, and
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:universal-lc-coefficient-carrier}
 M_D\ \cong\
 \left(\bigsqcup_{j\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R\right)
 \sqcup
 \left(\bigsqcup_{j\in\mathbb N}[0,\infty)\right)
\end{equation}
as a topological space.  Both families of connected components are
countably infinite.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The slice with integer coordinate zero is a clopen subspace of $M_D$
homeomorphic to $P$.  Condition~(1) therefore makes $P$ locally compact
at zero.  By Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:cone-lc-implies-group-lc}, $D$ is locally
compact.  The principal structure theorem supplies an open subgroup
$H\cong\mathbb R^n\times K$.  Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:no-compact-ordered-subgroup}
forces $K=\{0\}$, so $H\cong\mathbb R^n$ is open.

An ordered divisible abelian group is naturally a vector space over
$\mathbb Q$.  The subgroup $H$ is a $\mathbb Q$-subspace.  Choose an
algebraic vector-space complement $A$, so $D=H\oplus A$.  It is discrete
in its subspace topology because $H\cap A=\{0\}$ and $H$ is open.
There are only countably many $H$-cosets: a countable dense subset of
$D$ meets every open coset.  Thus $A$ is countable.  The addition map
$H\times A\to D$ is a topological isomorphism, since on each clopen
slice it is translation from $H$ onto an open coset.

The intersection $P\cap H$ is locally compact at zero and is the
nonnegative cone of the restricted order on $H\cong\mathbb R^n$.
Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:locally-closed-total-cone} gives $n\leq1$.  If $n=0$,
$D$ is countable and discrete.  If $n=1$, $D\cong\mathbb R\times A$.
This proves (1)$\Rightarrow$(3).

For the converse, the discrete case is immediate.  Suppose
$D\cong\mathbb R\times A$ with $A$ countable discrete.  The restricted
order on the open subgroup $\mathbb R\times\{0\}$ is Borel.  By
Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:borel-order-real-line}, after changing the orientation of
the real coordinate it is the usual order.  For each $a\in A$, each
section
\[
 S_a=\{r\in\mathbb R:(r,a)\succ0\}
\]
is an upper set for the usual real order.  It is consequently one of
\[
 \varnothing,\qquad\mathbb R,\qquad(b,\infty),\qquad[b,\infty)
 \quad (b\in\mathbb R).
\]
For $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$.  The corresponding nonnegative section
at $a=0$ is $[0,\infty)$; at $a\neq0$ the strict and nonstrict
sections agree.

The $(a,k)$-slices of $M_D$, for $(a,k)\in A\times\mathbb Z$, are
clopen and have one of these interval types, with the replacement
$(0,\infty)\mapsto[0,\infty)$ exactly when $a=0$ and $k\geq0$.
Every nonempty slice is locally compact and homeomorphic either to
$\mathbb R$ or to $[0,\infty)$.  There are countably many slices.
In particular, the slices $a=0$, $k<0$ give infinitely many line
components, while $a=0$, $k\geq0$ give infinitely many closed-ray
components.  This proves (3)$\Rightarrow$(2), the homeomorphism
\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:universal-lc-coefficient-carrier}, and Polishness.  Finally,
(2)$\Rightarrow$(1) is immediate.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Consequences and the precise boundary of the result}

\begin{corollary}\label{pma:lcc:cor:no-zero-dimensional-lc-coefficient}
The inherited coefficient construction produces no uncountable
zero-dimensional locally compact space.  Every uncountable locally
compact carrier it produces is homeomorphic to the carrier obtained
from $D=\mathbb R$.
\end{corollary}

The classification also excludes connected uncountable carriers inside
this construction; the discrete integer coordinate already supplies
clopen slices.  It gives a stronger conclusion than an existence
obstruction for one proposed space: the entire locally compact
homeomorphism type is fixed.

It is essential not to infer that the open connected subgroup
$\mathbb R\times\{0\}$ must be convex in the arithmetic order.
For example, put the lexicographic order with real coordinate first on
$D=\mathbb R\times\mathbb Q$ and give $\mathbb Q$ the discrete
topology.  Then $(0,1)$ lies between $(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$, although it
does not lie in that connected subgroup.  The coefficient cone remains
locally compact, as the theorem predicts.

Likewise, the theorem does not assert that every uncountable Polish
model of Presburger arithmetic with continuous addition has the carrier
\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:universal-lc-coefficient-carrier}.  A presentation whose
topology is not inherited from a Polish coefficient group can evade
these hypotheses.  The broader inherited-group statement is proved next. Further questions
are collected in Section~\ref{pma:lcc:sec:research-program}.

\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) Within inherited coefficient presentations,
\cref{pma:lcc:cor:no-zero-dimensional-lc-coefficient} answers Part~I's
\cref{pma:pr:q:zerodim} negatively and the remark after it excludes connected
carriers (\cref{pma:pr:q:connected}); \cref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones}
below extends both to every inherited Polish group cone. For presentations not
inherited from a Polish ordered group both questions stay open
(\cref{pma:lcc:question:zero-dimensional}). \Cref{pma:lcc:thm:lc-coefficient-classification}
extends part~(3) of source~08's \cref{pma:lc:thm:cones} by assuming local
compactness of the cone rather than of the coefficient group, and fixes the
carrier.

\section{The classification extends to arbitrary inherited group cones}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:general-inherited-cones}

The coefficient group need not be divisible, and the ambient ordered
group need not split as a coefficient group followed by its standard
integer part.  The same arguments classify every inherited positive
cone in a Borel ordered abelian Polish group.
Write $X_{\mathrm{lc}}$ for the countable disjoint union of lines and
closed rays displayed in~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:universal-lc-coefficient-carrier}.

\begin{theorem}[General inherited-cone classification; extends \cref{pma:lc:thm:lca,pma:lc:thm:classification}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones}
Let $G$ be an abelian Polish group with a translation-invariant linear
order whose nonnegative cone $P$ is Borel.  The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $P$ is locally compact at zero in the topology inherited from $G$;
\item $P$ is locally compact in that topology;
\item as a topological group, $G$ is either countable discrete, or
      $G\cong\mathbb R\times A$ for a countable discrete torsion-free
      abelian group $A$.
\end{enumerate}
If these equivalent local-compactness conditions hold and, in addition,
$G$ has a least positive element $e$ and $P$ is uncountable, then $P$
is homeomorphic to $X_{\mathrm{lc}}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:cone-lc-implies-group-lc}, local compactness of $P$ at
zero gives local compactness of $G$.  The principal structure theorem and
Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:no-compact-ordered-subgroup} supply an open subgroup
$H\cong\mathbb R^n$.  The cone $P\cap H$ is locally compact at zero,
so Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:locally-closed-total-cone} gives $n\leq1$.

Here is a direct splitting argument that does not assume divisibility of
$G$.  Since an ordered abelian group is torsion-free, it embeds in its
rational hull $G_{\mathbb Q}=G\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$, a
$\mathbb Q$-vector space.  The subgroup $H$ is divisible and is therefore
already a $\mathbb Q$-subspace of this hull.  Choose a vector-space
complement $B$ to $H$ in $G_{\mathbb Q}$ and put $A=G\cap B$.  For
$g\in G$, its decomposition $g=h+b$ has $h\in H\subseteq G$, so
$b=g-h$ lies in $A$.  Hence $G=H\oplus A$.  The subgroup $A$ is
torsion-free, is discrete because $H$ is open, and is countable because
there are only countably many open $H$-cosets.  Addition gives the
topological isomorphism $H\times A\cong G$, as in the earlier proof.
This proves (1)$\Rightarrow$(3).

For (3)$\Rightarrow$(2), the discrete case is immediate.  In the other
case Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:borel-order-real-line} orients the real subgroup in
its usual direction.  In each clopen coset of that subgroup, the positive
cone is an upper interval.  Each nonempty such interval is a line or an
open or closed ray, and is locally compact.  Condition (2) plainly
implies (1).

Suppose now that $G$ has a least positive element $e$ and is uncountable.
Then $H\cong\mathbb R$.  For every $h\in H$ with $h>0$ and every
standard $n\geq0$, divisibility of $H$ and minimality of $e$ give
\[
 \frac{h}{n+1}\geq e,
 \qquad\text{and consequently}\qquad h\geq(n+1)e>ne.
\]
In particular, $H\cap\mathbb Ze=\{0\}$, so the cosets $H+ke$,
$k\in\mathbb Z$, are pairwise distinct.  In an oriented real
coordinate on $H$, their intersections with $P$ are
\[
 P\cap(H+ke)\ \cong\
 \begin{cases}
 [0,\infty),&k\geq0,\\
 (0,\infty),&k<0.
 \end{cases}
\]
The dominance inequality just proved determines the sign away from the
real origin; the sign of $ke$ determines whether that endpoint belongs.
All other coset sections are again empty, lines, or open or closed rays.
There are countably many such clopen sections, with infinitely many line
components and infinitely many closed-ray components already supplied by
the standard integer translates.  Thus $P\cong X_{\mathrm{lc}}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{pma:lcc:cor:presburger-group-completion-carrier}
Suppose a locally compact Polish model of Presburger arithmetic is the
nonnegative cone, with its inherited topology, of a Borel ordered abelian
Polish group.  If the model is uncountable, its carrier is
$X_{\mathrm{lc}}$.  In particular, an uncountable zero-dimensional
locally compact continuous-addition Presburger model cannot admit such
an inherited Polish group presentation.
\end{corollary}

The condition concerns a compatible topology on the entire group of
differences, not merely the existence of that group algebraically.  Every
cancellative commutative monoid has an algebraic group of differences;
it is precisely the compatible Polish group topology and inherited-cone
condition that are additional here.  No algebraic splitting of a general
Presburger group over its standard $\mathbb Z$-subgroup is assumed.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones} strengthens
source~08's \cref{pma:lc:thm:lca,pma:lc:thm:classification}: no ambient local
compactness is assumed, and the homeomorphism type of the cone is determined.
For Part~III's \cref{pma:cp:q:spaces} it settles the locally compact
inherited case.

\subsection{A compact-open obstruction without a group topology}

One useful obstruction survives even when no ambient topological group
is available.

\begin{lemma}[compare \cref{pma:pr:lem:compactmonoid}]\label{pma:lcc:lem:no-compact-positive-subsemigroup}
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff commutative cancellative topological monoid whose
only invertible element is zero.  Its only nonempty compact
subsemigroup is $\{0\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $C$ be a nonempty compact subsemigroup.  For each $a\in C$, the
set $a+C$ is a nonempty compact subset of $C$.  These sets have the
finite intersection property: for $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in C$, their
intersection contains $a_1+\cdots+a_m+C$.  Choose
\[
 p\in\bigcap_{a\in C}(a+C).
\]
Since $p\in C$, the intersection condition includes $p\in p+C$.
Thus $p=p+c$ for some $c\in C$, and cancellation against $p=p+0$
gives $c=0$.  We have shown that every such $C$ contains zero.

For any $a\in C$, the translate $a+C$ is itself a nonempty compact
subsemigroup: the sum of $a+x$ and $a+y$ equals
$a+(a+x+y)$, with $a+x+y\in C$.  Applying the previous paragraph to
$a+C$ gives $0\in a+C$.  Hence $a$ is invertible in $M$ and must be
zero.  Therefore $C=\{0\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Compact-open neighborhoods force isolated zero]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:compact-open-isolated-zero}
Let $M$ be a Hausdorff commutative cancellative topological monoid with
jointly continuous addition and no nonzero invertible elements.  If
zero has a compact open neighborhood, then zero is isolated.
Consequently, zero is isolated in every zero-dimensional locally
compact Hausdorff continuous-addition Presburger presentation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $K$ be a compact open neighborhood of zero.  For each $x\in K$,
joint continuity at $(x,0)$ supplies neighborhoods $U_x$ of $x$ and
$V_x$ of zero such that $U_x+V_x\subseteq K$.  Finitely many $U_x$
cover $K$.  Intersecting their corresponding $V_x$, and then
intersecting with $K$, gives an open neighborhood $V$ of zero satisfying
\[
 V\subseteq K,\qquad K+V\subseteq K.
\]
If $v\in V$, every positive integer multiple of $v$ lies in $K$.
The closure of this set of multiples is a nonempty compact
subsemigroup: $K$ is closed because it is compact in a Hausdorff space,
and joint continuity preserves the subsemigroup condition under closure.
Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:no-compact-positive-subsemigroup} says that this closure
is $\{0\}$.  Since it contains $v$, we have $v=0$.  Hence $V=\{0\}$
is open.

Finally, a zero-dimensional locally compact Hausdorff space has a
compact open neighborhood at each point: inside an open neighborhood
with compact closure choose a clopen neighborhood, which is then
compact.  A Presburger monoid satisfies cancellation and has no nonzero
additive units, so the first assertion applies.
\end{proof}

This last conclusion concerns the topology at zero only.  It does not
rule out zero-dimensional locally compact Presburger presentations with
isolated zero, and it does not assert that every standard natural number
is isolated: continuity of addition alone does not make every
translation an open map.

\noindent\writetag{} \Cref{pma:lcc:thm:compact-open-isolated-zero} extends
Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:cor:compact} (no compact carrier) and
\cref{pma:pr:lem:compactmonoid}; compare source~06's \cref{pma:cp:thm:zero},
which isolates $0$ when addition and multiplication are both continuous.

\section{Arithmetic on the manifold boundary}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:arithmetic-boundary}

The countably many endpoints of the locally compact carrier have an
intrinsic arithmetic meaning.  Here $\partial_{\mathrm{man}}P$ denotes
the boundary of $P$ as a one-dimensional topological manifold with
boundary, rather than its boundary inside the ambient group.  On
$X_{\mathrm{lc}}$ these are exactly the endpoints of the closed-ray
components.

\begin{theorem}[The boundary is an elementary initial submodel]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:arithmetic-boundary}
Let $G$ be a Borel ordered abelian Polish group whose nonnegative cone
$P$, in its inherited topology, is an uncountable locally compact model
of Presburger arithmetic.  Put $H=G^0$, the connected component of zero,
and define
\[
 C=\{g\in G: |g|<h\ \text{for every }h\in H\text{ with }h>0\}.
\]
Then $H\cong\mathbb R$, $C$ is a countable discrete convex subgroup
containing the standard integer subgroup, and
\[
 \partial_{\mathrm{man}}P=C_{\geq0}.
\]
With its inherited arithmetic, this boundary is a countable elementary
initial submodel of $P$ and has the discrete subspace topology.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones} gives an open subgroup
isomorphic to $\mathbb R$.  An open subgroup is also closed; since this
one is connected, it is exactly $H=G^0$.

The set $C$ is a subgroup.  If $c,d\in C$ and $h\in H$ is positive,
then $|c|<h/2$ and $|d|<h/2$, whence $|c+d|<h$; closure under negation
is immediate.  It is convex because $0\leq x\leq |c|$ with $c\in C$
implies $x<h$ for every positive $h\in H$.  No nonzero element of $H$
lies in $C$, so $C\cap H=\{0\}$.  The quotient $G/H$ is countable,
and the map $C\to G/H$ is injective.  Thus $C$ is countable.  It is
discrete since $H$ is open and intersects it only at zero.  If $e$ is the
least positive element, the dominance inequality in
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones} shows that every standard
multiple of $e$ belongs to $C$.

Each $H$-coset meets $P$ in a line or an open or closed ray, or not at
all.  Suppose $c\in C_{\geq0}$.  For $h\in H$, the sign of $c+h$
is positive when $h>0$, negative when $h<0$, and nonnegative when
$h=0$.  Therefore
\[
 P\cap(c+H)=c+H_{\geq0},
\]
and $c$ is the endpoint of this closed ray.  Conversely, if $x\in P$
is such an endpoint in its $H$-coset, then $x-h<0$ for every positive
$h\in H$.  Consequently $0\leq x<h$ for every such $h$, so $x\in C$.
This proves the asserted identification with the intrinsic manifold
boundary.

Finally, $G$ is a Presburger ordered group, or $\mathbb Z$-group, and
$C$ inherits its least positive element $e$.  Division stays inside
$C$.  More explicitly, if
\[
 c=mq+r e,\qquad 0\leq r<m,
\]
with $c\in C$ and a standard positive integer $m$, then $mq=c-re\in C$.
Convexity gives $q\in C$, since $|q|\leq m|q|=|mq|$.  Thus $C$ is
itself a $\mathbb Z$-group and its inclusion into $G$ preserves and
reflects every congruence predicate.  Quantifier elimination for
Presburger arithmetic in the language with congruence predicates makes
this inclusion elementary.  Restricting to nonnegative cones gives
$C_{\geq0}\preccurlyeq P$.  Convexity makes it an initial submodel.
\end{proof}

The word ``initial'' is arithmetic: elements below a boundary element
are again boundary elements.  It does not mean that the endpoint set is
a connected interval in the ambient topology; that endpoint set is
discrete.

\noindent\writetag{} In source~08's notation (remark after
\cref{pma:lc:thm:classification}) source~15's $H=G^0$ is $C$ and its $C$ is
$B_C$: the letters are exchanged. The theorem shows that in the locally compact
case $B_C$ is a countable discrete convex elementary initial submodel.

\begin{theorem}[Every countable Presburger model occurs as a boundary; the construction of \cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:boundary-realization}
For every countable model $N$ of Presburger arithmetic, there is an
uncountable locally compact inherited Polish-group presentation $P$
with continuous addition such that
\[
 P\cong X_{\mathrm{lc}}\ \text{topologically},\qquad
 \partial_{\mathrm{man}}P\cong N\ \text{arithmetically}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $C=N-N$ be the countable ordered difference group of $N$ and give
$C$ the discrete topology.  It is a $\mathbb Z$-group.  Set
\[
 G=\mathbb R\lex C
\]
and give it the product topology, with the real coordinate dominant in
the arithmetic order.  This is an abelian Polish group with Borel order
and least positive element $(0,1_C)$.  Since
\[
 G/\mathbb Z(0,1_C)
 \cong\mathbb R\lex (C/\mathbb Z1_C)
\]
is divisible, $G$ is a $\mathbb Z$-group and $P=G_{\geq0}$ is a full
Presburger model.  Addition is continuous.  The general classification
gives its carrier $X_{\mathrm{lc}}$.  Its connected component is
$\mathbb R\times\{0\}$, and the infinitesimal subgroup relative to
that component is exactly $\{0\}\times C$.  The preceding theorem
identifies its manifold boundary with $\{0\}\times N$.
\end{proof}

\noindent\writetag{} The model in this proof is source~13's countable-core
transfer with $D=\R$ and $K=N-N$ (\cref{pma:nsp:thm:countable-core-transfer});
the identification of its boundary with $N$ is source~15's, through
\cref{pma:lcc:thm:arithmetic-boundary}.

\section{Continuum many models on one locally compact carrier}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:continuum-lc-models}

The topological rigidity in
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:lc-coefficient-classification} does not imply rigidity of
the arithmetic structure.  We now exhibit the maximum possible number
of pairwise nonisomorphic continuous-addition Presburger models on the
single carrier
\[
 X_{\mathrm{lc}}=
 \left(\bigsqcup_{j\in\mathbb N}\mathbb R\right)
 \sqcup
 \left(\bigsqcup_{j\in\mathbb N}[0,\infty)\right).
\]
The ingredients are ordinary finite-support ordered groups; no novelty
claim is made for the Hahn-group method itself.

\subsection{A recoverable continuum family of countable orders}

For a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb N$, put
\[
 k_n(S)=\begin{cases}1,&n\notin S,\\2,&n\in S,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 L_S=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\bigl(\mathbb Z+\mathbf{k_n(S)}\bigr),
\]
where $+$ and $\sum$ denote ordered sums, $\mathbb Z$ has its usual
two-sided order, and $\mathbf k$ is a finite chain of size $k$.
The countable order $L_S$ has neither a least nor a greatest element.

For elements of a linear order, define finite condensation by
\[
 x\sim_{\mathrm{fin}}y
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [\min(x,y),\max(x,y)]\text{ is finite}.
\]
This is an equivalence relation with convex classes and is preserved by
all order isomorphisms.  In $L_S$ its classes are, in succession,
\[
 \mathbb Z_0,\ \mathbf{k_0(S)},\ \mathbb Z_1,
 \ \mathbf{k_1(S)},\ \mathbb Z_2,\ \mathbf{k_2(S)},\ \ldots.
\]
Indeed, two points in one integer block have a finite interval between
them, as do two points in one finite block.  An interval crossing from
an integer block into the following finite block contains an infinite
terminal segment of that integer block.  An interval crossing from a
finite block into the following integer block contains an infinite
initial segment of the latter.  Every interval crossing farther contains
one of these infinite intervals.

Consequently the condensation quotient has order type $\omega$.
Every automorphism of $\omega$ is the identity, and an order isomorphism
of $L_S$ with $L_T$ must match the corresponding finite classes.  Their
cardinalities recover $k_n(S)$ for every $n$, and hence recover $S$.
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:LS-unique}
 L_S\cong L_T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S=T.
\end{equation}

\subsection{Encoding an order into Archimedean classes}

For a countable linear order $L$, let
\[
 V_L=\bigoplus_{\ell\in L}\mathbb Q
\]
be the group of finitely supported rational functions on $L$.  For a
nonzero $v\in V_L$, let $\lambda(v)$ be the least point in its finite
support and declare
\[
 v>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v(\lambda(v))>0.
\]
Every nonempty finite subset of a linear order has a least element, so
this definition requires no well-ordering of $L$.  It gives the usual
lexicographic ordered-group structure, with earlier indices dominating
later indices.  The group $V_L$ is countable and divisible.  Equip it
with the discrete topology and define
\[
 D_L=V_L\lex \mathbb R,
 \qquad
 G_L=D_L\lex \mathbb Z,
 \qquad
 M_L=(G_L)_{\geq0}.
\]
The topology of $D_L$ is the product of the discrete topology on $V_L$
and the usual topology on $\mathbb R$; the topology on $M_L$ is inherited
from $D_L\times\mathbb Z$.  The coefficient order is Borel: each
nonzero positive $V_L$-coset is wholly positive, each negative coset is
wholly negative, and the zero coset uses the usual real order.

The group $G_L$ is a discretely ordered abelian group with least positive
element $1=(0,0,1)$, and its quotient by $\mathbb Z1$ is the divisible
ordered group $D_L$.  Equivalently, for every standard $m\geq2$,
division by $m$ has precisely the usual residue representatives
$0,\ldots,m-1$.  In coordinates it is given by
\[
 (d,z)=m\left(\frac d m,\left\lfloor\frac z m\right\rfloor\right)
       +(0,z\bmod m).
\]
For a nonnegative input the quotient is again nonnegative.  By the
standard ordered-group characterization of Presburger models, $M_L$
is a model of the full first-order theory of
$(\mathbb N,0,1,+,<)$, including its entire induction scheme.  Addition
is continuous because it is the restriction of the group operation.
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:lc-coefficient-classification} gives
$M_L\cong X_{\mathrm{lc}}$ as a topological space.

For completeness, the invariant distinguishing these models can be
checked directly.  For positive elements of an ordered abelian group,
write
\[
 x\asymp y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (\exists m,n\in\mathbb N_{>0})\ (x\leq my\ \text{and}\ y\leq nx).
\]
This is Archimedean equivalence.  Order its classes by dominance:
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:dominance-convention}
 [x]\mathrel{\triangleleft}[y]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 x>ny\ \text{for every }n\in\mathbb N_{>0}.
\end{equation}
Thus a more dominant class is earlier.  The condition is independent of
the positive representatives and is invariant under ordered-group
isomorphisms.  In $V_L$, two positive elements are Archimedean equivalent
exactly when they have the same least support index.  Equality of the
indices allows integer multiples of either positive leading coefficient
to dominate the other; inequality of the indices makes the earlier
coordinate dominate every positive integer multiple of the later one.
Hence
\[
 \mathcal A(V_L)\cong L,\qquad
 \mathcal A(D_L)\cong L+\mathbf1,\qquad
 \mathcal A(G_L)\cong L+\mathbf2,
\]
where $\mathcal A$ denotes the set of positive Archimedean classes with
the convention~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:dominance-convention}.  The two appended classes
come respectively from the real summand and the integer summand.

An isomorphism of Presburger monoids $M_L\to M_{L'}$ extends uniquely
to an isomorphism of their Grothendieck groups, by
$x-y\mapsto h(x)-h(y)$.  It preserves the positive cones, and therefore
preserves the ordered groups and their Archimedean-class orders.  For
$L=L_S$, the order $L_S$ has no greatest element.  In
$L_S+\mathbf2$, the greatest class and its immediate predecessor are
therefore precisely the two appended classes.  Removing those two
intrinsically specified classes recovers $L_S$.  There is no absorption
of an end block.  We conclude from~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:LS-unique} that
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:models-distinct}
 M_{L_S}\cong M_{L_T}\text{ as Presburger structures}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S=T.
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp number of models on one locally compact carrier; compare \cref{pma:cp:thm:continuum}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:continuum-lc-models}
There are exactly $2^{\aleph_0}$ isomorphism classes of full Presburger
models with continuous addition whose underlying topological space is
$X_{\mathrm{lc}}$. The lower bound is realized by inherited
coefficient presentations.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lower bound is~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:models-distinct}.  Choose a homeomorphism
from each of the displayed carriers to the fixed space
$X_{\mathrm{lc}}$ and transport its arithmetic structure.

For the upper bound, a continuous map from $X_{\mathrm{lc}}^2$ to
$X_{\mathrm{lc}}$ is determined by its restriction to a countable dense
subset, because the target is Hausdorff.  Since
$|X_{\mathrm{lc}}|=2^{\aleph_0}$, there are at most
\[
 (2^{\aleph_0})^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}
\]
such maps.  Choosing the constants $0$ and $1$ does not increase this
bound.  The order is recovered from addition by
$x\leq y\Longleftrightarrow(\exists z)\,x+z=y$, so it contributes no
additional choices.  Hence there are at most continuum many such
structures, and in particular at most continuum many isomorphism
classes.
\end{proof}

This separates two classification problems.  The locally compact carrier
is unique inside the uncountable inherited coefficient construction, but
its arithmetic structures achieve the largest multiplicity permitted by
continuity on a separable space.  Further questions are to determine the
topological Presburger automorphism groups of these presentations and
to determine the descriptive complexity of isomorphism on the full
space of continuous Presburger operations on $X_{\mathrm{lc}}$.  Within
the displayed $S$-indexed family the isomorphism relation has already
been determined: it is exactly equality of the parameters.

In fact, the family above fixes even the boundary arithmetic.  In
$G_{L_S}=V_{L_S}\lex \mathbb R
\lex \mathbb Z$, the subgroup infinitesimal relative
to the open real component is precisely the final $\mathbb Z$ summand.
Thus $\partial_{\mathrm{man}}M_{L_S}$ is the standard model
$\mathbb N$ for every $S$.  The continuum lower bound therefore persists
after prescribing the boundary to be standard arithmetic.

\noindent\writetag{} The analogous counts on Baire space are Part~III's
\cref{pma:cp:thm:continuum,pma:cp:s06:thm:continuum}. Source~13's
\cref{pma:nsp:cor:continuum-polish-cores} gives $2^{\aleph_0}$ nonsplit
locally compact models; by \cref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones} they too
live on $X_{\mathrm{lc}}$, whereas the family above is split.

\section{Consequences for multiplication and for omnific arithmetic}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:synthesis-omnific}

\subsection{The locally compact obstruction is entirely algebraic}

The topological classification and the cardinality theorem combine to
give a conclusion stronger than the Borel multiplier obstruction in
this particular setting.

\begin{theorem}[No multiplication on an uncountable locally compact inherited cone; a case of \cref{pma:br:thm:semiring}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:lc-no-arbitrary-multiplication}
Let $G$ be an abelian Polish group with a Borel translation-invariant
linear order and least positive element $1$. Suppose that its positive
cone $M=G_{\geq0}$, with the inherited topology, is uncountable and
locally compact. There is no unital semiring multiplication on $M$
having its existing addition, zero, and distinguished unit $1$.
No continuity or measurability of the proposed multiplication is
assumed. Neither Presburger induction nor multiplication commutativity
is required for this conclusion.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:general-inherited-cones}, $G$ has an open subgroup
$H\cong\R$ and $G/H$ is countable. The order restricted to $H$ is
usual or reversed by Lemma~\ref{pma:lcc:lem:borel-order-real-line}; therefore
$H$ is an uncountable Archimedean subgroup in its induced order.

A proposed multiplication on $M$ extends uniquely by distributivity
to its additive group of differences $G$. The construction is the
algebraic version of~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:multiplier-group-completion}, and
does not use any Borel hypothesis. Products of nonnegative elements
remain nonnegative. Moreover, the product of two strictly positive
elements is strictly positive. Indeed, each can be written as $1+x$
with $x\geq0$, and
\[
 (1+x)(1+y)=1+x+y+xy>0.
\]
Thus the extension makes $G$ a discretely ordered unital ring.
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:archimedean-subgroup-cardinality} then injects the
uncountable group $H$ into the countable quotient $G/H$, a
contradiction.
\end{proof}

The topology is used to locate the Archimedean subgroup of countable
index. Once that subgroup has been found, the obstruction survives
every change of topology. In particular, refining one of these cones'
topologies to isolate its standard natural numbers cannot make its
\emph{unchanged additive structure} support a semiring multiplication.
The polynomial example in
Section~\ref{pma:lcc:sec:borel-multiplication-obstruction} has a different
ordered additive group and therefore does not contradict this theorem.

\subsection{Explicit finite normal forms in the omnific integers}

The family from Section~\ref{pma:lcc:sec:continuum-lc-models} can be placed
inside the omnific integers without invoking a topology on a proper
class, infinite support convergence, or a global choice of normal
forms. All the normal forms needed for each element are finite.
We use the standard convention that an omnific integer has real
coefficients at strictly positive surreal exponents and an integer
coefficient at exponent zero. The inspected ProveIt development realizes
this as a coefficient pullback inside its surreal normal-form ring
\cite{s15:proveitOmnific}.

\begin{lemma}\label{pma:lcc:lem:rational-exponent-embedding}
Every countable linear order $L$ admits an order-reversing embedding
$q:L\to\Q\cap(1,2)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Enumerate $L$. Assign exponents one at a time, maintaining the required
reversed inequalities. At each finite stage, the already assigned
elements above and below the next element determine an open interval
between finitely many rational bounds; use $1$ or $2$ when one side
has no assigned bound. The interval is nonempty because the finite
assignment respects the order. Density of $\Q$ supplies a new rational
strictly inside it. The union of these finite assignments is the
desired injection.
\end{proof}

For $v\in V_L$, $r\in\R$, and $k\in\Z$, define
\begin{equation}\label{pma:lcc:eq:omnific-embedding}
 \Phi_L(v,r,k)
   =\sum_{\ell\in\supp(v)}v(\ell)\,\omega^{q(\ell)}
      +r\omega+k.
\end{equation}
The convention is that zero coefficients are omitted. The finite
support has a well-defined greatest exponent, and every exponent
$q(\ell)$ lies strictly between $1$ and $2$.

\begin{theorem}[A set-sized omnific realization; compare \cref{pma:pr:thm:omnific,pma:cp:thm:omnific}]
\label{pma:lcc:thm:omnific-realization}
The map $\Phi_L$ is an injective order-preserving additive homomorphism
from
\[
 G_L=V_L\lex\R\lex\Z
\]
into the omnific integers, and sends its distinguished unit to $1$.
Its nonnegative image is an additive Presburger substructure of the
nonnegative omnific integers. With the topology transported from
$M_L$, this image is a locally compact Polish model on $\Xlc$.
For the orders $L_S$, these images yield continuum many nonisomorphic
such arithmetic structures with standard boundary.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The expression~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:omnific-embedding} has no negative exponent
and has integer constant term, so it is an omnific integer. Uniqueness
of finite normal forms gives injectivity. Addition is coefficientwise,
giving additivity and preservation of the unit.

If $v\neq0$, let $\ell_0$ be its least support index. Since $q$ reverses
the order, $q(\ell_0)$ is the greatest exponent appearing in the first
sum. It also exceeds the exponent $1$ of the real summand and the
exponent $0$ of the integer summand. The sign of the normal form is
therefore the sign of $v(\ell_0)$. If $v=0$ and $r\neq0$, its sign
is the sign of $r$; if $v=r=0$, its sign is the sign of $k$.
This is exactly the lexicographic order on $G_L$.

Transport the topology along the resulting bijection between $M_L$
and its positive image. The bijection is then a homeomorphism by
definition, and the already proved Presburger axioms, continuity of
addition, local compactness, and boundary statements are preserved.
Each image is a set of cardinality continuum: its parameters range
over the set $V_L\times\R\times\Z$, not over all surreal numbers.
\end{proof}

These are additive substructures, with the full Presburger theory
verified by their $\Z$-group certificate. They are not subrings for
the usual omnific multiplication. For example,
\[
 \omega=\Phi_L(0,1,0),\qquad \omega\cdot\omega=\omega^2,
\]
and uniqueness of normal forms shows that $\omega^2$ is outside the
image: every exponent allowed by~\eqref{pma:lcc:eq:omnific-embedding} is
less than $2$. Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:lc-no-arbitrary-multiplication}
says more than this failure of closure. No alternative multiplication
on the same positive image can satisfy the unital semiring laws with
its existing addition and unit.

The topology just transported is a coefficient topology. It is distinct
from the native order topology of the omnific integers, which is
discrete because $1$ is least positive. ProveIt's separate discreteness
development concerns the native fine order topology; it provides no
contradiction to the nondiscrete coefficient topology used here
\cite{s15:proveitOmnificTopology}. An assertion of ``a Polish topology on
the omnific integers'' without a set-sized carrier and an explicit
topology would obscure both of these distinctions.

\section{From mathematical proofs to a ProveIt formalization}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:formalization}

The repository offers a concrete starting point for formalizing these
results, but the distinction between a source-inspected existing declaration
and a proposed future theorem must be maintained. The source audit
establishes which declarations are present at the pinned commit.
The proofs in this article are mathematical proofs; no new Lean
kernel certificate accompanies them.

\subsection{Existing formal interfaces}

The Presburger files are under the directory
\begin{quote}\small
\mbox{\nolinkurl{Logic/PresburgerArithmetic/Lean/PresburgerArithmetic/}}.
\end{quote}
The actual semantics in \nolinkurl{Syntax.lean} use valuations of type
\texttt{List Int}; quantified variables range over \nolinkurl{Int}.
In \nolinkurl{Decision.lean}, the following declarations occur in
the namespace \mbox{\nolinkurl{PresburgerArithmetic.Formula}}
\cite{s15:proveitPresburger}:
\begin{itemize}
\item \mbox{\nolinkurl{quantifierEliminate}}: the elimination procedure;
\item \mbox{\nolinkurl{holds_iff_quantifierEliminate}}: its semantic equivalence;
\item \mbox{\nolinkurl{decideSentence_eq_true_iff}}: correctness for sentences;
\item \mbox{\nolinkurl{presburgerArithmetic_decidable}}: the resulting decision instance.
\end{itemize}
These support the executable integer
decision procedure. They do not by themselves instantiate that
procedure over an arbitrary nonstandard ordered group.

The omnific files are under
\nolinkurl{Algebra/SurrealNumbers/Surreal/Foundations/}.
The inspected \nolinkurl{OmnificIntegers.lean} supplies the following
chain of interfaces \cite{s15:proveitOmnific}:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \nolinkurl{normalFormHahnHom} turns the normal-form map into a
ring homomorphism, and \nolinkurl{nonnegativeSupportSubring} restricts
the permitted exponents.
\item \nolinkurl{constantCoeff} extracts the real constant coefficient;
\nolinkurl{omnificSubring} pulls it back along the integer embedding.
The abbreviation \nolinkurl{OmnificInteger} is a universe-indexed type,
and \nolinkurl{omnificToSurreal} embeds it into the actual surreal
construction.
\item \nolinkurl{omnificToSurreal_injective} records injectivity;
\nolinkurl{omnificConstantCoeff} extracts the integer constant;
\nolinkurl{omnificPurelyInfiniteIdeal} is its kernel; and
\mbox{\nolinkurl{omnificQuotientEquiv}} identifies the quotient with $\Z$.
\item In \nolinkurl{OmnificPurelyInfiniteModule.lean},
\nolinkurl{omnificPurelyInfiniteAddEquiv} transfers the established
purely infinite support module. The real and rational module
instances provide coefficient divisibility.
\end{enumerate}
These interfaces fit the finite normal-form construction above.
Their existence is source evidence for a formalization route, not
evidence that the new Polish topology or classification is already
implemented.

\noindent\writetag{} The declarations named in this subsection exist at the
current state under these names. They are about the ordinary integers and the
omnific coefficient construction; none of source~15's theorems is formalized.

\subsection{A dependency order for implementation}

\paragraph{Stage 1: algebraic certificates and the cardinal obstruction.}
Introduce a semantic interface for discretely ordered abelian groups
with standard residue representatives. Prove closure of positive cones,
the unique division statement, and extension of additive monoid maps
to differences. Then formalize
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:archimedean-subgroup-cardinality}: after the bounded
integer-interval lemma, its essential object is the additive map
$a\mapsto ah+H$ and the proof that its kernel is trivial. This is
the shortest substantial result in the article and needs no measure
theory or descriptive set theory.

\paragraph{Stage 2: nonstandard Presburger semantics.}
Parameterize the interpretation of affine terms and congruences by
the ordered group. The elimination proof must use the actual
subgroup $mG$, including nonstandard shifts. For example,
\[
 x\equiv y\pmod m\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 x-y\in mG
\]
is the semantic congruence relation. Proving a formula invariant under
standard iterations of the translation $x\mapsto x+m$ only covers
$m\Z1$, which can be a proper subgroup of $mG$. Generalized
elimination or a formal model-theoretic completeness argument closes
this gap. Its output should include elementary embeddings of pure
$\Z$-subgroups, the interface needed by the boundary theorem.

\paragraph{Stage 3: topology and local compactness.}
Build the coefficient models as explicit types with transported
product topologies. Prove the $G_\delta$ criterion and the
compact-neighborhood reflection lemma. The Euclidean closed-cone
argument is a small independent target. The full classification then
requires the principal LCA structure theorem and the measurable-order
compact-subgroup obstruction. Availability of these results in the
particular dependency version must be checked before estimating a
formalization budget; this manuscript does not assume that they are
already packaged in the required form.

\paragraph{Stage 4: the arithmetic boundary and continuum family.}
Formalize the infinitesimal subgroup $C$ relative to the open real
component, its convexity and countability, and its identification
with the endpoints. Prove purity under division and then apply the
semantic theorem from Stage~2. For the continuum family, finite
support makes the ordered-group construction elementary; the
recoverable finite-condensation pattern supplies an explicit
nonisomorphism certificate. The final omnific embedding uses finite
normal forms and the already inspected coefficient interfaces.

\paragraph{Stage 5: the Borel multiplier theorem.}
This stage requires Borel automatic continuity, a complete metric,
Cantor product probability, and a tail zero-one law. The proof is
organized so that each dependency can be isolated. The finite-block
estimate only counts $2^k$ assignments and avoids a measurable
inverse or an injective Cantor-space coding theorem. The order and
the topology must remain separate structures in the formal statement:
assuming an order topology would force discreteness at the outset
and erase the content of the result.

\subsection{What verification establishes}

The source comparison fixes the existing background; the proofs check
the new implications; and the counterexamples test the boundaries of
the hypotheses. Separate AI-assisted mathematical reviews focused on the
rational-hull splitting, endpoint identification, quotient injection,
finite-block probability argument, and recovery of the continuum
parameters. That review is useful error control, but it is not a
substitute for an independent referee or a proof assistant.

Finite numerical checks could illustrate the geometric growth
inequality, but they would not verify the uncountable cardinalities,
Polish completeness, elementarity, or all induction instances. The
article therefore supplies deductive arguments for those claims and
does not present finite computation as a mathematical certificate.

\section{Further research questions and a proposed program}
\label{pma:lcc:sec:research-program}

The following are proposed questions arising from the results. Their
status is deliberately local: they are not all asserted to be previously
published open problems. Where a question comes from Glazer's paper
or the earlier repository manuscript, that origin is stated. Questions
already settled above are separated from questions outside the proved
hypotheses.

\subsection{Questions now settled within the inherited-group framework}

For an uncountable Presburger positive cone inherited from a Borel
ordered abelian Polish group, the locally compact carrier is exactly
$\Xlc$. Thus connected and zero-dimensional locally compact carriers
are excluded in this framework. Every such cone forbids every unital
semiring multiplication on the same addition and unit. The fixed
carrier supports the maximum possible number, continuum, of
isomorphism classes, even with standard boundary. Its intrinsic
boundary is always a countable elementary initial submodel, and the
set of possible boundary models is exactly the set of countable
Presburger models. These are complete answers to the corresponding
restricted classification, expansion, multiplicity, and boundary
questions.

\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) For Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:zerodim} and
\cref{pma:pr:q:connected}, and Part~III's \cref{pma:cp:q:spaces} and
\cref{pma:cp:q:connected}, these settle the inherited-group case only.

\subsection{Presentations outside Polish group completions}

\begin{question}[Zero-dimensional locally compact arithmetic]
\label{pma:lcc:question:zero-dimensional}
Does any uncountable zero-dimensional locally compact Polish space
support a full Presburger model with jointly continuous addition?
\end{question}
This extends a follow-up question in the repository manuscript
\cite{s15:proveitPolish}. The classification proves that any affirmative
example cannot inherit its topology from a Borel ordered Polish group.
Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:compact-open-isolated-zero} adds that its zero must
be isolated. The remaining case is therefore precise: an example
with isolated zero and no compatible inherited Polish group
presentation. A global nonexistence proof must use information
beyond the compact-open neighborhood argument.

\noindent\writetag{} This is Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:zerodim}, re-scoped by
\cref{pma:lcc:cor:presburger-group-completion-carrier} and
\cref{pma:lcc:thm:compact-open-isolated-zero}.

\begin{question}[Connected Polish arithmetic]
Does a connected uncountable Polish space admit a full Presburger
model with jointly continuous addition? What changes if local
compactness or finite covering dimension is imposed?
\end{question}
The inherited locally compact case is excluded above. Connectedness
without a group-completion hypothesis remains outside these proofs.
One possible approach is to study the successor map and the images
of translations as topological embeddings; addition is cancellative,
but its inverses on these images need not be continuous automatically.
The degree-stratum polynomial example is disconnected and therefore
does not answer this question.

\noindent\writetag{} Compare Part~I's \cref{pma:pr:q:connected}, Part~III's
\cref{pma:cp:q:connected} and source~13's \cref{pma:nsp:q:connected}.

\begin{question}[A usable group-completion criterion]
Which intrinsic conditions on a locally compact Polish Presburger
monoid ensure that its topology is inherited from a Polish group
topology on its algebraic group of differences?
\end{question}
A useful answer should be stated using translations, the partial
difference map on ordered pairs, and neighborhood structure, so it
can be checked without first constructing a group topology. The
polynomial example shows that cancellation, joint continuity of
addition, local compactness, and a full Presburger reduct do not
suffice. This question would identify exactly where the classification
can be applied to presentations given without coefficient coordinates.

\noindent\writetag{} This is source~08's \cref{pma:lc:q:completion}
(= source~09's \cref{pma:ser:q:cones}); sources~12 and~10 ask it again in
\cref{pma:part:br}.

\subsection{Arithmetic invariants beyond the carrier}

\begin{question}[Classification with a prescribed boundary]
Fix a countable Presburger model $N$. Classify the locally compact
inherited-group presentations with manifold boundary isomorphic to
$N$, up to arithmetic isomorphism and up to topological arithmetic
isomorphism.
\end{question}
Existence is settled by Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:boundary-realization}, and
there are already continuum many classes when $N=\N$. The open
classification problem is to find complete invariants. Natural data
include the ordered quotient above the infinitesimal subgroup,
the placement of the real component, and extension data for the
standard integer subgroup. A homeomorphism of carriers alone
cannot recover these data.

\begin{question}[Threshold orders and automorphism groups]
For a fixed countable torsion-free abelian group $A$, classify Borel
translation-invariant linear orders on $\R\times A$ whose cones
are discretely ordered Presburger models. Determine their groups
of continuous Presburger automorphisms.
\end{question}
Each real-coset section is empty, full, or a ray. Its threshold,
whether an endpoint is present, and the arithmetic relations between
cosets satisfy compatibility conditions under addition. Making
these conditions explicit could turn the topological classification
into an arithmetic parametrization. The real component need not
be convex, so assuming a single lexicographic product would miss
part of the problem.

\begin{question}[Complexity of isomorphism]
In a precise standard Borel coding of continuous binary operations
and distinguished constants on $\Xlc$, what is the descriptive
complexity of the subset defining Presburger models? On that
subset, what is the complexity of arithmetic isomorphism and of
topological arithmetic isomorphism?
\end{question}
The family $S\mapsto M_{L_S}$ has its own isomorphism relation
completely determined: it is equality of the parameters. Cardinality
alone does not determine the complexity of isomorphism on the larger
space of presentations. A classification should distinguish
continuous changes of coordinates from abstract model isomorphisms.

\subsection{Strengthening and formalizing the obstructions}

\begin{question}[Smaller endomorphism hypotheses]
In Theorem~\ref{pma:lcc:thm:borel-multiplier-obstruction}, how far can the
assumption that every positive $a$ is $T_a(e)$ be weakened?
\end{question}
The proof actually uses only enough positive endomorphisms to
continue a sequence that is rapidly increasing in order while
topologically summable. A useful refinement would give an intrinsic
condition on the positive endomorphism orbit of $e$ that is both
necessary and sufficient for this recursion. Merely replacing the
orbit condition by an unexplained cofinality assumption would leave
the needed control of neighborhoods unproved.

\noindent\writetag{} (Batch 87.) Answered by \cref{pma:part:br}: by source~12's
\cref{pma:br:thm:unit-spectrum}, in an uncountable group with a Hausdorff Baire
ccc topology and a Baire-property cone every ordered additive self-embedding
$f$ satisfies $f(e)\le2a$ for the $a$ of
\cref{pma:br:lem:bounded-neighborhood}. So a single positive endomorphism $T$
with $T(e)>2a$ already forces countability, and no regularity of $T$ is needed.

\begin{question}[Regularity of the order]
Which conclusions survive when a Borel order is replaced by a
weaker measurable or category-theoretic regularity assumption?
\end{question}
Different steps use different regularity. The real-line lemma uses
the Baire property; the compact-subgroup lemma uses Haar measurability;
the probabilistic obstruction needs the inverse images of order
intervals under the Cantor limit map to be measurable. A satisfactory
weakening should state these requirements on the relevant maps and
subgroups, since an arbitrary weakening of ``Borel'' need not be
preserved by restriction or inverse image.

\noindent\writetag{} For the multiplier obstruction, the Baire property of the
cone suffices (\cref{pma:part:br}).

\begin{question}[Algebraic obstructions beyond one real subgroup]
What other additive invariants prevent a discretely ordered group
from admitting any unital ordered-ring multiplication?
\end{question}
The injection $H\hookrightarrow G/H$ compares the size of an
Archimedean subgroup with its quotient. One can ask for analogues
using a chain of Archimedean layers, ranks of quotients, or several
independent multiplier images. A useful classification would explain
which failures are purely algebraic and which arise only from
measurability. The polynomial ring supplies an example where an
infinite hierarchy of larger growth layers permits multiplication.

\begin{question}[Minimal metatheory and Glazer's Question 1]
What is the weakest subsystem of second-order arithmetic that proves
the particular obstruction theorems in this article? How does it
compare with Glazer's original question about proving his Theorem~2
in $\mathsf{ATR}_0$?
\end{question}
Glazer's Question~1 is an explicitly published problem
\cite[Further Work, Question~1]{Glazer}. This article does not answer it.
Its classical proofs use completeness, Baire category, product
probability, and, in the classification, algebraic complements and
LCA structure. The phrase ``induction-free'' in
Section~\ref{pma:lcc:sec:borel-multiplication-obstruction} refers to the
\emph{object arithmetic being modeled}, not to the strength of
the metatheory used to prove the theorem. Determining the latter
requires a separate reverse-mathematical analysis.

\noindent\writetag{} Source~14 (\cref{pma:part:atr}) claims an affirmative
answer to Glazer's Question~1, not independently reviewed; source~15's own
statement that it does not answer the question stands.

\begin{question}[A checked formalization]
Can the algebraic cardinality theorem, the generalized Presburger
semantic certificate, and the boundary theorem be formalized in
ProveIt as a coherent first milestone?
\end{question}
These three components connect the repository's current integer
elimination and omnific coefficient interfaces to the new structural
results. They also divide naturally into algebra, model theory, and
topology. The probability theorem can follow as a second milestone
once the needed measure-theoretic interfaces are explicit.

\subsection{Recommended order of work}

The most concrete next project is the algebraic obstruction and its
formal certificate: the statement is short, the proof has few
dependencies, and the conclusion is stronger than a continuity
obstruction. Classification of presentations with a prescribed boundary
is the next mathematical project, because the boundary supplies an
intrinsic invariant that the carrier alone misses. The broad existence
questions for connected or
zero-dimensional presentations should be pursued together with a
group-completion criterion, with the polynomial example serving as
a test case for every proposed general theorem.

\section{Worked examples and an audit of the hypotheses (source 05)}
\label{pma:pr:sec:audit}

\subsection{A negative constant term is compatible with positivity}

In $\MR$, take
\[
 x=(\tfrac32,-17),\qquad y=(\tfrac14,6).
\]
Both are positive, and
\[
 x+y=(\tfrac74,-11).
\]
Division of $x$ by $5$ gives
\[
 q_5(x)=(\tfrac3{10},-4),\qquad r_5(x)=3,
\]
because $-17=5(-4)+3$. The quotient is positive because its real
coordinate is positive. A definition that incorrectly demanded a
nonnegative integer coordinate for every element would break the
predecessor and division axioms.

\subsection{A nonstandard finite-candidate calculation}

Let $L=(\tfrac12,-5)$, $U=(\tfrac23,0)$, and require
\[
 y\equiv(\tfrac7{13},2)\pmod{3G}.
\]
The real coefficient of a congruence parameter is irrelevant because
$\R$ is divisible. Among $L,L+1,L+2$, the candidate $L+1$ has integer
coordinate $-4\equiv2\pmod3$, so it is a witness. Every candidate lies
below $U$, since its leading coefficient is $1/2<2/3$.
No iteration a nonstandard number of times is used: the finite search is
justified by full invariance on $3G$-cosets.

\subsection{A Baire convergence that order cannot detect continuously}

Let $e_j$ be the rational unit vector at coordinate $j$. Then
\[
 (e_j,0)\to(0,0),\qquad (e_j,0)>n\one
 \quad\text{for every fixed standard }n.
\]
The initial coefficients eventually agree with zero to every prescribed
finite length. In omnific notation this sequence is
\[
 \omega,\quad\omega^{1/2},\quad\omega^{1/3},\quad\ldots,
\]
which converges to zero in the \emph{specified coefficient topology},
not in the arithmetic order topology. This is a concrete illustration,
not a claim about an unspecified topology on surreal numbers.

\subsection{Hypothesis checklist}

\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.30\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{.62\textwidth}@{}}
\toprule
Potential pitfall & Resolution in the proofs\\
\midrule
\endhead
Only the division axioms are checked &
\Cref{pma:pr:thm:qe,pma:pr:cor:fullpresburger,pma:pr:prop:least} establish the complete theory
and every additive induction instance.\\[.6em]
An open ray is given an incomplete metric &
\Cref{pma:pr:sec:topology} provides a compatible logarithmic metric on each
open ray and a complete metric on the whole sum.\\[.6em]
The intended topology is silently replaced by the order topology &
Both topologies are explicitly distinguished; the arithmetic order
topology is discrete.\\[.6em]
Standard-shift invariance is used with a nonstandard quotient &
\Cref{pma:pr:ex:falseperiod} exhibits the failure; \cref{pma:pr:lem:finite} uses
invariance on $mG$-cosets instead.\\[.6em]
The all-zero rational branch is lost &
The nonnegative-cone tree in \eqref{pma:pr:eq:zerobranch} explicitly includes it.\\[.6em]
Computing an output tag secretly requires deciding equality of streams &
For a negative output integer coordinate, a negative input supplies a
finite bound on the first positive coefficient.\\[.6em]
A type-theoretic ``computable model'' is confused with a countable one &
The presentation is Type-2 on all Baire sequences; not every element is
computable, and order has only a limit decision procedure.\\[.6em]

It is only an additive fragment. \Cref{pma:pr:thm:no_semiring} rules out even
